In [Figure [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#fig3)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#fig3)a, for RuCp 2, the overall reaction energy is positive for the transfer of surface and bridging hydrogen on the NH _x_-terminated Si(100) surface, making CpH elimination clearly unfavorable. After the first CpH formation and desorption, the computed reaction energy is 0.83 eV for H transfer from surface NH 2 and 1.53 eV for H transfer from bridge NH. The computed reaction energies for the second H transfer continue to be positive for both types of H transfer: after formation of the second CpH, the computed reaction energy is as high as 3.62 eV for H transfer from surface NH 2 and 1.79 eV for H transfer from bridge NH.

In [Figure [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#fig3)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#fig3)b, for CoCp 2, the overall reaction energy is negative for the first Cp ligand elimination with H transfer from surface NH 2. A moderate energy barrier of 0.73 eV is computed for the surface H transfer step. The configuration of the transition state is shown in the [Supporting Information](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/acs.jpcc.3c02933/suppl_file/jp3c02933_si_001.pdf). After CpH formation and elimination, the computed energy gain is −0.21 eV. For the second surface H transfer, the computed reaction energy is positive. After the second CpH desorption, the computed reaction energy is positive at 1.86 eV. By contrast, for H transfer from bridge NH, the overall reaction energy is positive for the first and second Cp elimination. The computed reaction energies are 0.68 eV for the first CpH desorption and 0.49 for the second CpH desorption. Since the Cp ligand elimination process for this pathway is endothermic, no barrier calculations are performed for H transfer from bridge NH.

Transfer of surface H is preferred since it leaves an NH surface termination, while a bridging H will leave a bare, undercoordinated N atom, which we would expect to be unstable and hence unfavorable.

In our previous study of depositing Ru on NH _x_-terminated metal surfaces,[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#ref33) we discussed that the energy cost to break the Ru–C bond is higher due to the stronger Ru–C bond strength. The bond energies between the metal and the Cp rings in RuCp 2 and CoCp 2 were calculated as 3.05 eV per Ru–C bond and 2.96 eV per Co–C bond.[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#ref47) For depositing Ru thin films, Ru compounds with more complex Cp-based ligands are used experimentally rather than RuCp 2; these ligands appear to offer higher reactivity. For Co thin films, CoCp 2- and N-plasma-based PE-ALD processes have been demonstrated in the literature.[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#ref8)−[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#ref11),[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#ref24) Our DFT results indicate that RuCp 2 is not a favorable candidate for depositing Ru thin films. This is also consistent with the experimental work in which we found only one paper[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#ref48) in the literature that has used RuCp 2 and N plasma for PE-ALD of Ru thin-film deposition, while other reports have used ruthenium compounds with more complex Cp-based ligands such as Ru(EtCp)2 and (MeCpPy)Ru.[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#ref29),[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#ref30),[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#ref35)

For CoCp 2, when comparing H terminations and NH _x_ terminations, the energy gain on the NH _x_-terminated Si(100) surface, −0.21 eV, is more favorable than that on H-terminated Si, 0.12 eV. This provides further evidence that the plasma-generated N _x_ H _y_ radicals are essential to promote Co metal deposition in addition to preventing metal oxidation. From our results, we suggest that if we apply the N plasma (NH 3 or mixture of N 2 and H 2) treatment on the H:Si(100) substrate as the first step in Co ALD with CoCp 2, the nucleation delay can be reduced. In addition, the differences we see for surface reactivity also suggest the possibility of area-selective ALD mediated by these NH _x_ terminations and H terminations.

### Ligand Exchange Reactions on H:SiN _x_–Si(100) Terminations

3.4
In terms of growth behavior, the PE-ALD of metal thin films has two regions: an initial nucleation region and a steady growth region. In the steady growth region, the surface terminations are NH _x_-terminated Ru or Co surfaces (_x_ = 1 or 2).[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#ref41) Our previous studies have investigated the reaction mechanisms of eliminating the Cp ligand on these NH _x_-terminated Ru or Co surfaces in the metal precursor half-cycle and found that the Cp ligand is eliminated via H transfer, CpH formation, and CpH desorption.[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#ref32),[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#ref33) The remaining Cp rings after the metal precursor cycle are eliminated at the plasma cycle by reacting with plasma-generated •H radicals. This explains the low C impurity in the deposited Co thin films, where most of the Cp ligand is removed via CpH, and the decomposition of Cp is not preferred.

In addition to the two surface terminations of Si(100) described above, we further investigate the possible formation of SiN _x_/Si(100) and H:SiN _x_/Si(100) substrates. These can form via surface Si atoms reacting with plasma-generated •N and •H radicals, which can migrate through the Si surface. These surfaces were generated with ab initio MD calculations, and full details are given in the [Supporting Information](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/suppl/10.1021/acs.jpcc.3c02933/suppl_file/jp3c02933_si_001.pdf). The resulting SiN _x_/Si(100) and H;SiN _x_/Si(100) are shown in [Figures [4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#fig4)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#fig4) and [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#fig5).

Figure 4
[![Image 18: Figure 4](https://pmc-oa-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/PMC10364078.1/jp3c02933_0005.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=10364078_jp3c02933_0005.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/figure/fig4/)

Configurations of the stable structure of the SiN _x_/Si(100) substrate in (a) side view and (b) top view. Si and N atoms are represented by dark yellow and blue spheres, respectively.

Figure 5
[![Image 19: Figure 5](https://pmc-oa-opendata.s3.amazonaws.com/PMC10364078.1/jp3c02933_0006.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=10364078_jp3c02933_0006.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/figure/fig5/)

Configurations of the stable structure of the H:SiN _x_/Si(100) substrate in (a) side view and (b) top view. Si, N, and H atoms are represented by dark yellow, blue, and white spheres, respectively.

Precursors RuCp 2 and CoCp 2 adsorb at the SiN _x_/Si(100) and H:SiN _x_/Si(100) surfaces with computed adsorption energies summarized in [Table [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#tbl3)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#tbl3). The preferred binding mode is the horizontal mode, the same as on the other substrates, and this adsorption mode shows computed adsorption energies of −0.47 eV for RuCp 2 and −0.76 eV for CoCp 2 on the H:SiN _x_/Si(100) substrate and −0.53 eV for RuCp 2 and −1.74 eV for CoCp 2 on the SiN _x_/Si(100) substrate. Again, CoCp 2 shows stronger interaction on the surface compared to RuCp 2. The larger adsorption energy on SiN _x_ termination compared to that on H:SiN _x_ termination may reflect undercoordinated atoms on the surface terminating layer.

Table 3. Computed Adsorption Energies of Metal Precursors RuCp 2 and CoCp 2 with Horizontal and Upright Binding Modes on SiN _x_/Si(100), H:SiN _x_/Si(100), and Bare Si(100) Surfaces

|  | RuCp 2 _E_ ad/eV | CoCp 2 _E_ ad/eV |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| (3×3) | horizontal | horizontal |
| H:SiN _x_/Si(100) | –0.47 | –0.76 |
| SiN _x_/Si(100) | –0.53 | –1.74 |
| bare Si(100) | –5.87 | –6.07 |

[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/table/tbl3/)

On the H:SiN _x_/Si(100) surface, we consider the elimination of Cp via the H transfer, CpH formation, and CpH desorption pathway. RuCp 2 has a computed high energy cost at 2.37 eV for the H transfer step, regardless of which H is involved, that is, from H–Si, NH, or NH 2. Thus, no further calculations are performed to generate the full reaction pathway for RuCp 2. For CoCp 2, the computed reaction energy is exothermic for H transfer from NH to Cp, with a computed value of −0.81 eV, whereas H transfer from NH 2 or H–Si has endothermic reaction energy. Despite this exothermic H transfer step for CoCp 2, the overall reaction energy for first Cp ligand elimination is actually positive at 0.60 eV. Thus, the elimination of the Cp ligand via H transfer, CpH formation, and CpH desorption pathways on the H:SiN _x_/Si(100) surface is thermodynamically not favored. No full reaction pathway is plotted for H:SiN _x_/Si(100) due to unfavorable reactions. Compared to NH _x_ terminations of 1 ML NH + 1 ML NH 2 discussed in [Section [3.3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#sec3.3)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#sec3.3), this H:SiN _x_ termination has a thicker layer and lower activity toward Cp ligand elimination.

In addition to SiN _x_/Si(100) and H:SiN _x_(100), a bare Si(100) surface is applied to explore a case where surface NH _x_ terminations may have desorbed due to high operating temperatures. However, the bare Si(100) surface does not exist at typical ALD conditions; the Si surface is covered with NH _x_ terminations after reacting with plasma-generated N _x_ H _y_ radicals, but we include this surface for completeness. Both precursors have significantly more exothermic adsorption energies on bare Si(100). These more exothermic adsorption energies are due to the surface dangling Si atoms, indicating that hydrogen and NH _x_ terminations passivate Si. This is also observed by Phung[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078#ref49) et al., where adsorption of RuCp 2 was proposed to be less favorable on the H-terminated Ru(001) surface in comparison to that on the bare Ru(001) surface. The precursors dissociate into a bare metal atom and two adsorbed Cp species, and the adsorption energies suggest these will persist on the surface; this is reasonable since the adsorbed Cp will passivate the dangling Si bonds.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10364078)Conclusions

4
We studied the first reactions in PE-ALD of Ru and Co using cyclopentadienyl-based metal precursors RuCp 2 and CoCp 2 on various silicon substrates, including (1) H:Si(100), (2) NH _x_-terminated Si(100), (3) H:SiN _x_/Si(100), and (4) bare Si(100), to gain a systematic understanding of the reaction mechanism between these precursors and substrates. On the H:Si(100) surface, both precursors show a thermoneutral reaction energy for the elimination of the first Cp ligand via H transfer from the substrate. At most, only one Cp ligand is eliminated for both RuCp 2 and CoCp 2 on the H:Si(100) surface since the second Cp ligand elimination step is highly endothermic.

We can consider a modification to this Si(100) surface termination to surface NH _x_ terminations by running the plasma step first and exploiting radicals •NH and •NH 2 to modify to an NH _x_–Si(100) surface. The elimination of surface H terminations via H 2 formation and desorption with plasma radical •H is endothermic. The preferred NH _x_ termination on the Si(100) surface at a typical ALD operating temperature of 600 K is 1 ML NH + 1 ML NH 2, with NH 2 occupying surface top sites and NH occupying surface bridge sites. This is analogous to our previously analyzed mixed NH _x_ terminations on Ru(100) and Co(100) surfaces, where NH 2 occupies surface sites and NH prefers bridge sites on the metal surface.

On the NH _x_-terminated Si(100) surface, RuCp 2 shows endothermic reactions for elimination of both Cp ligands. On the contrary, NH _x_ terminations can promote the first Cp ligand elimination for CoCp 2 with the computed overall reaction energy at −0.21 eV, and the reaction energies to eliminate both Cp ligands on the NH _x_-terminated Si(100) surface is endothermic. The computed activation barrier for the first H transfer step is moderate at 0.73 eV. This difference is due to the stronger Ru–C bond strength compared to Co–C bond strength. This is also observed in the elimination of Cp ligands on NH _x_-terminated Ru and Co surfaces, where CoCp 2 has exothermic reaction energies and low activation barriers on NH _x_-terminated Co(001) and Co(100) surfaces, but RuCp 2 has endothermic reaction energies and high activation barriers on NH _x_-terminated Ru(001) and Ru(100) surfaces.

Both precursors have endothermic reactions of Cp ligand elimination on the H:SiN _x_/Si(100) surface. Compared to the NH _x_ termination, the H:SiN _x_ termination is thicker and shows less reactivity. This indicates that the surface reactivity is highly dependent on substrate terminations, which can also be utilized for area-selective deposition.

Therefore, in the initial stages of PE-ALD of Co with CoCp 2, our results show that N 2/H 2 plasma pretreatment on the Si substrates would generate surface NH _x_ terminations, which promote Cp ligand elimination and will reduce the nucleation delay relative to H-terminated silicon. The use of an initial NH 3 plasma pulse before the metal pulse would produce this substrate. However, the resulting surface should not have a thick Si–NH _x_ terminating region, which promotes nucleation delay and can be avoided with a short plasma pulse. In addition, endothermic reactions in some cases suggest that a long nucleation delay will be observed in an ALD process. The reactivity is highly dependent on Si(100) substrate terminations, which can also be utilized for area-selective deposition. For Ru deposition, RuCp 2 is not a useful precursor, showing highly endothermic ligand elimination reactions on all Si terminations.

The effect of modifying metal precursors, including ligand modification with MeCp or EtCp, on the reactions at the initial stages are the subject of ongoing work, while a complete understanding of the deposition of Ru or Co for Cu seed layers can be obtained from follow-up work investigating the precursor reaction mechanisms on TaN/SiO 2/Si and TiN/SiO 2/Si substrates.

This is a peer-reviewed scientific research article published in The Journal of Physical Chemistry C (Nanomaterials and Interfaces) on July 7, 2023 (DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcc.3c02933), from researchers at Tyndall National Institute (University College Cork, Ireland) and Fudan University (Shanghai, China). The study uses first-principles density functional theory (DFT) simulations to investigate the nucleation of ruthenium (Ru) and cobalt (Co) precursors on silicon substrates with different surface terminations, addressing the problem of "nucleation delay" in plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition (PE-ALD) for next-generation interconnects.

Key findings:
- Ru and Co are being investigated as replacements for Cu in next-generation interconnects due to scaling challenges with Cu at the nanoscale.
- The study examined reactions between precursors RuCp₂ and CoCp₂ with four Si substrate terminations: (1) H:Si(100), (2) NHₓ-terminated Si(100), (3) H:SiNₓ/Si(100), and (4) bare Si(100).
- Reported Ru nucleation delays range from <10 to >500 ALD cycles depending on precursor, substrate, and plasma type (documented in Table 1); no systematic data on Co nucleation delay existed in the literature.
- On H:Si(100), both precursors show thermoneutral energy for first Cp ligand elimination but highly endothermic second elimination (2.83 eV for CoCp₂, 2.09 eV for RuCp₂), meaning only one Cp ligand can be eliminated.
- On NHₓ-terminated Si(100), CoCp₂ shows favorable first Cp ligand elimination (−0.21 eV reaction energy, 0.73 eV activation barrier), while RuCp₂ shows endothermic reactions for both ligand eliminations.
- CoCp₂ adsorbs more strongly than RuCp₂ on all substrates (e.g., −0.98 eV vs −0.37 eV on H:Si(100) horizontal mode).
- On H:SiNₓ/Si(100), Cp ligand elimination is thermodynamically unfavored for both precursors (CoCp₂ overall reaction energy +0.60 eV).
- On bare Si(100), both precursors have strongly exothermic adsorption energies (−5.87 eV for RuCp₂, −6.07 eV for CoCp₂), but this surface is not realistic at ALD operating conditions.

Key conclusions:
- N₂/H₂ plasma pretreatment of Si substrates to generate NHₓ terminations promotes Cp ligand elimination for CoCp₂ and can reduce nucleation delay for Co PE-ALD.
- RuCp₂ is not a useful precursor for Ru deposition, showing highly endothermic ligand elimination on all Si terminations studied, explaining why more complex Cp-based Ru precursors (e.g., Ru(EtCp)₂, (MeCpPy)Ru) are used experimentally.
- Surface reactivity is highly dependent on substrate terminations, which may enable area-selective deposition.
- The thicker H:SiNₓ termination shows lower reactivity toward ligand elimination, suggesting short plasma pulses are preferable to avoid forming thick Si-NHₓ regions.

Computational methods: periodic spin-polarized DFT (VASP 5.4), PBE functional, PAW formalism, 400 eV cutoff, PBE-D3 van der Waals correction, Bader charge analysis, CI-NEB for activation barriers, ab initio MD at 600 K. Funding from Science Foundation Ireland (SFI-NSFC Partnership Program, Grant 17/NSFC/5279) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant 51861135105).

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Thin-film deposition technique that deposits one 1-atom thick layer at a time

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Schematic_illustration_of_atomic_layer_deposition.tif/lossless-page1-330px-Schematic_illustration_of_atomic_layer_deposition.tif.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Schematic_illustration_of_atomic_layer_deposition.tif)

Schematic illustration of one reaction cycle of the ALD process, using the trimethylaluminium (TMA) -water process to make thin aluminium oxide films as (simplified) example. There, the starting surface contains hydroxyls (OH groups) as reactive sites; Step 1 is the reaction of TMA; Step 2 is a purge or evacuation step, Step 3 is the reaction of water, and Step 4 is a purge or evacuation step.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-1)

**Atomic layer deposition** (**ALD**) is a [thin-film deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thin-film_deposition "Thin-film deposition") technique based on the sequential use of a gas-phase [chemical process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_process "Chemical process"); it is a subclass of [chemical vapour deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_vapour_deposition "Chemical vapour deposition"). The majority of ALD reactions use two chemicals called [precursors](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/precursor "wiktionary:precursor") (also called "reactants"). These precursors react with the surface of a material one at a time in a sequential, self-limiting, manner. A thin film is slowly deposited through repeated exposure to separate precursors. ALD is a key process in [fabricating semiconductor devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication"), and part of the set of tools for synthesizing [nanomaterials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanomaterials "Nanomaterials").

## Introduction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atomic_layer_deposition&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Introduction")]

During atomic layer deposition, a film is grown on a [substrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Substrate_(chemistry) "Substrate (chemistry)") by exposing its surface to alternate gaseous species (typically referred to as [precursors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precursor_(chemistry) "Precursor (chemistry)") or reactants). In contrast to [chemical vapor deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_vapor_deposition "Chemical vapor deposition"), the precursors are never present simultaneously in the reactor, but they are inserted as a series of sequential, non-overlapping pulses. In each of these pulses the precursor molecules react with the surface in a self-limiting way, so that the reaction terminates once all the available sites on the [surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_science "Surface science") are consumed. Consequently, the maximum amount of material deposited on the surface after a single exposure to all of the precursors (a so-called ALD cycle) is determined by the nature of the precursor-surface interaction.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-stam-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:4-3) By varying the number of cycles it is possible to grow materials uniformly and with high precision on arbitrarily complex and large substrates.

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/ALD_Periodic_Table_-_May_2019.png/330px-ALD_Periodic_Table_-_May_2019.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ALD_Periodic_Table_-_May_2019.png)

An overview of the materials synthesized by ALD with 1 or more publications describing the process[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-ALDDatabase-4)

ALD is a deposition method with great potential for producing very thin, conformal films with control of the thickness and composition of the films possible at the atomic level. A major driving force for the recent interest is the prospective seen for ALD in scaling down microelectronic devices according to [Moore's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore's_law "Moore's law"). ALD is an active field of research, with hundreds of different processes published in the [scientific literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_literature "Scientific literature"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-stam-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:4-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:5-5) though some of them exhibit behaviors that depart from that of an ideal ALD process.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:5-5) Currently there are several comprehensive review papers that give a summary of the published ALD processes, including the work of Puurunen,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:0-6) Miikkulainen _et al._,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:5-5) Knoops _et al._,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-7) and Mackus & Schneider _et al._.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-8) An interactive, community driven database of ALD processes is also available online[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-ALDDatabase-4) which generates an up-to-date overview in the form of an annotated [periodic table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_table "Periodic table").

The sister technique of atomic layer deposition, [molecular layer deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_layer_deposition "Molecular layer deposition") (MLD), uses organic precursors to deposit polymers. By combining the ALD/MLD techniques, it is possible to make highly conformal and pure hybrid films for many applications.

Another technology related to ALD is [sequential infiltration synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequential_infiltration_synthesis "Sequential infiltration synthesis") (SIS) which uses alternating precursor vapor exposures to infiltrate and modify polymers. SIS is also referred to as vapor phase infiltration (VPI) and sequential vapor infiltration (SVI).

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atomic_layer_deposition&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

### 1960s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atomic_layer_deposition&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1960s")]

In the 1960s, Stanislav Koltsov together with [Valentin Aleskovsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentin_Aleskovsky "Valentin Aleskovsky") and colleagues experimentally developed the principles of ALD at [Leningrad Technological Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leningrad_Technological_Institute "Leningrad Technological Institute") (LTI) in the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:02-9) The purpose was to experimentally build upon the theoretical considerations of the "framework hypothesis" coined by Aleskovsky in his 1952 [habilitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habilitation "Habilitation") thesis.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:02-9) The experiments started with metal chloride reactions and water with porous silica, soon extending to other substrate materials and planar thin films.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:02-9) Aleskovskii and Koltsov together proposed the name "Molecular Layering" for the new technique in 1965.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:02-9) The principles of Molecular Layering were summarized in the doctoral thesis ("professor's thesis") of Koltsov in 1971.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:02-9) Research activities of molecular layering covered a broad scope, from fundamental chemistry research to applied research with porous catalysts, sorbents and fillers to [microelectronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microelectronics "Microelectronics") and beyond.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:02-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:2-10)

In 1974, when starting the development of thin-film [electroluminescent displays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electroluminescent_display "Electroluminescent display") (TFEL) at Instrumentarium Oy in [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland"), [Tuomo Suntola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuomo_Suntola "Tuomo Suntola") devised ALD as an advanced thin-film technology.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:12-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:3-12) Suntola named it [atomic layer epitaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_epitaxy "Atomic layer epitaxy") (ALE) based on the meaning of "epitaxy" in Greek language, "arrangement upon".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:12-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:3-12) The first experiments were made with elemental Zn and S to grow ZnS.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:12-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:3-12) ALE as a means for growth of thin films was internationally patented in more than 20 countries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:12-11) A breakthrough occurred, when Suntola and co-workers switched from high vacuum reactors to [inert gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inert_gas "Inert gas") reactors which enabled the use of compound reactants like metal chlorides, [hydrogen sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_sulfide "Hydrogen sulfide") and [water vapor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_vapor "Water vapor") for performing the ALE process.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:12-11)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-13) The technology was first disclosed in 1980 SID conference.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:12-11) The TFEL display prototype presented consisted of a ZnS layer between two aluminum oxide dielectric layers, all made in an ALE process using ZnCl 2 + H 2 S and AlCl 3 + H 2 O as the reactants. The first large-scale proof-of-concept of ALE-EL displays were the flight information boards installed in the [Helsinki-Vantaa airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki-Vantaa_airport "Helsinki-Vantaa airport") in 1983.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:12-11) TFEL flat panel display production started in the mid-1980s by Lohja Oy in the Olarinluoma factory.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:12-11) Academic research on ALE started in [Tampere University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampere_University_of_Technology "Tampere University of Technology") (where Suntola gave lectures on electron physics) in 1970s, and in 1980s at [Helsinki University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki_University_of_Technology "Helsinki University of Technology").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:12-11) TFEL display manufacturing remained until the 1990s the only industrial application of ALE. In 1987, Suntola started the development of the ALE technology for new applications like [photovoltaic devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaic_device "Photovoltaic device") and [heterogeneous catalysts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterogeneous_catalyst "Heterogeneous catalyst") in Microchemistry Ltd., established for that purpose by the Finnish [national oil company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_oil_company "National oil company")[Neste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neste "Neste") Oy. In the 1990s, ALE development in Microchemistry was directed to semiconductor applications and ALE reactors suitable for silicon wafer processing. In 1999, Microchemistry Ltd. and the ALD technology were sold to the Dutch [ASM International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASM_International "ASM International"), a major supplier of semiconductor manufacturing equipment and Microchemistry Ltd. became ASM Microchemistry Oy as ASM's Finnish daughter company. Microchemistry Ltd/ASM Microchemistry Ltd was the only manufacturer of commercial ALD-reactors in the 1990s. In the early 2000s, the expertise on ALD reactors in Finland triggered two new manufacturers, Beneq Oy and Picosun Oy, the latter started by Sven Lindfors, Suntola's close coworker since 1975. The number of reactor manufacturers increased rapidly and semiconductor applications became the industrial breakthrough of the ALD technology, as ALD became an enabling technology for the continuation of [Moore's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore's_law "Moore's law").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:12-11) In 2004, [Tuomo Suntola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuomo_Suntola "Tuomo Suntola") received the European [SEMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_Equipment_and_Materials_International "Semiconductor Equipment and Materials International") award for the development of the ALD technology for semiconductor applications[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:12-11) and in 2018 the [Millennium Technology Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennium_Technology_Prize "Millennium Technology Prize").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-14)

The developers of ML and ALE met at the 1st international conference on atomic layer epitaxy, "ALE-1" in Espoo, Finland, 1990.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:12-11)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:02-9) An attempt to expose the extent of molecular layering works was made in a scientific ALD [review article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_article "Review article") in 2005[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:4-3) and later in the VPHA-related publications.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:62-15)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:02-9)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:72-16)

The name "atomic layer deposition" was apparently proposed for the first time in writing as an alternative to ALE in analogy with [CVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_vapor_deposition "Chemical vapor deposition") by Markku Leskelä (professor at the [University of Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Helsinki "University of Helsinki")) at the ALE-1 conference, Espoo, Finland. It took about a decade before the name gained general acceptance with the onset of the international conference series on ALD by [American Vacuum Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Vacuum_Society "American Vacuum Society").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-17)

### 2000s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atomic_layer_deposition&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2000s")]

In 2000, [Gurtej Singh Sandhu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurtej_Sandhu "Gurtej Sandhu") and Trung T. Doan of [Micron Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micron_Technology "Micron Technology") initiated the development of atomic layer deposition [high-κ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-%CE%BA_dielectric "High-κ dielectric") films for [DRAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") memory devices. This helped drive cost-effective implementation of [semiconductor memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_memory "Semiconductor memory"), starting with [90-nm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/90_nanometer "90 nanometer")[node](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_node "Semiconductor node") DRAM.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-ieee-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-19)[Intel Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intel_Corporation "Intel Corporation") has reported using ALD to deposit high-κ gate dielectric for its [45 nm CMOS technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/45_nanometer "45 nanometer").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-20)

ALD has been developed in two [independent discoveries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_discovery "Multiple discovery") under names [atomic layer epitaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_epitaxy "Atomic layer epitaxy") (ALE, Finland) and molecular layering (ML, Soviet Union).[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:62-15) To clarify the early history, the Virtual Project on the History of ALD (VPHA) has been set up in summer 2013.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-21) It resulted in several publications reviewing the historical development of ALD under the names [ALE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_epitaxy "Atomic layer epitaxy") and ML.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:62-15)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:12-11)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:02-9)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:72-16)

In 2009, multiple pulsed infiltration (MPI), later referred to as vapor phase infiltation (VPI), sequential vapor infiltration (SVI) or [sequential infiltration synthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequential_infiltration_synthesis "Sequential infiltration synthesis") (SIS), was first reported by researchers at the [Max-Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Planck_Institute_of_Microstructure_Physics "Max Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics") and added to the family of ALD-derived techniques.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-23)

## Surface reaction mechanisms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atomic_layer_deposition&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Surface reaction mechanisms")]

In a prototypical ALD process, a substrate is exposed to two reactants A and B in a sequential, non-overlapping way. In contrast to other techniques such as [chemical vapor deposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_vapor_deposition "Chemical vapor deposition") (CVD), where thin-film growth proceeds on a steady-state fashion, in ALD each reactant reacts with the surface in a self-limited way: the reactant molecules can react only with a finite number of reactive sites on the surface. Once all those sites have been consumed in the reactor, the growth stops. The remaining reactant molecules are flushed away and only then reactant B is inserted into the reactor. By alternating exposures of A and B, a thin film is deposited. This process is shown in the side figure. Consequently, when describing an ALD process one refers to both dose times (the time a surface is being exposed to a precursor) and purge times (the time left in between doses for the precursor to evacuate the chamber) for each precursor. The dose-purge-dose-purge sequence of a binary ALD process constitutes an ALD cycle. Also, rather than using the concept of growth rate, ALD processes are described in terms of their growth per cycle.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-24)

In ALD, enough time must be allowed in each reaction step so that a full adsorption density can be achieved. When this happens the process has reached saturation. This time will depend on two key factors: the precursor pressure, and the sticking probability.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-book-25) Therefore, the rate of adsorption per unit of surface area can be expressed as:

{\displaystyle {R_{abs}}=S*F}![Image 6: {\displaystyle {R_{abs}}=S*F}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/6eb95c9c25f3cb7ae4a840856b315ab545b8d75d)
Where R is the rate of adsorption, S is the sticking probability, and F is the incident molar flux.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-26) However, a key characteristic of ALD is the S will change with time, as more molecules have reacted with the surface this sticking probability will become smaller until reaching a value of zero once saturation is reached.

The specific details on the [reaction mechanisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reaction_mechanism "Reaction mechanism") are strongly dependent on the particular ALD process. With hundreds of process available to deposit oxide, metals, nitrides, sulfides, chalcogenides, and fluoride materials,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:5-5) the unraveling of the mechanistic aspects of ALD processes is an active field of research.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) Some representative examples are shown below.

### Thermal ALD

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atomic_layer_deposition&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Thermal ALD")]

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Al2O3_Reaction_Mechanism_for_ALD.png/500px-Al2O3_Reaction_Mechanism_for_ALD.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Al2O3_Reaction_Mechanism_for_ALD.png)

Proposed mechanism for Al 2 O 3 ALD during the a) TMA reaction b) H 2 O reaction

Thermal ALD requires temperatures ranging from room temperature (~20°C) to 350°C for ligand exchange or combustion type surface reactions.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-28) It occurs through surface reactions, which enables accurate thickness control no matter the substrate geometry (subject to aspect ratio) and reactor design.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-stam-2)

The synthesis of Al 2 O 3 from [trimethylaluminum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimethylaluminum "Trimethylaluminum") (TMA) and water is one of the best known thermal ALD examples. During the TMA exposure, TMA dissociatively chemisorbs on the substrate surface and any remaining TMA is pumped out of the chamber. The dissociative [chemisorption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemisorption "Chemisorption") of TMA leaves a surface covered with AlCH 3. The surface is then exposed to H 2 O vapor, which reacts with the surface –CH 3 forming CH 4 as a reaction byproduct and resulting in a hydroxylated Al 2 O 3 surface.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-stam-2)

### Plasma ALD

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atomic_layer_deposition&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Plasma ALD")]

In plasma-assisted ALD (PA-ALD), the high reactivity of the plasma species allows to reduce the deposition temperature without compromising the film quality; also, a wider range of precursors can be used and thus a wider range of materials can be deposited as compared to thermal ALD.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-stam-2) PA-ALD can also deliver higher thickness control as well as uniformity in deposition.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-29)

### Spatial ALD

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atomic_layer_deposition&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Spatial ALD")]

In temporal ALD the separate precursor and co-reactant doses are separated from each other in _time_ by a purge step. In contrast, in spatial ALD (s-ALD), these gases are delivered at different locations, so they are separated in _space_. In [atmospheric pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_pressure "Atmospheric pressure") s-ALD the precursor and co-reactant are delivered continuously and they are separated from each other by a gas curtain to prevent gas phase reactions. Such gas curtain typically consists of nitrogen injection and exhaust positions, see Figure 1. As a substrates moves through the different gas zones, self-limiting reactions take place at the substrate surface and the ALD process takes place. As this process can easily be accelerated, the deposition rate for spatial ALD can be much higher than for conventional ALD. For example, for ALD of Al 2 O 3 the deposition rate increases from 100-300 nm per hour to 60 nm per minute.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:0-6)

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Spatial_ALD_concept.png/250px-Spatial_ALD_concept.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Spatial_ALD_concept.png)

Schematic drawing of the spatial ALD concept

The inline nature of spatial ALD makes it suitable for high volume production lines and roll-to-roll production. In general, s-ALD has been employed to apply moisture permeation barriers, passivation layers in silicon solar cells and functional layers in batteries. The chemistry for spatial ALD processes is comparable with typical temporal ALD processes, and materials that have been explored include inorganic metal oxides such as Al 2 O 3, (Al- or Ga doped) ZnO, SiO 2, In 2 O 3, InZnO, LIPON, Zn(O,S), SnO x, and TiO x _,_ but also PMG metals (Pt, Ir, Ru) can be deposited. Additionally, organic molecules can be grown in combination with inorganic atoms to enable molecular layer deposition (MLD). Plasma- or ozon enhanced spatial ALD has been demonstrated which generally lowers the deposition temperatures required.

### Photo-assisted ALD

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atomic_layer_deposition&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Photo-assisted ALD")]

In this ALD variety, UV light is used to accelerate surface reactions on the substrate. Hence reaction temperature can be reduced, as in plasma-assisted ALD. As compared to plasma-assisted ALD, the activation is weaker, but is often easier to control by adjusting the wavelength, intensity and timing of illumination.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-stam-2)

### Metal ALD

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atomic_layer_deposition&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Metal ALD")]

Copper metal ALD has attracted much attention due to the demand for copper as an [interconnect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interconnects_(integrated_circuits) "Interconnects (integrated circuits)") material[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] and the relative ease by which copper can be deposited thermally.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:8-30) Copper has a positive [standard electrochemical potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_electrode_potential "Standard electrode potential")[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-31) and is the most easily reduced metal of the first-row transition metals. Thus, numerous ALD processes have been developed, including several using hydrogen gas as the coreactant.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:8-30)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-32) Ideally, copper metal ALD should be performed at ≤100°C to achieve continuous films with low surface roughness,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-33) since higher temperatures can result in agglomeration of deposited copper.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-34)

Some metals can be grown by ALD via fluorosilane [elimination reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elimination_reaction "Elimination reaction") using a [metal halide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal_halides "Metal halides") and a silicon precursor (e.g. [SiH 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silane "Silane"), [Si 2 H 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disilane "Disilane")) as the reactants. These reactions are very exothermic due to the formation of stable Si–F bonds.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) Metals deposited by fluorosilane elimination include tungsten[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:9-35) and molybdenum.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-36) As an example, the surface reactions for tungsten metal ALD using WF 6 and Si 2 H 6 as the reactants can be expressed as[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-:9-35)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-37)

WSiF 2 H* + WF 6 → WWF 5* + SiF 3 H WF 5* + Si 2 H 6 → WSiF 2 H* + SiF 3 H + 2 H 2
The overall ALD reaction is[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27)

WF 6 + Si 2 H 6 → W + SiF 3 H + 2 H 2, ∆H = –181 kcal
The growth rate can vary from 4 to 7 Å/cycle depending on the deposition temperature (177 to 325°C) and Si 2 H 6 reactant exposure (~10 4 to 10 6 L), factors that may influence Si 2 H 6[insertion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insertion_reaction "Insertion reaction") into Si–H bonds[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-39) and result in a silicon CVD contribution to the tungsten ALD growth.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27)

The thermal ALD of many other metals is challenging (or presently impossible) due to their very negative electrochemical potentials. Recently, the application of novel strong [reducing agents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reducing_agent "Reducing agent") has led to the first reports of low-temperature thermal ALD processes for several electropositive metals. Chromium metal was deposited using a chromium [alkoxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkoxide "Alkoxide") precursor and BH 3(NHMe 2).[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-40) Titanium and tin metals were grown from their respective metal chlorides (MCl 4, M = Ti, Sn) and a bis([trimethylsilyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trimethylsilyl "Trimethylsilyl")) six-membered ring compound.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-42) Aluminum metal was deposited using an aluminum [dihydride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydride "Hydride") precursor and [AlCl 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_chloride "Aluminium chloride").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-43)

### Catalytic SiO 2 ALD

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Atomic_layer_deposition&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Catalytic SiO2 ALD")]

The use of catalysts is of paramount importance in delivering reliable methods of SiO 2 ALD. Without [catalysts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalysis "Catalysis"), surface reactions leading to the formation of SiO 2 are generally very slow and only occur at exceptionally high temperatures. Typical catalysts for SiO 2 ALD include Lewis bases such as NH 3 or [pyridine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyridine "Pyridine") and SiO 2; ALD can also be initiated when these [Lewis bases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_bases "Lewis bases") are coupled with other silicon precursors such as [tetraethoxysilane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetraethoxysilane "Tetraethoxysilane") (TEOS).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27)[Hydrogen bonding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_bonding "Hydrogen bonding") is believed to occur between the Lewis base and the SiOH* surface species or between the H 2 O based reactant and the Lewis base. Oxygen becomes a stronger [nucleophile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleophile "Nucleophile") when the Lewis base hydrogen bonds with the SiOH* surface species because the SiO-H bond is effectively weakened. As such, the electropositive Si atom in the SiCl 4 reactant is more susceptible to nucleophilic attack. Similarly, hydrogen bonding between a Lewis base and an H 2 O reactant make the electronegative O in H 2 O a strong nucleophile that is able to attack the Si in an existing SiCl* surface species.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-44) The use of a Lewis base catalyst is more or less a requirement for SiO 2 ALD, as without a Lewis base catalyst, reaction temperatures must exceed 325°C and pressures must exceed 10 3 torr. Generally, the most favorable temperature to perform SiO 2 ALD is at 32°C and a common deposition rate is 1.35 angstroms per binary reaction sequence. Two surface reactions for SiO 2 ALD, an overall reaction, and a schematic illustrating Lewis base catalysis in SiO 2 ALD are provided below.

Primary reactions at surface: SiOH* + SiCl 4 → SiOSiCl 3* + HCl SiCl* + H 2 O → SiOH* + HCl Overall ALD reaction: SiCl 4 + 2H 2 O → SiO 2 + 4 HCl[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/SiO2_Reaction_Mechanism.png/250px-SiO2_Reaction_Mechanism.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SiO2_Reaction_Mechanism.png)

Proposed mechanism of Lewis base catalysis of SiO 2 ALD during a) an SiCl 4 reaction and b) an H 2 O reaction

ALD reaction mechanisms| Type of ALD | Temperature range | Viable substrates | Reactants | Applications |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Catalytic ALD | >32°C with Lewis base catalyst[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) | Metal oxides (i.e. TiO 2, ZrO 2,SnO 2)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) | (Metal)Cl 4, H 2 O[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) | High k-dielectric layers, protective layers, anti-reflective layers, etc.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) |
| Al 2 O 3 ALD | 30–300°C | Al 2 O 3, metal oxides[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-Florian-45) | (Metal)Cl 4, H 2 O, Ti(OiPr)4, (Metal)(Et)2[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) | Dielectric layers, insulating layers, etc., Solar Cell surface passivations[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-Florian-45) |
| Metal ALD using thermal chemistry | 175–400°C[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-kimreview-46) | Metal Fluorides, organometallics, catalytic metals[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-kimreview-46) | M(C 5 H 5)2, (CH 3 C 5 H 4)M(CH 3)3 ,Cu(thd)2, Pd(hfac)2, Ni(acac)2, H 2[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-kimreview-46) | Conductive pathways, catalytic surfaces, MOS devices[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-kimreview-46) |
| ALD on polymers | 25–100°C[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) | Common polymers (polyethylene, PMMA, PP, PS, PVC, PVA, etc.)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) | Al(CH 3)3, H 2 O, M(CH 3)3[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) | Polymer surface functionalization, creation of composites, diffusion barriers, etc.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) |
| ALD on particles | 25–100°C for polymer particles, 100–400°C for metal/alloy particles[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) | BN, ZrO 2, CNTs, polymer particles | Various gases: [Fluidized bed reactors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluidized_bed_reactor "Fluidized bed reactor") are used to allow coating of individual particles[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) | Deposition of protective and insulative coatings, optical and mechanical property modification, formation of composite structures, conductive mediums |
| Plasma or radical-enhanced ALD for single element ALD materials | 20–800°C[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-47)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) | Pure metals (i.e. Ta, Ti, Si, Ge, Ru, Pt), metal nitrides (i.e. TiN, TaN, etc.)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) | Organometallics, MH 2 Cl 2, tertbutylimidotris(diethylamido)tantalum (TBTDET), bis(ethylcyclopentadienyl)ruthenium), NH 3[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-GeorgeOverview-27) | DRAM structures, [MOSFET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MOSFET "MOSFET") and semiconductor devices, capacitors[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-48) |
| Plasma-enhanced ALD of metal oxides and nitrides | 20–300°C | Al 2 O 3, SiO 2, ZnO x, InO x, HfO 2, SiN x, TaN x[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition#cite_note-51) | Similar to thermal ALD |  |

## Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) - Wikipedia Article Summary

### Overview
Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is a thin-film deposition technique based on the sequential use of a gas-phase chemical process, classified as a subclass of chemical vapour deposition (CVD). Most ALD reactions use two chemicals called precursors (or "reactants") that react with a material's surface one at a time in a sequential, self-limiting manner. ALD is a key process in fabricating semiconductor devices and part of the toolset for synthesizing nanomaterials.

### Core Principles
- ALD grows films on a substrate by exposing its surface to alternate gaseous precursors in sequential, non-overlapping pulses (unlike CVD where precursors are present simultaneously).
- Each precursor reacts with the surface in a self-limiting way, terminating once all available surface sites are consumed.
- Growth is described in terms of "growth per cycle" rather than growth rate.
- The dose-purge-dose-purge sequence constitutes an ALD cycle; saturation depends on precursor pressure and sticking probability (R_abs = S × F, where S is sticking probability and F is incident molar flux).

### History
- **1960s (Soviet Union):** Stanislav Koltsov and Valentin Aleskovsky experimentally developed ALD principles at Leningrad Technological Institute (LTI), based on Aleskovsky's 1952 "framework hypothesis." They named the technique "Molecular Layering" (ML) in 1965.
- **1974 (Finland):** Tuomo Suntola independently devised ALD (initially called "atomic layer epitaxy" or ALE) at Instrumentarium Oy for thin-film electroluminescent (TFEL) displays. First experiments grew ZnS using elemental Zn and S. A breakthrough came with switching from high-vacuum to inert gas reactors, enabling compound reactants like metal chlorides, H2S, and water vapor.
- **1983:** First large-scale ALE-EL displays installed at Helsinki-Vantaa airport flight information boards.
- **1987:** Suntola began developing ALE for photovoltaic and catalyst applications at Microchemistry Ltd. (owned by Neste Oy).
- **1999:** Microchemistry Ltd. was sold to ASM International (Dutch), becoming ASM Microchemistry Oy — the only commercial ALD-reactor manufacturer in the 1990s.
- **2000s:** Beneq Oy and Picosun Oy emerged in Finland. In 2000, Gurtej Singh Sandhu and Trung T. Doan of Micron Technology developed ALD high-κ films for DRAM (starting at 90-nm node). Intel used ALD for high-κ gate dielectric in its 45 nm CMOS technology.
- **2004 & 2018:** Suntola received the European SEMI award (2004) and the Millennium Technology Prize (2018).
- **2009:** Sequential infiltration synthesis (SIS) / vapor phase infiltration (VPI) first reported by Max-Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics researchers.
- The name "atomic layer deposition" was first proposed by Markku Leskelä at the ALE-1 conference (Espoo, Finland, 1990). The Virtual Project on the History of ALD (VPHA) was established in 2013 to document the independent discoveries (ALE in Finland, ML in Soviet Union).

### Surface Reaction Mechanisms
- **Thermal ALD:** Operates at room temperature (~20°C) to 350°C. Best-known example: Al2O3 from trimethylaluminum (TMA) and water. TMA dissociatively chemisorbs, leaving AlCH3 on the surface; H2O reacts with –CH3 forming CH4 and a hydroxylated Al2O3 surface.
- **Plasma ALD (PA-ALD):** Uses high-reactivity plasma species to reduce deposition temperature without compromising film quality; enables wider range of precursors and materials, with better thickness control and uniformity.
- **Spatial ALD (s-ALD):** Precursors separated in space (not time) via gas curtains; suitable for high-volume and roll-to-roll production. Deposition rate for Al2O3 increases from 100–300 nm/hour to 60 nm/minute.
- **Photo-assisted ALD:** Uses UV light to accelerate surface reactions, reducing reaction temperature; weaker activation than plasma but easier to control.
- **Metal ALD:** Copper ALD is of interest for interconnects (best performed ≤100°C to avoid agglomeration). Metals like tungsten and molybdenum can be deposited via fluorosilane elimination (e.g., WF6 + Si2H6 → W + SiF3H + 2H2, ∆H = –181 kcal). Novel strong reducing agents enabled low-temperature ALD of electropositive metals (Cr, Ti, Sn, Al).
- **Catalytic SiO2 ALD:** Requires Lewis base catalysts (NH3, pyridine) to enable practical SiO2 deposition; without catalysts, temperatures must exceed 325°C and pressures exceed 10³ torr. Optimal temperature is 32°C with a common deposition rate of 1.35 Å per binary reaction sequence.

### Applications
- **Microelectronics:** Gate oxides, transition-metal nitrides, metal films, magnetic recording heads, DRAM capacitors (high-κ dielectric layers).
- **Photovoltaics:** Passivation layers in silicon solar cells.
- **Electro-optic:** Thin film couplers.
- **Biomedical:** Various applications.
- **Permeation barriers for plastics:** Moisture barrier coatings.
- **Quality control:** Process control mechanisms for film quality.

### Advantages
- Atomic-level thickness and composition control.
- Highly conformal films on arbitrarily complex and large substrates.
- Wide range of materials (oxides, metals, nitrides, sulfides, chalcogenides, fluorides) — hundreds of published processes with an interactive community database and annotated periodic table available.

### Disadvantages
- **Economic viability:** Slower process compared to other deposition methods.
- **Reaction time:** Sequential pulses and purge steps limit throughput.
- **Chemical limitations:** Some materials (especially electropositive metals) are difficult or impossible to deposit thermally.

### Related Techniques
- Molecular layer deposition (MLD) — uses organic precursors to deposit polymers.
- Sequential infiltration synthesis (SIS) / vapor phase infiltration (VPI) / sequential vapor infiltration (SVI) — alternates precursor exposures to infiltrate and modify polymers.
args.key_excerpts: "Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is a thin-film deposition technique based on the sequential use of a gas-phase chemical process; it is a subclass of chemical vapour deposition."

## Abstract

The relentless pursuit of device miniaturization and the emergence of complex three-dimensional integration in semiconductor manufacturing have revealed fundamental limitations in conventional deposition, lithography, and etching techniques at sub-10 nm scales. In this review, we examine emerging atomic layer processes: area-selective deposition (ASD), atomic layer annealing (ALA), and atomic layer etching (ALE), which collectively offer atomic-scale precision in material modification. ASD utilizes either intrinsic differences in substrate surface reactivity or chemically engineered surface inhibitors to achieve self-aligned, bottom-up patterning with high selectivity. ALA utilizes cycle-by-cycle, plasma-mediated ion interactions to enable localized crystallization and dopant activation at significantly reduced thermal budgets, thereby preserving underlying device structures while delivering the desired electrical and structural properties. ALE separates the etching process into self-limiting surface functionalization and selective removal steps, allowing Å-level etch depth control with minimal substrate damage, even in high-aspect-ratio features. This review elucidates the fundamental mechanisms of each process, summarizes recent technological advancements, and highlights their critical roles in enabling the continued evolution of semiconductor devices in the post-Moore era.

## 1 Introduction

The semiconductor industry has relentlessly followed Moore’s Law, continuously increasing transistor density on integrated circuits [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR1 "Moore, G. E. (1998). Cramming more components onto integrated circuits. Proceedings of the IEEE, 86(1), 82–85.")]. In response to the growing demand for smaller and more energy-efficient computing devices, the industry has achieved remarkable progress in miniaturizing electronic circuits over several decades [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR2 "Dennard, R. H., Gaensslen, F. H., Yu, H. N., Rideout, V. L., Bassous, E., & LeBlanc, A. R. (1974). Design of ion-implanted mosfet’s with very small physical dimensions. IEEE Journal of solid-state Circuits, 9(5), 256–268."), [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR3 "Mii, Y. J. (2024, December). Semiconductor Industry Outlook and New Technology Frontiers. In 2024 IEEE International Electron Devices Meeting (IEDM) (pp. 1–6). IEEE.")]. For example, planar field-effect transistors (FETs) were succeeded by multi-gate devices such as FinFETs at the 22-nm node and gate-all-around (GAA) architectures for nodes below 5 nm. These advancements have relied on numerous process innovations, including high-k/metal gate stacks to suppress leakage, extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography for ~ 7 nm patterning, and complex multi-patterning techniques to achieve sub-10 nm scaling [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR4 "Ball, P. (2022). Semiconductor technology looks up. Nature Materials, 21(2), 132–132.")].

More recently, the development of GAA structures has accelerated to overcome the scaling limitations of conventional silicon complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) and to usher in the 2-nm technology era. At the 2024 IEEE International Electron Devices Meeting (IEDM), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) unveiled a 2-nm nanosheet GAA process offering an increase in density along with significant improvements in speed or power efficiency over 3-nm technology. Meanwhile, Intel demonstrated a ribbon-style GAA FET capable of maintaining Mobility at silicon thicknesses as low as 3 nm [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR5 "Vaughan, O. (2024). Two nanometre CMOS technology. Nature Electronics, 7(12), 1063–1063.")].

However, as scaling approaches atomic dimensions, conventional two-dimensional (2D) device layouts are reaching their limits. Three-dimensional (3D) integration is now being aggressively explored to enhance both device density and performance. Vertical chip stacking holds the promise of creating smaller, faster devices with reduced power consumption. In heterogeneous 3D integration, multiple chips or “chiplets” optimized for different functions are stacked and interconnected within a single package. In Monolithic 3D integration, multiple layers of transistors are fabricated sequentially on the same wafer [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR6 "Swaminathan, R. (2022). The next frontier: Enabling moore’s law using heterogeneous integration. Chip Scale Review, 26, 1–8. 
                  https://www.chipscalereview.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Enabling-Moores-Law-using-heterogeneous.pdf
                  
                ")]. Both approaches significantly enhance transistor density by utilizing the vertical dimension, reducing interconnect lengths, and enabling novel computing paradigms, such as in-memory and in-sensor computing for edge applications.

At the device level, innovative architectures such as vertical-transport FETs are being actively researched. Similarly, researchers are investigating vertical 3D integration of 2D materials. These efforts illustrate a broader shift toward increasingly complex 3D architectures. Concurrently, challenges associated with power density and thermal budgets are becoming more pronounced [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR7 "Guo, Y., Li, J., Zhan, X., Wang, C., Li, M., Zhang, B., & Han, Z. (2024). Van der Waals polarity-engineered 3D integration of 2D complementary logic. Nature, 630(8016), 346–352.")].

### 1.1 Need for Novel Manufacturing Processes

As semiconductor devices continue to shrink and 3D architectures become more prevalent, conventional fabrication techniques are approaching their fundamental limits, particularly in patterning, deposition, and etching. At sub-10 nm dimensions, even atomic-level deviations can critically impact device performance [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR8 "Arts, K., Hamaguchi, S., Ito, T., Karahashi, K., Knoops, H. C., Mackus, A. J., & Kessels, W. M. E. (2022). Foundations of atomic-level plasma processing in nanoelectronics. Plasma Sources Science and Technology, 31(10), 103002.")]. Consequently, the industry is transitioning beyond conventional CMOS, necessitating unprecedented control over materials and geometries at the atomic scale. This transition is driving the development of novel atomic layer manufacturing processes capable of depositing, etching, or Modifying materials one atomic layer at a time, thus enabling continued progress in the 3D era of Moore’s Law.

As fabrication processes advance, several limitations arise (Fig. [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#Fig1)):

Furthermore, controlling film thickness at the atomic (sub-Å) level exceeds the capabilities of most conventional methods [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR9 "Johnson, R. Even with EUV lithography, achieving single-exposure patterning at ~ 5 nm pitch is extremely challenging, significantly increasing manufacturing costs and defect risk [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR11 "Neisser, M. Photon shot noise, electron scattering, and uneven resist reactions lead to rough edges and patterning failures, issues that require alternative solutions such as maskless lithography or directed self-assembly techniques [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR12 "Giannopoulos, I., Mochi, I., Vockenhuber, M., Ekinci, Y., & Kazazis, D. (2024). Extreme ultraviolet lithography reaches 5 Nm resolution. Nanoscale, 16(33), 15533–15543.")].

Etch rates can vary, and even Å-level overshoots may destroy delicate features. In HAR structures, plasma exposure can introduce defects, such as bowing, twisting, and striation, which are unacceptable in modern nanoscale devices [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR13 "Oehrlein, G. S., Brandstadter, S. M., Bruce, R. L., Chang, J. P., DeMott, J. C., Donnelly, V. M., & Ventzek, P. L. (2024). Future of plasma etching for microelectronics: Challenges and opportunities.                 ")].

These challenges in deposition, lithography, etching underscore the need for atomic-scale processes. Accordingly, the semiconductor industry is increasingly developing novel atomic layer techniques that can deposit and remove materials with atomic precision.

### 1.2 Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD)

Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is a thin-film growth technique uniquely suited for atomic-scale manufacturing [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR14 "Suntola, T. (1992). Atomic layer epitaxy. Thin Solid Films, 216(1), 84–89.")]. Originating in the 1970 s, initially referred to as atomic layer epitaxy, it gained prominence only in recent decades as device scaling demanded precise film deposition on increasingly complex topographies. By the late 1980 s, the technique transitioned into commercial reactor systems, and by the 1990 s, it supported dedicated atomic layer epitaxy workshops, which eventually evolved into the annual ALD conference launched in 2001. Around the year 2000, the broader term ALD was adopted to reflect the method’s applicability to both amorphous dielectrics and epitaxial films [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR15 "George, S. M. (2010). Atomic layer deposition: An overview. Chemical Reviews, 110(1), 111–131.")].

ALD is fundamentally based on sequential, self-limiting surface reactions. In a typical ALD cycle, two vapor-phase precursors are introduced sequentially into a reactor as follows (Fig. [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#Fig2)) [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR16 "Puurunen, R. L. (2005). Surface chemistry of atomic layer deposition: A case study for the trimethylaluminum/water process. Journal of applied physics, 97(12).")]:

**Fig. 2**

![Image 7: Fig. 2](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs12541-025-01337-z/MediaObjects/12541_2025_1337_Fig2_HTML.jpg)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z/figures/2)

Schematic of the ALD process. (reprinted from [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR24 "Go, D., Shin, J. W., Lee, S., Lee, J., Yang, B. C., Won, Y., … An, J. (2023). Atomic layer deposition for thin film solid-state battery and capacitor. International Journal of Precision Engineering and Manufacturing-Green Technology, 10(3), 851–873.")], © 2022, Springer Nature)

1.   (i)
Precursor pulse: A gaseous precursor (e.g., trimethylaluminum for aluminum) is pulsed into the chamber. It chemisorbs onto the substrate surface, reacting with available surface sites until saturation is reached. Because the surface quickly becomes fully covered, the reaction self-limits; once every reactive site is occupied, no further adsorption occurs.

2.   (ii)
Purge: An inert gas (typically N 2 or Ar) flushes out excess precursor and volatile reaction byproducts. No gas-phase reaction should occur between cycles.

3.   (iii)
Reactant pulse: A second reactant (often a co-reactant such as water, ozone, or a plasma species) is introduced. This reactant chemically reacts with the adsorbed first precursor, converting it into the desired compound (e.g., converting Al–CH 3 to Al–O during Al 2 O 3 deposition). This reaction is also self-limiting and proceeds until all reactive sites are consumed.

4.   (iv)
Purge: A second purge removes the excess reactant and byproducts.

Each cycle deposits approximately one atomic layer of material, often less than a full monolayer in practice. By repeating the cycle multiple times, films of precisely controlled thickness can be grown. The typical growth-per-cycle (GPC) varies depending on the precursor chemistry, but generally ranges from 0.05 to 0.1 nm per cycle for most oxides and nitrides [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR17 "Kim, J., Lee, S., Song, Y., Choi, S., An, J., & Cho, J. (2021). Thermal conductivity of plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposited hafnium zirconium oxide dielectric thin films. Journal of the European Ceramic Society, 41(6), 3397–3403."), [18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR18 "Shin, J. W., Lee, J., Kim, K., Kwon, C., Park, Y. B., Park, H., & An, J. (2022). Effect of nitrogen plasma on the mechanical and electrical properties of plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposited TiN films. Ceramics International, 48(17), 25651–25655.")]. Therefore, a 20-nm film may require 100 to 400 ALD cycles but offers layer-by-layer precision. Owing to the self-limiting nature of each reaction step, ALD inherently provides exceptional thickness control and uniformity. Its primary advantages can be summarized as follows [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR15 "George, S. M. (2010). Atomic layer deposition: An overview. Chemical Reviews, 110(1), 111–131.")]:

*   Precise thickness control: Each half-reaction halts when the surface reaches saturation, preventing overshoot and ensuring that each cycle contributes a nearly fixed amount of material. This permits sub-Å control of film thickness by simply adjusting the number of cycles, far exceeding the precision of conventional CVD or PVD techniques.

*   Extreme conformality: ALD achieves uniform coating over all exposed surfaces, even deep within trenches or around complex 3D structures. Because the gas-phase precursors diffuse into recessed features and react in a layer-by-layer manner, ALD can produce pinhole-free films on structures with aspect ratios of 10:1, 20:1, or higher. In contrast, PVD is limited by line-of-sight deposition.

*   Material and temperature versatility: A wide range of chemistries is available for ALD. Commonly deposited materials include oxides (Al 2 O 3, HfO 2, SiO 2), nitrides (TiN, AlN), sulfides, metals (Ru, Pt, W, etc.), and even complex materials such as doped oxides and alloys. Each process operates within a specific temperature window in which the reactions remain self-limiting. Within this window, the GPC remains independent of time or precursor flow rate once saturation is achieved, an essential characteristic of ALD.

Owing to these attributes, ALD is exceptionally well-suited for semiconductor fabrication [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR19 "Shin, J. W., Kang, M. H., Oh, S., Yang, B. C., Seong, K., Ahn, H. S., & An, J. (2018). Atomic layer deposited high-k dielectric on graphene by functionalization through atmospheric plasma treatment. Nanotechnology, 29(19), 195602."),[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR20 "Shim, J., Lim, J., Kim, I., Kim, S. K., Ahn, S. Y., Park, J., … Kim, S. (2023, December).Fully CMOS-compatible room-temperature waveguide-integrated bolometer based on germanium-on-insulator platform at mid-infrared operating beyond 4 µm. In 2023 International Electron Devices Meeting (IEDM) (pp. 1–4). IEEE."),[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR21 "Park, G., Go, D., Jo, S., Lee, T. H., Shin, J. W., & An, J. (2023). High-Performance graphene‐Dielectric interface by UV‐Assisted atomic layer deposition for graphene field effect transistor. Advanced Electronic Materials, 9(7), 2300074.")], as well as for applications in optics [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR22 "Kim, J., Kim, Y., Kim, W., Oh, D. K., Kang, D., Seong, J., & Rho, J. (2024). 8 ″wafer-scale,centimeter-sized, high-efficiency Metalenses in the ultraviolet. Materials Today, 73, 9–15.")], batteries [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR23 "Li, J., Wu, J., Wang, M., Wen, D., Liu, X., Shan, B., & Chen, R. (2025). Subnano Al2O3 coatings for kinetics and stability optimization of LiNi0. 83Co0. 12Mn0. 05O2 via O3-Based atomic layer deposition. ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces."), [24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR24 "Go, D., Shin, J. W., Lee, S., Lee, J., Yang, B. C., Won, Y., … An, J. (2023). International Journal of Precision Engineering and Manufacturing-Green Technology, 10(3), 851–873.")], and catalysis [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR25 "Kim, H. J., Li, H., Kim, D., Park, G., Jo, S. E., Ju, K., & An, J. (2025). Active and stable plasma-enhanced ALD pt@ Ni-YSZ hydrogen electrode for steam reversible solid oxide cells.
