However, the self-limiting nature of ALD growth results in long process times for moderate film thicknesses. Additionally, the requirement for volatile precursors constrains the range of compatible materials. Operating within a narrow temperature window (typically below ~ 350 °C) further limits substrate compatibility and may lead to non-ideal reactions outside this range. Finally, the need for precise control over vacuum, thermal, and flow parameters during the pulse and purge cycles increases both equipment and operational costs. Incomplete purging may also result in impurity incorporation [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR9 "Johnson, R. W., Hultqvist, A., & Bent, S. F. (2014). A brief review of atomic layer deposition: From fundamentals to applications. Materials Today, 17(5), 236–246.")].

### 1.3 Need for Novel Atomic Layer Processes

To address the previously discussed drawbacks of ALD and overcome interrelated bottlenecks in patterning fidelity, thermal budget, and etch precision, a new suite of “atomic layer” processes has emerged—namely, area-selective deposition (ASD), atomic layer annealing (ALA), and atomic layer etching (ALE) (Fig. [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#Fig3)).

*   ASD modifies ALD chemistries or introduces surface inhibitors to confine film growth exclusively to predefined regions. This considerably reduces the number of patterning steps and improves overlay accuracy in HAR architectures. Given the increasing demand for higher integration densities and more complex device designs, ASD plays a crucial role in overcoming the limitations of conventional patterning techniques in advanced semiconductor fabrication [[28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR28 "Fang, M., & Ho, J. C. (2015). Area-selective atomic layer deposition: Conformal coating, subnanometer thickness control, and smart positioning. ACS Nano, 9(9), 8651–8654."),[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR29 "Parsons, G. N. (2019). Functional model for analysis of ALD nucleation and quantification of area-selective deposition. Journal of Vacuum Science & Technology A, 37(2), 020911.

With the advent of plasma-enhanced ALE (PE-ALE) techniques, this method is well-positioned to meet the stringent requirements of next-generation transistor designs, including GAA transistors and other advanced logic devices [[33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR33 "Kanarik, K. The growing complexity of semiconductor devices necessitates the adoption of atomic layer processes to overcome the thermal, patterning, and etching limitations of conventional techniques. ASD, ALA, and ALE provide critical solutions that enhance precision, scalability, and material integrity in the fabrication of advanced semiconductor devices. These innovations are not merely incremental improvements; they are essential enablers for sustaining Moore’s Law and realizing the next generation of electronic technologies.

Accordingly, this review presents the fundamentals and representative case studies of these novel atomic layer processes, specifically, area-selective ALD (AS-ALD), ALA, and ALE.

## 2 Area-Selective Atomic Layer Deposition (AS-ALD)

### 2.1 Introduction to AS-ALD

As technology scales beyond the 3-nm node, achieving high-resolution patterning with minimal misalignment and reduced process complexity has become increasingly critical [[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR35 "Cao, W., Bu, H., Vinet, M., Cao, M., Takagi, S., Hwang, S., & Banerjee, K. (2023). The future transistors. Nature, 620(7974), 501–515.")]. Conventional top-down fabrication methods in the semiconductor industry, such as EUV lithography and etching, face significant challenges related to overlay, edge placement error, and high lithography costs, all of which collectively limit scalability and yield [[36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR36 "Varnava, C. (2022). Extreme-ultraviolet lithography packs more transistors on chip. Nature Electronics, 5(7), 406–406."), [37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR37 "Liu, T. L., & Bent, S. (2025). Nanostructure fabrication by area selective deposition: A brief review. Materials Horizons, 12, 1711–1725. 
                  https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2025/mh/d4mh01472c
                  
                ")].

To address these challenges, AS-ALD has gained significant attention as a promising bottom-up approach. AS-ALD enables self-aligned patterning by confining deposition to predefined areas, thereby reducing the reliance on multiple lithography steps [[37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR37 "Liu, T. L., & Bent, S. (2025). Nanostructure fabrication by area selective deposition: A brief review. Materials Horizons, 12, 1711–1725. 
                  https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlehtml/2025/mh/d4mh01472c
                  
                "),[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR38 "Clark, R., Tapily, K., Yu, K. H., Hakamata, T., Consiglio, S., O’meara, D., … Leusink,G. (2018). Perspective: New process technologies required for future devices and scaling.Apl Materials, 6(5)."),[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR39 "Mackus, A. J., Merkx, M. J., & Kessels, W. M. (2018). From the bottom-up: Toward area-selective atomic layer deposition with high selectivity. Chemistry of Materials, 31(1), 2–12.")]. Unlike conventional patterning methods, which require repeated lithographic definition of each layer, AS-ALD achieves selective film growth through surface-specific deposition strategies that allow material formation only on targeted regions. This approach offers an effective solution to the aforementioned process limitations.

The fundamental principle of AS-ALD lies in the differential nucleation behavior of ALD chemistries on distinct surfaces. This enables film growth on the “growth area (GA)” while suppressing deposition on the “non-growth area (NGA)” through controlled nucleation delay. Selective behavior is governed by factors such as surface energy, chemical functionalization, and process conditions, which collectively facilitate precise deposition without the need for additional pattern transfer steps.

The difference in nucleation onset between GA and NGA can be characterized by a “selectivity window,” defined as the number of ALD cycles during which deposition remains effectively confined to GA. However, over extended cycles, selectivity may degrade owing to phenomena such as precursor adsorption and eventual nucleation on NGA, leading to unintended film growth [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR39 "Mackus, A. J., Merkx, M. J., & Kessels, W. M. (2018). From the bottom-up: Toward area-selective atomic layer deposition with high selectivity. Chemistry of Materials, 31(1), 2–12.")]. Therefore, various strategies have been developed to prolong the selectivity window and maintain deposition fidelity across longer ALD processes.

In this section, recent developments in AS-ALD are categorized based on four key mechanisms used to achieve high selectivity: intrinsic material properties, reaction inhibition, surface treatment, and process engineering.

### 2.2 Intrinsic Material Selectivity

Inherent or substrate-dependent selectivity refers to the natural differences in surface chemistry, where certain ALD precursors fail to nucleate on some materials without additional surface treatments. This type of selectivity arises from fundamental differences in surface reactivity, such as the presence of functional groups or variations in surface energy, which influence nucleation kinetics. These differences can enable self-aligned deposition, particularly during the initial ALD cycles, effectively guiding film formation onto desired regions [[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR38 "Clark, R., Tapily, K., Yu, K. H., Hakamata, T., Consiglio, S., O’meara, D., … Leusink,G. (2018). Perspective: New process technologies required for future devices and scaling.Apl Materials, 6(5)."), [39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR39 "Mackus, A. J., Merkx, M. J., & Kessels, W. M. (2018). From the bottom-up: Toward area-selective atomic layer deposition with high selectivity. Chemistry of Materials, 31(1), 2–12.")].

One of the most widely recognized examples of inherent AS-ALD is the contrast in nucleation behavior between metallic and dielectric surfaces [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR40 "Singh, J. A., Thissen, N. F., Kim, W. H., Johnson, H., Kessels, W. M., Bol, A. A.,… Mackus, A. J. (2018). Area-selective atomic layer deposition of metal oxides on noble metals through catalytic oxygen activation. Chemistry of Materials, 30(3), 663–670."),[41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR41 "Saha, S., Jursich, G., Phakatkar, A. H., Shokuhfar, T., & Takoudis, C. G. (2022). Order of magnitude enhancement of inherently selective atomic layer deposition of zirconia on silicon without deposition on copper: The role of precursor. Vacuum, 195, 110686."),[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR42 "Li, Y. C., Cao, K., Lan, Y. X., Zhang, J. M., Gong, M., Wen, Y. W., … Chen, R. (2021).Inherently area-selective atomic layer deposition of manganese oxide through electronegativity-induced adsorption. Molecules, 26(10), 3056."),[43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR43 "Lee, J. M., Lee, J. H., Lee, S. H., Oh, J., Kim, H., Oh, J., & Kim, W. H. (2025). Deposition selectivity on oxide versus metal surfaces via catalyzed atomic layer deposition of SiO2 and vapor-dosed phosphonic acid inhibitors. Applied Surface Science, 688, 162337.")]. In a study by Kim et al. [[44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR44 "Kim, H. B., Lee, J. M., Sung, D., Ahn, J. H., & Kim, W. H. (2024). Highly area-selective atomic layer deposition of device-quality Hf1-xZrxO2 thin films through catalytic local activation. Chemical Engineering Journal, 488, 150760.")], AS-ALD of Hf 1−x Zr x O 2(HZO) thin films was achieved by utilizing intrinsic differences in surface reactivity between metal and dielectric substrates. The researchers demonstrated that catalytic metal surfaces, such as Pt and Ru, selectively promoted HZO growth, whereas inert dielectric surfaces, such as SiO 2, exhibited minimal or no deposition (Fig. [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#Fig4)a). This selectivity was accomplished without additional surface passivation or etching steps, relying entirely on localized catalytic activation during ALD.

A similar approach has recently been extended to 2D material systems. For instance, Park et al. [[45](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR45 "Park, J., Kwak, S. J., Kang, S., Oh, S., Shin, B., Noh, G., … Kang, K. (2024). Area-selective atomic layer deposition on 2D monolayer lateral superlattices. Nature Communications, 15(1), 2138.")] investigated AS-ALD on MoS 2–MoSe 2 monolayer lateral superlattices by exploiting the intrinsic surface chemical differences between the two materials. During Al 2 O 3 deposition, nucleation occurred preferentially on MoSe 2, while MoS 2 regions showed no growth during the initial ALD cycles (Fig. [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#Fig4)b and c). This behavior was attributed to variations in precursor adsorption, surface diffusion, and desorption mechanisms. Consequently, well-defined nanoscale patterns were formed along the MoS 2–MoSe 2 interface, indicating the potential of inherent selectivity-based AS-ALD for precision patterning in 2D material heterostructures.

### 2.3 Reaction Inhibitors

In AS-ALD via reaction inhibition, selectivity is maintained by applying surface passivation layers, such as self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) [[46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR46 "Liu, T. L., Harake, M., & Bent, S. F. (2023). Sequential use of orthogonal Self-Assembled monolayers for Area‐Selective atomic layer deposition of dielectric on metal. Advanced Materials Interfaces, 10(5), 2202134."),[47](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR47 "Chang, C. W., Tseng, Y. H., Hsu, C. S., & Chen, J. T. (2023). Area-Selective atomic layer deposition on metal/dielectric patterns: Amphiphobic coating, vaporizable inhibitors, and regenerative processing. ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, 15(23), 28817–28824."),[48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR48 "Lee, J., Oh, J., Kim, J., Oh, H., Shong, B., & Kim, W. H. (2024). Area-selective atomic layer deposition of Ru thin films by chemo-selective Inhibition of alkyl aldehyde molecules on nitride surfaces. Applied Surface Science, 662, 160099."),[49](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR49 "Lee, S. H., Lee, J. M., Lee, J. H., Kwak, J., Chung, S. W., & Kim, W. H. (2022). Area-selective atomic layer deposition of Ru thin films using phosphonic acid self-assembled monolayers for metal/dielectric selectivity. Materials Letters, 328, 133187.")] or small molecular inhibitors (SMIs), to block precursor adsorption on NGA. In contrast, GA is designed to remain unaffected by these inhibitors, allowing for ASD. These inhibition layers typically remain stable for a specific number of ALD cycles (known as the “selectivity window”), but may eventually degrade or detach, resulting in reduced selectivity.

A classic example of this strategy is the use of SAMs applied before the ALD precursor pulse. Bobb-Semple et al. Area-selective atomic layer deposition assisted by self-assembled monolayers: a comparison of Cu, Co, W, and Ru. Chemistry of Materials, 31(5), 1635–1645.")] demonstrated that alkyl-terminated SAMs, such as octadecylphos phonic acid (ODPA), effectively inhibit metal precursor adsorption on various metal surfaces, thereby enabling AS-ALD of ZnO or Al 2 O 3. These SAMs form a dense, hydrophobic organic layer that resists precursor chemisorption, while unmodified SiO 2 surfaces remain receptive to film growth. However, SAMs face limitations, including lengthy processing times resulting from their low volatility, and their bulky molecular structures can hinder effectiveness at sub-10 nm nodes, especially in HAR features [[51](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR51 "Lee, Y., Rothman, A., Shearer, A. B., & Bent, S. F. (2025). Molecular design in Area-Selective atomic layer deposition: Understanding inhibitors and precursors. Chemistry of Materials, 37(5), 1741–1758.")].

To overcome these limitations, SMIs have been introduced as an alternative [[52](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR52 "Merkx, M. J., Vlaanderen, S., Faraz, T., Verheijen, M. A., Kessels, W. M., & Mackus, A. J. (2020). Area-selective atomic layer deposition of TiN using aromatic inhibitor molecules for metal/dielectric selectivity. Chemistry of Materials, 32(18), 7788–7795."),[53](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR53 "Yarbrough, J., Pieck, F., Grigjanis, D., Oh, I. K., Maue, P., Tonner-Zech, R., & Bent, S. F. (2022). Tuning molecular inhibitors and aluminum precursors for the area-selective atomic layer deposition of Al2O3. Chemistry of Materials, 34(10), 4646–4659."),[54](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR54 "Cho, E. H., Kong, D., Cho, I., Leem, Y., Lee, Y. M., Kim, M., & Lee, H. B. R. (2024). Area-Selective atomic layer deposition of ruthenium via reduction of interfacial oxidation. Chemistry of Materials, 36(18), 8663–8672."),[55](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR55 "Merkx, M. J., Tezsevin, I., Yu, P., Janssen, T., Heinemans, R. H., Lengers, R. J.,… Mackus, A. J. (2024). In situ formation of inhibitor species through catalytic surface reactions during area-selective atomic layer deposition of TaN. The Journal of Chemical Physics, 160(20)."),[56](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR56 "Park, H., Oh, J., Lee, J. M., & Kim, W. H. (2024). Selective nitride passivation using vapor-dosed aldehyde inhibitors for area-selective atomic layer deposition. Materials Letters, 366, 136570.")]. SMIs are vapor-phase molecules that are pulsed intermittently during the ALD process to block precursor adsorption on NGA surfaces. In a recent study, Nguyen et al. [[57](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z#ref-CR57 "Nguyen, C. T., Cho, E. H., Gu, B., Lee, S., Kim, H. S., Park, J., … Lee, H. B. R.(2022). This approach effectively suppressed TiO 2 deposition up to a thickness of 49 nm. Additionally, the geometric constraints affected the spatial distribution of inhibitor Molecules, leading to a gradient in selective deposition, particularly evident within 3D nanohole structures.

### 2.4 Surface Pretreatment

Surface treatment in AS-ALD refers to any physical or energetic preprocessing of a substrate that modifies its surface chemistry to define GA and NGA. By “predefining” areas with different chemical reactivities, ALD precursors can be directed to adsorb and react selectively on the desired locations. This is a review paper published in the International Journal of Precision Engineering and Manufacturing (Volume 26, pages 2551–2571, published 15 September 2025) titled "Novel Atomic Layer Processes for Semiconductor Manufacturing: Area Selective Deposition, Atomic Layer Annealing, and Atomic Layer Etching." Authors include Sangwon Lee, Gyuha Lee, Jeongmin Oh, and Jihwan An (ORCID: 0000-0002-7697-9935). The open-access article has 11k accesses and 17 citations.

The review addresses fundamental limitations of conventional deposition, lithography, and etching techniques at sub-10 nm scales in semiconductor manufacturing, driven by device miniaturization and complex 3D integration. It examines three emerging atomic layer processes:

1. **Area-Selective Deposition (ASD)**: Utilizes intrinsic differences in substrate surface reactivity or chemically engineered surface inhibitors (such as self-assembled monolayers/SAMs or small molecular inhibitors/SMIs) to achieve self-aligned, bottom-up patterning with high selectivity. The review categorizes AS-ALD approaches into four mechanisms: intrinsic material selectivity (e.g., HZO growth promoted on catalytic Pt/Ru surfaces but not SiO2; selective nucleation on MoSe2 vs MoS2 in 2D lateral superlattices), reaction inhibitors (SAMs like octadecylphosphonic acid, and SMIs that block precursor adsorption on non-growth areas), surface pretreatment, and process engineering.

2. **Atomic Layer Annealing (ALA)**: Incorporates localized, cycle-by-cycle plasma-mediated thermal treatments into ALD sequences, enabling sub-nanometer dopant activation or crystallization at significantly reduced thermal budgets, preserving thermally sensitive underlying device structures while achieving desired electrical and structural properties.

3. **Atomic Layer Etching (ALE)**: Separates etching into self-limiting surface functionalization and selective removal steps, allowing Å-level etch depth control with minimal substrate damage, even in high-aspect-ratio features. Plasma-enhanced ALE (PE-ALE) is positioned to meet stringent requirements of next-generation transistor designs including GAA transistors.

Key context: The semiconductor industry has progressed from planar FETs to FinFETs (22-nm node) to gate-all-around (GAA) architectures below 5 nm, and is entering the 2-nm era (TSMC's 2-nm nanosheet GAA process and Intel's ribbon-style GAA FET at 3 nm silicon thickness, both unveiled at 2024 IEDM). Conventional CVD/PVD struggle with high-aspect-ratio conformality; EUV lithography faces shot noise and random defect challenges; RIE lacks atomic-level control in HAR structures.

The review details ALD fundamentals (sequential, self-limiting surface reactions with four steps: precursor pulse, purge, reactant pulse, purge; typical growth-per-cycle of 0.05–0.1 nm/cycle; advantages including precise thickness control, extreme conformality, and material versatility; limitations including slow process times, narrow temperature windows below ~350°C, and high costs).

## Abstract

Atomic layer deposition (ALD) has become an indispensable thin-film technology in the contemporary microelectronics industry. The unique self-limited layer-by-layer growth feature of ALD has outstood this technology to deposit highly uniform conformal pinhole-free thin films with angstrom-level thickness control, particularly on 3D topologies. Over the years, the ALD technology has enabled not only the successful downscaling of the microelectronic devices but also numerous novel 3D device structures. As ALD is essentially a variant of chemical vapor deposition, a comprehensive understanding of the involved chemistry is of crucial importance to further develop and utilize this technology. To this end, we, in this review, focus on the surface chemistry and precursor chemistry aspects of ALD. We first review the surface chemistry of the gas–solid ALD reactions and elaborately discuss the associated mechanisms for the film growth; then, we review the ALD precursor chemistry by comparatively discussing the precursors that have been commonly used in the ALD processes; and finally, we selectively present a few newly-emerged applications of ALD in microelectronics, followed by our perspective on the future of the ALD technology.

## Highlights

* The surface chemistry of the gas–solid ALD reactions is reviewed, and the associated mechanisms are elaborately discussed.
* The ALD precursor chemistry is reviewed by comparatively discussing the precursors that have been commonly used.
* Newly-emerged applications of ALD in microelectronics are presented.
* Future perspectives of the ALD technology are outlined.

## 1. Introduction

Following the Moore’s law, the critical size of the microelectronic devices has been continually shrinking over the decades to boost the performance of the integrated circuits (ICs) [[1](#ijemacd88ebib1)]. As the device critical size gradually approaches its limit, more efforts have been made to explore new materials and 3D device structures to further extend the Moore’s law. Owing to the limitation by short-channel effects, non-planer field-effect transistors (FETs), such as fin FETs (FinFETs) [[2](#ijemacd88ebib2)] and gate-all-around (GAA) FETs [[3](#ijemacd88ebib3)], have been gradually adopted in the microelectronics industry. To meet the requirements of fabricating chips with these complex structures, it is very important to use a deposition technology that can controllably afford highly uniform conformal thin films on 3D topologies. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is an essential technology for these purposes. ALD is based on sequential and self-limiting gas–solid chemical reactions, and owing to the self-limiting nature, the composition and thickness of the deposited thin films can be precisely controlled at the atomic scale [[4](#ijemacd88ebib4)–[6](#ijemacd88ebib6)]. Also, ALD is able to deposit highly uniform films in trench or hole structures with a high aspect ratio, which can hardly be achieved by the conventional physical vapor deposition (PVD) or chemical vapor deposition (CVD). Over the past decades, along with the downscaling of the microelectronic devices, ALD has become extensively used in numerous key process steps in the advanced technology nodes of the IC fabrication, such as the deposition of ultrathin high-k oxides for the gate-dielectrics in FETs [[7](#ijemacd88ebib7), [8](#ijemacd88ebib8)] and the capacitor-dielectrics in dynamic random access memory (DRAM) [[9](#ijemacd88ebib9), [10](#ijemacd88ebib10)], the deposition of the spacers for self-aligned multi-patterning [[11](#ijemacd88ebib11), [12](#ijemacd88ebib12)], etc. Also, ALD is essential for the preparation of many newly-emerged microelectronic devices, such as the back-end-of-line (BEOL)-compatible oxide-based transistors [[13](#ijemacd88ebib13)–[15](#ijemacd88ebib15)]. Therefore, the ALD technology has been considered as a vital enabler to realize new device structures for ICs.

The ALD technology relies heavily on the involved surface chemistry, which can significantly influence the properties of the deposited films, such as film thickness, morphology, conformality, and composition. Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of the surface chemistry and associated mechanisms is very important. The ALD precursors are also very important; they are usually metalorganic compounds, and their volatility, thermal stability, and self-limiting reactivity can substantially affect the growth behavior of the ALD films. Therefore, the design of the precursor chemical structures is of the pivot for the ALD technology.

To address the above issues, this review focuses on the chemistry aspect of the ALD technology. The chemistry involved in the ALD surface reactions is firstly reviewed, and the associated mechanisms are elaborately discussed. Then follows the review of the precursor chemistry, and the precursors that have been commonly used are carefully discussed. Finally, the applications of the ALD technology for some newly-emerged areas in microelectronics are discussed. Certainly, we cannot review every aspect of the ALD technology, given its already very wide applications, and the readers may refer to some other published reviews for more information about ALD [[16](#ijemacd88ebib16)–[30](#ijemacd88ebib30)].

## 2. Surface chemistry of ALD

ALD is essentially a variant of CVD. An ALD process relies on two or more self-limiting gas–solid chemical reactions, which are controlled to proceed in an alternate and cyclic manner. As shown in figure [1](#ijemacd88ef1)(a), a typical ALD process consists of a cycling of four steps: (I) excessive amount of precursor A is dosed into the chamber to react with the functional groups on the solid surface, and the reaction is self-limiting and the byproduct is volatile; (II) the chamber is purged by inert gas to completely remove the byproduct and unreacted A; (III) excessive amount of precursor B is dosed into the chamber to react with the functional groups formed in (I), and the reaction is also self-limiting and the byproduct is also volatile; and (IV) the chamber is again purged by inert gas to completely remove the byproduct and unreacted B.

![Figure 1. Refer to the following caption and surrounding text.](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)

**Figure 1.** Characteristics of ALD. (a) Schematic illustration of an ALD cycle. (b) Saturation behavior of the precursor chemisorption. (c) Temperature dependence of the ALD film growth rate.

Download figure:

The key point of ALD is that the gas–solid chemical reactions should be self-limiting, and this feature is illustrated in figure [1](#ijemacd88ef1)(b), where the gas–solid chemical reactions can be regarded as the chemisorption of the precursor on the solid surface and the chemisorption saturates as the precursor exposure amount exceeds a certain point. The saturated chemisorption can afford a fixed amount of material grown on the surface in each ALD cycle. Therefore, a uniform thin film of material can be conformally coated on any structured surfaces, and at the same time, the film thickness can be precisely controlled by the number of the ALD cycles. On the other hand, insufficient precursor exposure would lead to unsaturated chemisorption on the surface, and the remaining active surface sites are still capable of adsorbing a second type of precursor. This strategy has been used in the ALD of multi-element compounds. For instance, a ternary oxide A*x*B*y*O*z* can be deposited by the pulsing sequence of the A, B, and O precursors, where the pulse of A is set in the subsaturation regime [[31](#ijemacd88ebib31), [32](#ijemacd88ebib32)].

The surface chemical reactions are normally temperature dependent (figure [1](#ijemacd88ef1)(c)), and the temperature range where the surface reactions are self-limiting is regarded as the ALD window. Although the film growth rate (also known as growth per cycle, GPC) is often a constant within the window, the range of the ALD window is actually bounded by the fulfillment of the self-limiting conditions; and therefore, GPC in the window may increase or decrease as well. Precursor condensation or incomplete reaction may occur below the window; whereas precursor decomposition or desorption may occur above the window.

As the surface chemical reactions are crucial for ALD, a thorough understanding of the associated mechanisms is very important to develop and optimize the ALD processes in order to achieve the desired film properties, such as the film thickness, morphology, conformality, and composition. Among the ALD processes that have been so far realized for numerous materials, the involved ALD surface chemistry mechanisms can be generally classified into four categories, which are the ligand-exchange, dissociative or non-dissociative chemisorption, oxidation, and reduction mechanisms. The attributes of these mechanisms are elaborated as follows.

### 2.1. Ligand-exchange mechanism

The ligand-exchange mechanism (figure [2](#ijemacd88ef2)(a)) is the most common mechanism for ALD, and it can be described as the following general reaction scheme:

![Equation (1)](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)![Figure 2. Refer to the following caption and surrounding text.](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)

**Figure 2.** Schematic illustration of the chemisorption mechanisms: (a) ligand-exchange, (b) dissociative chemisorption, and (c) non-dissociative chemisorption mechanisms.

Download figure:

where || denotes the surface, *a* is a surface group, *M* is a metal atom, and *L* is a ligand of the precursor. During the ligand-exchange reaction, a ligand (*L*) of the gaseous precursor molecule (*ML*n) is displaced by the surface species (||−*a*), forming the volatile byproduct of *aL*, and meanwhile, the remainder of the precursor molecule bonds to the surface, forming a chemisorbed new surface species of ||−*ML*n−1. The ligand-exchange reaction may continue to occur between the chemisorbed ||−*ML*n−1 and another nearby ||-*a* surface group, and therefore, multiple chemical bonds may be formed between the precursor and surface as the following:

![Equation (2)](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)

A common example of the ligand-exchange mechanism is the proton transfer scheme, in which a Brønsted base abstracts a proton from a Brønsted acid. As the scheme shown in equation ([1](#ijemacd88eeqn1)), the metal precursor (*ML*n) serves as a Brønsted base, and it can abstract protons (*a* = H) from the Brønsted acidic surface groups, such as hydroxyls. In this respect, the metal precursor with a stronger ionic character of its metal–ligand bond is more favorable for the proton transfer reaction, because in this case the ligand is more analogous to a free anion and hence more effective to abstract a positively charged proton. The acidity of the ligand itself is also very important; a stronger basic ligand is more effective to abstract a proton, and this effect is well manifested when comparing the precursors of metalorganics and metal halides.

The ALD of Al2O3 from the precursors of trimethylaluminum (TMA) and H2O is a typical process that follows the proton-transfer ligand-exchange mechanism. This ALD process has been extensively studied both experimentally and theoretically [[33](#ijemacd88ebib33)–[35](#ijemacd88ebib35)]. In the TMA half-cycle, the surface terminal –OH groups react with the TMA via the proton-transfer ligand-exchange reaction, forming the O–Al bonds and releasing the volatile byproduct of CH4, and then, in the subsequent H2O half-cycle, the remaining surface methyl ligands are displayed by hydroxyls via another proton-transfer ligand-exchange reaction with the incoming H2O molecules:

![Equation (3)](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)![Equation (4)](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)

The formation of the strong Al–O bonds is the main driving force for the surface reactions, and the reaction enthalpy was reported to be one of the highest among all ALD reactions [[4](#ijemacd88ebib4)]. Both the above reactions are efficient and self-limiting, which makes the ALD of Al2O3 an almost ideal case for ALD.

The halogen transfer is another example of the ligand-exchange mechanism. The halogen transfer appears in the thermal ALD of W and Mo metals [[36](#ijemacd88ebib36), [37](#ijemacd88ebib37)], where Si2H6 is typically used with the metal fluorides of WF6 and MoF6. In these ALD processes, the silane can abstract the fluorine atoms from the surface, forming volatile fluorosilanes, such as SiF4 and SiHF3, along with H2 and HF. For instance, the chemical reaction for the ALD of W from WF6 and Si2H6 were found to be [[38](#ijemacd88ebib38)]

![Equation (5)](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)![Equation (6)](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)

These reactions are highly exothermic, owing to the formation of the strong Si–F bonds. Simultaneously, the H2 gas is produced by the reductive elimination of the hydrogen atoms of the unstable intermediate metal hydrides, which are formed by the fluorine-transfer ligand-exchange reaction. The reductive elimination also affords the desired metal films, and further details of the reduction mechanism will be discussed in section [2.4](#ijemacd88es2-4).

Another type of the ligand-exchange mechanism is based on the exchange of the ligands between two metal precursors, which appears in the ALD of Cu and Co metals [[39](#ijemacd88ebib39), [40](#ijemacd88ebib40)]. As an example, Cu metal can be deposited from bis(dimethylamino-2-propoxy)copper(II) [Cu(dmap)2] and diethylzinc (DEZ). In this ALD process, the surface dmap groups from Cu(dmap)2 are displaced by the ethyls from DEZ via the ligand exchange reaction, forming volatile Zn(dmap)2. The afforded –Cu(C2H5) surface species are not stable and readily forms Cu metal and butane through the reductive elimination as the following:

![Equation (7)](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)![Equation (8)](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)

Notably, for all these ligand-exchange mechanisms, it is important that one of the exchanged products is sufficiently volatile to be liberated from the surface, as otherwise, nonideal issues would occur, as will be discussed later. Generally, the ligand-exchange mechanisms are essential for the majority of the ALD processes.

### 2.2. Dissociative or non-dissociative chemisorption

The chemisorption of the precursors can also follow a dissociative or non-dissociative mechanism. In the dissociative chemisorption scheme (figure [2](#ijemacd88ef2)(b)), the precursor molecule dissociates into two or more parts when it is chemisorbed on the surface,

![Equation (9)](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAQAAAC1HAwCAAAAC0lEQVR42mNkYAAAAAYAAjCB0C8AAAAASUVORK5CYII=)

This mechanism often occurs on the surfaces with catalytic activity. For instance, noble metals, such as Ru, have good catalytic nature, and therefore, the ALD processes to deposit Ru often involve the dissociative chemisorption of the ruthenium precursors [[41](#ijemacd88ebib41), [42](#ijemacd88ebib42)]. Similar processes were also observed on Ni [[43](#ijemacd88ebib43), [44](#ijemacd88ebib44)] and Cu [[45](#ijemacd88ebib45)] surfaces. The dissociative chemisorption can also occur on the SiO2 surface, where strained siloxane (Si–O–Si) bridges are present. --- SOURCE 3: Physical Vapor Deposition (PVD) | SemiFlows Blog ---
URL: https://semiflows.com/blog/what-is-physical-vapor-deposition-in-semiconductor-manufacturing

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This SemiFlows blog article by Joseph Swann provides a comprehensive overview of Physical Vapor Deposition (PVD) in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, covering its physics, processes, challenges, evolution across technology nodes, related processes, and future outlook.

**Definition & Fundamentals:** PVD is a high-vacuum thin-film deposition technique that uses physical methods (as opposed to chemical reactions in CVD) to produce constituent atoms that travel through a low-pressure gas phase and condense on a substrate. It encompasses two primary techniques: evaporation (heating a source until it vaporizes) and sputter deposition (bombarding a solid source with energetic plasma ions). Sputtering is the chief method for depositing aluminum, copper seeds, and other metals in modern manufacturing. PVD requires extremely low-pressure environments to enable transport without excessive scattering, and it avoids complex by-product contamination common in CVD.

**Physics & Mechanism:** Sputter deposition relies on momentum transfer. The chamber is evacuated, argon sputtering gas is admitted, and an interelectrode voltage ionizes the argon to create plasma. The negatively biased target causes positively charged argon ions to accelerate toward it, physically ejecting target atoms via billiard-ball-like collisions. Sputter yield (atoms ejected per incident ion) peaks at an angle less than 90 degrees—glancing angles reflect ions while perfectly normal angles push atoms deeper into the target. Ejected atoms follow an approximately cosine angular distribution.

**Process Principles:** Modern PVD systems primarily use DC magnetron sputtering, where a magnetic field confines electrons on a closed path near the target, creating a dense argon plasma at lower pressures. This enables high sputtering rates with lower applied potential, lower operating pressures, and less gas trapping in films. DC sputtering cannot deposit dielectric materials (charge buildup neutralizes cathode potential), requiring RF power supplies for insulating films. Reactive sputtering (e.g., titanium in nitrogen plasma to form TiN) combines sputtering with chemical reactions. Key process parameters—power, chamber pressure, gas flow ratios—govern mean free path, kinetic energy of arriving atoms, and film stress/density. Advantages include low operational cost, good film adhesion, and ability to deposit very high melting point materials.

**Challenges & Failure Modes:**
- Poor conformality: line-of-sight deposition causes shadowing effects in high-aspect-ratio structures, with overhang pinch-off before trench bottoms are filled
- Ion-induced surface damage: high-energy bombardment creates unwanted interfacial electronic states that degrade device mobility and reliability
- Target impurity/grain issues: e.g., PVD TiN films show small grains with (111) plane dominance, inducing higher interfacial oxidation and defect densities compared to ALD alternatives (relevant in ferroelectric memory with HfZrOx films)
- Adhesion/wetting failures: copper on improperly formed barriers exhibits 3D island growth rather than smooth wetting, causing adhesion failure during mechanical polishing

**Technology Node Evolution:** PVD was heavily used for all BEOL barrier layers (Ta/TaN) and copper seed layers at the 28nm planar node due to acceptable step coverage, high throughput, and material purity. However, at 14nm FinFET and 7nm FinFET nodes, extreme aspect-ratio vias made PVD unsuitable for continuous diffusion barriers due to shadowing. The industry transitioned to hybrid integration—using ALD for ultra-thin conformal barrier layers (like ALD TaN) while retaining specialized ionized PVD for copper seed layers requiring high purity and good wetting.

**Related Processes:** PVD is a critical precursor to electroplating (copper seed provides conductivity, followed by CMP). In FEOL, PVD deposits work-function tuning metals and barrier layers in high-k metal gate processes. PVD liners enable orthogonal metal line patterning at the same metal level. In advanced packaging, PVD sputtering universally deposits under bump metallurgy (UBM) layers with titanium/tantalum diffusion barriers and copper seeds for electroplated pillars.

**Future Outlook:** PVD is evolving toward highly ionized PVD (iPVD), which uses secondary RF coils to heavily ionize sputtered metal flux, enabling directional control via substrate biasing to defeat shadowing in deep trenches. Research is also exploring novel barrier materials like ruthenium and cobalt with superior copper wettability and lower size-effect resistivity than tantalum-based systems.
</summary>

Desirable barrier properties include: (1) good adhesion to Cu and dielectric; (2) immiscibility with Cu and high-temperature diffusion prevention; (3) good conductivity for direct ED of Cu; (4) simple ultra-thin uniform deposition.

--- SOURCE 15: Tungsten Metallization in Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing: Materials Physics, Deposition Mechanisms, and Integration Challenges | SemiFlows Blog ---
URL: https://semiflows.com/blog/what-is-tungsten-in-semiconductor-manufacturing

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from SemiFlows Blog provides a comprehensive technical overview of tungsten (W) metallization in advanced semiconductor manufacturing. Tungsten is a refractory metal primarily used to form contact plugs, local interconnects, and vias, serving as the critical conductive bridge between front-end-of-line (FEOL) active transistor structures and back-end-of-line (BEOL) multi-level wiring. It is selected for its high melting point, electromigration resistance, and excellent step coverage, while its low diffusivity in silicon dioxide and silicon substrates (compared to copper) prevents deep-level contamination.

**Physics & Mechanism**: Tungsten deposition typically uses tungsten hexafluoride (WF₆) as the gaseous precursor. Two main reduction pathways exist: silane (SiH₄) reduction for the nucleation phase (forming a thin continuous seed layer, reacting rapidly at lower temperatures), followed by hydrogen (H₂) reduction for bulk film growth. The hydrogen reduction reaction (WF₆ + 3H₂ → W + 6HF) is thermally driven and surface-catalyzed. Hot-wire assisted ALD (HWALD) uses atomic hydrogen for low-temperature, self-limiting deposition, though this competes with fluorine-based etching reactions. A diffusion barrier—typically TiN or a Ti/TiN bilayer—is required between tungsten and silicon to prevent silicide consumption and fluorine penetration. Ohmic contact behavior is achieved through heavy doping to narrow the Schottky barrier, enabling field emission tunneling.

**Process Principles**: Deposition temperature and chamber pressure are key parameters. Higher temperatures increase deposition rate (Arrhenius kinetics) but can cause rougher, non-conformal films; lower temperatures improve step coverage but reduce throughput. Tungsten crystallizes in two phases: the desired low-resistivity α-W (body-centered cubic) and the high-resistivity metastable β-W (A15 cubic), the latter stabilized by fluorine/oxygen impurities. High precursor purity and optimized H₂/WF₆ ratios are critical for α-W nucleation.

**Challenges & Failure Modes**: Key failure modes include: (1) Fluorine attack causing "volcano" defects—when WF₆ penetrates thin/discontinuous barriers and reacts with silicon or TiSi₂ to form volatile SiF₄ or TiF₄, creating voids that erupt during heating; (2) Grain boundary scattering—as contact dimensions shrink below 20nm, resistivity rises sharply due to electron scattering at surfaces/grain boundaries and fluorine impurities; (3) Loading effects during SF₆/Ar etchback—redeposition of tungsten or Ti-N-F byproducts causing incomplete clearing and electrical shorts; (4) High tensile stress leading to cracking, wafer warpage, or delamination.

**Technology Node Evolution**: At 28nm, contacts used TiSi₂ or CoSi₂ with Ti/TiN barrier + CVD W plug. At 14nm, ultra-thin ALD TiN barriers and NiSi silicide were adopted. At 7nm and beyond, the TiN barrier and nucleation layer occupied over half the contact volume, driving innovations including barrierless tungsten (selective CVD directly on silicide), alternative metals (cobalt, ruthenium with shorter electron mean free paths), and dual-metal stacked vias (e.g., Mo or W stacks on primary contact metal).

**Related Processes**: Upstream processes include ion implantation and rapid thermal annealing (RTA) for silicidation, and anisotropic contact hole etching. Downstream processes include tungsten CMP (using alumina/silica slurries with oxidizing agents) and BEOL copper dual damascene metallization.

**Future Outlook**: Trends include fully selective ALD/CVD for bottom-up tungsten growth without CMP, and renewed use of tungsten in high-temperature electronics such as GaN power devices (aluminum-free gate stacks and backend interconnects capable of operating beyond silicon thermal limits).
</summary>

<summary>
This webpage from Korvus Technology, a UK-based PVD (Physical Vapour Deposition) system manufacturer, provides a detailed comparison between evaporation and sputtering as the two primary PVD methods for thin film deposition.

**Key Content:**

**PVD Overview:** PVD deposits thin films of a source material onto a substrate inside a vacuum chamber using either thermal evaporation or magnetron sputtering. Sputtering is preferred for materials with very high melting points (as it doesn't rely on vaporisation temperature) and can produce compound films via reactive sputtering. E-beam evaporation offers higher deposition rates and excellent uniformity, popular in aerospace, tool manufacturing, and semiconductor industries.

**Evaporation Methods (3 types):**
1. **Resistive Thermal Evaporation** - target material heated in a boat/crucible via high current through a resistive coil (e.g., Korvus TES system)
2. **Electron Beam Evaporation** - electrons bombard and heat a target directly via thermionic emission (e.g., Korvus TAU E-Beam source)
3. **Low Temperature Thermal Evaporation** - combines resistive/e-beam evaporation with cooling for precise control via PID thermal feedback loop (e.g., Korvus ORCA system)

**Evaporation Pros:** Wide range of sources, high deposition rate, excellent uniformity with masks/planetary, good for high melting point materials (e-beam), high throughput, simple and cost-effective (thermal). **Cons:** Poor uniformity without planetary/masks, moderate complexity (e-beam).

**Sputtering Methods:** Magnetron sputtering (most scalable PVD process), ion beam sputtering (IBS), reactive sputtering, plasma sputtering. Used for semiconductor circuits, thin film transistors, anti-reflective glass coatings, and low-e architectural glass coatings.

**Sputtering Pros:** High deposition rate, high throughput, best uniformity (IBS), highest quality films (IBS), dense films with strong adhesion, ideal for optical/electrical applications. **Cons:** Poor deposition rate for dielectrics, high complexity and cost, substrate heating, low deposition rates for IBS.

**Selection Guidance:** Evaporation is more cost-effective, less complex, offers higher deposition rates for high-volume production. Sputtering offers better film quality, uniformity, and scalability at higher cost/complexity. Sputtering is better for thicker metallic/insulation coatings; resistive thermal evaporation suits thinner films with lower melting temperatures; e-beam evaporation suits improved step coverage and wide material selection.

--- SOURCE 2: E-Beam Evaporation vs. Sputter Deposition ---
URL: https://roguevalleymicrodevices.com/e-beam-evaporation-vs-sputter-deposition

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Rogue Valley Microdevices (a pure play MEMS foundry) is a technical guide comparing electron beam (e-beam) evaporation and sputter deposition for MEMS metallization—the two primary physical vapor deposition (PVD) methods used in MEMS fabrication, sensor manufacturing, and semiconductor wafer processing.

**How Each Method Works:**
- **E-beam evaporation:** A focused electron beam heats a small spot on a source material in a water-cooled crucible within a high-vacuum chamber, causing thermal evaporation. The vapor travels in a straight line (line of sight) to the wafer, producing high-purity films and enabling multiple materials to be evaporated in sequence via multiple source pockets without breaking vacuum.
- **Sputter deposition:** A target material is bombarded with energetic argon ions generated in a plasma (at low pressure). Momentum transfer ejects atoms that arrive at the wafer from many directions due to collisions with process gas, producing dense, well-adhered, conformal films. DC power is used for conductive targets; RF power for insulating targets.

**Key Differences:**
- **Step coverage:** Evaporation provides poor step coverage (directional flux); sputtering provides good step coverage (omnidirectional flux).
- **Lift-off compatibility:** Evaporation is excellent for lift-off (sidewalls stay uncoated); sputtering is poor for lift-off (coats sidewalls).
- **Alloy fidelity:** Evaporation struggles with alloys due to differing vapor pressures; sputtering preserves target composition faithfully.
- **Adhesion and density:** Sputtered films are denser and adhere better (high-energy arrival, plus in situ RF etch); evaporated films often need a thin adhesion layer.
- **Deposition rate:** Evaporation offers generally higher rates, useful for thick films.
- **Film purity:** Evaporation yields very high purity; sputtered films are high purity.
- **Substrate heating:** Evaporation causes low heating; sputtering causes higher heating.

**Rogue Valley Microdevices Capabilities:** E-beam evaporation with up to six in-situ materials, PVD sputter on 50.8mm–300mm substrates with in-situ RF etch and optional HF dip for aluminum films, precious metals (gold, platinum, silver, copper), Au/Sn multilayer solder stacks, reactively sputtered dielectrics, and metal anneal services.

**Selection Workflow:** (1) Lift-off patterning → e-beam evaporation; (2) Conformal step coverage → sputter; (3) Alloy/compound composition fidelity → sputter; (4) Precious/refractory metals, multilayer stacks, thick high-purity films → e-beam evaporation; (5) Many successful flows use both methods at different steps.

**Typical applications:** E-beam for lift-off metallization, precious metal contacts, multilayer stacks, thick high-purity films, optical coatings, refractory metals. Sputtering for alloy films (aluminum alloys, TiW), adhesion/barrier layers, conformal coatings, reactively sputtered dielectrics, interconnect metallization, and large-diameter wafers.
</summary>

URL: https://www.aemdeposition.com/blog/thin-film-deposition-methods.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an informational blog article from AEM Deposition (a Chinese manufacturer of thin film deposition materials, based in Changsha, Hunan Province) explaining thin film deposition methods, specifically focusing on Physical Vapor Deposition (PVD), sputtering, and evaporation. The article was published/updated on 2025-08-08.

KEY CONTENT:

**Thin Film Deposition Basics:** Thin film deposition adds a very thin layer (a few nanometers to a few micrometers) onto a substrate surface, changing surface properties while preserving the base material's structure. Applications include semiconductors, camera lenses, solar panels, medical implants, and aerospace components.

**Physical Vapor Deposition (PVD):** The core technique that vaporizes solid material inside a vacuum chamber and condenses it onto the substrate. Advantages include cleaner films (due to vacuum), strong adhesion, and compatibility with metals, alloys, and ceramics. The two main sub-methods are sputtering and evaporation.

**Sputtering:** Uses energetic ions (typically from argon plasma) to knock atoms off a solid sputtering target, which then deposit onto the substrate. Advantages: works with metals, alloys, and ceramics; produces dense, high-quality films with strong adhesion; precise control over thickness and composition; suitable for R&D and industrial production. Applications: semiconductor manufacturing, optical coatings, transparent conductive layers in displays/solar cells, protective coatings. Types include DC sputtering, RF sputtering, and magnetron sputtering.

**Evaporation:** Heats specially prepared evaporation materials until they vaporize and condense on the substrate. Two main heating methods: thermal evaporation (resistive heating element like tungsten filament or boat) and electron beam (e-beam) evaporation (focused high-energy electron beam, allows high-melting-point metals). Advantages: high deposition rates, simpler equipment, cost-effective for certain metals. Limitations: best for materials that vaporize cleanly; coatings are line-of-sight (limited coverage on complex geometries); film density often lower than sputtered films.

**Sputtering vs. Evaporation Comparison Table:**
- Sputtering: solid target, ion bombardment, moderate deposition rate, dense/uniform films, metals/alloys/ceramics, excellent coverage on complex shapes, higher equipment cost.
- Evaporation: solid evaporation materials, thermal vaporization, high deposition rate, less dense (possible columnar structure), best for cleanly vaporizing metals, line-of-sight coverage, generally lower equipment cost.

**Selection Guidance:** Choose sputtering for high-density uniform coatings or complex geometries; choose evaporation for faster deposition rates, simpler equipment, or cleanly vaporizing metals. Key factors: material type, coating requirements, substrate shape, production scale, and budget. Expert tip emphasizes partnering with a reliable supplier for high-purity sputtering targets and evaporation materials.

--- SOURCE 10: Molecular-beam epitaxy - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular-beam_epitaxy

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE) is an epitaxy method for thin-film deposition of single crystals, widely used in the manufacture of semiconductor devices including transistors, diodes, and MOSFETs at microwave frequencies, as well as lasers used to read optical discs (CDs and DVDs).

**History:** The original ideas of the MBE process were first established by K. G. Günther (1958), though his films were not epitaxial (deposited on glass). The process was first demonstrated for epitaxial growth by John Davey and Titus Pankey, who grew GaAs films on single-crystal GaAs substrates. Major development was enabled by J.R. Arthur's investigations of growth kinetics and Alfred Y. Cho's in situ observation of the MBE process using reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) in the late 1960s.

**Method:** MBE takes place in high or ultra-high vacuum (10⁻⁸–10⁻¹² Torr). Key features include:
- Deposition rates typically less than 3,000 nm per hour, allowing films to grow epitaxially
- The absence of carrier gases and ultra-high vacuum result in the highest achievable film purity
- In solid-source MBE, elements like gallium and arsenic are heated in quasi-Knudsen effusion cells or electron-beam evaporators until they sublime; gaseous elements then condense on the wafer and may react (e.g., forming single-crystal gallium arsenide)
- RHEED is used to monitor crystal growth during operation
- Computer-controlled shutters allow precise layer thickness control, down to a single layer of atoms
- Ultra-high vacuum maintained by cryopumps and cryopanels chilled with liquid nitrogen (~77 K) in systems requiring cooled substrates; other systems use rotating platters heated to several hundred degrees Celsius
- Also used for organic semiconductors (molecules rather than atoms evaporated), with variations like gas-source MBE resembling chemical vapor deposition
- Systems can be modified with oxygen sources for depositing oxide materials for advanced electronic, magnetic, and optical applications

**Quantum nanostructures:** MBE enables atomically flat and abrupt hetero-interfaces, allowing construction of nanowires and quantum structures for information processing, quantum communication/computing, and monolithical integration on silicon. Heterostructure nanowire lasers built using advanced MBE techniques enable picosecond signal processing.

**Asaro–Tiller–Grinfeld (ATG) instability:** An elastic instability encountered during MBE where lattice mismatch between growing film and substrate accumulates elastic energy. At a critical height, the film breaks into isolated islands to relax lateral tension. Critical height depends on Young's modulus, mismatch size, and surface tension. Applications include self-assembly of quantum dots; also known as Stranski–Krastanov growth.

**Notable figures and related topics:** Key people include Colin P. Flynn, Arthur Gossard, Herbert Kroemer, and Ben G. Streetman. Related technical topics include HEMT, heterojunction bipolar transistors, pulsed laser deposition, metalorganic vapour phase epitaxy, quantum cascade lasers, solar cells, thermal laser epitaxy, and wetting layers.
</summary>

"Molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE) is an epitaxy method for thin-film deposition of single crystals. MBE is widely used in the manufacture of semiconductor devices, including transistors."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, part of a 3-issue series on 3D packaging technologies from Oerlikon Balzers Ltd., describes an integrated deep silicon etch (DSE) and advanced directional sputtering (PVD) process for achieving high aspect ratio (AR) through-silicon vias (TSVs) up to 30:1. The driving force is that many proposed interconnect structures require ARs greater than 10:1, which exceeds the current reliable fill limit of 5:1–10:1 using conventional PVD techniques.

The DSE process uses a time division multiplexed (TDM) Bosch process with alternating SF6 etch steps and C4F8 polymer deposition steps to create vertical via profiles. Scallop (sidewall roughness) is minimized by reducing etch step duration to 0.5–1.0 seconds, achieved through optimized system design including fast gas switching, proprietary throttle valve pressure control algorithms, and RF matching networks using fixed capacitors with frequency variation. This yields etch rates of 8–10 µm/min for larger features while maintaining good sidewall smoothness.

Advanced directional sputtering (ADS) uses a large target-to-substrate distance (~1.5× substrate diameter) plus RF bias to achieve perpendicular deposition and good step coverage. This approach provides 15% bottom coverage for Ti and 10% for Cu in 8:1 AR trenches, suitable for current TSV applications like flash memory, DRAM, and image sensors.

To extend capabilities further, a high power pulsed magnetron sputtering (HPPMS) technology called "highly ionized sputtering" (HIS) was developed. It uses short (<0.2ms) high-current pulses (several hundred to >1000A) to achieve >90% ionization of Ti near the target surface. HIS operates at small TSD (30–80mm) and pressures <1Pa, unlike conventional ionized PVD. The Ti process achieves up to 20% bottom coverage in 10:1 AR trenches at 26 Å/s deposition rate, and Ta deposition was demonstrated at 30:1 AR with substantial bottom and lower sidewall coverage, including in the shadow of DSE scallops. These processes extend the limits of PVD + electroplated Cu metallization schemes for 3D packaging.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 12: Electron Beam Evaporation: For High-Melting-Point Materials ---
URL: https://www.samaterials.com/content/electron-beam-evaporation.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an article from Stanford Advanced Materials (samaterials.com) as part of their "PVD Basics" series, explaining Electron Beam Evaporation (e-beam evaporation), a physical vapor deposition (PVD) technique used for depositing high-melting-point materials.

**How It Works:**
- A focused beam of high-energy electrons (5-10 kV, generated by a tungsten or tantalum filament) heats and evaporates a target material called the "evaporant," which sits in a water-cooled copper crucible.
- Magnetic steering coils bend and direct the electron beam across the evaporant surface to control evaporation rate and uniformity.
- The vapor travels through a vacuum chamber (typically 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁷ Torr) and condenses onto the substrate.
- The electron beam can be focused to a spot of just a few millimeters, producing extremely high power density, allowing melting of virtually any material regardless of melting point.

**Key Advantage - Water Cooling:**
Unlike thermal evaporation where the entire crucible heats up (causing contamination), in e-beam evaporation only the spot where the beam hits gets hot. The evaporant forms a "self-crucible"—a molten pool surrounded by solid material of the same composition—eliminating container contamination. This allows evaporation of reactive materials (e.g., aluminum, which reacts with tungsten crucibles) and ultra-high-purity materials.

**Materials That Can Be E-Beam Evaporated (with melting points):**
- Platinum (1,768°C) - electrodes, Schottky contacts
- Gold (1,064°C) - electrical contacts, corrosion protection
- Aluminum (660°C) - semiconductor interconnects, mirrors
- Copper (1,085°C) - chip wiring
- Titanium (1,668°C) - adhesion layers, biomedical
- Tantalum (3,017°C) - diffusion barriers, capacitors
- Tungsten (3,422°C) - X-ray targets, high-temperature electrodes
- Molybdenum (2,623°C) - electrodes, solar cells
- Silicon (1,414°C) - thin-film transistors
- SiO₂ (1,710°C) - optical coatings, insulators
- TiO₂ (1,843°C) - optical coatings, photocatalysts
- ITO (~1,800°C) - transparent conductive films

**Advantages:**
1. Handles high-melting-point materials (tungsten, tantalum, platinum, ceramics) that thermal evaporation cannot process.
2. High purity due to elimination of crucible contamination.
3. High deposition rates (hundreds of nanometers per minute), much faster than sputtering for many materials.
4. Low film stress compared to sputtered films—important for precision optics and thin membranes.
5. No substrate damage (mostly) since there is no plasma involved.

The page also notes that if a material cannot be melted (some ceramics decompose before melting), e-beam evaporation may still work through sublimation. The broader site navigation shows Stanford Advanced Materials offers a wide range of materials, products (metals, ceramics, compounds, opticals, magnets, sputtering targets, lab equipment), and services across multiple industries and global regions.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a PhD dissertation by Jun Feng, submitted to Harvard University's Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology in June 2017, under the advisorship of Professor Roy G. Gordon. The dissertation focuses on advanced metallization processes for complex structures in microelectronics using Direct-Liquid-Evaporation Chemical Vapor Deposition (DLE-CVD).

**Key Topics Covered:**

1. **Background (Chapter 1):** The dissertation addresses challenges in modern microelectronics as devices scale below 10nm, requiring 3D architectures and flexible electronics. Key challenges include copper interconnect diffusion barriers (Ta, TaN, TiN, WN, MnNx, CoNx), silicide contacts (NiSi, CoSi2, TiSi2, PtSi), and tungsten plug replacement by cobalt. The chapter compares PVD vs. CVD methods, explaining that CVD offers conformal coating capabilities essential for high-aspect-ratio structures, while PVD lacks conformality.

2. **DLE-CVD Technology:** Unlike conventional CVD with bubbler sources, DLE-CVD stores liquid precursor solutions unheated and injects them directly into a heated evaporation region. This avoids precursor decomposition, provides stable and controllable delivery rates via liquid mass flow controllers, and enables higher gas-phase precursor concentrations for superior conformality. Precursors are metalorganic compounds with acetamidinate ligands dissolved in solvents like tetradecane and trihexylamine. Co, Ni, and Cu depositions use vaporization at 150°C under 5-30 Torr vacuum, with chamber temperatures of 180-280°C.

3. **Self-Smoothing Al-Catalyzed SiO2 ALD (Chapter 2):** The dissertation details a process to fabricate high-aspect-ratio trench structures via Bosch-type RIE and an Al-catalyzed SiO2 ALD process that exhibits a self-smoothing effect. The Al-SiO2 process deposits >1 nm/cycle (vs. ~0.1 nm/cycle for conventional ALD) and reduced surface roughness 68% (from ~47nm to ~15nm) on zig-zag patterned substrates. Two mechanisms are proposed: "concave filling" (SiO2 chains crosslink at valley bottoms, filling depressions) and "convex collapsing" (chains on convex surfaces lack support and collapse). Optimized RIE conditions include 700 uC/cm2 e-beam dosage, 500nm 950PMMA C4 resist, 10°C temperature, and 75-140W platen power, achieving 25:1 and 10:1 aspect ratio trenches.

4. **DLE-CVD Cobalt for Cu Interconnect Encapsulation (Chapter 3):** The dissertation describes deposition of highly conformal, pure, smooth nanocrystalline Co films and demonstrates all-around encapsulation of nano-scale copper interconnects by DLE-CVD Co as an effective strategy for enhancing interconnect reliability, stability, and operation life.

5. **Atom Probe Tomography Studies (Chapter 4):** APT is used to acquire compositional and structural information of DLE-CVD-deposited metals (Co, Ni, NiSi) at atomic resolution, including samples from deep inside high-aspect-ratio trenches.

6. **Polymer Fiber Metallization (Chapter 5):** DLE-CVD Co is explored as an initial metallization layer on Kevlar polymer fibers for creating conductive flexible interconnects. CVD is identified as the most promising method for conformal coating of fiber bundles compared to PVD and DVD methods. DLE-CVD overcomes traditional CVD limitations (high temperature requirements and inadequate step coverage at aspect ratios >10:1), and electroplating on DLE-CVD Co-seeded Kevlar fibers is demonstrated.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 14: Electron-Beam Evaporation - an overview ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/electron-beam-evaporation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from ScienceDirect provides a comprehensive overview of Electron-Beam Evaporation (EBE), a physical vapor deposition (PVD) technique used in engineering applications. The AI-generated definition states that EBE involves accelerated electrons bombarding a target surface in a high-vacuum environment to evaporate and deposit coating material onto a substrate, achieving temperatures of 3000–6000 °C with energy densities over 100 W/cm². It is commonly used for depositing high-melting-point alloys or oxides.

KEY TECHNICAL DETAILS:
- EBE is a PVD method where an electron gun generates high-speed electrons using electric and magnetic fields to bombard a target source (usually a metal or oxide) in a vacuum chamber
- Electrons emitted from a heated tungsten filament are accelerated (up to 100 kV) and focused onto the target material in a water-cooled crucible
- Kinetic energy of electrons converts to thermal energy, causing evaporation of the target material which deposits onto a substrate as a thin film
- Working distance between source and substrate typically ranges from 300 mm to 1 m, with thermal energy below 1 eV for coating
- Deposition rates are 2-3 orders of magnitude higher than sputtering: compounds can be deposited at ~100 nm/s, metals at ~1 µm/s
- EBE can heat target materials up to 6000°C, making it suitable for high-melting-point materials

APPLICATIONS:
- Thin film deposition for solar cells (dye-sensitized, perovskite, CZTS-based photovoltaic devices)
- Gate dielectric deposition (e.g., Sm2O3 thin films on Si substrates for MOS devices)
- Protective coating on porous metal supports for solid oxide cells
- Synthesis of 2D and 3D nanoparticle assemblies, carbon nanotubes, and graphene layers
- Silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries (graphene/Si multilayer structures)
- High barrier plastics using nanoscale inorganic films (SiO, SiO_x, Al2O3)

ADVANTAGES:
- Higher deposition rates than sputtering and thermal evaporation
- High purity films (crucible materials practically excluded from evaporation)
- Suitable for high-melting-point materials and high-density films
- Better surface morphology, phase matching, and optical performance vs. other methods
- Lower contamination than thermal evaporation (only source material is heated, not the whole crucible)

DISADVANTAGES:
- Secondary electrons may ionize residual gas molecules, causing contamination
- Compounds may decompose when bombarded by high-energy electrons, affecting final film composition
- Short filament lifetime, deposition non-uniformity, and spatter
- Thickness control less precise than sputtering systems
- Preferential evaporation of multi-component precursors with different melting points can affect film composition

PROCESS PARAMETERS affecting film properties include chamber pressure, deposition rate, substrate temperature, powder particle size, and applied bias voltage. Increasing substrate temperature decreases porosity and enhances density; increasing electron gun power raises film thickness and crystallite size.

SPECIFIC RESEARCH EXAMPLES from the page:
- TiO2 passivation layers via EBE achieved 4.93% PCE in dye-sensitized solar cells
- CZTS photovoltaic devices fabricated via EBE achieved efficiencies up to 5.43%
- SiO coatings by electron-beam reactive evaporation showed 10-60 fold reductions in oxygen permeation rates
- 3D aligned CNT/Si hybrid anodes achieved 93% capacity retention after 100 cycles and 1055 mAh/g after 1000 cycles at 5 A/g with 99.7% Coulombic efficiency
- Graphene/Si multilayer structures showed >1600 mAh/g discharge capacity at 100 mA/g over 30 cycles

Related terms include Physical Vapor Deposition, Chemical Vapor Deposition, Thin Films, Nanoparticles, Carbon Nanotubes, Magnetron, and Pulsed Laser deposition. Recommended publications include Thin Solid Films, Journal of Alloys and Compounds, Microelectronic Engineering, and Optical Materials.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: Atomic Layer Deposition in Semiconductors: How It Works ---
URL: https://eureka.patsnap.com/blog/material-tech-resources/what-is-atomic-layer-deposition-technology

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Patsnap Eureka blog explains Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) in semiconductors — a critical vapor-phase thin-film deposition technique that deposits materials one atomic layer at a time. ALD is a specialized form of Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD) offering superior control over film thickness, uniformity, and conformality.

**How ALD Works (5-step process):**
1. Precursor A exposure (e.g., metal-containing compound) forms a monolayer, saturating reactive sites on the substrate
2. Purge with inert gas (nitrogen/argon) to remove excess precursor and byproducts
3. Precursor B exposure (e.g., water or ozone) reacts with the chemisorbed layer to form a stable material layer
4. Second purge step
5. Repeat cycle — each cycle deposits approximately 0.1–0.2 nanometers; hundreds to thousands of cycles control total film thickness

**Key characteristics of ALD films:** atomic-level thickness control, excellent uniformity over large wafers, superior conformality on 3D structures, dense and pinhole-free layers, and low-temperature processing capability.

**ALD vs CVD comparison:** ALD uses sequential, self-limiting surface reactions for atomic-precision control and excellent conformality on high-aspect-ratio structures, but has slower deposition rates. CVD introduces all reactants simultaneously for continuous film growth, offering higher deposition rates but less thickness control and conformality. CVD is better suited for bulk films and simple geometries.

**Semiconductor applications of ALD:**
- Gate dielectrics (high-k materials like HfO₂ replacing SiO₂)
- 3D NAND flash memory (uniform coatings in deep trenches)
- FinFET and GAAFET transistors (coating non-planar surfaces)
- Hard mask layers (etch-resistant layers for lithography)
- Barrier and encapsulation layers (preventing metal diffusion/moisture)

**Common materials deposited:** metal oxides (Al₂O₃, HfO₂, TiO₂, ZnO), metal nitrides (TiN, TaN), metals (Pt, Ru, Co), dielectrics (SiO₂, Si₃N₄), and conductors (W, Mo, Cu — emerging).

**Challenges:** slow deposition rates, higher production costs than CVD, complex precursor chemistry, need for highly pure precursors, and equipment cost/throughput limitations. Innovations like spatial ALD and plasma-enhanced ALD are addressing these issues.

**Future trends:** ALD for sub-5nm/3nm logic nodes, advanced DRAM and NAND scaling, integration with EUV lithography, new precursor development, ALD for 2D materials, and hybrid ALD-CVD processes.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 12: Atomic layer deposition ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_layer_deposition

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) - Wikipedia Article Summary

### Overview
Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is a thin-film deposition technique based on the sequential use of a gas-phase chemical process, classified as a subclass of chemical vapour deposition (CVD). Most ALD reactions use two chemicals called precursors (or "reactants") that react with a material's surface one at a time in a sequential, self-limiting manner. ALD is a key process in fabricating semiconductor devices and part of the toolset for synthesizing nanomaterials.

### Core Principles
- ALD grows films on a substrate by exposing its surface to alternate gaseous precursors in sequential, non-overlapping pulses (unlike CVD where precursors are present simultaneously).
- Each precursor reacts with the surface in a self-limiting way, terminating once all available surface sites are consumed.
- Growth is described in terms of "growth per cycle" rather than growth rate.
- The dose-purge-dose-purge sequence constitutes an ALD cycle; saturation depends on precursor pressure and sticking probability (R_abs = S × F, where S is sticking probability and F is incident molar flux).

### History
- **1960s (Soviet Union):** Stanislav Koltsov and Valentin Aleskovsky experimentally developed ALD principles at Leningrad Technological Institute (LTI), based on Aleskovsky's 1952 "framework hypothesis." They named the technique "Molecular Layering" (ML) in 1965.
- **1974 (Finland):** Tuomo Suntola independently devised ALD (initially called "atomic layer epitaxy" or ALE) at Instrumentarium Oy for thin-film electroluminescent (TFEL) displays. First experiments grew ZnS using elemental Zn and S. A breakthrough came with switching from high-vacuum to inert gas reactors, enabling compound reactants like metal chlorides, H2S, and water vapor.
- **1983:** First large-scale ALE-EL displays installed at Helsinki-Vantaa airport flight information boards.
- **1987:** Suntola began developing ALE for photovoltaic and catalyst applications at Microchemistry Ltd. (owned by Neste Oy).
- **1999:** Microchemistry Ltd. was sold to ASM International (Dutch), becoming ASM Microchemistry Oy — the only commercial ALD-reactor manufacturer in the 1990s.
- **2000s:** Beneq Oy and Picosun Oy emerged in Finland. In 2000, Gurtej Singh Sandhu and Trung T. Doan of Micron Technology developed ALD high-κ films for DRAM (starting at 90-nm node). Intel used ALD for high-κ gate dielectric in its 45 nm CMOS technology.
- **2004 & 2018:** Suntola received the European SEMI award (2004) and the Millennium Technology Prize (2018).
- **2009:** Sequential infiltration synthesis (SIS) / vapor phase infiltration (VPI) first reported by Max-Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics researchers.
- The name "atomic layer deposition" was first proposed by Markku Leskelä at the ALE-1 conference (Espoo, Finland, 1990). The Virtual Project on the History of ALD (VPHA) was established in 2013 to document the independent discoveries (ALE in Finland, ML in Soviet Union).

### Surface Reaction Mechanisms
- **Thermal ALD:** Operates at room temperature (~20°C) to 350°C. Best-known example: Al2O3 from trimethylaluminum (TMA) and water. TMA dissociatively chemisorbs, leaving AlCH3 on the surface; H2O reacts with –CH3 forming CH4 and a hydroxylated Al2O3 surface.
- **Plasma ALD (PA-ALD):** Uses high-reactivity plasma species to reduce deposition temperature without compromising film quality; enables wider range of precursors and materials, with better thickness control and uniformity.
- **Spatial ALD (s-ALD):** Precursors separated in space (not time) via gas curtains; suitable for high-volume and roll-to-roll production. Deposition rate for Al2O3 increases from 100–300 nm/hour to 60 nm/minute.
- **Photo-assisted ALD:** Uses UV light to accelerate surface reactions, reducing reaction temperature; weaker activation than plasma but easier to control.
- **Metal ALD:** Copper ALD is of interest for interconnects (best performed ≤100°C to avoid agglomeration). Metals like tungsten and molybdenum can be deposited via fluorosilane elimination (e.g., WF6 + Si2H6 → W + SiF3H + 2H2, ∆H = –181 kcal). Novel strong reducing agents enabled low-temperature ALD of electropositive metals (Cr, Ti, Sn, Al).
- **Catalytic SiO2 ALD:** Requires Lewis base catalysts (NH3, pyridine) to enable practical SiO2 deposition; without catalysts, temperatures must exceed 325°C and pressures exceed 10³ torr. Optimal temperature is 32°C with a common deposition rate of 1.35 Å per binary reaction sequence.

### Applications
- **Microelectronics:** Gate oxides, transition-metal nitrides, metal films, magnetic recording heads, DRAM capacitors (high-κ dielectric layers).
- **Photovoltaics:** Passivation layers in silicon solar cells.
- **Electro-optic:** Thin film couplers.
- **Biomedical:** Various applications.
- **Permeation barriers for plastics:** Moisture barrier coatings.
- **Quality control:** Process control mechanisms for film quality.

### Advantages
- Atomic-level thickness and composition control.
- Highly conformal films on arbitrarily complex and large substrates.
- Wide range of materials (oxides, metals, nitrides, sulfides, chalcogenides, fluorides) — hundreds of published processes with an interactive community database and annotated periodic table available.

### Disadvantages
- **Economic viability:** Slower process compared to other deposition methods.
- **Reaction time:** Sequential pulses and purge steps limit throughput.

The authors are affiliated with Peking University Shenzhen Graduate School and Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. The article has a DOI of 10.1088/2631-7990/acd88e and received 15,389 total downloads.

The review focuses on the chemistry of atomic layer deposition (ALD), a critical thin-film technology in modern microelectronics. ALD is characterized by self-limited layer-by-layer growth that enables deposition of highly uniform, conformal, pinhole-free thin films with angstrom-level thickness control, particularly on 3D topologies.
