URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12541-025-01337-z

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review paper published in the International Journal of Precision Engineering and Manufacturing (Volume 26, pages 2551–2571, published 15 September 2025) titled "Novel Atomic Layer Processes for Semiconductor Manufacturing: Area Selective Deposition, Atomic Layer Annealing, and Atomic Layer Etching." Authors include Sangwon Lee, Gyuha Lee, Jeongmin Oh, and Jihwan An (ORCID: 0000-0002-7697-9935). The open-access article has 11k accesses and 17 citations.

The review addresses fundamental limitations of conventional deposition, lithography, and etching techniques at sub-10 nm scales in semiconductor manufacturing, driven by device miniaturization and complex 3D integration. It examines three emerging atomic layer processes:

1. **Area-Selective Deposition (ASD)**: Utilizes intrinsic differences in substrate surface reactivity or chemically engineered surface inhibitors (such as self-assembled monolayers/SAMs or small molecular inhibitors/SMIs) to achieve self-aligned, bottom-up patterning with high selectivity. The review categorizes AS-ALD approaches into four mechanisms: intrinsic material selectivity (e.g., HZO growth promoted on catalytic Pt/Ru surfaces but not SiO2; selective nucleation on MoSe2 vs MoS2 in 2D lateral superlattices), reaction inhibitors (SAMs like octadecylphosphonic acid, and SMIs that block precursor adsorption on non-growth areas), surface pretreatment, and process engineering.

2. **Atomic Layer Annealing (ALA)**: Incorporates localized, cycle-by-cycle plasma-mediated thermal treatments into ALD sequences, enabling sub-nanometer dopant activation or crystallization at significantly reduced thermal budgets, preserving thermally sensitive underlying device structures while achieving desired electrical and structural properties.

3. **Atomic Layer Etching (ALE)**: Separates etching into self-limiting surface functionalization and selective removal steps, allowing Å-level etch depth control with minimal substrate damage, even in high-aspect-ratio features. Plasma-enhanced ALE (PE-ALE) is positioned to meet stringent requirements of next-generation transistor designs including GAA transistors.

Key context: The semiconductor industry has progressed from planar FETs to FinFETs (22-nm node) to gate-all-around (GAA) architectures below 5 nm, and is entering the 2-nm era (TSMC's 2-nm nanosheet GAA process and Intel's ribbon-style GAA FET at 3 nm silicon thickness, both unveiled at 2024 IEDM). Conventional CVD/PVD struggle with high-aspect-ratio conformality; EUV lithography faces shot noise and random defect challenges; RIE lacks atomic-level control in HAR structures.

The review details ALD fundamentals (sequential, self-limiting surface reactions with four steps: precursor pulse, purge, reactant pulse, purge; typical growth-per-cycle of 0.05–0.1 nm/cycle; advantages including precise thickness control, extreme conformality, and material versatility; limitations including slow process times, narrow temperature windows below ~350°C, and high costs).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"ASD utilizes either intrinsic differences in substrate surface reactivity or chemically engineered surface inhibitors to achieve self-aligned, bottom-up patterning with high selectivity." "ALA utilizes cycle-by-cycle, plasma-mediated ion interactions to enable localized crystallization and dopant activation at significantly reduced thermal budgets, thereby preserving underlying device structures while delivering the desired electrical and structural properties." "ALE separates the etching process into self-limiting surface functionalization and selective removal steps, allowing Å-level etch depth control with minimal substrate damage, even in high-aspect-ratio features." "These innovations are not merely incremental improvements; they are essential enablers for sustaining Moore's Law and realizing the next generation of electronic technologies." "Each cycle deposits approximately one atomic layer of material... The typical growth-per-cycle (GPC) varies depending on the precursor chemistry, but generally ranges from 0.05 to 0.1 nm per cycle for most oxides and nitrides."

--- SOURCE 14: Atomic layer deposition of thin films: from a chemistry perspective - IOPscience ---
URL: https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/2631-7990/acd88e

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article titled "Atomic layer deposition of thin films: from a chemistry perspective" published in the International Journal of Extreme Manufacturing (Volume 5, Number 3) on June 14, 2023, by Jinxiong Li, Gaoda Chai, and Xinwei Wang. The authors are affiliated with Peking University Shenzhen Graduate School and Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. The article has a DOI of 10.1088/2631-7990/acd88e and received 15,389 total downloads.

The review focuses on the chemistry of atomic layer deposition (ALD), a critical thin-film technology in modern microelectronics. ALD is characterized by self-limited layer-by-layer growth that enables deposition of highly uniform, conformal, pinhole-free thin films with angstrom-level thickness control, particularly on 3D topologies.

Key content covered in the article:
1. Introduction: ALD has become essential for fabricating advanced microelectronic devices including FinFETs and gate-all-around (GAA) FETs, high-k gate dielectrics, DRAM capacitor dielectrics, spacers for self-aligned multi-patterning, and BEOL-compatible oxide-based transistors.

2. Surface Chemistry of ALD: A typical ALD cycle consists of four steps: (I) dosing precursor A to react with surface functional groups (self-limiting reaction producing volatile byproducts), (II) purging with inert gas, (III) dosing precursor B to react with newly formed functional groups, and (IV) purging again. The self-limiting nature of the gas-solid reactions is key; insufficient precursor exposure leads to unsaturated chemisorption which can be exploited for depositing multi-element compounds. The ALD window is the temperature range where surface reactions remain self-limiting.

The surface chemistry mechanisms are classified into four categories:
- Ligand-exchange mechanism (most common): Includes proton-transfer (e.g., Al2O3 ALD from trimethylaluminum and H2O), halogen transfer (e.g., W and Mo ALD from WF6/MoF6 with Si2H6), and ligand exchange between two metal precursors (e.g., Cu deposition from Cu(dmap)2 and diethylzinc).
- Dissociative chemisorption: Precursor dissociates into parts upon chemisorption, often occurring on catalytic surfaces like Ru, Ni, and Cu, and on SiO2 surfaces with strained siloxane bridges.
- Non-dissociative chemisorption.
- Oxidation and reduction mechanisms.

Key highlights of the paper include: reviewing surface chemistry of gas-solid ALD reactions with detailed discussion of growth mechanisms; reviewing ALD precursor chemistry with comparative discussion of commonly used precursors; presenting newly-emerged applications of ALD in microelectronics; and outlining future perspectives of ALD technology.
</summary>

"The unique self-limited layer-by-layer growth feature of ALD has outstood this technology to deposit highly uniform conformal pinhole-free thin films with angstrom-level thickness control, particularly on 3D topologies."

- Tungsten-based ALD, pioneered by Lam, has been the predominant metallization technique for over two decades, but chipmakers need to shift beyond tungsten for future NAND, DRAM, and logic scaling.

--- SOURCE 7: Metallization: Copper Damascene, Cobalt & Ruthenium Interconnects | SemiconductorX ---
URL: https://semiconductorx.com/mfg-front-end-metallization.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage covers wafer metallization in semiconductor manufacturing, the process that builds the interconnect network wiring billions of transistors into functional circuits. It forms local contacts (middle-of-line, MOL) from transistor source, drain, and gate to the first interconnect layer, then builds multiple metal levels (back-end-of-line, BEOL) for routing signals and power. A leading-edge logic chip has 10-15+ metal layers, each patterned, etched, filled, and planarized before the next.

The metallization equipment market is spread across four vendors: Applied Materials (leading in PVD, ALD barriers, electroplating, and CMP), EBARA (primary CMP alternative), Lam Research (metal etch and deposition integration), and Tokyo Electron (BEOL etch, deposition, cleaning). Consumables concentration is deeper: copper electroplating chemistry concentrates at Dow/DuPont, BASF, and Atotech (now part of MKS Instruments); specialty metal precursors for cobalt and ruthenium ALD come from an even narrower supplier base (Entegris, Merck/EMD, UP Chemical, Adeka, DNF); sputtering targets concentrate at JX Advanced Metals, Materion, and Honeywell.

The dominant integration approach is damascene processing (dual damascene etches via and trench in one cycle, filling both together). Each metal layer follows a cycle: dielectric deposition, via/trench patterning, barrier/liner deposition (TaN, TiN, Ru, Co via ALD/PVD), copper seed layer, electroplating fill, CMP planarization, and cap layer deposition.

Interconnect metals have transitioned through generations: Aluminum (legacy, displaced below 250nm, still used in mature-node/power/analog ICs and bond pads), Tungsten (MOL contacts, still extensively used), Copper (industry standard for BEOL since ~180nm, now approaching scaling limits), Cobalt (adopted from 10nm onward for MOL and lower BEOL due to better electromigration at small dimensions), Ruthenium (emerging at 3nm and below, potentially barrierless integration), and Molybdenum (research stage for post-copper and 3D NAND word lines).

The central engineering challenge is the resistance problem: as line widths shrink, cross-section shrinks quadratically so resistance grows quadratically, driving RC delay growth. A 2nm barrier in a 10nm trench consumes 40% of the trench, driving adoption of thinner ALD barriers and alternative liner materials. Low-k/ultra-low-k dielectrics reduce capacitance; cobalt, ruthenium, and molybdenum reduce resistance.

The cobalt/ruthenium transition is gradual because each new metal requires requalification of barrier, liner, CMP slurry, cleaning chemistry, and reliability models. Ruthenium supply is particularly constrained: it's one of the rarest platinum-group metals, produced as a byproduct of platinum and nickel refining, concentrated in South Africa and Russia, with annual global production measured in tens of tonnes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The bottom layers are pitch-limited by transistor density; the top layers are resistance-limited by current-carrying requirements."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Interconnects Approach Tipping Point ---
URL: https://semiengineering.com/interconnects-approach-tipping-point

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Semiconductor Engineering (published February 20, 2025, by Laura Peters) examines how the semiconductor industry's interconnects are approaching a critical tipping point as leading-edge logic devices move to next-generation nanosheets. The 1nm (10Å) node will have 20nm pitch metal lines, but the interconnect stack already consumes a third of device power and accounts for 75% of chip RC delay. This is forcing a potential transition from copper to ruthenium (Ru) interconnects at the lowest, tightest levels, possibly as soon as the 14 Å node, and from tungsten to molybdenum (Mo) in DRAM and 3D NAND applications.

Key technical points:
- Ruthenium appears furthest along in demonstrating manufacturability and reliability, and can be deposited by PVD, CVD, ALD, or electroless plating. It requires no barrier layer, doesn't oxidize easily, has a shorter electron mean free path, and is compatible with air gaps (k=1.0) to reduce RC delay, though air gaps reduce mechanical stability and would be used sparingly on alternating layers.
- The switch from damascene processing to subtractive (deposition-etch) schemes is likely because it enables more flexible, scalable paths to connect taller CFET devices, provides better line height control than CMP, and allows higher aspect ratio lines (beyond 2:1). imec's "semi-damascene" process is a two-layer module that could extend to multi-layer stacks, with data showing stacked via resistance remains important up to M5.
- Molybdenum is emerging as the successor to tungsten for word lines in DRAM, contacts and plugs in 3D NAND, and contacts in logic. It offers low resistance at nanometer dimensions, requires no barrier layer (little intrinsic diffusivity into dielectrics), is low cost, and can be deposited via ion beam deposition at 400°C to achieve lower resistivity than tungsten. Nearly all major chipmakers are in various stages of molybdenum qualification.
- Copper extension efforts include lower-resistance via processes, thinner TaN diffusion barriers via ALD, Ru-Co alternative liners, elimination of barrier layers at via bottoms, and self-aligned or fully aligned vias. Samsung reported a Ru-Co bilayer liner producing 87% fewer voids and 14% better line resistance at tight dimensions.
- Backside power delivery (BPD) moves power delivery to the wafer backside so frontside interconnect levels only carry signals, potentially delaying ruthenium introduction by a device node.
- Thermal concerns (Joule heating, electromigration, stress migration, TDDB) are exacerbated by scaling and low-k dielectric/air gap transitions, with heating now affecting more than just the first metal level.
- imec's Zsolt Tokei notes that at 36nm pitches ruthenium performance is already slightly better than copper, but the change is disruptive and requires full self-alignment, via-to-line leakage in spec, correct DPPM, air-gap compatibility, and passing electromigration and reliability testing.
- Lam Research's Kaihan Ashtiani states moly is emerging as the most suitable material to replace tungsten, creating a major inflection point.

The article concludes that material and architectural changes only happen when existing flows absolutely cannot meet performance specifications, so any metal replacement will occur gradually and step-wise due to massive existing investments in copper dual-damascene and tungsten metallization tooling.
</summary>

"There are a number of factors to consider in the selection of a metal, and resistivity is among the most important. At the atomic dimensions required for advanced chipmaking, moly is emerging as the most suitable material to replace tungsten, creating a major inflection point in the industry." - Kaihan Ashtiani, Lam Research

--- SOURCE 10: Depositing ruthenium layers in interconnect metallization ---
URL: https://patents.google.com/patent/US10731250B2/en

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Google Patents page for US Patent US10731250B2, titled "Depositing ruthenium layers in interconnect metallization," assigned to Lam Research Corporation. The patent was filed as US15/996,925 and published as US20180347041A1 before being granted. Inventors include Do Young Kim, Jeong-Seok Na, Chiukin Steven Lai, Raashina Humayun, and Michal Danek.

**Core Technology:**
The patent describes methods and apparatus for depositing ruthenium (Ru) layers in semiconductor interconnect metallization, particularly for sub-10nm technology nodes. The key innovation involves a two-step process:
1. **Ru liner layer deposition** via multiple atomic layer deposition (ALD) cycles performed under reducing conditions (using a reducing agent such as H2 or NH3, either thermal or plasma-enhanced)
2. **Ru fill operation** where the feature is at least partially filled with ruthenium by reacting a ruthenium precursor with an oxidant

The protective Ru liner layer (typically 1-2 nm thick) prevents oxidation of underlying adhesion/barrier layers and metal substrates during the subsequent oxidative fill step. It also serves as a barrier preventing oxygen from penetrating into underlying metal layers.

**Technical Details:**
- Addresses the problem that copper interconnects are challenging at sub-10nm nodes because copper has an electron mean free path of ~39 nm, and no barrier material maintains integrity below 2.5nm thickness (barriers consume >50% of line cross-section at small dimensions)
- Ruthenium has a short inelastic mean free path, allowing better resistivity scaling than copper at sub-10nm dimensions, and can be used without a diffusion barrier
- ALD dose sequences include: Ru precursor → reductant; Ru precursor → oxidant → reductant; Ru precursor → oxidant mixed with reductant; etc.
- Ru precursors include Ru(0) and Ru(II) organometallic compounds (e.g., (arene)(diene)Ru(0), (cyclopentadienyl)(ethyl)Ru(II)dicarbonyl)
- Two approaches for protective layer: (1) cycling oxidation-reduction chemistries, or (2) reduction-only chemistry
- Applications include sub-10nm MOL and BEOL logic interconnects, source/drain contact fill, vias, and trenches
- Features may be fully filled with Ru or other metals (Cu, W, Co, Mo, Ni, Al)
- Liner layers can be deposited on WCN, TiN, WN, WC, or TaN
- Process parameters: temperatures 150-450°C, pressures 0.1-10 Torr, carrier gas flows 25-1000 sccm, dose times 0.5-20 seconds

**Apparatus Claims:**
The patent also covers an apparatus with process chambers, gas inlets for Ru precursor, oxidant, and reducing agent sources, plus a controller with machine-readable instructions for performing the Ru liner deposition cycles and fill process.

**Classifications:** Covers C23C (chemical coating/CVD), C23C16/455 (ALD), H01L21/768 (interconnect manufacturing), H10P14 (formation of materials), and H10W20 (interconnections) classifications.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"One aspect of the disclosure relates to a method including receiving a substrate including a feature; performing multiple atomic layer deposition (ALD) cycles to deposit a ruthenium (Ru) liner layer in the feature, wherein each of the ALD cycles include a dose of a reducing agent; and after depositing the Ru liner layer, at least partially filling the feature with ruthenium by reacting a first ruthenium precursor with an oxidant."
</key_excerpts>

# Ruthenium Interconnects On Tap

Chipmakers will stall as long as possible, but copper’s days are numbered.

June 20th, 2024 - By: [Katherine Derbyshire](https://semiengineering.com/author/katherine/)

![popularity](https://semiengineering.com/wp-content/themes/se_current/images/pop_ratings/pop_rating_lev4.png "popularity")

Chipmakers’ focus on new interconnect technology is ramping up as copper’s effectiveness continues to diminish, setting the stage for a significant shift that could improve performance and reduce heat at future nodes and in advanced packages.

The introduction of copper interconnects in 1997 upended the then-standard tungsten via/aluminum line metallization scheme. Dual damascene integration schemes replaced “dry” steps like plasma etch and deposition with “wet” processes like electroplating and CMP. At the time, manufacturers were struggling to minimize RC delay in the face of more complex interconnect structures.

Nearly three decades later, the semiconductor industry is at a similar crossroads. Shrinking line dimensions are approaching copper’s electron mean free path. Barrier layers are consuming a larger share of the total available line width. The need for an alternative to copper is growing. Like most radical changes, though, manufacturers hope to delay this one as long as they can.

Results presented at the recent IEEE Interconnect Technology Conference showed that opportunities for copper optimization remain.

**Getting the most out of copper**  
 As interconnects shrink, interfaces and their properties become more relevant to electrical performance than the bulk material properties. Jongmin Baek, senior engineer at Samsung Semiconductor, and his colleagues looked specifically at how optimizing the barrier and etch stop layers needed for copper can improve overall performance. For example, in a contact metal-spacer test vehicle, the group used a sidewall plasma pre-treatment to reduce the sidewall barrier thickness by a third, improving contact resistance by 2%. [⁠1]

The Samsung researchers paid particular attention to the via bottom barrier. Because metal vias rest on metal lines, this barrier is not needed as either an electrical insulator or a diffusion barrier. It exists only as an artifact of the sidewall deposition, yet it can account for more than 60% of via resistance. [Selective deposition methods](https://semiengineering.com/sidestepping-lithography-in-chip-manufacturing/) often are used to reduce via bottom deposition. In Baek’s work, a polymeric inhibitor improved selectivity relative to the self-assembled monolayers that are commonly used, giving a 20% resistance reduction.

Modern interconnect schemes depend on a variety of carbon-doped oxides for the “C” part of the circuit’s RC delay. Less dense materials are attractive because they have lower dielectric constants (k). Additional work by Samsung’s Kang Sub Yim considered the depletion of dielectric surface carbon by plasma etching.[⁠2] Etching damage to low-k dielectrics raises the effective dielectric constant, and therefore the capacitance of the circuit. Higher-density materials, typically with k values above 3.0, are more resistant to plasma etching damage, potentially giving them a lower effective k value in sub-30nm features. For features smaller than about 30nm, surface carbon depletion has a larger impact than the bulk dielectric constant.

Yim’s group also used surface silylation to restore etch damage. However, Baek pointed out that surface treatment of the dielectric sidewalls risks contamination of the exposed metal at the via bottom. Instead, Baek’s group used a thermal recovery process with proprietary chemistry to revert the post-etch Si-OH terminated surface to one terminated with Si-CH3.

Full encapsulation of copper lines includes a metal cap layer — usually cobalt — to reduce electromigration, followed by an insulating etch stop and barrier layer. Due to pitch scaling, these layers are becoming a larger fraction of the total line thickness. To improve the interface with the cap layer, Baek added a plasma pretreatment before the etch stop layer deposition. As a result, they saw a 30% reduction in stress in the copper lines, and a 10% reduction in via resistance. Separately, Yim achieved similar results.

**Ruthenium vias, then lines**  
 While all these developments are promising, a long-term successor to copper is still needed. Vias in particular are coming to dominate the overall interconnect resistance because of their small size and their sheer numbers. In the first four or five interconnect levels, the metal lines are very short and don’t contribute much resistance. One alternative, then, is to use a transitional hybrid metallization scheme, combining copper lines with a material like tungsten, ruthenium, or molybdenum for vias.

Simulations at imec showed that using ruthenium vias for the first four layers of the interconnect stack reduces overall resistance by as much as 60%.[⁠3] To integrate ruthenium vias with copper lines, they suggested depositing a TaN barrier layer on dielectric sidewalls only, landing the ruthenium directly on exposed copper. Any such scheme requires good dielectric surface passivation and good control of ruthenium selectivity. A cluster tool process is preferred, because removing native oxide from exposed copper can damage the dielectric passivation.

**Fig. 1: Schematic comparing two self-aligned double patterning processes. Source: imec**

Because ruthenium can be deposited or etched in a variety of ways and does not require a barrier layer, it opens the door to much more flexible integration schemes. For example, Giulio Marti, imec R&D engineer, and his colleagues benchmarked three different fully self-aligned via processes.[⁠4] The first, and most conventional, used EUV self-aligned double-patterning, with the spacer lines that process creates serving to define the metal lines (SADP-SIM). After transferring the spacer pattern to a SiN hard mask, selective RIE etching patterned a ruthenium metal layer, followed by SiO2 deposition. A highly selective etch aligned the via openings to the remaining SiN features, followed by CVD ruthenium deposition to fill them.

The other two options Marti considered, both based on pillar vias, deposited a second ruthenium layer on top of the first, with an etch stop layer separating the two. In these schemes, pattern transfer uses a two-step ruthenium etch. First, a high-aspect ratio etch cuts the desired metal lines in both layers. Then, a spin-on dielectric fills these trenches, with a hard mask on top. Tone-inversion EUV patterns the hard mask to protect the desired via pillars, while the previous etch stop layer protects the underlying metal lines. Marti found that the two pillar via options increased the number of process steps, but increased the process window. In particular, this approach prevents bridging between vias and adjacent lines.

![](https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/20240619_IITC_CW.png?resize=676%2C599&ssl=1)  
 **Fig. 1: Schematic comparing SADP-SIM and SADP-SID processes. Source: imec**

Another alternative, proposed by Chen Wu, another imec R&D engineer, and his colleagues uses the SADP spacers to define the dielectric features, rather than the metal.[⁠5] In this SADP-SID scheme, a hard mask material is deposited between spacer pillars, which are then removed. Though this approach adds process complexity, it means that metal features are defined directly by the mask, giving designers more flexibility and control over feature dimensions.

Regardless of the specific approach, though, Wu emphasized that optimized ruthenium etch and deposition processes will be critical. Tapered Ru profiles, footings at the base of ruthenium features, and incomplete removal of the TiN adhesion layer can reduce the spacing between adjacent lines, leading to leakage.

**An integration scheme is just the beginning**  
 A successful process integration scheme requires careful attention to all the component layers. For ruthenium, that optimization process is just beginning. Jack Rogers and colleagues at TEL’s Albany Technology Center investigated the effects of adhesion layer process conditions on ruthenium’s deposition behavior. Ruthenium films on PVD and ALD TiN had different grain orientations, different grain orientation distributions, and different resistivities. Larger and more uniform Ru grains appear to reduce resistivity, at least when grains are smaller than the overall interconnect dimensions.[⁠6]

Though ruthenium interconnects will require fewer auxiliary layers than copper — that’s part of the point — the re-introduction of metal etch and dielectric fill processes are sure to keep process engineers busy for years to come.

**References**

1. Jongmin Baek, et al., “Interface engineering for performance and reliability boosting of logic devices,” International Interconnect Technology Conference, San Jose, 2024, paper 2.5.
2. Kang Sub Yim, Jong Min Baek, Hoon Seok Seo, “Advanced interconnect capacitance and interface engineering beyond 1.4nm Logic Devices,” International Interconnect Technology Conference, San Jose, 2024, paper 2.1.
3. Marleen H. van der Veen, et al., “Low Resistance Stacked Via Metallization for Future Interconnects,” International Interconnect Technology Conference, San Jose, 2024, paper 12.1.
4. Giulio Marti, et al., “Redefining 2-Level Semi-Damascene Interconnect Technology: Benchmarking three different Fully Self- aligned Via options,” International Interconnect Technology Conference, San Jose, 2024, poster 9.1.
5. Chen Wu, et al., “Demonstration of MP18-26nm Ru Semi-Damascene Spacer-is-Dielectric SADP Integration,” International Interconnect Technology Conference, San Jose, 2024, poster 9.3.
6. Jack Rogers, et al., “Process Control for the Modification of Ruthenium Resistivity in Scaled Subtractive Interconnects,” International Interconnect Technology Conference, San Jose, 2024, paper 2.4.

args.summary:
This article from Semiconductor Engineering (June 20, 2024, by Katherine Derbyshire) discusses the transition away from copper interconnects in semiconductor manufacturing as copper's effectiveness diminishes at shrinking node dimensions. The article reports on findings presented at the IEEE Interconnect Technology Conference (IITC 2024 in San Jose).

Key points covered:

1. **Copper's limitations**: Shrinking line dimensions are approaching copper's electron mean free path, and barrier layers consume an increasing share of line width. The industry introduced copper interconnects in 1997 (dual damascene scheme with electroplating and CMP), and is now approaching a similar crossroads nearly three decades later.

2. **Copper optimization efforts**: Samsung researchers (Jongmin Baek and colleagues) presented work on optimizing barrier and etch stop layers. Key findings include: a sidewall plasma pre-treatment reduced sidewall barrier thickness by a third (improving contact resistance by 2%); a polymeric inhibitor improved via-bottom selectivity (20% resistance reduction); via bottom barrier can account for more than 60% of via resistance; surface silylation/thermal recovery chemistry (Si-OH to Si-CH3 termination) restores etch damage; and a plasma pretreatment before etch stop deposition gave 30% stress reduction in copper lines and 10% via resistance reduction.

3. **Low-k dielectric considerations**: Samsung's Kang Sub Yim examined carbon depletion from dielectric surfaces by plasma etching. For features smaller than ~30nm, surface carbon depletion impacts capacitance more than the bulk dielectric constant. Higher-density materials (k>3.0) are more resistant to plasma damage and may have lower effective k in sub-30nm features.

4. **Ruthenium vias as transition**: imec simulations showed ruthenium vias for the first four interconnect layers reduce overall resistance by up to 60%. A transitional hybrid scheme would combine copper lines with tungsten, ruthenium, or molybdenum vias. Ruthenium requires no barrier layer and can be deposited or etched in multiple ways, enabling flexible integration.

5. **Self-aligned via processes**: imec's Giulio Marti benchmarked three fully self-aligned via processes — including SADP-SIM (spacer-defined metal lines with EUV self-aligned double patterning) and two pillar-via options that increased process steps but improved process window and prevented via-to-line bridging. Chen Wu proposed a SADP-SID scheme using spacers to define dielectric features instead of metal, offering more design flexibility.

6. **Ruthenium process optimization**: TEL's Albany Technology Center (Jack Rogers) investigated how adhesion layer process conditions affect ruthenium deposition. Ru films on PVD vs. ALD TiN showed different grain orientations and resistivities; larger, more uniform Ru grains reduce resistivity. Optimized ruthenium etch/deposition is critical — tapered Ru profiles, footings, and incomplete TiN adhesion layer removal can cause leakage between lines.

The article notes that while copper optimization opportunities remain, the long-term shift to ruthenium interconnects will require years of process engineering work, including re-introduction of metal etch and dielectric fill processes.
args.key_excerpts: "Because metal vias rest on metal lines, this barrier is not needed as either an electrical insulator or a diffusion barrier. It exists only as an artifact of the sidewall deposition, yet it can account for more than 60% of via resistance."

# Abhishekkumar Thakur’s Post

[Abhishekkumar Thakur](https://de.linkedin.com/in/abhishekkumar-thakur-16081991?trk=public_post_feed-actor-name)

* [Report this post](/uas/login?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Fposts%2Fabhishekkumar-thakur-16081991_semiconductor-semiconductorindustry-tsmc-activity-7368382730876731392-bmrJ&trk=public_post_ellipsis-menu-semaphore-sign-in-redirect&guestReportContentType=POST&_f=guest-reporting)

Why Ruthenium would take over Copper in critical metal interconnects? Copper's resistivity increases up to 10x due to electron scattering, as its line width falls below its 40nm mean free path. Copper requires a 3-4nm thick diffusion barrier, reducing the effective copper width in a 10nm line to 2-4nm, complicating fabrication and increasing resistance. Copper lacks a manufacturable etching process; lines are formed by etching dielectrics, depositing barriers and seed layers, and filling with copper. Ruthenium as an Alternative: Ruthenium offers lower resistance at line widths ≤17nm, better electromigration resistance, and easier etching compared to copper. Ruthenium’s etchability enables a semidamascene approach, combining additive and subtractive metallization, simplifying air-gap dielectric schemes. Ruthenium deposition (e.g., PVD, CVD, ALD) faces adhesion issues on SiO2, requiring liners like TiN, though thinner films improve adhesion. Sputtering ruthenium in a nitrogen atmosphere or alloying with tungsten/cobalt creates amorphous structures, enhancing barrier properties against copper diffusion. Low-temperature electroless plating of ruthenium with succinic acid and post-annealing reduces resistivity by removing impurities, offering a viable deposition method. Ruthenium’s resistivity varies by crystal orientation, with 25% lower resistance along the [001] axis, but epitaxial integration into CMOS is complex, requiring layer transfer.   10 Polysilicon & Semiconductor Terms Everyone Should Know In the world of semiconductors, understanding key technical terms helps decode how chips — the brains behind all modern electronics — are made.  Here are 10 essential terms every enthusiast, student, or professional should know 👇 1. Polysilicon (Poly-Si): A purified form of silicon used as a raw material to produce silicon wafers — the foundation of every chip. 2. Wafer: A thin slice of semiconductor material, usually silicon, on which microcircuits are built. 3. Ingot: A cylindrical block of purified silicon, sliced into wafers for chip manufacturing. 4. Czochralski Process: A method used to grow single-crystal silicon ingots from molten silicon. 5. Doping: The process of adding impurities to silicon to modify its electrical properties — crucial for creating transistors. 6. Photolithography: A technique that uses light to transfer circuit patterns onto a wafer — similar to printing microscopic blueprints. 7. Etching: The process of removing layers from the wafer surface to create circuit patterns. 8. Deposition: Adding thin films of materials onto the wafer surface, layer by layer. 9. CMP (Chemical Mechanical Polishing): A smoothing process that ensures wafer surfaces are perfectly flat for precision layering. 10. Clean Room: A controlled environment free of dust and contaminants where wafers are manufactured — even a single particle can ruin a chip!   Every Fab Plays a Different Game: Nodes, Pixels, Power & Pitches 1. What is a Node in CMOS Fab? • In logic/CMOS fabs (the Intels, TSMCs, Samsungs of the world), a node traditionally referred to the minimum feature size of a transistor (like the gate length). • Example: 180 nm node, 65 nm node, 7 nm node. 👉 But today, “node” is more of a marketing label than an exact physical dimension. For instance, TSMC’s 5 nm node doesn’t literally mean transistors are 5 nm wide — it’s a bundle of improvements in: • Transistor density (more transistors per area). • Performance (speed). • Power efficiency (less leakage, lower voltage). So in CMOS fabs, node ≈ generation of process technology. 2. What about Other Types of Fabs? Other fabs don’t always follow the same “node” naming convention. Their key parameter depends on what the fab is optimizing for: Power Semiconductor Fabs (Si, SiC, GaN): • Parameter = Voltage/Current rating (e.g., 600 V SiC MOSFET, 1200 V IGBT). • Instead of “node,” the figure of merit is how efficiently they handle high power without heating up or failing. Display Fabs (LCD, OLED, MicroLED): • Parameter = Pixel Pitch / Resolution (e.g., 4K UHD, 8K, microdisplay in µm). • It’s about how small and uniform you can make each pixel and the backplane transistors. Packaging Fabs (OSAT, ATMP): • Parameter = Interconnect pitch (distance between bumps, wires, or TSVs). • For advanced packaging, the “node” could be 2.5D/3D integration, chiplet pitch, or bump pitch in microns. Analog/MEMS/Legacy Fabs: • Parameter = Device characteristics like voltage tolerance, MEMS dimensions, or sensor sensitivity. • They don’t chase “nm scaling” but stability, yield, and reliability. 3. Analogy (Simple Way to Remember) Think of each fab type like a different kind of sport. Each has its own “scoring system” (what matters most): CMOS Fab (Logic/CPU/GPU): Like sprinting → the score is time (nm node = faster & smaller steps). Power Fab: Like weightlifting → the score is how much load you can carry (voltage/current rating). Display Fab: Like painting/art → the score is detail and sharpness (pixel resolution). Packaging Fab: Like Lego building → the score is how tightly and cleverly you can pack blocks (interconnect pitch, 3D stacking). Analog/MEMS Fab: Like craftsmanship → the score is precision, balance, and reliability rather than size. ✅ So, to sum up: • In CMOS fabs, node = process generation (historically feature size, now a branding of density/power/performance). • In other fabs, “node” doesn’t mean much; instead, they have their own key figure of merit — voltage, resolution, interconnect pitch, or device reliability. ~~~~~ If you are looking to invest in semiconductors and need expert insights, drop us a DM.

This is a LinkedIn post by Abhishekkumar Thakur discussing why Ruthenium (Ru) would replace Copper (Cu) in critical metal interconnects for advanced semiconductor manufacturing.

Key points from the post:
- Copper's resistivity increases up to 10x due to electron scattering as its line width falls below its 40nm mean free path.
- Copper requires a 3-4nm thick diffusion barrier, reducing effective copper width in a 10nm line to only 2-4nm, complicating fabrication and increasing resistance.
- Copper lacks a manufacturable etching process; lines are formed by etching dielectrics, depositing barriers and seed layers, then filling with copper (damascene approach).

Ruthenium advantages:
- Offers lower resistance at line widths ≤17nm
- Better electromigration resistance
- Easier etching compared to copper
- Enables a semidamascene approach (combining additive and subtractive metallization), simplifying air-gap dielectric schemes

Ruthenium challenges:
- Deposition (PVD, CVD, ALD) faces adhesion issues on SiO2, requiring liners like TiN
- Sputtering Ru in a nitrogen atmosphere or alloying with tungsten/cobalt creates amorphous structures enhancing barrier properties
- Low-temperature electroless plating with succinic acid and post-annealing reduces resistivity by removing impurities
- Ru resistivity varies by crystal orientation (25% lower resistance along the [001] axis), but epitaxial integration into CMOS is complex, requiring layer transfer

Comments provide additional expert perspectives:
- Dr. My Nghe Tran: questioned cost comparison of metals
- Avron Ger: noted IMEC has been working on this path and questioned when it will go into HVM (High Volume Manufacturing), noting it would only apply to the first metal levels
- Rubina Sultan: noted key challenge is polishing and etching; unlike Cu with decades of well-established CMP and etch processes, Ru needs further development
- James Swonger: raised molybdenum (Mo) and alloy alternatives (CuW, CuMo, AgW, AgMo) rather than damascene
- Bernd Wildpanner: questioned reliability data and formation of ruthenium chloride compounds
- Kwanghyun Kim: asked about Mo as alternative; mentioned integration challenges (anisotropic conductivity, grain structure control, adhesion)
- Simon Kirk: noted post-etch residue cleaning and selectivity challenges
- Ed Korczynski: noted volatile toxic oxides form in CMP of Ru, increasing tool and process costs
- Bijan Nowroozi: noted Ru is hexagonal, making it an anisotropic conductor

The post has 284 reactions and 13 comments. It includes links to further details (https://lnkd.in/dNSr4Ddx and https://lnkd.in/dthMBKUg).

The page also includes related semiconductor posts on VLSI oxidation processes, RC extraction at advanced nodes, polysilicon terminology, integrated circuits, and fab node naming conventions (though these are secondary content from the "More Relevant Posts" section).

# Molybdenum-Based Metallization: Unlocking New Economies of Scale in Semiconductor Manufacturing
## Counterpoint Research
10600 subscribers
717 likes

### Description
38121 views
Posted: 14 May 2025
AI is driving technological shifts and breakthrough innovations to address the challenges of intense complexities required in the semiconductor industry. Traditional metallization schemes are finding it challenging to support the aggressive scaling demands driven by the next-gen computing era. In this CP conversations, Counterpoint’s VP of Research, Ross Young discusses with Dr. Kaihan Ashtiani, CVP and GM, ALD/CVD metals at Lam Research on the Lam Research’s leadership in Atomic Layer Deposition and how it is driving the transition to Moly. Dr. Kaihan talks about how Lam is enabling the evolution from Tungsten which has been the metal of choice for over two decades is reaching its limits and how Lam has been at the forefront in enabling the transition to Moly.

Follow us on social media platforms: 
Twitter - https://twitter.com/counterpointtr
LinkedIn - https://www.linkedin.com/company/counterpoint-technology-market-research/
Instagram - https://www.instagram.com/counterpointresearch/

2 comments
### Transcript:
Data-intensive applications like AI are fueling intense demand for more advanced computation capabilities. As a result, chipmakers are pushing the limits of what's possible in the race for the next generation semiconductor devices. Atom-by-atom deposition of metal is essential in manufacturing these advanced chips. From creating complex patterns to memory word lines and to logic contacts. And tungsten has been the metal of choice for more than a couple of decades. But traditional metallization schemes can no longer support this kind of aggressive scaling demands. With this in background, Lam Research recently introduced Altus Halo, the world's first atomic layer deposition tool that harnesses the capabilities of the metal molybdenum to enable scaling on in the AI era. My colleague Ross Young had an opportunity to sit down with Kayhan Ashtiani from Lam Research to learn more about this innovation. Hello Kayhan. Thanks for taking the time to meet with us today. Tell me a little bit more about what you do at Lam Research. Yeah. Hi. My name is Kayhan Ashtiani. I'm a vice president general manager of ALD CBD metal deposition group at Lam Research. I've been with the company for 27 years. It's been a fun journey. Please explain the role of deposition in semiconductor manufacturing. Yeah. Deposition generally refers to forming thin films on a semiconductor chip. Those films generally come in two different categories, dielectric films and metal films. And the idea of having two different films is to form the interconnects that connect billions of devices on a semiconductor chip such that they can talk to each other and perform the performance the function that they're they're supposed to do. So dielectrics provide the insulation just like wiring in our homes and metals have the role of carrying the current electrical current in these devices. So uh we deposit these films uh via PVD, CVD, and now ALD. The difference between ALD and PVD and CVD is uh related to the precision of how we deposit the films. So, CVD refers to chemical vapor deposition. It deposits film at a uh much higher rate and faster rate and deposits bulk material uh into devices. PVD refers to physical vapor deposition where a target is used of the material that needs to be deposited on the on the semiconductor chip and that material is transferred from the target to the wafer. So, uh both of those techniques were viable when people were looking at very high uh uh dimensions of the features in these uh semiconductor chips. As the dimensions shrink uh and get smaller we need a more precision uh or precise method of depositing these materials. So, uh with the metals, atomic layer deposition ALD is used such that we deposit these uh films one atomic layer at a time on a semiconductor chip. Therefore, achieving the the precision that we need to fill the dimensions that are getting smaller and smaller. So, it's uh it's a it's something that uh Lam started um uh more than 20 years ago in terms of developing the atomic layer deposition. And we were the first company actually introducing ALD of metals in the industry uh with our ALD tungsten. And now we are transitioning to ALD moly, which is a uh very important significant point uh for the industry uh transition. So, please tell us a little bit more about why Lam is transitioning from tungsten to to moly. Yeah, so uh when we look at the uh technology roadmap that our customers have in terms of advancing their devices to to address the needs of the industry in AI and cloud in high-speed IO. All the applications that are very demanding from a computing perspective. There is a need to lower the resistivity of the metal that they use for the interconnect. And Molly is is able to address that compared to other materials that have been used in the past. So, resistivity is a very important part metallization in semiconductor chips. And as it the name says, resistivity is resistance towards the flow of electrical currents, which determines the speed of the device, therefore performance of the device. So, this transition to Molly is very important from that perspective because we offer lower resistivity metal compared to what is used today such that our customers can advance their devices to to the to the future. What devices are are you expecting to use Molly for? This is the Yeah. So, there are two questions in that. I think it's what devices need to use Molly and which ones are going to happen first in terms of adoption. I think from a device perspective and we see that in the industry today is that literally all devices and all customers are looking into this transition to Molly. And but it's in terms of adoption the the timing slightly different even though they're close enough that it becomes a challenge to to some degree. I would say literally all devices will shift towards Molly from the priority perspective in terms of adoption perhaps demand in memory is first adopter and it's going to be followed very closely that in logic and DRAM. And which is the most challenging to adopt? Uh, would say most uh challenging perhaps is NAND and uh and that's uh because of the the the way the devices laid out. Uh NAND devices are formed in three dimensions and have a two-dimensional aspect to them as well. That makes the surface area that we need to deposit the moly film into uh a very large surface area with the challenges of different aspect ratios both in vertical and lateral dimensions. So, because of that the uh process sequences that are required to do uh moly deposition in these uh devices as well as the hardware features that are necessary to make the process happen is uh more sophisticated than the other two. Even though the challenges of integration remain for all devices logic and memory and memory being NAND and DRAM, the those challenges are uh unique to each device. So, we have to address uh all of those uh independently. So, why is Lam best positioned to lead the transition to a moly ALD? Jeff? Uh I would say that uh uh over the past 20 years uh we have introduced technologies in uh in terms of atomic layer deposition of uh metals that have been uh uh pioneering and leading in the industry. So, 20 years ago we uh we came out with our atomic layer deposition of tungsten uh and that uh started being used in high-volume manufacturing. So, I would say with that leading uh position that we had in terms of ALD deposition of metals, it puts us in a very good uh and significant position to have a leading position in ALD of moly as well which uh shows in our uh adoption of our hafnium moly today in the industry. So, it's going to be tough for your competition to to break into this segment. Uh I would say that we have a good lead over our competitors. Uh this is a a inflection in the industry and I'm sure our competitors are as hungry as we are in terms of developing these technologies. But in terms of our lead in the in the area in terms of the technology that we develop, and also with the Molly itself, where we started close to 10 years ago, that we have a significant lead in terms of development of technology that I would say that we are in a very good position to to lead the industry. And how is it positive? Is it a gas? Is it it's in the target? So, how do you source the Molly? Yeah. The the Molly is sourced through a through a chemical precursor. So, the chemical precursor comes in a in in different forms as like any other chemical component or precursors. There could be different composition. We developed those techniques starting I would say close to 7 years ago with some of our vendors developing those techniques of who delivered material to the chamber such that we can run the processes and deposit the films. So, and we've made significant improvements and advancements in delivering these materials. Is that another competitive advantage for Lam? I would say so because this the what we call the bulk delivery a first in the industry at this scale. So, we developed a delivery system that goes in the sub fab of our customers, not the main fab, where usually the chemicals and the facilities are supposed to be, and then it's delivered to the tool in the in the fab itself. This was I would say a first as well given the scale of the material that we are putting down. So, and I would say that is competitive advantage for Lam as well. So, it takes up less clean room space. Correct. And what was the role of your customers in in defining the requirements for this tool? Uh Yeah, so uh we we developed this process, what we call the unit film, and the tool, uh we started developing it starting 10 years ago. So, uh developing the unit film is one part of the process uh to make these materials be accepted in the industry. Next is to put it that our customer sites and uh look at the integration of this film with the rest of the device. And also uh validate the economic viability of the of the tool. So, uh uh we started that development, but we needed a collaboration with our customers to validate uh what is uh uh the rest of the environment that needs to support uh the position of Molly. And that's uh what we've done with a number of customers over the years. Um what can you say about what this tool means for your customers' road maps? Yeah, our our customers look for uh advancing their devices. Part of the advancement of devices is related to making metals being lower resistivity, essentially having faster speed. So, um on their road map, there was an anticipation of the need, but uh whether Molly or other materials could satisfy that, that that's the big question that uh vendors like Lamb address. So, uh we've addressed that part of their technology road map that they would need a lower resistivity metal, and we proved out that ALD Molly could satisfy those requirements that they have. And uh now we have the validations that in fact we were correct in our prediction that Molly is the right material to address those challenges. This is a significant inflection in the industry. It uh obviously uh enables uh the our customers to advance their technology given the acceptance and the shift that we're seeing from other materials to Molly. Uh it creates obviously an opportunity for Lamb to uh to participate in this inflection in a significant way. And uh for our customers also to show the benefit on their devices for their customers. Their customers being uh either consumers or enterprise. Uh either way they they're they're able to demonstrate the uh the benefit to their customers as well. So, I would say it's a win-win situation for all in a very significant inflection in the industry. When do you think we'll see the first Molly ALD devices in the market or are they already out there? Um I would I would say most of our customers are in various stages of uh development uh right now. Uh and that means uh certain customers may be at the very beginning of that uh validation. And some customers we're already seeing in ramp and close to production. Well, that must be very satisfying to see something you've worked on for so many years come to market and will be in consumers' hands. Absolutely. It uh it was a great challenge uh and uh and we are happy that we are addressing a need for the for the industry while uh I think uh both us and our customers will benefit from. Seems like a real breakthrough. Is there anything else you'd like to add? Uh I would like to come back to uh saying that uh we've enabled uh deposition of Molly uh via atomic layer deposition for the first time in production for our customers. And that's a significant shift uh from uh the metallization schemes that we've had before. And uh Lamb in his leading position to uh to take our customers through this journey and uh make him uh advance in their customer uh needs and advance in their devices as well as moving the industry to the next phase. Very exciting. Congratulations. Thank you so much. Mhm.

The topic is Lam Research's leadership in Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) and the industry transition from tungsten to molybdenum (moly) metallization for semiconductor manufacturing.

Key points covered:
- Deposition in semiconductor manufacturing forms thin films (dielectric and metal) that create interconnects connecting billions of devices on a chip. Dielectrics provide insulation while metals carry electrical current.
- Three deposition methods exist: PVD (physical vapor deposition), CVD (chemical vapor deposition), and ALD (atomic layer deposition). As feature dimensions shrink, ALD's atomic-layer precision becomes necessary.
- Lam introduced ALD of metals over 20 years ago with ALD tungsten and is now transitioning to ALD molybdenum (Moly).
- The transition is driven by the need for lower resistivity metals to support AI, cloud, and high-speed IO applications, as resistivity determines device speed and performance.
- All device types and customers are shifting toward Moly. Memory (particularly NAND) is expected to be the first adopter, followed closely by logic and DRAM.
- NAND is the most challenging to adopt Moly due to its 3D architecture with large surface areas and complex aspect ratios in both vertical and lateral dimensions.
- Lam began developing Moly technology close to 10 years ago, positioning them with a significant lead over competitors.
- Moly is sourced through a chemical precursor delivered via a bulk delivery system that Lam developed (a first in the industry) — the system sits in the sub-fab (not the main fab), taking up less cleanroom space.
- Lam worked with customers over the years to validate the integration of Moly films with the rest of the device and confirm economic viability.
- Customers are at various stages of development — some at the beginning of validation, while some are already in ramp and close to production.
- Ashtiani describes this as a significant inflection in the industry, a win-win for Lam and its customers.

They dig into the [advantages of molybdenum](https://www.counterpointresearch.com/insight/scaling-3d-chips-with-molybdenumbased-metallization/) and discuss how [Lam](https://www.counterpointresearch.com/insight/top-five-wafer-fab-equipment-manufacturers-q1-2025-performance/) is enabling the transition from traditional tungsten metallization to [molybdenum (moly)](https://www.counterpointresearch.com/insight/post-insight-research-notes-blogs-molybdenum-the-metal-enabling-next-big-leap-in-chip-manufacturing-for-the-ai-era/) via atomic layer deposition (ALD).

## The Interview

## Key Takeaways from the Discussion

### Role of Deposition in Semiconductor Manufacturing

* Deposition refers to the formation of thin films on semiconductor chips, categorized into dielectric and metal films, to create interconnects that connect billions of devices on a chip, enabling communication.

  * Dielectric films provide insulation, similar to home wiring, while metal films carry electrical current.
  * Earlier techniques, such as physical vapor deposition (PVD) and chemical vapor deposition (CVD), were more suitable for larger feature dimensions. As dimensions shrink, ALD is used to deposit films one atomic layer at a time, achieving the required precision and uniformity.

  ### Technology and Transition to Moly

  + Lam was the first to introduce tungsten ALD, with the development spanning more than 20 years.
  + As semiconductors continue to shrink and performance demands grow, chipmakers are reaching the limit of what is possible with tungsten. Enter moly, which has lower resistance than tungsten in nano-scale wires and does not require a barrier layer. These qualities help boost efficiency and chip speed and reduce the number of process steps required in manufacturing.
  + In an industry first, Lam has developed techniques to deliver solid precursor materials to the chamber to enable the atomic layer deposition of moly.

  ### Adoption of Moly in End Devices

  + NAND is expected to adopt moly first, followed by logic and DRAM. However, Moly’s adoption in NAND is challenging due to the device structure.
  + Lam has developed the necessary process sequences and hardware features to address these challenges, leveraging decades of expertise.
  + With a significant lead in moly development over the past decade, the new solution positions Lam to lead the transition in the industry.

  ## Analyst Takes

  + AI is pushing the boundaries of what is possible in the race to scale, driving the evolution from traditional scaling to more complex architectures, including 3D structures, integration and heterogeneous designs, to meet demands for increased computational capabilities.
  + The path forward demands transformative uses of new materials and innovation in tools and equipment to enable the precision required for HVM.
  + Paving the way for post-GAAFET technologies, such innovations in process and manufacturing will enable seamless transition to next-generation architectures like Complementary FETs (CFETs) and 2D materials. This will be critical for extending Moore’s Law and unlocking new scaling frontiers beyond 2030.

# Molybdenum – The Metal Enabling Next Big Leap In Chip Manufacturing for the AI Era

![](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/image005-1.png)

In 2024 alone, an astonishing one trillion semiconductor chips were produced – or 100 chips for every human being on earth. Behind this number is an industry racing to overcome the physical limits of semiconductors to deliver higher performance and meet soaring demand coming from the advanced AI, efficient edge computing, and premiumization in smartphone and other smart devices.

**Metallization in Manufacturing & Evolution of New Materials**

Today’s smart devices are performing a greater number of functions than their predecessors, particularly with the rise of AI. This has been enabled by technologies like 3D [NAND](https://www.counterpointresearch.com/insights/scaling-to-1000-layer-3d-nand-in-the-ai-era/) in flash memory, where layers of memory are stacked vertically like skyscrapers and interconnects must be fast, precise, and defect-free.

To address higher performance requirements, one area in chip manufacturing that is undergoing transformation is metallization – the process of depositing thin metal layers on chips to form electrical pathways. Atom-by-atom deposition of metal is essential in manufacturing advanced chips — from creating complex patterns, to memory wordlines, to logic contacts.

**Seven Key Stages In Semiconductor Manufacturing**

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

However, as layer counts increase and wordline connections – the ‘wire’ connections to memory cells – shrink, resistance and reliability become bottlenecks. This is becoming the case with Tungsten, which has been the primary element used for interconnection in the past 25 years. But as chip structures become more complex, especially with the evolution of 3D NAND and DRAM, tungsten is hitting its limits. Enter molybdenum, the metal which will propel the next leap in advanced chip manufacturing as we enter the AI era.

**Why Moly, Now?**

Molybdenum is superior to tungsten and offers three key breakthroughs:

These benefits translate into faster chips, higher yields, and more efficient production—all critical for next-gen devices from smartphones to servers utilizing the three major segments across NAND, DRAM and logic chips.

**Resistance Comparison**

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

Despite its numerous benefits, molybdenum has not been used in the metallization process until now because atomic layer deposition (ALD) methods had not been developed to meet molybdenum metallization requirements. Specifically:

**Cracking the Manufacturing Code For Moly:**

**ALTUS® Halo by Lam Research – A Milestone for Molybdenum in Metallization**

Lam Research’s newly launched ALTUS® Halo is the world’s first ALD tool which overcomes the technical hurdles of molybdenum deposition at scale. It delivers:

**Lam Research’s ALTUS® Halo: World First Molybdenum Atomic Layer Deposition Tool**

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

![](data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAAAAACH5BAEKAAEALAAAAAABAAEAAAICTAEAOw==)

**Commercial Milestones**

Lam’s ALTUS Halo has made it possible to bring molybdenum into mass production. Molybdenum is now being adopted in high-volume 3D NAND and advanced logic fabs, with DRAM in development. Micron is an early adopter using ALTUS Halo in the production of its advanced NAND products.

**The Bottom Line for Industry Partners and Investors**

Innovation has always been a driver of value across the manufacturing chain taking the semiconductor industry forward.

*“As Moore’s Law slows and semiconductor architectures become more advanced, materials innovation is the next competitive frontier,” notes*[*Neil Shah*](https://www.counterpointresearch.com/opinion_leader/neil)*, VP of research. “Molybdenum represents a rare and pivotal inflection point—a change not just in materials, but in terms of performance and economics of advanced chipmaking.”*

Lam Research is leading this shift and delivering on innovation that will bring faster processes, better chips and more value.

**Molybdenum In Semiconductor Manufacturing 101:**

Download the latest **whitepaper** from Counterpoint and Lam Research for context around chip production processes and Molybdenum.

[‘Scaling 3D Chips With Molybdenum-Based Metallization’](https://www.counterpointresearch.com/insight/scaling-3d-chips-with-molybdenumbased-metallization?utm_source=research&utm_medium=abm_landing&utm_campaign=mbu&utm_id=mbu_abm_landing_mar_q3_2025&utm_content=counterpoint)

Watch the **Counterpoint Conversations**with Lam Research’s VP & GM Kaihan Ashtiani explaining the innovation around Molybdenum.

[Molybdenum-Based Metallization: Unlocking New Economies of Scale in Semiconductor Manufacturing](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MnE7FjLySZQ)

# Endura® Volta® Cobalt CVD

![video-altText](/content/dam/site/prod-tech/semi/img/volta-animation.jpg)

Thin, conformal CVD cobalt liners and selective cobalt caps encapsulate copper interconnects, improving reliability and scalability beyond the 2Xnm node.

The Applied Endura VoltaCVD Cobalt system sustains Applied’s technical leadership in [CVD](/us/en/glossary.html#cvd), introducing the first material change in more than 15 years of copper barrier/seed (CuBS) development to enable continued high-performance interconnect scaling. The first-of-its-kind technology makes possible deposition of seed-enhancing liner and selective cap layers less than 20Å thick that improve interconnect yield and reliability at the 2Xnm node and beyond. It is the industry’s only vacuum-based [electro-migration](/us/en/glossary.html#electro-migration) (EM) mitigation solution and the only CVD cobalt liner product integrated on the same platform with pre-clean, barrier, and copper seed processes.

Driven by the demand for complex mobile technologies, multi-component system-on-chip (SoC) designs are proliferating to deliver desired functionality and compact form factor. Aggressive pitch scaling for these modern processors in turn is driving greater circuit density and necessity for high performance from interconnects that run for literally miles through these multi-level devices. These trends make it more challenging to achieve the coverage, adhesion, and fill that produces the void-free copper interconnects essential for device operation. Even a single void can render portions of the chip useless.

The Volta CVD Cobalt system introduces a new materials era for extending copper interconnect technology. It promotes copper seed layer coverage by improving copper [wetting](/us/en/glossary.html#wetting), resulting in a thin, continuous, conformal layer that facilitates repair of discontinuities and formation of a robust seed layer. This high-quality layer in turn promotes void-free copper gap fill at the most advanced nodes.

Shrinking geometries also result in higher resistance as well as greater susceptibility to EM failures in the copper lines. A high-quality bond at the interface between the copper and dielectric barrier layer is vital for avoiding EM failures. The Volta system’s best-in-class (>100:1) selective metal capping process strengthens adhesion at the copper-dielectric interface to improve EM performance by an order of magnitude without increasing line resistance or degrading time-dependent dielectric breakdown.

The combined use of Volta CVD Cobalt as both liner and selective metal cap enables complete encapsulation of copper lines and ensures the most robust interconnect reliability for the 2Xnm node and beyond.

This is a product page from Applied Materials describing the Endura® Volta® Cobalt CVD system, a semiconductor manufacturing tool for advanced copper interconnect technology.

**Key Details:**
- The system deposits thin, conformal CVD cobalt liners and selective cobalt caps that encapsulate copper interconnects, improving reliability and scalability beyond the 2Xnm node.
- It represents the first material change in more than 15 years of copper barrier/seed (CuBS) development, sustaining Applied Materials' technical leadership in CVD.
- The technology enables deposition of seed-enhancing liner and selective cap layers less than 20Å thick, improving interconnect yield and reliability at the 2Xnm node and beyond.
- It is described as the industry's only vacuum-based electro-migration (EM) mitigation solution and the only CVD cobalt liner product integrated on the same platform with pre-clean, barrier, and copper seed processes.

**Market Context & Problem:**
- Demand for complex mobile technologies is driving proliferation of multi-component system-on-chip (SoC) designs for functionality and compact form factor.
- Aggressive pitch scaling increases circuit density and creates need for high-performance interconnects running miles through multi-level devices.
- These trends challenge coverage, adhesion, and fill needed for void-free copper interconnects — even a single void can render portions of a chip useless.

**Technology Benefits:**
- The cobalt liner improves copper wetting, promoting a thin, continuous, conformal seed layer that facilitates repair of discontinuities and forms a robust seed layer, enabling void-free copper gap fill at advanced nodes.
- The best-in-class (>100:1) selective metal capping process strengthens adhesion at the copper-dielectric interface, improving electro-migration performance by an order of magnitude without increasing line resistance or degrading time-dependent dielectric breakdown.
- Combined use as both liner and selective metal cap enables complete encapsulation of copper lines, ensuring robust interconnect reliability for the 2Xnm node and beyond.

The page is part of Applied Materials' Semiconductor Products & Technologies section, featuring product imagery and technical specifications.

SAN JOSE, Calif., Nov. 24, 2004--Novellus Systems, Inc. (Nasdaq NM: NVLS), the productivity and technology leader in advanced deposition, surface preparation and chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) processes for the global semiconductor industry, today announced the introduction of ALTUS DirectFill--a single-system solution designed to meet contact and via-fill needs at 65 nm and below. Leveraging Novellus' production-proven ALTUS platform, DirectFill eliminates the need for conventional titanium/titanium nitride (Ti/TiN) toolsets. This advanced plug-fill technique can reduce contact resistance (Rc) and lower overall cost of ownership (CoO) by 50 percent or more when compared to existing processes.

Novellus' ALTUS DirectFill simplifies the tungsten deposition process by replacing the standard multi-tool, Ti/TiN/W approach with a single system. This system integrates an advanced preclean process in one process module, followed by Novellus' proprietary, pulsed nucleation layer (PNL) deposition of tungsten nitride (WN) in a second module, and then a combined PNL and chemical vapor deposition (CVD) tungsten (W) deposition in a third module. The multi-station sequential deposition process modules used for WN and W deliver high productivity and process reproducibility.

ALTUS DirectFill technology provides several key technical benefits. First, the tungsten nitride barrier exhibits atomic layer deposition (ALD) conformality and is substantially thinner than the Ti/TiN liner-barrier it replaces, allowing more of the contact to be filled with lower resistivity tungsten. The tungsten nitride/low resistivity tungsten DirectFill process can reduce contact plug resistance by as much as 50 percent at the 45-nm node. Additionally, PNL tungsten nitride provides excellent barrier characteristics for tungsten and adheres to a variety of dielectric materials. All process temperatures are below 400°C, providing compatibility with future process integration requirements. Unlike competitive systems, ALTUS DirectFill technology solves fill problems at advanced nodes without compromising resistivity.

"ALTUS DirectFill combines an innovative new model for advanced contact fill with the benefits of a proven Novellus platform," said Karl Levy, vice president and general manager of Novellus' Tungsten Business Unit. "Unlike the conventional PVD/MOCVD process sequence, our integrated single-architecture technology approach enhances current tungsten deposition applications, such as contact and bit line, while enabling future applications, such as capacitor electrode and metal gate electrode, where tungsten nitride and tungsten are currently being evaluated. It is a system that carries significant technical advantages without sacrificing productivity," added Levy.

The new tool is available in both 200-mm (Concept Two ALTUS DirectFill) and 300-mm (Concept Three ALTUS DirectFill) configurations. Novellus is actively engaged in joint development projects and working with more than two dozen customers worldwide to develop processes for a wide range of applications and emerging technologies.

# Endura® Volta® Selective W CVD

![video-altText](/content/dam/site/prod-tech/semi/img/SelectiveW-Chen-rev3-thumb.jpg)

Tungsten (W) has been widely used as a gapfill material in middle-of-line (MOL) [contacts](/us/en/glossary.html#contact) for its low resistivity and bulk fill characteristics. MOL contacts form the critical electrical link between the [transistors](/us/en/glossary.html#transistor) and the [interconnects](/us/en/glossary.html#interconnect). Hence, ensuring low resistivity contacts is crucial for overall device performance.

With continued scaling, however, contact dimensions have decreased to the point at which contact [resistance](/us/en/glossary.html#resistance) is becoming a bottleneck in realizing optimum device performance. As the cross-sectional area of the contact shrinks, a growing proportion of the volume is occupied by metal liner/barrier and [nucleation layers](/us/en/glossary.html#nucleation_layer), leaving less volume for the conducting metal fill. In addition, multiple resistive interfaces in the plug contribute to higher contact resistance.

The Applied Endura Volta Selective W CVD system offers an Integrated Materials Solution™ that relieves these adverse effects with a breakthrough in 2D scaling. The system combines surface treatment chambers with selective tungsten deposition chambers. The selective deposition is enabled by both the unique process capabilities of the deposition chambers and the various surface treatments that use specialized chemistries to prepare the underlying metal and [dielectrics](/us/en/glossary.html#dielectric) of the contact to enable bottom-up, metal-on-metal deposition. The selective process eliminates both liner/barrier and nucleation layers to alleviate the bottleneck in device performance, and produces void- and seam-free gapfill.

As all process steps are performed in an ultra-clean, continuous high-vacuum environment, the integrated materials solution ensures a pristine interface and defect-free contact fill. With the volume of conducting metal maximized, contact resistivity is substantially improved compared to conventional liner/barrier contact fabrication. This lower resistance facilitates higher device density and extends 2D scaling.

![video-altText](/content/dam/site/prod-tech/semi/img/previous-tungsten-thumb.jpg)

*In conventional contact gapfill, the volume of conducting**metal is limited by the liner/barrier and nucleation layer.*

![video-altText](/content/dam/site/prod-tech/semi/img/new-tungsten-thumb.jpg)

**Selective tungsten makes the entire volume* *of the contact available for conducting metal**

![video-altText](/content/dam/site/prod-tech/semi/img/wafer-sidebyside-thumb.jpg)

*\*

*The Integrated Materials Solution for selective deposition combines**specialized pre-treatment of surfaces with a unique tungsten deposition process.*

![Endura Volta Selective W CVD](/content/dam/site/prod-tech/semi/img/2020_Selective%20W_endura_i10000w.png)

# Applied Materials Says New Tool Breaks Chip Resistance Bottleneck

## The smallest vertical connections were becoming unworkable for new generations of chips

[Samuel K. Moore](https://spectrum.ieee.org/u/samuel-k-moore)

07 Aug 2020

2 min read

Samuel K. Moore is IEEE Spectrum’s semiconductor editor.

Applied Materials' Endura Volta Selective Tungsten CVD system.

Image: Applied Materials

The regular scaling down in the size of transistors has always had a similar scaling down in the size of the vertical metal contacts that bridge the devices themselves to the wiring that links them up to form [logic gates](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/logic-gates).

But in the last few generations the resistance of those [tungsten](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/tungsten) contacts has become a drag on performance, and chip makers had been eyeing moves to alternative materials for future generations. Chip equipment supplier [Applied Materials](https://www.appliedmaterials.com/) says it’s come up with a machine that reverses this resistance problem, boosting the performance of today’s chips and allowing fabs to continue using tungsten into the future.

For devices on today’s most advanced chips “resistance is your key issue,” says Zhebo Chen, global product manager. “With the transistor you’ve taken an economy car and turned it into a race car, but if the roads are congested it doesn’t matter.”

The heart of the problem is that in the existing manufacturing process, tungsten contacts must be clad in a layer of titanium nitride. The process involves first forming a hole in a layer of dielectric to contact the transistor, then adding a layer of titanium nitride to line that hole and the surface of the dielectric. The next step uses a process called chemical vapor deposition to put tungsten on all the surfaces at once, growing from the nitride layer inwards within the holes until the hole is filled. Finally, the surface layer of tungsten is removed, leaving just the nitride-clad contacts.

The purpose of the nitride is two-fold. First, it helps the tungsten stick to the walls as the contact grows, preventing flaking. Second, it blocks fluorine used in the growth process from fouling the chip.

The problem is that even as the diameter of the contact has been shrunk down, the thickness of the cladding has not. In 7-nanometer chips today, contacts are only 20 nanometers wide, and only 25 percent of their volume is tungsten, explains Chen. The rest is cladding.

In July, [Applied Materials](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/applied-materials) released a machine that can make tungsten contacts with no cladding at all, reducing resistance by 40 percent. This “selective gapfill process” deposits tungsten from the bottom of the contact hole up instead of on all the surfaces at once. Because it uses a different chemistry than the previous process, there’s no need for a liner’s adhesion enhancement nor its fluorine-blocking ability. However, the process does need to be accomplished completely in a vacuum, so the company built it around a sealed system capable of moving wafers through multiple process steps without exposing them to air.

Although the new machine, called the [Endura Volta Selective Tungsten CVD](https://www.appliedmaterials.com/products/endura-selective-w-cvd) system, was introduced in July, Chen says it’s already being used in high-volume manufacturing by leading manufacturers.

“There’s more than 100 kilometers of tungsten contact on a [300-millimeter] wafer,” says Chen. “Doing this right in high-volume manufacturing is exceedingly difficult.”
