# Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects

###### Abstract

Today, interconnect resistance and reliability are key limiters for the performance of advanced CMOS circuits. As transistor scaling is slowing, interconnect scaling has become the main driver for circuit miniaturization, and interconnect limitations are expected to become even more stringent in future CMOS technology nodes. Current Cu dual-damascene metallization is also becoming increasingly challenging as critical interconnect dimensions approach 10 nm, alternative metallization schemes are researched with increasing intensity for about a decade. The selection of alternative metals is a highly multifaceted task and includes many criteria, covering the resistivity at reduced dimension, reliability and thermal aspects, as well as a sustainability perspective. In this tutorial, we introduce the basic criteria for alternative metal benchmarking and selection, and discuss the current state of the art of the field. The tutorial covers materials close to manufacturing introduction, materials under actual research, as well as future directions for fundamental research. While first alternatives to Cu metallization in commercial CMOS devices have become a reality recently, research for the ultimate interconnect metal is ongoing.

###### Contents

## I Introduction

Microelectronic circuits are central elements in myriads of electronic appliances in almost every aspect of today’s life. Logic circuits, memory cells, and sensors are used to process, store, and detect information not only in computers or cell phones but also in automobiles or medical applications. The success of microelectronics relies on the relentless miniaturization of the underlying building blocks, which, in the case of logic circuits based on transistors, has been epitomized by the famed Moore’s law.[moore\_cramming\_1965](#bib.bib1) Equivalent scaling laws exist also for other devices, for example for memory cells. The reduction of device dimensions in combination with the enormous increase of device density[burg\_moores\_2021](#bib.bib2) has led to large performance benefits, but also to lower energy consumption, and, at least for older generations, much reduced cost per function. As an example, the cost to fabricate one transistor has been reduced by a factor of 10910^{9} from 1970 to today.[moore\_11\_2003](#bib.bib3)

In the public perception, the focus has been historically on the scaling of transistors or memory cells. However, the scaling of the interconnect is of identical importance to uphold Moore’s law. Interconnect lines and vias provide signal, power, and clock to the active components of the circuits, such as complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) transistors or memory elements, and thus are central in the creation of complex microelectronic circuits and systems with advanced functionality (Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")a). As an example, the area of a SRAM cell that is used as cache memory in logic processors is determined in one direction by the gate pitch (also termed “contacted poly pitch”) of the transistors (the transistor size) and by the pitch of the metal lines (the interconnect pitch) in the orthogonal direction (Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")b). Hence, to reduce the SRAM cell area, both transistor and interconnect dimensions should be scaled.

![Refer to caption](2406.09106v1/Interconnect_SRAM.png)

Historically, the transistor performance has improved when dimensions were reduced, leading to the aforementioned performance benefits. By contrast, this does not hold for interconnects. Decreasing the cross-sectional area of a wire invariably increases its resistance per unit length, leading to larger energy dissipation and increased R​CRC-delay. Today, at interconnect line dimensions on the order of 12 to 15 nm (see Sec. [I.1](#S1.SS1 "I.1 Technology targets for future interconnects ‣ I Introduction ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")), the interconnect performance is typically the major limitation for the overall performance of advanced microelectronic circuits.[bohr\_interconnect\_1995](#bib.bib7); [meindl\_beyond\_2003](#bib.bib8); [ekekwe\_power\_2010](#bib.bib9); [baklanov\_advanced\_2012](#bib.bib10); [clarke\_process\_2014](#bib.bib11); [hauschildt\_advanced\_2014](#bib.bib12); [brain\_interconnect\_2016](#bib.bib13); [vyas-chip\_2018](#bib.bib14); [bonilla\_interconnect\_2020](#bib.bib15); [tokei\_inflection\_2020](#bib.bib16); [li\_interconnect\_2022](#bib.bib17); [nogami\_interconnect\_2023](#bib.bib18) For transistors, miniaturization has been accompanied by changes in the device architecture.[auth\_22nm\_2012](#bib.bib19); [loubet\_stacked\_2017](#bib.bib20); [jagannathan\_vertical-transport\_2021](#bib.bib21) However, for interconnects, architectural options are limited and therefore, performance improvements have to occur through materials and process innovation. Interconnect capacitance reduction can be achieved by using dielectrics with lower permittivity (low-κ\kappa dielectrics)[baklanov\_advanced\_2012](#bib.bib10) or air gaps.[gosset\_advanced\_2005](#bib.bib22); [chang\_airgap\_2023](#bib.bib23) However, progress has been stymied by the reduced mechanical stability of the resulting interconnects, which has led to reliability issues during packaging.

As a result, the optimization of the metallization scheme has become a major focus of interconnect research in recent years.[adelmann\_alternative\_2014](#bib.bib24); [hauschildt\_advanced\_2014](#bib.bib12); [zhang\_ruthenium\_2016](#bib.bib25); [wen\_ruthenium\_2016](#bib.bib26); [edelstein\_20\_2017](#bib.bib27); [adelmann\_alternative\_2018](#bib.bib28); [lin\_future\_2018](#bib.bib29); [gall\_resistivity\_2020](#bib.bib30); [gall\_search\_2020](#bib.bib31); [gall\_materials\_2021](#bib.bib32); [adelmann\_intermetallic\_2023](#bib.bib33); [nogami\_interconnect\_2023](#bib.bib18) The current Cu dual-damascene metallization scheme (Fig. [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")) that replaced Al-based metallization after 1999[edelstein\_full\_1997](#bib.bib34); [kriz\_overview\_2008](#bib.bib35); [gupta\_copper\_2009](#bib.bib36); [baklanov\_advanced\_2012](#bib.bib10) is facing growing issues for several reasons. First, Cu requires diffusion barriers and adhesion liners to ensure the interconnect reliability. Without diffusion barriers (typically TaN-based), Cu drift into surrounding dielectrics leads to rapid dielectric breakdown and shorting between adjacent lines (see Sec. [III](#S3 "III Interconnect reliability ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects") ). Moreover, Cu electromigration becomes and increasing issue at scaled dimensions (see Sec. [III](#S3 "III Interconnect reliability ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")). This can be mitigated by adhesion liner layers (typically Co) between the TaN barrier and Cu as well as by capping layers.[gupta\_copper\_2009](#bib.bib36); [baklanov\_advanced\_2012](#bib.bib10); [oates\_strategies\_2014](#bib.bib37); [hu\_future\_2018](#bib.bib38) However, the thickness of barrier and liner layers cannot be scaled below a combined thickness on the order of 2–3 nm without losing their function. Hence, for lines with reduced width, barrier and liner layers (with high resistivity) occupy an increasingly large volume fraction of the total metallization, leaving less and less space for Cu, while contributing little to the conductance of the wire. In addition, as it will be discussed below, the resistivity of Cu increases strongly for scaled dimensions due to an increasing influence of grain boundary and surface scattering. Both effects—higher resistivity and decreasing Cu volume fraction—contribute to an extremely rapid increase of the line and via resistances per unit length when the interconnect is scaled. This leads to a rapid deterioration of the interconnect performance even for short lines in. Finally, the dual-damascene metallization manufacturing scheme requires progressively disruptive modifications to allow for void- and defect-free interconnects with high mechanical stability.

![Refer to caption](2406.09106v1/Dual_Damascene.png)

These issues can be mitigated by selecting alternative metals that ideally do not require barrier and liner layers while showing a weaker sensitivity of the resistivity to small dimensions. While this cannot revert the increase of the line resistance per unit length, we will demonstrate below that alternative metals and metallization schemes can outperform Cu at sufficiently small line widths. In this tutorial, we will describe the different aspects relevant for the selection of potential alternative metals for advanced interconnects. The selection process is multifaceted and needs to address numerous aspects. We have therefore developed a multistage process to identify, downselect, and benchmark alternative metals for interconnect applications (Fig. [3](#S1.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")). The tutorial is organized as follows. We will first address the sensitivity of the resistivity to nanoscale dimensions and introduce a material screening process. This will then be followed by the introduction of reliability aspects, including the assessment and understanding of time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) and electromigration (EM). We then show the application of this process to elemental, binary, as well as ternary metals, and discuss current and future research directions. Since there is a strong relation between metal selection and future integration schemes, we will address integration and process aspects for alternative metals in future technology nodes. Finally, sustainability topics are increasingly becoming important to reduce the ecological footprint of the microelectronic industry. We will therefore introduce a life cycle assessment scheme for interconnect metals and apply it to various promising metals identified based on the previous criteria.

![Refer to caption](2406.09106v1/Figure_Workflow.png)

### I.1 Technology targets for future interconnects

Historically, the scaling of interconnect dimensions has been driven by industry-wide roadmaps, such as the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS),[noauthor\_itrs\_2015](#bib.bib39) presently called International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (ITRDS).[noauthor\_itrs\_nodate](#bib.bib40) However, today, no industry-wide roadmap exists and also technology node nomenclature has become ambiguous. Presently, minimum interconnect pitches in commercial advanced microelectronic chips are on the order of 25 nm[wu\_3nm\_2022](#bib.bib41) and are expected to decrease further during the coming decade (see Tab. [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ I.1 Technology targets for future interconnects ‣ I Introduction ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")), reaching predicted line width below 10 nm in the near future. This is of particular importance since the contacted poly pitch (the transistor gate pitch) cannot be miniaturized much further. Hence, future important area gains for, e.g., SRAM cells need to come mainly from transistor architecture as well as interconnect pitch scaling.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Year of HVM | 2024/25 | 2027/28 | 2029 | 2031 | 2033 | 2035 |
| Technology node | 2nm | 14A | 10A | 7A | 5A | 3A |
| Transistor technology | GAA | GAA | CFET | CFET | CFET | 2D |
| Min. metal pitch (nm) | 23 | 20 | 18 | 16 | 14 | 12 |
| Gate pitch (nm) | 45 | 42 | 42 | 39 | 39 | 36 |

As pointed out above, such small line widths may not be compatible with Cu dual-damascene metallization (Fig. [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")), used in today’s interconnects. Although additional optimizations of Cu dual-damascene processing are still ongoing, the minimum interconnect dimensions in the roadmap in Tab. [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ I.1 Technology targets for future interconnects ‣ I Introduction ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects") will require ultimately disruptive approaches using potentially novel materials, processes, as well as integration schemes. As the table indicates, relevant dimensions for interconnect lines and vias will be in the range between about 5 and 10 nm, which can be used as a guidance for both metal selection as well as process development.

## II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions

It has been known for several decades that the resistivity of metallic nanostructures, such as thin films or nanowires, is typically much higher than that of the corresponding bulk metals.[fuchs\_conductivity\_1938](#bib.bib44); [sondheimer\_mean\_1952](#bib.bib45); [soffer\_statistical\_1967](#bib.bib46); [mayadas\_electrical\_1969](#bib.bib47); [mayadas\_electrical-resistivity\_1970](#bib.bib48); [sambles\_electrical\_1980](#bib.bib49) This is a major issue for interconnect scaling since this leads to a line and via resistance increase that is much faster than expected from the reduction of the geometrical dimensions alone, especially in the targeted range of dimension below 10 nm. The resistivity increase has been attributed to the combined effect of scattering at (rough) surface or interfaces [fuchs\_conductivity\_1938](#bib.bib44); [sondheimer\_mean\_1952](#bib.bib45) as well as at grain boundaries. [mayadas\_electrical\_1969](#bib.bib47); [mayadas\_electrical-resistivity\_1970](#bib.bib48) For a quantitative description, various transport models have been developed for thin films with top and bottom surfaces/interfaces.[mayadas\_electrical-resistivity\_1970](#bib.bib48); [namba\_resistivity\_1970](#bib.bib50); [marom\_effect\_2006](#bib.bib51); [timoshevskii\_influence\_2008](#bib.bib52); [feldman\_dependence\_2008](#bib.bib53); [ke\_resistivity\_2009](#bib.bib54); [rickman\_resistivity\_2012](#bib.bib55); [moors\_resistivity\_2014](#bib.bib56); [moors\_modeling\_2015](#bib.bib57); [zhou\_resistivity\_2018](#bib.bib58); [zhou\_electrical\_2018](#bib.bib59) We note however that currently no equivalent one-dimensional transport model exists that can describe wires with four surrounding surfaces. Yet, the basic qualitative behavior is expected to be rather similar and therefore “thin-film-derived” resistivity models have been used to understand the scaling performance of nanowires also.[hinode\_resistivity\_2001](#bib.bib60); [steinhogl\_size-dependent\_2002](#bib.bib61); [maitrejean\_experimental\_2006](#bib.bib62); [marom\_size\_dependent\_2006](#bib.bib63); [khoo\_aspect\_2007](#bib.bib64); [graham\_resistivity\_2010](#bib.bib65); [kim\_structural\_2011](#bib.bib66); [chawla\_electron\_2011](#bib.bib67); [smith\_evaluation\_2019](#bib.bib68)

In this section, we introduce the underlying physics of the resistivity of metal nanostructures. It will be shown that the mean free path of the charge carriers in bulk metals is a key parameter to characterize the dependence of the resistivity on nanostructure dimensions. Subsequently, we address additional scattering contributions in compound metals. Finally, we then introduce ab initio screening methods to compute the mean free path and to identify promising metals with potentially lower resistivity than Cu at the nanoscale.[gall\_electron\_2016](#bib.bib69); [dutta\_thickness\_2017](#bib.bib70); [moors\_first-principles-based\_2022](#bib.bib71)

### II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures

#### II.1.1 Semiclassical description of electron transport

The most common approach to understand the increase of resistivity at low dimensions relies on the Boltzmann Transport Equation (BTE). The BTE describes the statistics of the carriers distribution out-of-equilibrium, e.g., when an electrical field is applied.

In absence of temperature and composition gradients or magnetic field, the BTE can be written as

Matthiessen’s rule may be violated in the case of nanocrystalline nearly-amorphous films with large disorder.[mooij\_electrical\_1973](#bib.bib76); [gurvitch\_ioffe-regel\_1981](#bib.bib77); [tsuei\_nonuniversality\_1986](#bib.bib78) In such films, localization effects become important,[imry\_possible\_1980](#bib.bib79); [lee\_disordered\_1985](#bib.bib80) which is typically accompanied by a significantly reduced temperature dependence (the temperature coefficient of the resistivity) with respect to the bulk behavior.[mooij\_electrical\_1973](#bib.bib76); [tsuei\_nonuniversality\_1986](#bib.bib78) However, the derivation of Eq. ([7](#S2.E7 "In II.1.1 Semiclassical description of electron transport ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")) does not require Matthiessen’s rule to hold for surface scattering and grain boundary or phonon scattering. As a matter of fact, Matthiessen’s rule is typically not cromulent for surface scattering and grain boundary scattering in thin metallic films, as already pointed out in Ref. [mayadas\_electrical-resistivity\_1970](#bib.bib48) due to the “renormalization” of the mean free path by grain boundary scattering. This renders the separate quantification of bulk, surface scattering, and grain boundary scattering contributions to the thin film resistivity difficult[dutta\_thickness\_2017](#bib.bib70) and certain approximate versions of Eq. ([7](#S2.E7 "In II.1.1 Semiclassical description of electron transport ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")) that separate contributions from surface and grain boundary scattering should be used with caution.

#### II.1.2 Material dependence of thin film resistivity scaling

Equation ([7](#S2.E7 "In II.1.1 Semiclassical description of electron transport ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")) contains five independent material parameters of the problem: the bulk single-crystal conductivity, the electron mean free path, the specularity of the scattering at film surfaces/interfaces, the average grain size, and the grain reflection coefficient. In practice, one often finds a strong dependence of the grain size on film thickness, which leads to a second indirect source of thickness dependence for the thin film resistivity, besides surface scattering. The relation between grain size and film thickness ℓ⁡(h)\ell(h) depends strongly on deposition process parameters and is not a unique function of the material itself. Although sometimes a linear relation has been assumed, this is experimentally typically not observed in the relevant thickness range (see Fig. [4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ II.1.2 Material dependence of thin film resistivity scaling ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")a). It can also be affected by post-deposition annealing, which can lead to grain growth or recrystallization.[doherty\_current\_1997](#bib.bib81); [humphreys\_recrystallization\_2004](#bib.bib82)

![Refer to caption](2406.09106v1/MFP_MS_simul.png)

Consequently, it is impossible to quantitatively predict the resistivity of metallic nanostructures based on bulk properties alone. As mentioned before, the relation ℓ⁡(h)\ell(h) depends on deposition process characteristics and thermal budget; no predictive models are available for grain structures and grain sizes beyond general trends.[thompson\_structure\_2000](#bib.bib83); [petrov\_microstructural\_2003](#bib.bib84) Since experiments have shown that grain boundary scattering can dominate the thin film resistivity,[dutta\_thickness\_2017](#bib.bib70) the screening of metals should include the possibility of obtaining large grain films (or nanowires), which can however not be achieved by (ab initio) calculations and therefore experimental studies of grain size and annealing behavior need to complement the transport and reliability proxies for more realistic metal assessments.

A second limitation of is the difficulty to compute or predict realistic values for parameters RR and pp. RR describes the reflection probability of an electron at a grain boundary, which depends in general on the (relative) orientation of the grains at both sides of the boundary and the atomic configuration of grain boundary. In general, calculations[zhou\_first-principles\_2022](#bib.bib85); [feldman\_simulation\_2010](#bib.bib86); [zhou\_ab\_2010](#bib.bib87); [cesar\_calculated\_2014](#bib.bib88) and experiments[kim\_large\_2010](#bib.bib89); [kim\_structural\_2011](#bib.bib66) have consistently observed large differences in RR between small angle or coincidence grain boundaries (with low RR) and large angle random grain boundaries (large RR). In polycrystalline films, the relevant RR will be an effective average over all grain boundary configurations and therefore dependent on the microstructure. While some trends with cohesive energy—larger cohesive energies are expected to lead to larger RR—appear plausible,[zhu\_electron\_2010](#bib.bib90) RR cannot be considered to depend on the metal only. In addition, the surface scattering specularity pp depends not only on the metal but also the properties of the surrounding interfaces or surfaces. Both the cladding material[rossnagel\_alteration\_2004](#bib.bib91); [tay\_electrical\_2005](#bib.bib92); [feldman\_calculation\_2009](#bib.bib93); [ke\_resistivity\_2009](#bib.bib54) and the interface or surface roughness are expected to play major roles. While surface scattering rates have been studied as a function of surface roughness theoretically[feldman\_dependence\_2008](#bib.bib53); [timoshevskii\_influence\_2008](#bib.bib52); [ke\_resistivity\_2009](#bib.bib54); [rickman\_resistivity\_2012](#bib.bib55); [moors\_resistivity\_2014](#bib.bib56); [moors\_modeling\_2015](#bib.bib57); [zhou\_electrical\_2018](#bib.bib59) and experimentally,[marom\_effect\_2006](#bib.bib51); [feldman\_dependence\_2008](#bib.bib53) quantitative agreement between theory and experiment is not established. Hence, calculations are not predictive and cannot be used for screening. Moreover, due to the potential dependence on cladding material and surface roughness, surface scattering cannot be considered a materials property.

The above section shows however that the resistivity increase, both due to surface or grain boundary scattering, scales with the bulk mean free path of the charge carriers, λ\lambda. Therefore, the impact of large RR, small grains, or diffusive interfaces can be mitigated by a short λ\lambda. This is illustrated in Fig. [4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ II.1.2 Material dependence of thin film resistivity scaling ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")b, which depicts the dependence of the thin film resistivity on the grain size, calculated using Eq. ([7](#S2.E7 "In II.1.1 Semiclassical description of electron transport ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")), for ρ0=5.3\rho\_{0}=5.3 μ​Ω\mu\Omegacm, R=0.45R=0.45, p=0p=0 (diffuse surface scattering), and a fixed thickness of 20 nm, as an example. The results indicate that a shorter mean free path λ\lambda leads to a weaker dependence of the resistivity on grain size, thus mitigating the effects of grain boundary scattering. A similar behavior can be found for the dependence of the thin film resistivity on the film thickness in presence of diffuse surface scattering. Consequently, This has led to the search of metals with short λ\lambda as alternatives to Cu. Cu mean free path can reach value as high as 40 nm,[gall\_electron\_2016](#bib.bib69) which is large compared to typical interconnect dimensions and grain sizes. Therefore, metals with much shorter mean promise to be much less sensitive to interconnect scaling. An ab-initio-based methodology to screen for short-λ\lambda metals will be described in Sec. [II.3](#S2.SS3 "II.3 Ab initio screening of alternative metals ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects"). The full alternative metal screening process including its current status will be detailed in Sec. [IV](#S4 "IV Downselection of alternative metals ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects").

#### II.1.3 Anisotropy effects on thin film resistivity scaling

The above models assume a spherical isotropic Fermi surface (a free electron gas with effective mass) and therefore both bulk and thin film resistivities do not depend on the crystallographic direction of the current. This allows for the derivation of the Fuchs–Sondheimer Eq. ([5](#S2.E5 "In II.1.1 Semiclassical description of electron transport ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")) and the Mayadas–Shatzkes Eq. ([7](#S2.E7 "In II.1.1 Semiclassical description of electron transport ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")). Due to the large complexity, currently no thin film resistivity model exists that considers the detailed band structure of the metal in combination with both surface and grain boundary scattering. While the Mayadas–Shatzkes model (Eq. ([7](#S2.E7 "In II.1.1 Semiclassical description of electron transport ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects"))) has been able to describe well experimental measurements,[learn\_resistivity\_1985](#bib.bib94); [zhang\_influence\_2006](#bib.bib95); [zhang\_influence\_2006b](#bib.bib96); [camacho\_surface\_2006](#bib.bib97); [sun\_dominant\_2009](#bib.bib98); [sun\_surface\_2010](#bib.bib99); [chawla\_electron\_2011](#bib.bib67); [barmak\_surface\_2014](#bib.bib100); [dutta\_thickness\_2017](#bib.bib70); [founta\_properties\_2022](#bib.bib101) the missing quantitative understanding of the model parameters RR and pp limits the assessment of the accuracy of the spherical Fermi surface approximation for different metals.

It should be noted that from a macroscopic point of view, the conductivity of cubic systems is isotropic and therefore, the approximation by a spherical Fermi surface may be appropriate. However, other less symmetric (hexagonal, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, trigonal) structures lead to anisotropic conductivity in the bulk metal. An example is hexagonal Ru, which has a lower resistivity along the hexagonal axis that in the two perpendicular (in-plane) directions.[volkenshtejn\_electric\_1978](#bib.bib102); [savitskii\_research\_1979](#bib.bib103) To describe this situation, a semiclassical Mayadas–Shatzkes-derived model was developed for ellipsoidal Fermi surfaces.[de\_clercq\_resistivity\_2018](#bib.bib104). Such a model can represent metals with hexagonal, tetragonal, or orthorhombic crystal symmetry, Mathematical details are beyond the scope of this tutorial, but the model finds a strong impact of Fermi surface anisotropy on surface scattering, while not affecting grain boundary scattering. This is illustrated in Fig. [5](#S2.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ II.1.3 Anisotropy effects on thin film resistivity scaling ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects"), which shows the bulk resistivity vs. films as a function of the effective mass anisotropy of the Fermi surface, using the model in Ref. [de\_clercq\_resistivity\_2018](#bib.bib104). Here, grain boundary scattering was neglected (R=0R=0) and only surface scattering was active. The results show that for a two-dimensional metal with large in-plane conductivity (small in-plane effective mass) and small out-of-plane conductivity (large in-plane effective mass) leads to the gradual suppression of surface scattering and an associated reduction of the thickness dependence of the thin film resistivity due to surface scattering.

![Refer to caption](2406.09106v1/Aniso_simul.png)

In principle, this effect can be utilized to reduce the resistivity of nanowires and therefore, the usage of two-dimensional and one-dimensional metals (with a single high conductivity crystallographic direction) for interconnect applications has been proposed.[kumar\_ultralow\_2022](#bib.bib105) Two points are however noteworthy. Since Matthiessen’s rule is generally not applicable, the presence of strong grain boundary scattering (which is not affected by the reduced dimensionality) leads to a suppression of surface scattering in two-dimensional metals, reducing the advantages due to anisotropy for small-grain metals. Furthermore, the usage of one-dimensional metals in interconnects requires single crystal metals so that the current direction is always aligned with the high-conductivity crystallographic direction. Presently, there is no practicable integration route for single crystal lines in commercial interconnects and therefore, such considerations are currently limited to fundamental material science.

### II.2 Point defects, disorder, and alloy scattering in metals

Before introducing first-principles screening methodologies to identify and downselect promising metals for interconnect applications based on the mean free path λ\lambda, we shortly introduce additional sources of scattering that are of great importance for compound metals.

In general, any deviation from periodicity in a crystal can scatter electrons.[ashcroft\_solid\_1976](#bib.bib106) Elemental metals contain vacancy (or vacancy cluster) defects or impurities. In typical polycrystalline high-quality thin films of relevant metals, vacancies and impurities limit the resistivity at low temperature but are typically negligible at room temperature, where scattering by phonons, grain boundaries, and surfaces dominate.

However, the situation is very different for compound metals. Alloys are intrinsically disordered materials with random distributions of the different atoms on the lattice sites. The resulting crystal is therefore not periodic, leading to high resistivity due to alloy scattering. This is illustrated in Fig. [6](#S2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ II.2 Point defects, disorder, and alloy scattering in metals ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects") for the seminal case of the Cu–Au system.[Johansson\_CuAu\_1936](#bib.bib107) For disordered random CuxAu1-x alloys, the resistivity is much larger than for the elemental metals Cu and Au, with a resistivity maximum at 50% of Au, where disorder is largest. By contrast, the system also contains two ordered intermetallic phases: Cu3Au and CuAu. Close to the stoichiometries of these ordered phases, the resistivity shows a sharp minimum, much lower than for disordered random alloys.

These observations indicate that alloy scattering needs to be avoided to achieve resistivities for compound metals that are relevant for interconnect applications. Hence, in addition to elemental metals, for which these issues do not arise, only ordered intermetallics are of potential interest in alternative metal screening exercises. This issue is aggravated by the challenge to measure and optimize the intermetallic ordering for thin films. More details and a summary of the state of the art can be found in Secs. [IV.3](#S4.SS3 "IV.3 Binary intermetallics ‣ IV Downselection of alternative metals ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects") and [IV.4](#S4.SS4 "IV.4 Ternary compounds ‣ IV Downselection of alternative metals ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects").

![Refer to caption](2406.09106v1/Alloy_Intermetallic.png)

### II.3 Ab initio screening of alternative metals

The discussion in Secs. [II.1.2](#S2.SS1.SSS2 "II.1.2 Material dependence of thin film resistivity scaling ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects") and [II.1.3](#S2.SS1.SSS3 "II.1.3 Anisotropy effects on thin film resistivity scaling ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects") signifies that predictive calculations of the resistivity of a thin film or a nanowire are not possible without detailed knowledge about microstructure, which is process dependent. Moreover, resistivity models such as Eq. ([7](#S2.E7 "In II.1.1 Semiclassical description of electron transport ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")) assume a spherical Fermi surface (free electron gas) and metal-specific scaling properties are only represented by a single mean free path value. While it is possible to compute the electron-phonon-limited resistivity of metals from first principles considering detailed band structures,[Ponce2020](#bib.bib108) this remains still today computationally very intensive, limiting practicable system sizes to a few atoms per unit cell. The main bottleneck is the computation of the relaxation time from the electron–phonon coupling. Furthermore, including grain boundaries with such a formalism is cumbersome. All these points restrict the possibility to set up fully predictive downselection methodology, which immediately identifies the most promising metal candidates for direct interconnect applications. Therefore, the metal selection problem needs to be tackled in a staged approach, as illustrated in Fig. [3](#S1.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects"). Nonetheless, screening of metals of potential interest is possible via the so-called ρ0​λ\rho\_{0}\lambda figure of merit, which can be calculated by ab initio methods with limited computational effort. The application of the overall methodology to screen elemental and compound metals will be described below in Sec. [IV](#S4 "IV Downselection of alternative metals ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects").

Within the BTE approach, the conductivity tensor of a (bulk) metal film is given by Eq. ([3](#S2.E3 "In II.1.1 Semiclassical description of electron transport ‣ II.1 Electron transport in bulk metals and nanostructures ‣ II Metal resistivity at nanoscale dimensions ‣ Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects")) as

This is a scientific tutorial paper (arXiv preprint 2406.09106) titled "Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects." The paper addresses the critical challenge that interconnect resistance and reliability are becoming key limiters for advanced CMOS circuit performance as transistor scaling slows and interconnect dimensions approach 10 nm.

**Key Context:** Current Cu dual-damascene metallization (which replaced Al-based metallization after 1999) faces growing issues at scaled dimensions. Cu requires diffusion barriers (typically TaN-based) and adhesion liners (typically Co) that cannot scale below a combined 2-3 nm thickness without losing function, leaving less space for actual Cu conductance. Additionally, Cu resistivity increases strongly at small dimensions due to grain boundary and surface scattering.

**Technology Roadmap:** The paper presents projected interconnect scaling targets through 2035, showing minimum metal pitch decreasing from 23 nm (2024/25, 2nm node) to 12 nm (2035, 3A node), with relevant interconnect line and via dimensions expected in the 5-10 nm range.

**Physics of Resistivity at Nanoscale:** The paper details the Boltzmann Transport Equation (BTE) framework, the Fuchs-Sondheimer equation for thin-film conductivity with surface scattering, and the Mayadas-Shatzkes model incorporating grain boundary scattering. Key material parameters affecting thin-film resistivity include: bulk single-crystal conductivity, electron mean free path, surface specularity (p), average grain size, and grain reflection coefficient (R).

**Key Finding:** The mean free path (λ) of charge carriers is a critical parameter. Cu's mean free path can reach up to 40 nm, which is large compared to interconnect dimensions. Metals with shorter λ are much less sensitive to interconnect scaling and grain boundary scattering effects. This has driven the search for alternative metals with short λ.

**Ab Initio Screening Methodology:** The paper introduces a ρ₀λ figure of merit that can be calculated via ab initio methods with limited computational effort, using either the constant relaxation time approximation or the constant mean free path approximation. This allows screening of candidate metals without full electron-phonon coupling calculations, which remain computationally prohibitive for large systems.

**Important Considerations:**
- Predictive calculations of thin-film resistivity are impossible without detailed knowledge of microstructure, which is process-dependent
- Grain size dependence on film thickness depends on deposition process parameters, not uniquely on material
- The reflection coefficient R and specularity p cannot be reliably predicted and are not purely materials properties
- Alloy scattering must be avoided in compound metals; only ordered intermetallics (not random alloys) are of potential interest for interconnects
- Anisotropy in Fermi surface can suppress surface scattering in 2D metals, but requires single-crystal lines with no current integration route yet
- Matthiessen's rule is typically not valid for surface and grain boundary scattering in thin metallic films

The paper describes a multistage screening process covering elemental, binary, and ternary metals, integration/process aspects for future nodes, and sustainability/life cycle assessment considerations.

# Molybdenum’s Role in Ultra-Fast Computing: The Metal Behind the Speed

* [Tweet](https://twitter.com/share)

Molybdenum’s Role in Ultra-Fast Computing: The Metal Behind the Speed

As the world races toward faster, smarter, and more connected technologies, the demand for ultra-fast computing is reshaping the semiconductor landscape. From AI and autonomous systems to 5G and edge computing, modern applications are generating massive volumes of data that must be processed, transmitted, and stored with unprecedented speed and reliability.

To keep up, we need advanced logic devices, the brains behind modern computing. These chips are evolving rapidly to deliver greater power and speed. Innovations like smaller transistors, new design architectures, and high-performance materials have already pushed performance boundaries.

As we scale below the 10 nm threshold and embrace 3D architectures like gate-all-around (GAA) transistors and backside power delivery, chip manufacturing becomes significantly more complex. New metals are being introduced to reduce wiring delays and improve reliability, and at the heart of this transformation is a surprising hero: molybdenum.

Why Molybdenum?

Traditionally, materials like tungsten (W) and copper (Cu) have been used in semiconductor interconnects. But as device geometry shrinks and performance requirements soar, these materials are hitting their limits. Molybdenum (Mo) is a promising metal for contacts and local interconnects because it offers a combination of low resistivity, high melting point, excellent thermal and chemical stability, and good electromigration resistance. It also is barrierless. This makes molybdenum well suited for advanced nodes, where traditional materials like Cu and W face scaling limitations.

With a set of properties that make it ideal for next-generation logic devices, molybdenum offers:

* Lower resistivity at nanoscale: molybdenum offers up to 30% lower resistivity than tungsten in thin films, enabling faster signal transmission and reduced power loss.
* Barrierless integration: Unlike tungsten and copper, molybdenum doesn’t require a barrier layer to prevent diffusion, simplifying manufacturing and improving yield.
* Scalability: molybdenum supports high aspect ratio features and 3D architectures like gate-all-around (GAA) transistors and backside power, which are essential for advanced logic chips.

Unlike copper and tungsten, molybdenum does not require a liner between itself and the dielectric because it forms a stable, low-resistance interface with the dielectric, and its high melting point and resistance to oxidation enables its direct deposition and integration. The lower resistance in the interconnects means that electrical signals can travel faster through the structure – reducing wiring delays and improving reliability. This is essential for high-speed data processing and retrieval, which are critical for the performance of logic devices.

Overall, molybdenum offers a balance of conductivity, scalability, and process simplicity. Its ability to perform without barrier layers and maintain low resistivity in thin films makes it a strong candidate for next-gen logic devices.

  

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  |  |
|  | **Cu** Copper | **W** Tungsten | **Mo** Molybdenum |
| Bulk Resistivity (μΩ-cm) | Very low (~1.68 µΩ·cm) | Higher (~5.6 µΩ·cm) | Moderate (~5.3 µΩ·cm) |
| Thin Film Resistivity | High in small features due to scattering | High in nanoscale features | Lower than W in small features |
| Barrier Layer Requirement | Requires barrier (e.g.TaN) | Requires barrier (e.g.TiN) | No barrier needed |
| Scalability to Advanced Nodes | Challenging below 10 nm | Used but reaching limits | Highly scalable |
| Deposition Method | Damascene | CVD/ALD | ALD, CVD, Selective ALD |
| Thermal Conductivity (W/m-K) | 400 | 170 | 138 |
| Mean-Free Path Suitability | Too long for nanoscale | Long: resistivity increases | Shorter: ideal for nanoscale |
| Corrosion Resistance | Moderate; needs protection | Good | Requires tailored CMP/etch |
| Industry Trend | Being phased out at local interconnects | Being phased out at contacts and vias | Emerging as successor to W and CU |

Scaling Interconnects with Molybdenum

As chip dimensions shrink, wires that connect transistors on a chip require new metallurgies with lower resistivity to avoid signal delays and improve reliability. Copper has long been the preferred metal for interconnect wiring, but in recent years, interconnects have had to scale down in size due to shrinking dimensions resulting in new limitations for Cu. As chip dimensions shrink, copper's resistivity increases, leading to higher resistance and power consumption in devices.

Copper interconnects also use liner and barrier layers to prevent copper diffusion and enhance adhesion. At smaller scales, these added layers increasingly contribute to the overall resistance and volume of the interconnect creating even more challenges for device makers.

Today, traditional copper interconnects are hitting a major barrier to continued scaling, a barrier known as the RC challenge. The RC challenge refers to the increasing resistance (R) and capacitance (C) in interconnects as devices scale down, which leads to signal delay, power loss, and performance degradation in integrated circuits.

![14325 blog image for recreation v2](https://blog.entegris.com/hs-fs/hubfs/14325%20blog%20image%20for%20recreation%20v2.jpg?width=1200&height=600&name=14325%20blog%20image%20for%20recreation%20v2.jpg)Engineers are now introducing materials such as cobalt, molybdenum, and ruthenium in select contacts and local interconnect layers, where copper’s liner and barrier requirements dominate resistance and limit further scaling. Precursors for these materials and the processes used to deposit these films are still maturing but companies like Entegris are at the forefront of these innovations. Once a distant vision, the molybdenum transition is now a reality.

As logic devices continue to scale, it’s important to distinguish where new metals can realistically be introduced and where fundamental architectural constraints remain.  
While copper faces increasing resistance challenges at extremely small dimensions, it is not expected to be replaced at tight-pitch interconnect (TPI) levels such as Metal 1 through Metal 4. These layers sit adjacent to SRAM structures, most critically the L1 cache, where low resistance is essential for performance.

The critical dimension (CD) of SRAM features is four to five times larger than the smallest CDs at TPI, driving a strong requirement for very low sheet resistance (Rs). Alternative metals such as molybdenum, tungsten, and iridium simply cannot meet this requirement at those levels today.

Even as advanced packaging technologies pull L2 and L3 caches off chip using hybrid bonding, L1 cache is expected to remain on chip for the foreseeable future, reinforcing copper’s continued role in these critical layers.

Precision Manufacturing with Mo

Molybdenum is emerging as a key replacement for tungsten and a selective enabler of next-generation logic integration. Thanks to innovations in Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD), Area Selective Deposition (ASD) and Chemical Mechanical Planarization (CMP), molybdenum can be deposited with atomic-level precision. This ensures defect-free contacts and interconnects and streamlined process steps making it viable for high-volume manufacturing.

Real-World Impact

From smartphones and data centers to AI accelerators and autonomous vehicles, molybdenum is helping power the next wave of ultra-fast computing. Its unique properties make it a strategic upgrade for select logic layers where legacy materials no longer scale effectively.

This webpage is an Entegris "Ensights" blog article titled "Molybdenum's Role in Ultra-Fast Computing: The Metal Behind the Speed," published in May 2026. The article discusses how molybdenum (Mo) is emerging as a critical replacement metal for tungsten (W) and copper (Cu) in advanced semiconductor interconnects as the industry scales below the 10 nm threshold and adopts 3D architectures like gate-all-around (GAA) transistors and backside power delivery.

Key content includes:

WHY MOLYBDENUM: Molybdenum offers a combination of low resistivity, high melting point, excellent thermal/chemical stability, good electromigration resistance, and is barrierless (no barrier layer needed). Its key advantages include up to 30% lower resistivity than tungsten in thin films, barrierless integration that simplifies manufacturing and improves yield, and scalability supporting high aspect ratio features and 3D architectures.

COMPARISON TABLE (Cu vs W vs Mo): Copper has very low bulk resistivity (~1.68 µΩ-cm) but high thin film resistivity in small features and requires a barrier (e.g., TaN); tungsten has higher resistivity (~5.6 µΩ-cm), requires barrier (e.g., TiN), and is reaching limits; molybdenum has moderate bulk resistivity (~5.3 µΩ-cm), lower thin film resistivity than tungsten in small features, and requires no barrier. Molybdenum uses ALD, CVD, and selective ALD deposition methods. Industry trend: copper is being phased out at local interconnects, tungsten at contacts and vias, with molybdenum emerging as the successor.

THE RC CHALLENGE: Traditional copper interconnects are hitting a scaling barrier due to increasing resistance (R) and capacitance (C) as devices scale down, causing signal delay, power loss, and performance degradation. Copper's liner and barrier layers increasingly dominate resistance at smaller scales. Engineers are introducing cobalt, molybdenum, and ruthenium in select contacts and local interconnect layers.

LIMITATIONS: Copper is NOT expected to be replaced at tight-pitch interconnect (TPI) levels (Metal 1 through Metal 4) because these layers sit adjacent to SRAM structures (especially L1 cache) where low resistance is essential. The critical dimension of SRAM features is 4-5 times larger than the smallest CDs at TPI, and molybdenum, tungsten, and iridium cannot meet the very low sheet resistance (Rs) requirements at those levels today. L1 cache is expected to remain on chip for the foreseeable future, even as L2 and L3 caches are pulled off-chip via hybrid bonding.

PRECISION MANUFACTURING: Innovations in Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD), Area Selective Deposition (ASD), and Chemical Mechanical Planarization (CMP) enable molybdenum to be deposited with atomic-level precision, ensuring defect-free contacts and interconnects viable for high-volume manufacturing.

Entegris is positioned as a leader enabling molybdenum integration for advanced logic, supporting transitions across contacts, vias, backside power delivery, and selective prefilling schemes. A link is provided to learn more about Entegris molybdenum offerings (entegris.info/moly).

--- SOURCE 1: Silicon Manufacturing: Comparing Physical Vapor, Atomic Layer, and Chemical Vapor Deposition | Wafer World ---
URL: https://www.waferworld.com/post/silicon-manufacturing-comparing-physical-vapor-atomic-layer-and-chemical-vapor-deposition

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Wafer World Inc. (a silicon wafer manufacturer based in West Palm Beach, FL) provides a comprehensive comparison of the three primary thin-film deposition techniques used in silicon manufacturing: Physical Vapor Deposition (PVD), Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD), and Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD). Published September 1, 2025, the article explains that thin-film deposition is a critical step in semiconductor fabrication involving ultra-thin material layers deposited onto silicon wafers.

**Key Content:**

- **PVD** is a physical process (sputtering or evaporation) where material is vaporized from a solid source and condensed onto the wafer. Benefits include high deposition rates, low cost, and versatility with many materials. Limitations include poor step coverage on high-aspect-ratio structures, difficulty controlling film thickness at atomic scales, and line-of-sight shadowing effects. Best for thicker films, larger feature sizes (≥100 nm), and budget-conscious/high-throughput applications.

- **CVD** deposits solid material via gas-phase chemical reactions. It produces high-purity, conformal coatings including SiO₂, Si₃N₄, polysilicon, and tungsten. Advantages include uniform thickness on complex 3D geometries and dense, low-defect coatings. Limitations include high temperature requirements (400–900°C) and hazardous gases (silane, ammonia, hydrogen chloride). Best for high-purity conformal films and complex compounds.

- **ALD** deposits films one atomic layer at a time using sequential, self-limiting reactions. Used for high-k dielectrics (HfO₂, Al₂O₃) in CMOS, barrier layers in 3D NAND and DRAM, and MEMS/nanodevice coatings. Offers atomic-level thickness control, excellent step coverage on 3D geometries, and pinhole-free films. Limitations include slower deposition rates, higher costs, and limited material systems. Best for sub-10nm technologies and high-aspect-ratio features.

The article emphasizes that in advanced manufacturing, these techniques are often combined within the same process stack (e.g., PVD seed layers, CVD interlayer dielectrics, ALD barrier layers) to balance cost, speed, and precision.

The page also notes Wafer World's acquisition of Micro Reclaim Technologies completed January 1, 2026, and provides company contact information (1100 Technology Place, Suite 104, West Palm Beach, FL 33407; phone 561-842-4441; sales@waferworld.com). The company holds AS9100D with ISO 9001 certification.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In the world of silicon manufacturing, the precision and performance of every thin film layer matter. Whether you're building transistors, MEMS devices, or optical coatings, choosing the right deposition technique can significantly impact yield, reliability, and device performance."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: US10847463B2 - Seed layers for copper interconnects - Google Patents ---
URL: https://patents.google.com/patent/US10847463B2/and

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Google Patents page for US Patent US10847463B2, titled "Seed layers for copper interconnects," assigned to Applied Materials, Inc. The patent was filed on August 13, 2018 (priority date August 22, 2017), and granted/published on November 24, 2020. The inventors are Zhiyuan Wu, Meng Chu Tseng, Mehul B. Naik, and Ben-Li Sheu. The patent has family members in the US, EP, JP, KR, CN, and TW, and is legally active.

**Technical Content:** The patent relates to semiconductor device manufacturing, specifically methods of forming ruthenium (Ru) doped copper (Cu) seed layers for copper interconnects. As circuit densities increase and transistor dimensions shrink, wire interconnect resistance and conductivity dominate device performance metrics including power consumption, RC delay, and reliability.

**Problem Addressed:** Copper seed layers deposited by PVD suffer from coverage gaps caused by copper agglomeration and discontinuous deposition (shadowing effects), which lead to voids in bulk copper, electromigration failures, and reduced device reliability.

**Solution/Method:** The patent describes forming a seed layer with a stacked structure comprising:
1. A first copper layer (deposited by ALD, CVD, or PVD; typically ~0.5-20 nm thick, ~4 nm preferred)
2. A ruthenium layer disposed on the first copper layer (typically 1-20 Å thick)
3. A second copper layer disposed on the ruthenium layer (typically 0.5-200 nm, ~2 nm preferred)

The ruthenium layer is deposited between the copper layers. Since copper and ruthenium are generally immiscible, the ruthenium pins the copper at grain boundaries, preventing copper agglomeration and electromigration. The method also involves a barrier layer (e.g., tantalum nitride) on the dielectric material layer to prevent copper diffusion, and subsequent bulk copper deposition via electroplating or reflow/gap fill, followed by CMP.

**Key Process Details:**
- ALD deposition of copper uses copper-containing organometallic precursors (e.g., Cu(DEAB)2, Cu(DMAP)2) with hydrogen, at chamber pressures of 1-30 Torr, substrate temperatures of 50-400°C, and plasma power of 100-1000 W (e.g., 400 W at 13.56 MHz).
- Ruthenium layer deposited using ruthenium-containing organometallics (e.g., methyl-cyclohexadine ruthenium tricarbonyl) with hydrogen, at 1-50 Torr and 100-400°C.
- The ratio of copper to ruthenium in the seed layer is between 99.9:1 and 4:1.

**Benefits:** Suppressed copper agglomeration, reduced minimum seed layer thickness for continuous coverage, improved reflow fill, reduced liner thickness requirements (increasing bulk copper volume and reducing line resistance), suppressed copper electromigration for increased circuit density and reliability, and ruthenium diffuses more slowly into copper than cobalt or manganese so line resistance is not negatively impacted.

**Equipment:** Methods can be performed in ENDURA® PVD, PRODUCER® CVD, and OLYMPIA® ALD chambers from Applied Materials, Inc. (Santa Clara, CA). Chambers can be connected under vacuum via a transfer chamber to prevent surface oxidation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Copper agglomeration occurs when the deposited copper coalesces into thicker coverage in some areas by pulling copper away from surrounding areas. Discontinuous deposition on the walls of the openings is typically due to a shadowing effect inherent to the copper seed physical vapor deposition (PVD) process for some opening geometries."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Physical Vapor Deposition (PVD) | SemiFlows Blog ---
URL: https://semiflows.com/blog/what-is-physical-vapor-deposition-in-semiconductor-manufacturing

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This SemiFlows blog article by Joseph Swann provides a comprehensive overview of Physical Vapor Deposition (PVD) in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, covering its physics, processes, challenges, evolution across technology nodes, related processes, and future outlook.

**Definition & Fundamentals:** PVD is a high-vacuum thin-film deposition technique that uses physical methods (as opposed to chemical reactions in CVD) to produce constituent atoms that travel through a low-pressure gas phase and condense on a substrate. It encompasses two primary techniques: evaporation (heating a source until it vaporizes) and sputter deposition (bombarding a solid source with energetic plasma ions). Sputtering is the chief method for depositing aluminum, copper seeds, and other metals in modern manufacturing. PVD requires extremely low-pressure environments to enable transport without excessive scattering, and it avoids complex by-product contamination common in CVD.

**Physics & Mechanism:** Sputter deposition relies on momentum transfer. The chamber is evacuated, argon sputtering gas is admitted, and an interelectrode voltage ionizes the argon to create plasma. The negatively biased target causes positively charged argon ions to accelerate toward it, physically ejecting target atoms via billiard-ball-like collisions. Sputter yield (atoms ejected per incident ion) peaks at an angle less than 90 degrees—glancing angles reflect ions while perfectly normal angles push atoms deeper into the target. Ejected atoms follow an approximately cosine angular distribution.

**Process Principles:** Modern PVD systems primarily use DC magnetron sputtering, where a magnetic field confines electrons on a closed path near the target, creating a dense argon plasma at lower pressures. This enables high sputtering rates with lower applied potential, lower operating pressures, and less gas trapping in films. DC sputtering cannot deposit dielectric materials (charge buildup neutralizes cathode potential), requiring RF power supplies for insulating films. Reactive sputtering (e.g., titanium in nitrogen plasma to form TiN) combines sputtering with chemical reactions. Key process parameters—power, chamber pressure, gas flow ratios—govern mean free path, kinetic energy of arriving atoms, and film stress/density. Advantages include low operational cost, good film adhesion, and ability to deposit very high melting point materials.

**Challenges & Failure Modes:**
- Poor conformality: line-of-sight deposition causes shadowing effects in high-aspect-ratio structures, with overhang pinch-off before trench bottoms are filled
- Ion-induced surface damage: high-energy bombardment creates unwanted interfacial electronic states that degrade device mobility and reliability
- Target impurity/grain issues: e.g., PVD TiN films show small grains with (111) plane dominance, inducing higher interfacial oxidation and defect densities compared to ALD alternatives (relevant in ferroelectric memory with HfZrOx films)
- Adhesion/wetting failures: copper on improperly formed barriers exhibits 3D island growth rather than smooth wetting, causing adhesion failure during mechanical polishing

**Technology Node Evolution:** PVD was heavily used for all BEOL barrier layers (Ta/TaN) and copper seed layers at the 28nm planar node due to acceptable step coverage, high throughput, and material purity. However, at 14nm FinFET and 7nm FinFET nodes, extreme aspect-ratio vias made PVD unsuitable for continuous diffusion barriers due to shadowing. The industry transitioned to hybrid integration—using ALD for ultra-thin conformal barrier layers (like ALD TaN) while retaining specialized ionized PVD for copper seed layers requiring high purity and good wetting.

**Related Processes:** PVD is a critical precursor to electroplating (copper seed provides conductivity, followed by CMP). In FEOL, PVD deposits work-function tuning metals and barrier layers in high-k metal gate processes. PVD liners enable orthogonal metal line patterning at the same metal level. In advanced packaging, PVD sputtering universally deposits under bump metallurgy (UBM) layers with titanium/tantalum diffusion barriers and copper seeds for electroplated pillars.

**Future Outlook:** PVD is evolving toward highly ionized PVD (iPVD), which uses secondary RF coils to heavily ionize sputtered metal flux, enabling directional control via substrate biasing to defeat shadowing in deep trenches. Research is also exploring novel barrier materials like ruthenium and cobalt with superior copper wettability and lower size-effect resistivity than tantalum-based systems.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"PVD is fundamentally a line-of-sight deposition process, which results in non-conformal step coverage caused by the shadowing effect in small feature size, high-aspect-ratio via geometries."
</key_excerpts>

This webpage from Patsnap Eureka provides a comprehensive technical and market analysis of Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) seed layer engineering for subsequent electroplating steps in semiconductor manufacturing.

As features shrank below 22nm, ALD became essential for conformal deposition in high-aspect-ratio structures (>100:1). Key objectives include creating optimal interfaces between diffusion barriers and bulk conductors, ensuring adhesion, uniform nucleation, low electrical resistance, and electromigration resistance. Emerging focus areas include materials beyond copper (ruthenium, platinum, palladium, cobalt) and compatibility with Gate-All-Around (GAA) transistors, 3D NAND, and advanced logic interconnects.

The market value exceeds $500 million annually.

**Current Challenges:** Key challenges include nucleation control on complex 3D structures, adhesion limitations leading to delamination, diminishing conformality beyond 10:1 aspect ratios, higher resistivity in ultra-thin layers, integration issues with pre-electroplating cleaning steps, material selection constraints (especially for direct copper ALD), and scalability/throughput limitations.

**Critical Patents:** Includes US20110017139A1 (Modulated Ion-Induced ALD using microwave plasma) and US20150144061A1 (Combinatorial Plasma Enhanced Deposition).

**Environmental Impact:** ALD can reduce water consumption by 30-40%, achieve up to 95% material utilization efficiency, yield 15-25% net energy savings, and reduce overall environmental impact by 20-35% compared to conventional approaches. Low-temperature ALD variants (80-120°C) further enhance sustainability.

**Interface Engineering:** Key considerations include substrate surface chemistry compatibility, adhesion-promoting interlayers, gradient composition layers, chemical stability of seed layers in electroplating baths, thermal expansion coefficient matching, and post-deposition annealing treatments.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"ALD emerged as a solution by offering superior conformality even in complex 3D structures with aspect ratios exceeding 100:1, enabling void-free metallization."

This blog post from AtomicLimits (published January 13, 2022, by Marc Merkx and Adrie Mackus of Eindhoven University of Technology) analyzes why area-selective deposition (ASD) of cobalt has been successfully adopted by the semiconductor industry for metal capping of Cu interconnects, whereas area-selective CVD of tungsten failed decades earlier for metal gapfill applications in back-end-of-line (BEOL) fabrication.

**Historical context of W ASD:** Area-selective CVD of W using WF6 and H2 was studied since the 1980s for metal gapfill. Both precursors contribute to selectivity (WF6 adsorbs on metals/Si but not SiO2; H2 dissociates selectively on metals). However, the process failed commercially due to selectivity loss from two main causes: (1) pre-existing impurities on non-growth areas, and (2) intermediate reaction products (WFx and HF) formed during precursor adsorption that re-volatilize and re-adsorb on the SiO2 non-growth area, causing undesired nucleation. In the 1980s, the technology node was ~1 µm, requiring 100 nm–1 µm of selective deposition—far more challenging than current applications.

**Why Co ASD succeeded for metal capping:** Co ASD is currently in production in high-volume manufacturing for capping Cu interconnects to improve electromigration (EM) reliability. Key reasons for success include: (1) Co capping only requires a few nanometers of deposition (as thin as 1.6 nm), while gapfill required 10s of nanometers—most ASD processes lose selectivity after several nanometers; (2) Cu lines are slightly recessed after CMP (due to corrosion and dishing), which confines lateral growth (mushrooming) as long as Co thickness doesn't exceed recess depth; (3) the thinner deposition requirement makes selectivity more achievable.

**Technical details:** CMP leaves 10^11–10^12 atoms/cm² metal defects on dielectric surfaces; post-CMP cleaning reduces but doesn't eliminate them, causing nucleation even with perfect intrinsic selectivity. Yield and leakage current degrade for Co capping layers thicker than 3 nm. Co precursors studied include Co2(CO)8, Co2(CO)6(C6H10), and CoCp(CO)2. Co-based alloys like CoWxPy can further improve EM reliability. Co, Ru, Mn, and W have been reported as candidate capping materials, with Co currently the material of choice.

**Future outlook:** Applied Materials is selling a dedicated tool for area-selective CVD of W for metal gapfill, suggesting renewed industry interest. With Intel and TSMC implementing Co interconnects for bottom metal layers, ASD of Co for metal gapfill is being considered, especially since ASD of Co is already in use for metal capping. The authors note that ASD is likely best suited for target thicknesses below 10 nm.

SUMMARY:

This article from SemiFlows Blog provides a comprehensive technical overview of tungsten (W) metallization in advanced semiconductor manufacturing. Tungsten is a refractory metal primarily used to form contact plugs, local interconnects, and vias, serving as the critical conductive bridge between front-end-of-line (FEOL) active transistor structures and back-end-of-line (BEOL) multi-level wiring. It is selected for its high melting point, electromigration resistance, and excellent step coverage, while its low diffusivity in silicon dioxide and silicon substrates (compared to copper) prevents deep-level contamination.

**Physics & Mechanism**: Tungsten deposition typically uses tungsten hexafluoride (WF₆) as the gaseous precursor. Two main reduction pathways exist: silane (SiH₄) reduction for the nucleation phase (forming a thin continuous seed layer, reacting rapidly at lower temperatures), followed by hydrogen (H₂) reduction for bulk film growth. The hydrogen reduction reaction (WF₆ + 3H₂ → W + 6HF) is thermally driven and surface-catalyzed. Hot-wire assisted ALD (HWALD) uses atomic hydrogen for low-temperature, self-limiting deposition, though this competes with fluorine-based etching reactions. A diffusion barrier—typically TiN or a Ti/TiN bilayer—is required between tungsten and silicon to prevent silicide consumption and fluorine penetration. Ohmic contact behavior is achieved through heavy doping to narrow the Schottky barrier, enabling field emission tunneling.

**Process Principles**: Deposition temperature and chamber pressure are key parameters. Higher temperatures increase deposition rate (Arrhenius kinetics) but can cause rougher, non-conformal films; lower temperatures improve step coverage but reduce throughput. Tungsten crystallizes in two phases: the desired low-resistivity α-W (body-centered cubic) and the high-resistivity metastable β-W (A15 cubic), the latter stabilized by fluorine/oxygen impurities. High precursor purity and optimized H₂/WF₆ ratios are critical for α-W nucleation.

**Challenges & Failure Modes**: Key failure modes include: (1) Fluorine attack causing "volcano" defects—when WF₆ penetrates thin/discontinuous barriers and reacts with silicon or TiSi₂ to form volatile SiF₄ or TiF₄, creating voids that erupt during heating; (2) Grain boundary scattering—as contact dimensions shrink below 20nm, resistivity rises sharply due to electron scattering at surfaces/grain boundaries and fluorine impurities; (3) Loading effects during SF₆/Ar etchback—redeposition of tungsten or Ti-N-F byproducts causing incomplete clearing and electrical shorts; (4) High tensile stress leading to cracking, wafer warpage, or delamination.

**Technology Node Evolution**: At 28nm, contacts used TiSi₂ or CoSi₂ with Ti/TiN barrier + CVD W plug. At 14nm, ultra-thin ALD TiN barriers and NiSi silicide were adopted. At 7nm and beyond, the TiN barrier and nucleation layer occupied over half the contact volume, driving innovations including barrierless tungsten (selective CVD directly on silicide), alternative metals (cobalt, ruthenium with shorter electron mean free paths), and dual-metal stacked vias (e.g., Mo or W stacks on primary contact metal).

**Related Processes**: Upstream processes include ion implantation and rapid thermal annealing (RTA) for silicidation, and anisotropic contact hole etching. Downstream processes include tungsten CMP (using alumina/silica slurries with oxidizing agents) and BEOL copper dual damascene metallization.

**Future Outlook**: Trends include fully selective ALD/CVD for bottom-up tungsten growth without CMP, and renewed use of tungsten in high-temperature electronics such as GaN power devices (aluminum-free gate stacks and backend interconnects capable of operating beyond silicon thermal limits).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"At the 7nm FinFET node and beyond, the volume of the contact plug became so small that the conventional TiN barrier and tungsten nucleation layer occupied more than half of the contact volume."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 18: Atomic layer Deposition - A semiconductor solution | GP Plasma ---
URL: https://gpplasma.com/atomic-layer-deposition

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from GP Plasma provides an educational introduction to Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD), a vacuum deposition technique offering digital control over thickness on high aspect ratio substrates. ALD relies on self-limiting surface reactions between vapor phase reactants that are separated in time, providing sequential exposures of the surface. The technique was first referenced in 1965 as "Molecular Layering," with the first production plant using ALD built for Electroluminescent Displays. ALD is now widely used across semiconductors, batteries, microelectronics, and photovoltaics, with over a thousand well-characterized ALD chemistries.

Key advantages over other deposition techniques include: high aspect ratio substrates up to 4000:1 (compared to HiPIMS at 30:1), compatibility with large 3D structures, small feature sizes below 10 nm, tuning of metal-semiconductor and semiconductor-semiconductor interfaces (fermi-states), and production of amorphous films. ALD has been shown to coat aspect ratios of 5000:1 with high conformality (Elam, 2003), and uniformities below 4% are achievable for high aspect ratio substrates (Elers, 2006), with 1% uniformity common for low aspect ratio wafers.

A standard ALD cycle consists of four stages: Precursor A Dose, Precursor A Purge, Precursor B Dose, Precursor B Purge. Purge stages use inert gas to remove excess precursor and reaction products, preventing CVD-style deposition. "Super cycles" (multiple material cycles) enable deposition of nanolaminate materials, graded layers, and alloys. Nanolaminates (repeated units of 2-3 layers) can regulate crystal size and enable applications like free-standing x-ray mirrors on polymer substrates (Fabreguette, 2007).

Growth rates typically range from 0.2 to 1.3 Å/cycle. The page argues that slow growth rates are a misconception as a disadvantage, since the pinhole-free nature of ALD films allows thinner films meeting the same performance criteria as other methods—ALD water/oxygen diffusion barriers can show superior performance at just 15 nm thickness (Higgs et al., 2014).

GP Plasma, together with Maxima Sciences, builds lab-scale ALD equipment for new market entrants, including the RALD machine for cost-effective R&D ALD coating of 3D geometries. GP Plasma also represents Swiss Cluster for North America for high-throughput batch applications with hybrid deposition capability mixing ALD with PVD and PECVD. The page includes references to key ALD literature (Elam 2003, Elers 2006, Fabreguette 2007, Higgs et al. 2014, Kessels/AtomicLimits sources).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) is a vacuum deposition technique that provides digital control over thickness on high aspect ratio substrates. ALD relies on self-limiting surface reactions between vapor phase reactants."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Patsnap Eureka provides a comprehensive technical overview of optimizing Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) for high aspect ratio structures in semiconductor manufacturing.

**ALD Technology Background**: ALD emerged in the 1970s, developed by Tuomo Suntola for electroluminescent displays, and gained momentum in the semiconductor industry in the 1990s. The technique uses sequential, self-limiting surface reactions for conformal coating with sub-nanometer precision. High aspect ratio structures (exceeding 10:1) present challenges including non-uniform film thickness and precursor penetration issues.

**Key Optimization Goals**: Achieving uniform film thickness (>95% conformality) throughout deep features, complete precursor penetration, and minimizing process time while maintaining quality.

**Market Demand**: Modern 3D NAND flash and DRAM devices require conformal deposition in structures with aspect ratios exceeding 100:1. Foundry sector demand is driven by FinFET and gate-all-around transistor architectures. Emerging applications in power semiconductors and wide bandgap materials expand the market.

**Core Challenges**: Mass transport limitations in narrow geometries, precursor depletion (especially for high sticking coefficient precursors), temperature gradients within deep features, purging inefficiency leading to parasitic CVD reactions, and complex surface chemistry variations along sidewalls.

**Existing Solutions**: Five main solution categories are outlined: (1) ALD process optimization (precursor flow, pulse timing, purge cycles), (2) specialized precursor delivery systems for deep features, (3) substrate preparation and surface modification (plasma treatments, seed layers), (4) multi-step deposition sequences (super-cycles, gradient depositions), and (5) specialized reactor designs with enhanced gas flow and temperature control.

**Key Players**: Applied Materials (Olympia ALD platform, PEALD, >95% conformality in high aspect ratios exceeding 50:1), ASM IP Holding (spatial ALD EmerALD system, >90% step coverage up to 100:1 aspect ratios), along with Tokyo Electron, Lam Research, Picosun, NEXUSBE, and Atlant 3D Nanosystems. Research institutions include University of California and Max Planck Society.

**Patent Innovations**: Two highlighted patents include a temperature-cycling method (WO2024233857A9) that varies substrate temperature between diffusion and purge stages, and a surface poisoning method (US20150132951A1) for high selectivity deposition with straight sidewalls without etching or lithography.

**Environmental Considerations**: Precursor materials like trimethylaluminum (TMA) and tetrakis(dimethylamido)titanium (TDMAT) present toxicity and bioaccumulation risks. Emerging green chemistry approaches include water-based ALD processes, reduced precursor quantities, and bio-derived molecules. REACH and TSCA regulations influence precursor selection.

**Quality Control Standards**: Requires in-situ monitoring (spectroscopic ellipsometry, quartz crystal microbalance, mass spectrometry), specialized metrology (cross-sectional TEM, FIB analysis, X-ray reflectometry), and statistical process control with six-sigma performance levels. Acceptance criteria typically require less than 5% thickness variation across aspect ratios exceeding 20:1.
</summary>

"ALD operates on sequential, self-limiting surface reactions that enable conformal coating of complex three-dimensional structures with sub-nanometer precision."

The authors note that further studies are needed to fully understand the effect of Kr, but they anticipate this superconformal ALD approach could be applicable to many ALD processes.
