--- SOURCE 1: US10731250B2 - Depositing ruthenium layers in interconnect metallization - Google Patents ---
URL: https://patents.google.com/patent/US10731250B2/en

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Google Patents page for US Patent US10731250B2, titled "Depositing ruthenium layers in interconnect metallization," assigned to Lam Research Corporation. The patent, filed as application US15/996,925, was published as US10731250B2 and is currently active. Inventors include Do Young Kim, Jeong-Seok Na, Chiukin Steven Lai, Raashina Humayun, and Michal Danek. The patent has related priority filings in Korea, PCT, Japan, Taiwan, and China.

**Technical Content:** The patent addresses challenges in fabricating copper interconnects at sub-10nm technology nodes. Copper's electron mean free path (~39nm) causes increased resistance at small dimensions, and scaling barrier layers below 2.5nm is problematic, consuming over 50% of line cross-section at sub-10nm nodes. The invention proposes using ruthenium (Ru) for interconnect metallization instead.

**Core Method:** The patent describes a two-step deposition process: (1) depositing a thin (1-2nm) protective ruthenium liner layer using reducing (non-oxidizing) chemistry via multiple ALD cycles, and (2) filling the feature with ruthenium by reacting a Ru precursor with an oxidant. The protective Ru liner prevents oxidation of underlying adhesion/barrier layers and metal substrates during the oxidizing fill step. The liner layer can be deposited on materials including WCN, TiN, WN, WC, and TaN.

**ALD Cycle Variations:** Multiple ALD dose sequences are described for depositing the Ru liner: Ru precursor → reductant; Ru precursor → oxidant → reductant; Ru precursor → oxidant mixed with reductant; and others. The reducing agent may be H2 or NH3 (thermal or plasma). ALD cycles may be thermal ALD or plasma-enhanced ALD (PEALD). The reducing dose removes oxygen incorporated into the Ru liner or underlying metallic layers.

**Ru Precursors:** The patent lists Ru(0) and Ru(II) organometallic precursors. Precursors for oxidative reactions include (ethylbenzyl)(1-ethyl-1,4-cyclohexadienyl)Ru(0), (1-isopropyl-4-methylbenzyl)(1,3-cyclohexadienyl)Ru(0), and (cyclopentadienyl)(ethyl)Ru(II)dicarbonyl. Precursors for reducing reactions include bis(5-methyl-2,4-hexanediketonato)Ru(II)dicarbonyl and bis(ethylcyclopentadienyl)Ru(II). The same or different Ru precursor may be used for liner and fill operations.

**Process Parameters:** Example substrate temperatures range 150-450°C (typically 200-400°C); chamber pressures 0.1-10 Torr; carrier gas (Ar) flows 25-1000 sccm; precursor dose times 0.5-20 seconds; purge times 0.1-10 seconds.

**Applications:** The methods apply to sub-10nm node MOL and BEOL logic interconnects, source/drain contact fill, and via/trench filling. Ruthenium has a short inelastic mean free path, allowing better resistivity scaling at sub-10nm dimensions than copper, and can be implemented without a diffusion barrier layer. Fill may be by ALD, CVD, electrochemical plating, or electroless plating. Features may also be filled with Cu, W, Co, Mo, Ni, or Al.

**Apparatus Claim:** The patent also covers an apparatus with process chambers, gas inlets for Ru precursor/oxidant/reducing agent sources, and a controller with instructions for the Ru liner deposition cycles and subsequent fill process.
</summary>

"One aspect of the disclosure relates to a method including receiving a substrate including a feature; performing multiple atomic layer deposition (ALD) cycles to deposit a ruthenium (Ru) liner layer in the feature, wherein each of the ALD cycles include a dose of a reducing agent; and after depositing the Ru liner layer, at least partially filling the feature with ruthenium by reacting a first ruthenium precursor with an oxidant."

URL: https://allanchem.com/advances-barrier-layers-cu-interconnects

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Allan Chemical Corporation (allanchem.com), a specialty chemicals supplier based in Ringwood, New Jersey, provides a technical article on "Advances in Barrier Layers for Cu Interconnects" in semiconductor manufacturing. The article traces the evolution of copper interconnect barrier materials as the semiconductor industry scales to 2 nm nodes and beyond.

**Historical Development of Barrier Materials:**
- Late 1990s: Tantalum (Ta) and Tantalum Nitride (TaN) became the standard barrier materials, applied via physical vapor deposition (PVD), to prevent copper diffusion into dielectric layers.
- By 2013 (16nm/14nm nodes): Cobalt (Co) liners replaced tantalum liners due to superior wetting properties, better copper adhesion, improved gap fill, and lower electrical resistance.
- Current (2nm and beyond): Ruthenium-Cobalt (RuCo) alloys now dominate advanced nodes, combining ruthenium's diffusion-blocking strength with cobalt's conductivity and adhesion.

**Key Performance Improvements:**
- RuCo alloys reduce barrier thickness by 33% (down to just 20 angstroms) and cut resistance by up to 25% compared to tantalum-based processes.
- Applied Materials demonstrated a 2.5% performance boost in 2 nm test chips using RuCo liners alongside advanced Black Diamond low-k dielectric materials.
- Advanced barriers enable void-free copper reflow, seedless copper electroplating (eliminating PVD seed layers), and improved thermal management for high-power chiplets and stacked devices.
- Advanced β-phase tantalum or ruthenium-based formulations achieve resistivities below 60 Ω/cm.

**Dual-Damascene Manufacturing:**
The article details three main deposition stages: conformal barrier layer application (diffusion block), copper seed layer deposition via PVD, and copper electroplating to fill etched features. Deposition methods include PVD, CVD/PECVD, and Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD), which achieves exceptional uniformity even in features with aspect ratios above 10:1. Barrier thicknesses typically range from 10 to 250 angstroms, with combined seed and barrier layers kept under 120 angstroms. Chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) compatibility is essential for multilayer integration.

**Future Developments:**
- Researchers are screening ternary and quaternary alloys (CoMo, CoRu, CoTa, CoW, MoRu, RuTa, RuW, plus ternaries like CoMoTa, CoRuTa, MoRuTa) using the Miedema model, targeting barrier thicknesses as low as 15 nm.
- Backside power delivery (BPD) relocates the power grid to the wafer's backside to lower resistance and reduce congestion.
- Advanced ALK films reduce capacitance by ~9% at 18 nm metal pitch, with an additional 14% reduction from airgaps.
- The copper market for 2025 is projected at $489–$495 million for device interconnects and $509 million for advanced packaging.

**Key Expert Quote:**
Gaurav Thareja, director of logic and memory process integration at Applied Materials, cited the industry's "urgent need for process innovations which enable resistance and capacitance reduction without compromising reliability and yield."

The article concludes that copper remains the preferred interconnect material even at 2 nm dimensions, with the focus on refining barrier and liner systems rather than replacing copper. Allan Chemical Corporation positions itself as a supplier of specialty chemicals supporting these semiconductor advancements.

--- SOURCE 3: Ruthenium: Metallization Physics, Process Principles, and Advanced Node Integration | SemiFlows Blog ---
URL: https://semiflows.com/blog/what-is-ruthenium-in-semiconductor-manufacturing

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This SemiFlows blog article provides a comprehensive technical overview of ruthenium (Ru) metallization in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, covering its physics, process principles, integration challenges, and technology node evolution.

**Key Physics & Mechanisms:**
- Ruthenium is thermodynamically immiscible with copper (zero solid solubility), making it an effective plateable Cu diffusion barrier without needing a separate seed layer.
- Sputter-deposited Ru films grow in columnar grain structures that force copper atoms along tortuous grain-boundary paths, extending barrier lifetime under thermal stress.
- Ru has a much shorter bulk electron mean free path than copper, meaning its resistivity rises far more gradually with linewidth scaling—allowing Ru to outperform Cu in RC delay at extremely small dimensions.
- PVD Ru on organosilicate glass (OSG) grows via Stranski-Krastanov (island) mode, creating weak adhesion requiring interface chemical modification (silicate layers or self-limiting precursors).
- During CMP, Ru must be oxidized (using H2O2-containing slurries), then dissolved via organic complexing agents like ethylenediamine (EDA) that coordinate with Ru d-orbitals. Galvanic corrosion between Cu and Ru is suppressed using pyridine carboxylate inhibitors (e.g., nicotinic acid) that form protective monolayers on copper.

**Process Principles:**
- Deposition: CVD/ALD provide conformal coverage in high-aspect-ratio features but introduce impurities (C, O, N) that raise resistivity; PVD used for liner applications.
- Thermal annealing: Hydrogen-assisted RTA drives grain coalescence and removes interstitial impurities, dramatically reducing resistivity.
- Subtractive dry etching: Uses Cl2/O2 chemistries forming volatile RuOxCly species; cryogenic chuck temperatures and passivation layer formation control anisotropy and line-edge roughness.
- CMP parameter interactions: Oxidizer concentration (excessive amounts cause pitting and Cu corrosion), complexing agent concentration (too high causes isotropic etching), and mechanical downforce (excessive causes dielectric erosion and dishing) are all non-linearly coupled.

**Challenges & Failure Modes:**
- Barrier breakdown under excessive thermal budgets (grain-boundary diffusion of Cu into silicon causing junction leakage).
- Interfacial delamination of Ru from low-k dielectrics under mechanical stress.
- Galvanic corrosion of Cu during CMP causing recess defects and voiding.
- Via loss and IMD dishing during planarization due to endpoint detection difficulties and polishing rate mismatch between hard Ru and soft dielectric.

**Technology Node Evolution:**
- 28nm–14nm nodes: Cu with Ta/TaN barriers sufficient; barrier thickness not yet restrictive.
- 7nm node: Barrier scaling to a few nanometers forced Ta/TaN replacement; Ru introduced as ultrathin liner enabling seedless direct Cu electroplating.
- Sub-3nm nodes: Shift to subtractive Ru metallization using EUV lithography and anisotropic dry etching, eliminating damascene trench filling bottlenecks; supports sub-30nm pitches with high current density and EM resistance.

**Future Outlook:**
Ru is expanding into FEOL applications (work-function metal in HKMG stacks for FinFET/nanosheet devices), buried power rails (BPR) for standard cell height optimization, and integration with air-gap schemes to reduce parasitic capacitance in the angstrom era.

**Related processes:** EUV lithography, low-k dielectric deposition, planarization stop layers (SiN/SiCN) to prevent via loss, and highly selective wet clean chemistries.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Ruthenium is an air-stable noble metal featuring a low bulk resistivity, an exceptionally high melting point, and a near-complete lack of solid solubility with copper. These intrinsic material properties allow ruthenium to function as a plateable copper diffusion barrier, enabling the direct electrodeposition of copper without requiring a conventional copper seed layer."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Vik's Newsletter discusses why ruthenium (Ru) is emerging as a replacement for copper (Cu) in low-level metal interconnects as pitch drops below 20nm in sub-2nm class advanced technology nodes.

**Context and Key Development:**
At IEDM 2024 in San Francisco, Intel unveiled a "subtractive" ruthenium process that reduces line-to-line capacitance between metals smaller than 25nm in pitch. Intel claimed to be the first to demonstrate a practical, cost-efficient, high-volume manufacturing compatible subtractive Ru integrated process with airgaps that does not require expensive lithographic airgap exclusion zones around vias or self-aligned via flows requiring selective etches. The airgaps provided up to 25% line-to-line capacitance reduction at pitches ≤25nm, and this solution could appear on Intel Foundry's future nodes.

**The Problem with Copper Interconnects:**
Copper has been the interconnect material of choice for three decades. Advanced nodes have 12-15 metal levels. Two major limitations emerge as features shrink:
- **Resistance**: Smaller cross-sectional area means increased resistance, voltage drop, and thermal dissipation.
- **Capacitance**: Lines too close together increase crosstalk; low-k dielectrics (εr ~2.5 vs 4.2 for SiO2) provided partial help, but resistance problems were unsolvable.

The dual-damascene process requires a tantalum nitride barrier layer and cobalt liner, reducing copper's effective cross-section by ~4nm total (2nm per side). Barrier and liner layers can make up ~30% of interconnect line width (~10nm at sub-25nm pitch), significantly increasing resistance. Future nodes project metal pitches approaching 10nm.

**Material Advantages of Ruthenium over Copper:**
1. **Bulk resistivity**: Copper is superior at 1.68 μΩ-cm vs ruthenium's 7.1 μΩ-cm.
2. **Mean free path (MFP)**: Copper has high MFP (~40nm), causing resistance to severely increase at small dimensions due to scattering. Ruthenium has low MFP (~6-8nm), making it insensitive to resistance increase at small sizes—this is the key advantage for narrow interconnects.
3. **Cohesive energy**: Ruthenium has ~6.7 eV/atom vs copper's ~3.5 eV/atom. This provides:
   - Lower diffusion (ruthenium can be used without barrier layers, recovering cross-sectional area for current flow)
   - Better electromigration resistance (atoms less prone to movement under current flow, reducing reliability concerns like opens and shorts)

**Subtractive Processing:**
Ruthenium can be patterned with subtractive etching (like aluminum interconnects from the late 1990s) rather than requiring the complex dual-damascene process used for copper.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a blog post from Lam Research (lamresearch.com) presenting a pathfinding study on hybrid metallization using molybdenum (Mo) for scaling back-end-of-line (BEOL) interconnects in advanced semiconductor logic devices. The article is authored by TY Oh, a staff semiconductor process and integration engineer with Korea Semiverse Solutions R&D.

**Key Topic:** As device dimensions shrink, traditional copper (Cu) conductors in BEOL metal lines and vias have become problematic due to increased resistance from small critical dimensions (CD). The study compares a conventional Cu dual damascene (DD) scheme against a hybrid metallization scheme using molybdenum (Mo) with barrierless metal deposition.

**Key Findings:**
1. **Hybrid Metallization Technique:** Uses bottom-up deposition to prefill vias with barrierless metals (which don't require a separate diffusion barrier layer), followed by conventional Cu DD processing. Can be initially adopted in bottom via contact areas and could eventually replace all Cu lines and vias.

2. **Resistance Benefits:** The Mo hybrid scheme provides approximately 55% total resistance benefit compared to conventional Cu DD. Adding selective barrier deposition (SBD) techniques reduces total resistance by an additional 15%, avoiding barrier metal deposition on top of vias.

3. **Current Density:** Mo via schemes (V1 Mo and V1/V2 Mo) exhibit much higher current density than Cu DD schemes because additional current can flow when barrier metal is not used.

4. **Stress Analysis:** Cu DD schemes show greater stress gaps in the Z direction between M1 and V1 compared to Mo via schemes, with higher probability of stress-induced voids at via bottoms. Hydrostatic stress gradients increase with increasing Mo height, while total M1-M3 resistance decreases. The optimal Mo height was identified as the amount needed to fill to via height (resistance slope saturates beyond 25 nm).

5. **Process Optimization:** Via stress can be controlled through material intrinsic stress (compressive intrinsic stress of Mo reduces via hydrostatic stress) and process temperature. Keeping temperature at approximately 400°C is preferred to minimize stress differences between via and M2, since M2 stress can change from tensile to compressive at higher temperatures.

6. **Methodology:** The study used SEMulator3D® virtual fabrication software with a uniform Monte-Carlo simulation of 400 experimental runs and linear regression analysis to identify four key parameter candidates for optimal via metal line profiles. As via top and bottom CD increase, via stress and total resistance decrease; as via height increases, via stress and total resistance increase. Capacitance between M1 and M2 increases as via height decreases and via CD increases, but there's a limit to reducing via height due to leakage current and time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) risks.

**Conclusion:** Virtual fabrication and virtual Design of Experiment (DOE) enabled identification of the optimal Mo via profile that minimizes mechanical stress (contributing to voids) and RC parasitic effects, allowing prediction of process changes without the time and cost of extensive wafer-based experimentation.
</summary>

<summary>
This webpage is a news article from Semiconductor Engineering (published June 21, 2024, by Katherine Derbyshire) titled "Ruthenium Interconnects On Tap," posted on the International Precious Metals Institute (IPMI) website. The article discusses how chipmakers are approaching a significant shift in interconnect technology as copper's effectiveness diminishes, with ruthenium emerging as a leading successor material.

Key content:

1. **Context**: Copper interconnects were introduced in 1997, replacing the tungsten via/aluminum line scheme, using dual damascene integration with wet processes (electroplating, CMP). Now, shrinking line dimensions are approaching copper's electron mean free path, and barrier layers are consuming more line width, driving the need for alternatives.

2. **Copper optimization research** (presented at IEEE Interconnect Technology Conference):
   - Samsung's Jongmin Baek found that sidewall plasma pre-treatment reduced barrier thickness by one-third and improved contact resistance by 2%.
   - The via bottom barrier (an artifact of sidewall deposition) can account for more than 60% of via resistance; a polymeric inhibitor improved selectivity and gave a 20% resistance reduction.
   - Samsung's Kang Sub Yim studied dielectric surface carbon depletion by plasma etching — for sub-30nm features, surface carbon depletion has a larger impact than bulk dielectric constant; surface silylation was used to restore etch damage.
   - Baek's group used a thermal recovery process to revert post-etch Si-OH surfaces to Si-CH3, and added plasma pretreatment before etch stop layer deposition, achieving 30% stress reduction in copper lines and 10% reduction in via resistance.

3. **Ruthenium vias and lines**: 
   - imec simulations show using ruthenium vias for the first four interconnect layers reduces overall resistance by up to 60%.
   - Transitional hybrid metallization (copper lines with tungsten, ruthenium, or molybdenum vias) is proposed.
   - Ruthenium doesn't require a barrier layer, enabling more flexible integration schemes.
   - Giulio Marti (imec) benchmarked three fully self-aligned via processes (SADP-SIM and two pillar via options), finding the pillar via options increased process steps but improved the process window and prevented via-line bridging.
   - Chen Wu (imec) proposed a SADP-SID scheme where spacers define dielectric features rather than metal, giving more control over feature dimensions.

4. **Ruthenium process optimization**: Jack Rogers and colleagues at TEL's Albany Technology Center studied adhesion layer effects on ruthenium deposition — larger and more uniform Ru grains appear to reduce resistivity. Optimized ruthenium etch and deposition processes are critical, as tapered profiles, footings, and incomplete TiN adhesion layer removal can cause leakage.

The article concludes that while copper optimization continues, a long-term successor is needed, and ruthenium interconnect integration will require years of process engineering work.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 17: Can binary or ternary compounds beat Cu in future interconnect applications? | imec ---
URL: https://www.imec-int.com/en/articles/can-binary-or-ternary-compounds-beat-cu-future-interconnect-applications

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a longread article published by imec (October 12, 2022) exploring whether binary or ternary compounds can replace copper (Cu) in future interconnect applications for advanced semiconductor manufacturing. The article is authored by imec researchers Geoffrey Pourtois (imec fellow), Christoph Adelmann (Scientific Director driving research on advanced metals), and Zsolt Tokei (imec fellow and incoming program director of 3D system integration).

BACKGROUND: Copper has been the mainstream conductor metal for interconnect lines and vias in logic back-end-of-line (BEOL) applications since the mid-1990s. However, as technology nodes shrink below ~10nm, Cu resistivity increases dramatically, and its required barrier/liner/cap layers (with high resistivity) occupy an ever-increasing portion of the metal volume. This has driven the interconnect community to seek alternative metals, initially focusing on pure metals like cobalt (Co), ruthenium (Ru), rhodium (Rh), iridium (Ir), and molybdenum (Mo), which perform better at small dimensions despite higher bulk resistivity.

RESEARCH INITIATIVE: About five years ago (around 2017), imec began exploring binary and ternary ordered compounds (intermetallics) that could outperform Cu at small dimensions in terms of resistance and reliability, ideally without requiring diffusion barriers or adhesion liners. First results were presented at IITC 2018, sparking a new global research field with several R&D groups worldwide now investigating candidate alloys, focusing mainly on binaries.

METHODOLOGY: Imec developed a unique down-selection and ranking methodology based on two key figures of merit:
1. **Bulk resistivity × mean free path (ρ0×λ)** — to predict resistivity increase at small dimensions. Cu has bulk resistivity of 1.7 µΩcm and mean free path of 39nm at room temperature. Candidates must have a lower product than Cu.
2. **Cohesive energy** — as a proxy for intrinsic reliability (resistance to electromigration and dielectric diffusion). Cu's value is ~4 eV; candidates must have comparable or higher cohesive energy.

These figures of merit are derived from ab-initio atomistic calculations (solid-state physics descriptions of electronic structures) and visualized in benchmarking graphs. Additional considerations include dielectric adhesion, thermodynamic stability of phases, annealing temperature compatibility with BEOL processing, toxicity, and material cost.

EXPERIMENTAL VALIDATION: The ab-initio sub-list is validated through experiments on 300mm wafers: (1) blanket thin films with varying thicknesses to measure resistivity, and (2) patterned t-shaped structures to investigate scaling potential in narrow lines. Candidates with higher bulk resistivity than Cu must show slower resistivity increase with scaling, with cross-over points around 10nm or higher.

CANDIDATES IDENTIFIED: Promising binary alloys include Al-, Cu-, and Ru-based compounds (e.g., AlNi, AlCu reported at IITC 2021). For ternary compounds, the number of combinations is too large even for ab-initio pre-screening, so imec focused on MAX phases — layered structures composed of an early transition metal (M), an A-group element (columns 13 or 14), and carbon or nitrogen (X). Some MAX phases (211, 312, and 413 stoichiometries) show favorable figures of merit compared to Cu and Ru.

NEXT STEPS: The team plans to implement the most promising candidates in relevant metallization schemes using a semi-damascene interconnect module (direct etching of a patternable metal for high-aspect-ratio lines), aimed at the most critical local interconnect layers as a far-out option. Cu is expected to remain the metal of choice for upper interconnect layers. Key integration challenges include controlling film stoichiometry and surface oxidation, and optimizing etching strategies. Future work will expand into sustainability assessments, including environmental footprint of process flows (etch chemistries, annealing steps, byproducts).
</summary>

URL: https://patents.google.com/patent/US10731250B2/en

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Google Patents page for US Patent US10731250B2, titled "Depositing ruthenium layers in interconnect metallization," assigned to Lam Research Corporation. The patent was filed as US15/996,925 and published as US20180347041A1 before being granted. Inventors include Do Young Kim, Jeong-Seok Na, Chiukin Steven Lai, Raashina Humayun, and Michal Danek.

**Core Technology:**
The patent describes methods and apparatus for depositing ruthenium (Ru) layers in semiconductor interconnect metallization, particularly for sub-10nm technology nodes. The key innovation involves a two-step process:
1. **Ru liner layer deposition** via multiple atomic layer deposition (ALD) cycles performed under reducing conditions (using a reducing agent such as H2 or NH3, either thermal or plasma-enhanced)
2. **Ru fill operation** where the feature is at least partially filled with ruthenium by reacting a ruthenium precursor with an oxidant

The protective Ru liner layer (typically 1-2 nm thick) prevents oxidation of underlying adhesion/barrier layers and metal substrates during the subsequent oxidative fill step. It also serves as a barrier preventing oxygen from penetrating into underlying metal layers.

**Technical Details:**
- Addresses the problem that copper interconnects are challenging at sub-10nm nodes because copper has an electron mean free path of ~39 nm, and no barrier material maintains integrity below 2.5nm thickness (barriers consume >50% of line cross-section at small dimensions)
- Ruthenium has a short inelastic mean free path, allowing better resistivity scaling than copper at sub-10nm dimensions, and can be used without a diffusion barrier
- ALD dose sequences include: Ru precursor → reductant; Ru precursor → oxidant → reductant; Ru precursor → oxidant mixed with reductant; etc.
- Ru precursors include Ru(0) and Ru(II) organometallic compounds (e.g., (arene)(diene)Ru(0), (cyclopentadienyl)(ethyl)Ru(II)dicarbonyl)
- Two approaches for protective layer: (1) cycling oxidation-reduction chemistries, or (2) reduction-only chemistry
- Applications include sub-10nm MOL and BEOL logic interconnects, source/drain contact fill, vias, and trenches
- Features may be fully filled with Ru or other metals (Cu, W, Co, Mo, Ni, Al)
- Liner layers can be deposited on WCN, TiN, WN, WC, or TaN
- Process parameters: temperatures 150-450°C, pressures 0.1-10 Torr, carrier gas flows 25-1000 sccm, dose times 0.5-20 seconds

**Apparatus Claims:**
The patent also covers an apparatus with process chambers, gas inlets for Ru precursor, oxidant, and reducing agent sources, plus a controller with machine-readable instructions for performing the Ru liner deposition cycles and fill process.

**Classifications:** Covers C23C (chemical coating/CVD), C23C16/455 (ALD), H01L21/768 (interconnect manufacturing), H10P14 (formation of materials), and H10W20 (interconnections) classifications.
</summary>

- Ruthenium is thermodynamically immiscible with copper (zero solid solubility), making it an effective plateable Cu diffusion barrier without needing a separate seed layer.
- Sputter-deposited Ru films grow in columnar grain structures that force copper atoms along tortuous grain-boundary paths, extending barrier lifetime under thermal stress.
- Ru has a much shorter bulk electron mean free path than copper, meaning its resistivity rises far more gradually with linewidth scaling—allowing Ru to outperform Cu in RC delay at extremely small dimensions.
- PVD Ru on organosilicate glass (OSG) grows via Stranski-Krastanov (island) mode, creating weak adhesion requiring interface chemical modification (silicate layers or self-limiting precursors).
- During CMP, Ru must be oxidized (using H2O2-containing slurries), then dissolved via organic complexing agents like ethylenediamine (EDA) that coordinate with Ru d-orbitals. Galvanic corrosion between Cu and Ru is suppressed using pyridine carboxylate inhibitors (e.g., nicotinic acid) that form protective monolayers on copper.

**Process Principles:**
- Deposition: CVD/ALD provide conformal coverage in high-aspect-ratio features but introduce impurities (C, O, N) that raise resistivity; PVD used for liner applications.
- Thermal annealing: Hydrogen-assisted RTA drives grain coalescence and removes interstitial impurities, dramatically reducing resistivity.
- Subtractive dry etching: Uses Cl2/O2 chemistries forming volatile RuOxCly species; cryogenic chuck temperatures and passivation layer formation control anisotropy and line-edge roughness.
- CMP parameter interactions: Oxidizer concentration (excessive amounts cause pitting and Cu corrosion), complexing agent concentration (too high causes isotropic etching), and mechanical downforce (excessive causes dielectric erosion and dishing) are all non-linearly coupled.

**Challenges & Failure Modes:**
- Barrier breakdown under excessive thermal budgets (grain-boundary diffusion of Cu into silicon causing junction leakage).
- Interfacial delamination of Ru from low-k dielectrics under mechanical stress.
- Galvanic corrosion of Cu during CMP causing recess defects and voiding.
- Via loss and IMD dishing during planarization due to endpoint detection difficulties and polishing rate mismatch between hard Ru and soft dielectric.

**Technology Node Evolution:**
- 28nm–14nm nodes: Cu with Ta/TaN barriers sufficient; barrier thickness not yet restrictive.
- 7nm node: Barrier scaling to a few nanometers forced Ta/TaN replacement; Ru introduced as ultrathin liner enabling seedless direct Cu electroplating.
- Sub-3nm nodes: Shift to subtractive Ru metallization using EUV lithography and anisotropic dry etching, eliminating damascene trench filling bottlenecks; supports sub-30nm pitches with high current density and EM resistance.

**Future Outlook:**
Ru is expanding into FEOL applications (work-function metal in HKMG stacks for FinFET/nanosheet devices), buried power rails (BPR) for standard cell height optimization, and integration with air-gap schemes to reduce parasitic capacitance in the angstrom era.

**Related processes:** EUV lithography, low-k dielectric deposition, planarization stop layers (SiN/SiCN) to prevent via loss, and highly selective wet clean chemistries.

**Context and Key Development:**
At IEDM 2024 in San Francisco, Intel unveiled a "subtractive" ruthenium process that reduces line-to-line capacitance between metals smaller than 25nm in pitch. Intel claimed to be the first to demonstrate a practical, cost-efficient, high-volume manufacturing compatible subtractive Ru integrated process with airgaps that does not require expensive lithographic airgap exclusion zones around vias or self-aligned via flows requiring selective etches. The airgaps provided up to 25% line-to-line capacitance reduction at pitches ≤25nm, and this solution could appear on Intel Foundry's future nodes.

**The Problem with Copper Interconnects:**
Copper has been the interconnect material of choice for three decades. Advanced nodes have 12-15 metal levels. Two major limitations emerge as features shrink:
- **Resistance**: Smaller cross-sectional area means increased resistance, voltage drop, and thermal dissipation.
- **Capacitance**: Lines too close together increase crosstalk; low-k dielectrics (εr ~2.5 vs 4.2 for SiO2) provided partial help, but resistance problems were unsolvable.

The dual-damascene process requires a tantalum nitride barrier layer and cobalt liner, reducing copper's effective cross-section by ~4nm total (2nm per side). Barrier and liner layers can make up ~30% of interconnect line width (~10nm at sub-25nm pitch), significantly increasing resistance. Future nodes project metal pitches approaching 10nm.

**Material Advantages of Ruthenium over Copper:**
1. **Bulk resistivity**: Copper is superior at 1.68 μΩ-cm vs ruthenium's 7.1 μΩ-cm.
2. **Mean free path (MFP)**: Copper has high MFP (~40nm), causing resistance to severely increase at small dimensions due to scattering. Ruthenium has low MFP (~6-8nm), making it insensitive to resistance increase at small sizes—this is the key advantage for narrow interconnects.
3. **Cohesive energy**: Ruthenium has ~6.7 eV/atom vs copper's ~3.5 eV/atom. This provides:
   - Lower diffusion (ruthenium can be used without barrier layers, recovering cross-sectional area for current flow)
   - Better electromigration resistance (atoms less prone to movement under current flow, reducing reliability concerns like opens and shorts)

**Subtractive Processing:**
Ruthenium can be patterned with subtractive etching (like aluminum interconnects from the late 1990s) rather than requiring the complex dual-damascene process used for copper.

However, as contact dimensions continue to scale down, contact resistance is becoming a performance bottleneck. As the contact cross-sectional area shrinks, an increasing proportion of volume is consumed by metal liner/barrier and nucleation layers, leaving less room for conducting metal fill, and multiple resistive interfaces contribute to higher contact resistance.

- **Key Benefits**:
  - Eliminates liner/barrier and nucleation layers, alleviating the device performance bottleneck
  - Produces void-free and seam-free gapfill
  - All process steps performed in an ultra-clean, continuous high-vacuum environment, ensuring a pristine interface and defect-free contact fill
  - Maximizes conducting metal volume, substantially improving contact resistivity compared to conventional liner/barrier contact fabrication
  - Lower resistance facilitates higher device density and extends 2D scaling

- **Visual Comparisons**: The page includes images comparing conventional contact gapfill (where metal volume is limited by liner/barrier and nucleation layers) versus selective tungsten (where the entire contact volume is available for conducting metal), as well as images of the system itself.

--- SOURCE 15: Applied Materials Says New Tool Breaks Chip Resistance Bottleneck - IEEE Spectrum ---
URL: https://spectrum.ieee.org/applied-materials-says-new-tool-breaks-chip-resistance-bottleneck

SUMMARY:
<summary>
IEEE Spectrum news article (August 7, 2020, by semiconductor editor Samuel K. Moore) reports that Applied Materials has released a new chip manufacturing tool called the Endura Volta Selective Tungsten CVD system that solves the growing resistance bottleneck in vertical tungsten contacts used to connect transistors to chip wiring. As transistor and contact sizes have shrunk across generations, the resistance of these tungsten contacts has become a major performance drag. In existing manufacturing processes, tungsten contacts must be clad in titanium nitride, which serves two purposes: helping tungsten adhere to the hole walls (preventing flaking) and blocking fluorine used in the growth process from fouling the chip. However, while contact diameters have shrunk to 20 nanometers in 7-nanometer chips, the cladding thickness has not scaled down—leaving only 25% of the contact volume as tungsten, with the rest being cladding. The new machine deposits tungsten from the bottom of the contact hole upward (a "selective gapfill process") using different chemistry that eliminates the need for cladding entirely, reducing resistance by 40%. The process must be performed entirely in a vacuum, so the system is built around a sealed environment that moves wafers through multiple process steps without air exposure. The tool was introduced in July 2020 and is already being used in high-volume manufacturing by leading chipmakers. Zhebo Chen, global product manager at Applied Materials, noted there is more than 100 kilometers of tungsten contact on a 300-millimeter wafer, making high-volume precision "exceedingly difficult." The solution allows fabs to continue using tungsten rather than switching to alternative materials.
</summary>

The rest is cladding.", "In July, Applied Materials released a machine that can make tungsten contacts with no cladding at all, reducing resistance by 40 percent.", "'There's more than 100 kilometers of tungsten contact on a [300-millimeter] wafer,' says Chen. 'Doing this right in high-volume manufacturing is exceedingly difficult.'", "The purpose of the nitride is two-fold. --- SOURCE 16: IRDS 2022 More Moore - IEEE ---
URL: https://irds.ieee.org/images/files/pdf/2022/2022IRDS_MM.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the "More Moore" chapter of the International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IRDS) 2022 Update, published by IEEE. It provides physical, electrical, and reliability requirements for logic and memory technologies to sustain power, performance, area, cost (PPAC) scaling over a 15-year horizon for mainstream/high-volume manufacturing (HVM).

**Purpose and Scope:** The More Moore International Focus Team (IFT) addresses system scaling challenges driven by big data and instant data applications, including mobile (edge computing, VR/AR, AI-enhanced connectivity), data/HPC servers (AI accelerators, ADAS chips, memory/IO solutions), and novel compute fabrics (neural processing units, fine-pitch 3D stacking, reconfigurable fabrics, smart 2.5D interposers).

**Key Scaling Targets (every 2-3 years):** Performance >10% more operating frequency at scaled supply voltage; Power >20% less energy per switching; Area >30% less chip area footprint; Cost <30% more wafer cost (15% less die cost). System scaling targets include 2.0-2.4x scaling of TOPSxTOPS/W/Area per node.

**Key Predictions and Findings:**
- Ground rule scaling expected to slow and saturate around 2028; EUV will be the enabler of ground rule scaling while controlling cost.
- FinFET architecture expected to sustain scaling until 2025, with transition to gate-all-around (GAA) devices thereafter (sustaining another decade+); transition from 3 to 4 GAA devices around 2031.
- Physical channel length projected to saturate around 12nm due to worsening electrostatics.
- SiGe and 2D material channels gaining importance to complement Si channels.
- Interconnect resistance has entered exponential increase regime due to non-ideal barrier scaling for Cu; need for new barrier materials, ALD-based barriers, or non-Cu metallization. TDDB limits minimum spacing between adjacent lines for low-κ dielectrics.
- After 2031, no room for 2D geometry scaling; 3D VLSI (sequential/stacked integration) becomes necessary, along with Beyond CMOS devices.
- Power density and thermal issues are significant challenges, particularly with 3D integration after 2031.
- Energy per switching reduction limited to less than 20% node-to-node on average.

**Memory Technologies:**
- DRAM: If cost scaling efficiency becomes poor, DRAM scaling will stop and 3D DRAM cell stacking or new DRAM concepts will be adopted.
- Flash: 96 layers currently at volume production; 128 layers achievable, with 192 and 256 possible. Density increase continues via vertical stacking of memory layers (3D Flash).
- Emerging NVM: FeRAM suitable for RFID/smart card/embedded applications; HfO2-based ferroelectric FET proposed as low-power Flash-like memory; STT-MRAM seen as embedded (not standalone) memory, potential NOR Flash replacement for low-power IoT; 3D cross-point memory demonstrated for storage class memory (SCM); high-density ReRAM limited by selector device issues; PCM provides good scaling trajectory.
- Compute-in-memory (CIM) arrays expected to evolve for edge-AI applications, taking advantage of embedded NVM integrated in BEOL stack.

**Challenges:**
- Near-term (2022-2028): Power scaling (voltage/capacitance scaling slowdown), parasitics scaling in stacked devices, cost reduction through EUV/DTCO/3D stacking, SRAM density scaling slowdown (enabling stacked SRAM-cache dies), interconnect scalability (resistance, EM, TDDB).
- Long-term (2028-2037): Power scaling (steep-subthreshold devices as only solution beyond CMOS), thermal issues from power density in 3D stacking, cost management of 3D integration, integration of non-Cu metallization (buried power rails).

**Performance Boosters:** Strain engineering (SiGe S/D EPI, SRB), high-mobility channels (Ge, III-V) for 3D stacked tiers, low-κ spacers/air spacers to reduce parasitic capacitance, MIS contacts to reduce Schottky barrier height, fin depopulation, CFET (P-over-N stacked devices), improved electrostatics via LGAA, and reduced process/material variability (CDU, LWR, LER control). Beyond CMOS adoption (ferroelectric-FET, BEOL oxide transistors, IGZO, 2D materials, memristors) projected around 2028 for ultra-low-power and neuromorphic applications.

The document includes technology roadmaps (tables) for logic core devices, DRAM, Flash, and NVM, and provides detailed lists of the More Moore team members from industry and academia (IBM, Intel, TSMC, Samsung, Applied Materials, NIST, Stanford, etc.).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 17: Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2406.09106v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific tutorial paper (arXiv preprint 2406.09106) titled "Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects." The paper addresses the critical challenge that interconnect resistance and reliability are becoming key limiters for advanced CMOS circuit performance as transistor scaling slows and interconnect dimensions approach 10 nm.

**Key Context:** Current Cu dual-damascene metallization (which replaced Al-based metallization after 1999) faces growing issues at scaled dimensions. Cu requires diffusion barriers (typically TaN-based) and adhesion liners (typically Co) that cannot scale below a combined 2-3 nm thickness without losing function, leaving less space for actual Cu conductance. Additionally, Cu resistivity increases strongly at small dimensions due to grain boundary and surface scattering.

**Technology Roadmap:** The paper presents projected interconnect scaling targets through 2035, showing minimum metal pitch decreasing from 23 nm (2024/25, 2nm node) to 12 nm (2035, 3A node), with relevant interconnect line and via dimensions expected in the 5-10 nm range.

**Physics of Resistivity at Nanoscale:** The paper details the Boltzmann Transport Equation (BTE) framework, the Fuchs-Sondheimer equation for thin-film conductivity with surface scattering, and the Mayadas-Shatzkes model incorporating grain boundary scattering. Key material parameters affecting thin-film resistivity include: bulk single-crystal conductivity, electron mean free path, surface specularity (p), average grain size, and grain reflection coefficient (R).

**Key Finding:** The mean free path (λ) of charge carriers is a critical parameter. Cu's mean free path can reach up to 40 nm, which is large compared to interconnect dimensions. Metals with shorter λ are much less sensitive to interconnect scaling and grain boundary scattering effects. This has driven the search for alternative metals with short λ.

**Ab Initio Screening Methodology:** The paper introduces a ρ₀λ figure of merit that can be calculated via ab initio methods with limited computational effort, using either the constant relaxation time approximation or the constant mean free path approximation. This allows screening of candidate metals without full electron-phonon coupling calculations, which remain computationally prohibitive for large systems.

**Important Considerations:**
- Predictive calculations of thin-film resistivity are impossible without detailed knowledge of microstructure, which is process-dependent
- Grain size dependence on film thickness depends on deposition process parameters, not uniquely on material
- The reflection coefficient R and specularity p cannot be reliably predicted and are not purely materials properties
- Alloy scattering must be avoided in compound metals; only ordered intermetallics (not random alloys) are of potential interest for interconnects
- Anisotropy in Fermi surface can suppress surface scattering in 2D metals, but requires single-crystal lines with no current integration route yet
- Matthiessen's rule is typically not valid for surface and grain boundary scattering in thin metallic films

The paper describes a multistage screening process covering elemental, binary, and ternary metals, integration/process aspects for future nodes, and sustainability/life cycle assessment considerations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Today, interconnect resistance and reliability are key limiters for the performance of advanced CMOS circuits. As transistor scaling is slowing, interconnect scaling has become the main driver for circuit miniaturization."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 18: A view on the logic technology roadmap ---
URL: https://www.imec-int.com/en/articles/view-logic-technology-roadmap

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## imec's View on the Logic Technology Roadmap

This article, authored by imec researchers Naoto Horiguchi (Director of the logic CMOS scaling program) and Zsolt Tokei (Program director nano-interconnects), presents imec's joint technology roadmap for advancing front-end-of-line (FEOL), middle-of-line (MOL), and back-end-of-line (BEOL) semiconductor processing toward the 1nm technology generation. Originally published in the Semiconductor Digest (August/September 2020 issue), the article outlines both near-term and long-term innovation options.

### Key Components of Logic Chips
- **FEOL**: Processing of active transistors (gate, source, drain) at the bottom of the chip
- **BEOL**: Interconnects/wiring in the top of the chip, organized in up to 15 metal layers (3-6 local Mx layers)
- **MOL**: Tiny metal contacts connecting FEOL transistors to BEOL local interconnects

### State-of-the-Art Technologies and Bottlenecks
- **FinFETs**: Industry moved from planar MOSFET to FinFET architecture; first commercial 22nm FinFETs introduced in 2012; current 7nm chips use FinFETs with 6T standard cells, 2 fins per device, and contact pitches as small as 57nm
- **Cu-based dual damascene** is the workhorse process for BEOL interconnects; most critical local interconnects (M1, M2) now have metal pitches as tight as 40nm
- **EUV lithography** has been adopted by all leading logic manufacturers for cost-effective patterning at tight pitches
- Bottlenecks: routing congestion and dramatic RC delay; Co is being adopted as an alternative metal at local level; airgaps used as alternative low-k dielectric at intermediate layers
- **MOL**: source/drain contact resistance has become a major concern due to shrinking contact areas; imec has improved contact schemes through increased doping and optimized metal-semiconductor interface quality
- **Self-aligned gate contacts (SAGCs)** allow gate contacts to be placed directly on top of the active device, improving routability

### Next Innovation Options (Near-Term)

**FEOL - Nanosheet and Forksheet Devices:**
- **Gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors**: Natural evolution of FinFET; gate fully wraps around horizontal Si sheets providing superior channel control; imec has worked on this since 2015; developed processes to reduce vertical nanosheet separation below 10nm to cut parasitic capacitance
- **Forksheet devices**: Proposed for the 2nm node and beyond; a dielectric wall isolates p- and nMOS gates allowing much tighter n-to-p spacing; expected to shrink track heights from 5T to 4.3T with lower parasitic capacitance and reduced SRAM cell area

**BEOL - Hybrid Metallization and Semi-Damascene:**
- Metal pitches of M1/M2 will reach 21nm; via critical dimensions as small as 12-14nm
- **Hybrid metallization**: Alternative via metal (Ru, W, or Mo) connects barrierless to the bottom of Cu lines, allowing thinner (2nm) Cu line barriers while maintaining electromigration reliability and lowering via resistance
- **Semi-damascene**: Proposed for metal pitches below 21nm; omits the CMP step; enables higher aspect ratio lines with lower resistance; uses patternable alternative metals (Ru, Mo) and eventually airgaps; envisioned for M1 and M2 layers

**MOL - Connectivity Revolution:**
- **Buried power rails (BPRs)**: Power rails buried in the FEOL instead of BEOL to free routing resources; at VLSI 2020, imec demonstrated a tungsten BPR in a FinFET CMOS test vehicle without adversely impacting CMOS characteristics
- **VBPRs**: Via to BPR stitching with the MOL layer (M0A line); imec showed W-based BPR interfaced with Ru via for excellent resistance and electromigration results
- **Wrap-around contacts** (enabled by atomic layer deposition of metal) proposed to replace diamond epi contacts, re-enlarging contact area and decreasing contact resistance

### Further-Out Options (Toward 1nm Nodes)

**FEOL - CFET:**
- **Complementary FET (CFET)**: Folds nFET on top of pFET (fin-on-fin or sheet-on-sheet), fully exploiting 3D device scaling; strongest advantage is area scaling, eventually enabling 3T logic standard cells and significantly smaller SRAM cells
- At VLSI 2020, imec demonstrated first experimental proof-of-concept of CFET fabricated in a monolithic process flow
- **Sequential CFET** being explored as less complex alternative, allowing more flexible choice of channel materials

**BEOL - Hybrid Height with Zero Via and Alternative Conductors:**
- **Hybrid height with zero via**: Splits each metal layer into three sub-layers (center line, extension above/below), allowing resistance/capacitance exchange flexibility within the same footprint; realized by metal recess etching steps
- **New conductor materials**: Ordered binary intermetallic compounds with low resistivity at scaled dimensions (e.g., AlNi, RuV3-based compounds); figure of merit defined as product of bulk resistivity times mean free path
- **Hybrid graphene/metal conductors**: Metal (Cu, Ru, Mo) encapsulated by graphene; imec demonstrated low electrical resistivity and high thermal stability

**MOL:**
- Novel solutions needed for contacting the common gate in CFET structures
- High-aspect ratio vias will interconnect 3D building blocks; ruthenium-based advanced MOL contacts proposed to reduce parasitic resistance of deep vias

### Summary
As scaling continues beyond 5nm, chip makers may gradually move away from mainstream technologies (FinFETs in FEOL, Cu dual damascene in BEOL, traditional contact schemes in MOL). Imec's roadmap presents a possible path toward the 1nm technology node through new device architectures, materials (Ru, Mo, metal alloys), and integration schemes (hybrid metallization, semi-damascene, hybrid-height with zero-via structures).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Chipmakers are moving ahead with technology generations. But maintaining the same timeline for scaling transistors in the front-end-of-line (FEOL), contacts and interconnects in the middle- (MOL) and back-end-of-line (BEOL) has become challenging."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 19: Molybdenum's Role in Ultra-Fast Computing: The Metal Behind the ... ---
URL: https://blog.entegris.com/molybdenums-role-in-ultra-fast-computing-the-metal-behind-the-speed

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an Entegris "Ensights" blog article titled "Molybdenum's Role in Ultra-Fast Computing: The Metal Behind the Speed," published in May 2026. The article discusses how molybdenum (Mo) is emerging as a critical replacement metal for tungsten (W) and copper (Cu) in advanced semiconductor interconnects as the industry scales below the 10 nm threshold and adopts 3D architectures like gate-all-around (GAA) transistors and backside power delivery.

Key content includes:

WHY MOLYBDENUM: Molybdenum offers a combination of low resistivity, high melting point, excellent thermal/chemical stability, good electromigration resistance, and is barrierless (no barrier layer needed). Its key advantages include up to 30% lower resistivity than tungsten in thin films, barrierless integration that simplifies manufacturing and improves yield, and scalability supporting high aspect ratio features and 3D architectures.

COMPARISON TABLE (Cu vs W vs Mo): Copper has very low bulk resistivity (~1.68 µΩ-cm) but high thin film resistivity in small features and requires a barrier (e.g., TaN); tungsten has higher resistivity (~5.6 µΩ-cm), requires barrier (e.g., TiN), and is reaching limits; molybdenum has moderate bulk resistivity (~5.3 µΩ-cm), lower thin film resistivity than tungsten in small features, and requires no barrier. Molybdenum uses ALD, CVD, and selective ALD deposition methods. Industry trend: copper is being phased out at local interconnects, tungsten at contacts and vias, with molybdenum emerging as the successor.

THE RC CHALLENGE: Traditional copper interconnects are hitting a scaling barrier due to increasing resistance (R) and capacitance (C) as devices scale down, causing signal delay, power loss, and performance degradation. Copper's liner and barrier layers increasingly dominate resistance at smaller scales. Engineers are introducing cobalt, molybdenum, and ruthenium in select contacts and local interconnect layers.

LIMITATIONS: Copper is NOT expected to be replaced at tight-pitch interconnect (TPI) levels (Metal 1 through Metal 4) because these layers sit adjacent to SRAM structures (especially L1 cache) where low resistance is essential. The critical dimension of SRAM features is 4-5 times larger than the smallest CDs at TPI, and molybdenum, tungsten, and iridium cannot meet the very low sheet resistance (Rs) requirements at those levels today. L1 cache is expected to remain on chip for the foreseeable future, even as L2 and L3 caches are pulled off-chip via hybrid bonding.

PRECISION MANUFACTURING: Innovations in Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD), Area Selective Deposition (ASD), and Chemical Mechanical Planarization (CMP) enable molybdenum to be deposited with atomic-level precision, ensuring defect-free contacts and interconnects viable for high-volume manufacturing.

Entegris is positioned as a leader enabling molybdenum integration for advanced logic, supporting transitions across contacts, vias, backside power delivery, and selective prefilling schemes. A link is provided to learn more about Entegris molybdenum offerings (entegris.info/moly).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Molybdenum (Mo) is a promising metal for contacts and local interconnects because it offers a combination of low resistivity, high melting point, excellent thermal and chemical stability, and good electromigration resistance. It also is barrierless."
</key_excerpts>

Technology Overview

## From Foundational Reactors to AI-Driven Process Intelligence

Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) is a cyclical, self-limiting thin-film deposition technique that enables angstrom-level thickness control and conformal coverage across complex three-dimensional structures — capabilities that are indispensable as semiconductor nodes continue to shrink below 5 nm. The foundational principle — alternating, self-terminating surface reactions between sequential precursor pulses separated by purge cycles — appears consistently across all jurisdictions and filing eras tracked by [PatSnap's patent analytics platform](https://www.patsnap.com/products/analytics/).

The technology is undergoing rapid diversification. Filings from 2001–2010 concentrate on batch and single-wafer reactor architectures, while filings from 2018 onward increasingly address throughput limitations via spatial separation of precursor zones, intelligent gas flow control, and AI-driven process optimization. According to [WIPO](https://www.wipo.int) global patent trend data, semiconductor process patents have accelerated significantly since 2018, with ALD-adjacent filings tracking this broader surge.

Innovation is **moderately concentrated**: ASM-family entities hold the broadest reactor architecture IP, but the dataset reveals a long tail of Korean SMEs, Chinese integrated circuit manufacturers, and academic institutions generating significant filings, particularly post-2020. The [life sciences](https://www.patsnap.com/solutions/lifesciences/) and advanced materials sectors are increasingly adopting ALD for barrier coatings and functional surface engineering beyond core semiconductor manufacturing.

Key ALD Sub-Domains

* Thermal ALD (TALD) — sequential gas-phase precursor/oxidant cycling under vacuum
* Plasma-Enhanced ALD (PEALD) — RF plasma sources at lower substrate temperatures
* Spatial ALD — physical separation of precursor zones replacing temporal purge cycles
* Area-Selective ALD (AS-ALD) — SAM inhibitors restrict deposition to defined regions
* Roll-to-Roll ALD — continuous web-based deposition for flexible substrates
* Hybrid ALD/ALE Integration — combined deposition and etch cycles for atomic-scale pattern fidelity

## Four Primary ALD Innovation Clusters Identified

Patent analysis across 2001–2026 reveals four distinct technology clusters, each reflecting a different phase and strategic focus in ALD development.

Cluster 1

### Thermal & Plasma-Enhanced ALD Reactor Hardware

The most densely populated cluster in the dataset, covering chamber geometry, gas distribution, susceptor heating, and plasma source design. The core mechanism relies on alternating saturating doses of two or more precursors separated by inert purge steps, with plasma variants lowering required substrate temperatures. Key contributors include ASM Genitech Korea (2006–2009), Donghua University (2011), and Samsung Electronics (2025) with multi-zone reactant supply and in-situ thickness measurement per substrate zone for real-time uniformity correction.

Most active filing cluster

Cluster 2

### Spatial & High-Throughput ALD

Spatial ALD physically separates precursor zones, eliminating temporal purge cycles and dramatically increasing throughput. Substrate or deposition-head motion replaces sequential pulsing, enabling near-continuous deposition. ASM IP Holding B.V. (2019) introduced rotary deposition heads with hydraulic gas curtains; LG Electronics (2021) developed inline spatial ALD for flat display substrates; TNO (2014) pioneered rotating drum deposition heads for continuous substrate motion. [Advanced materials applications](https://www.patsnap.com/solutions/chemicals/) including OLED encapsulation and flexible electronics are key growth areas.

High commercial growth potential

Cluster 3

### Area-Selective & Process-Enhanced ALD

This cluster addresses depositing films on designated surface regions only — a critical enabler for self-aligned multi-patterning — using SAM inhibitor layers, transient enhancement strategies, or hybrid processes. KAIST (2026) demonstrated a solution-shear method for SAM deposition independent of substrate type. Genus Inc. (2006) introduced sub-saturation precursor dosing achieving 10–50% metal incorporation versus 5–20% in conventional ALD. Tokyo Electron (2024) developed a hybrid wet ALE process bridging ALD and wet etch in a single cyclic process. According to [EPO](https://www.epo.org) patent landscape reports, selective deposition is among the fastest-growing semiconductor process IP categories.

Approaching productization

Cluster 4

### In-Situ Monitoring, AI Integration & Process Intelligence

Emerging since 2018, this cluster addresses the "black box" problem in ALD: limited visibility into film quality during deposition without breaking vacuum. Changchun University (2018) integrated RHEED for real-time crystallographic quality feedback. Korea University (2018) embedded in-situ XRF for real-time film composition and thickness analysis. Korea Institute of Fusion Energy (2025) introduced deep learning-based multivariate process prediction using 2D ALD image datasets. HKUST Guangzhou (2025) developed an AI-driven recommendation engine for precursor and process parameter selection. ## Where ALD Is Being Deployed Across Industry

ALD patent activity spans semiconductor logic and memory, EUV lithography infrastructure, display, photonics, compound semiconductors, and industrial coatings.

💾

### Semiconductor Device Manufacturing

The largest application domain across all retrieved results. ALD is used for gate dielectrics, diffusion barriers, capacitor dielectrics, and metal fill in sub-10 nm devices. Fujian Jinhua (2023) addresses multi-wafer uniformity correction in DRAM-era process chambers. Xinen IC (2024) incorporates annealing chambers co-located with ALD reaction chambers for in-line crystallization of deposited films. The [Semiconductor Industry Association](https://www.semiconductors.org) projects continued ALD adoption as nodes shrink below 3 nm.

🔬

### EUV Lithography Infrastructure

ALD has become a materials enabler for EUV optics and mask components. Carl Zeiss SMT GmbH (2024) describes macro-cycle ALD with partial back-etching for controlled deposition of capping layers on EUV optics. Frequently asked questions

## Atomic Layer Deposition — Key Questions Answered

Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) is a cyclical, self-limiting thin-film deposition technique that enables angstrom-level thickness control and conformal coverage across complex three-dimensional structures — capabilities that are indispensable as semiconductor nodes continue to shrink below 5 nm.

Key ALD sub-domains include Thermal ALD (TALD) using sequential gas-phase precursor/oxidant cycling under vacuum, Plasma-Enhanced ALD (PEALD) using RF plasma sources at lower substrate temperatures, Spatial ALD with physically separated precursor zones, Area-Selective ALD (AS-ALD) using SAM inhibitors, Roll-to-Roll ALD for flexible substrates, and Hybrid ALD/ALE Integration for atomic-scale pattern fidelity.

ASM Genitech Korea Ltd. / ASM IP Holding B.V. are the most prolific ALD-specific assignees in this dataset, with multiple filings across 2006–2019. Other key assignees include Samsung Electronics, Carl Zeiss SMT GmbH, Applied Materials, and Beneq Oy. Domestic Chinese companies including SMIC, Fujian Jinhua, Wuhan China Star, and Wuxi Yiwen represent a coordinated coverage of ALD for logic, memory, display, and equipment control.

The two most recent (2025) AI-focused patents signal a structural shift. Deep Learning-Based ALD Process Multivariate Prediction (Korea Institute of Fusion Energy, 2025) and Process Data Push Method for Atomic-Scale Processing (HKUST Guangzhou, 2025) both leverage neural networks and intelligent data recommendation to replace empirical trial-and-error in precursor selection and cycle optimization.

Area-Selective ALD (AS-ALD) uses self-assembled monolayer (SAM) inhibitors to restrict deposition to defined surface regions — a critical enabler for self-aligned multi-patterning. The emergence of substrate-agnostic SAM-based AS-ALD (KAIST 2026) alongside existing inhibitor chemistry patents signals that AS-ALD is approaching productization.

ALD has become a materials enabler for EUV optics and mask components. Carl Zeiss SMT GmbH uses ALD for capping layers on EUV optics and smoothing layers on metal mirror substrates. Applied Materials applies ALD to deposit protective coatings (AlN, Al₂O₃, BN, Ru, TaN, SiC, etc.) on carbon nanotube EUV pellicle membranes, maintaining greater than 90% EUV transmittance.

5. Preserve any lists or step-by-step instructions if present.
6. Include relevant dates, names, and locations that are crucial to understanding the content.
7. Summarize lengthy explanations while keeping the core message intact.

When handling different types of content:

- For news articles: Focus on the who, what, when, where, why, and how.
- For scientific content: Preserve methodology, results, and conclusions.
- For opinion pieces: Maintain the main arguments and supporting points.
- For product pages: Keep key features, specifications, and unique selling points.

Your summary should be significantly shorter than the original content but comprehensive enough to stand alone as a source of information. Aim for about 25-30 percent of the original length, unless the content is already concise.

```
}
```

E.|Meija, J.",,14,,,,EGU2012-1495-1,2012,2012,,,,Geophysical Research Abstracts,"European Geosciences Union (EGU) General Assembly 2012, April 22-27, 2012, Vienna, Austria",,,,,,"Today, MC-ICPMS has become a powerful research tool for the high precision isotope ratio measurements with over five-hundred papers published annually in the past several years1-2. This bias needs to be properly corrected in order to obtain accurate isotope amount ratio measurements. The choice of the fractionation law to calibrate (correct) measured isotope ratios is crucial in isotope science. Over the last decades, the Russell law mass bias correction model (Eq. 1)4 which is applicable only for mass-dependent fractionation and assumes identical mass bias for both the calibrator and measurand elements, has become a standard curriculum in isotope ratio measurements. However, it has been reported that not only mass bias is different for different elements but also that the mass bias is different for different isotope pairs of a same element5-6. Mass-independent fractionation in MC-ICPMS has been observed for elements such as Nd, W and Cd5-7. Ri,j = ri,j(mi/mj)-f (1) Here Ri,j = n(iE)/n(jE), ri,j is the measured (uncorrected) isotope ratio and E is the element of interest, f is the fractionation function and mi,mj are the nuclide masses. In this program, initial testing of four methods was carried out at the Mears Group Inc, test site that had been modified with additional grounding systems to simulate a nuclear power plant. This was followed by testing of the same methods at the AECL Nuclear Laboratories Chalk River site. This paper will discuss the results of those studies and present some of the findings that were made that can help to overcome the challenges faced by Nuclear Power Plants.",,10.1115/PVP2012-78794,23001887,,,,1dd78ce1-0b98-4802-852c-68e907e1a063,article,eng Unsupervised data analysis methods used in qualitative and quantitative metabolomics and metabonomics,"Cuperlovic-culf, Miroslava",,,,1,28,,2012,2012,Advances in Bioinformatics and Biomedical Engineering,,2327-7033|2327-7041,,,Systemic Approaches in Bioinformatics and Computational Systems Biology,,Medical Information Science Reference,9781613504352|9781613504369,,"Metabolomics or metababonomics is one of the major high throughput analysis methods that endeavors holistic measurement of metabolic profiles of biological systems. In this work, the author will demonstrate the benefits and limitations of different unsupervised analysis tools currently utilized in qualitative and quantitative metabolomics data analysis. Following a detailed literature review outlining different applications of unsupervised methods in metabolomics, the author shows examples of an application of the major previously utilized unsupervised analysis methods. The testing of these methods was performed using qualitative as well as corresponding quantitative metabolite data derived to represent a large set of 2,000 objects. Spectra of mixtures were obtained from different combinations of experimental NMR measurements of 13 prevalent metabolites at five different groups of concentrations representing different phenotypes. The analysis shows advantages and disadvantages of standard tools when applied specifically to metabolomics.",,10.4018/978-1-61350-435-2.ch001,23001800,,,,c5de7866-858f-4239-bcfe-85d27de1f2a7,chapter,eng Abstract 2532: integrated therapeutic antibody development at the National Research Council of Canada,"Jaramillo, Maria Luz|O'connor-McCourt, Maureen",Cancer Research,72,8 Supplement,2532,2532,,2012,15/04/2012,,,0008-5472|1538-7445,,,,,American Association for Cancer Research,,,"Advances in genomics and antibody engineering have enabled the development of an innovative class of targeted therapies to provide new treatment options for diseases with significant unmet medical needs such as cancer. Therapeutic antibodies represent one of the fastest growing classes of medications with sales anticipated to exceed $30 billion globally by 2012. The NRC has built a chain of cutting edge technology platforms needed to discover, engineer and produce therapeutic monoclonal antibodies with the goal of partnering with industrial and academic centers to advance research and development of this important class of therapeutics. Target Identification- To establish and validate the technology platform, tumor targets for candidate therapeutic antibody production were identified using a combination of proteomics, transcriptomics and bioinformatic approaches. Out of these lists, approximately 40 tumor targets were selected (known therapeutic antibody targets were excluded), and over 2,000 antibodies of mouse and camelid origin were then generated against these targets. Antibody generation- Once identified, the recombinant target protein of interest can be produced using the NRC's high efficiency cell expression platforms in CHO or HEK293 cells and purified protein used for immunization or panning. For targets which are difficult to express or purify, the capabilities for direct immunization with plasmid DNA constructs provides another option. Clone selection is carried out by ELISA and typically 50 antibodies/target are identified for further characterization. Antibody characterization and validation- The affinities of the antibodies are determined by SPR biosensor analysis. Reverse phase protein arrays and Western blot analysis on protein mixes and cell lines allow the characterization of the specificity of the antibodies. Epitope mapping can be carried out so that representative antibodies from each epitope bin can be selected for further validation in appropriate cell-based assays (many of which are established at NRC) and animal models. Therapeutic antibody Optimization, Bioprocessing and Biomanufacturing- Therapeutic antibodies selected for development can be further optimized using antibody engineering technologies to humanize them and/or modify their glycosylation patterns to improve their effector function, pharmacokinetics, solubility and stability as well as reduce their immunogenicity. The NRC platform for large scale protein production has the capacity to manufacture up to 13.5 g of commercial grade antibody using serum free, low endotoxin media in a cGMP certified CHO cell line which is ready for transfer to CMOs or other industrial partners.",,10.1158/1538-7445.AM2012-2532,23001785,,,,43e3adb3-7a37-4997-8810-9a01dd13295c,article,eng "Application of metabolomics in drug discovery, development and theranostics","Cuperlovic-Culf, Miroslava|S. Analysis of metabolic changes in patients and in disease models following treatments provides new methods for investigation of therapeutic response. Combined examination of disease metabolic characteristics and treatment response provides markers for personalization of therapies. Metabolomics finds itself at an increasingly important junction in all of these applications. Assessment of efficacy and specificity of drugs that directly or indirectly target metabolism through analyses of metabolic changes will also be presented. The focus of this review will be directed towards cancer, however, the overarching ideas as well as experimental and analysis approaches are easily transferable to other applications. In cancer research, metabolism is once again raising interest due to a better appreciation of the significance of altered metabolic phenotype in cancer development and progression. Additionally, it affects production of several enzymes leading to the reduction of glycerides and modification of the fatty acid profile, important quality determinants of seed oil. Additionally, different strategies employed by crop plants against salt stress as well as research reports describing genetic and transgenic approaches designed for improving plants ability to overcome salt stress are discussed.",Plant breeding|Plant genetics|Plant physiology,10.1007/978-1-4614-4747-4\_9,23000578,,,,ff848714-46c9-44ba-96d5-bc46a96244e6,chapter,eng Advances in microspore culture technology: a biotechnological tool for the improvement of medicinal plants,"Ferrie, Alison M. # ESA project develops Tanbium alloy for AM rocket engine parts

[Companies & Markets](/category/companies-markets)[Materials](/category/materials)[News](/category/news)

November 6, 2025

![ESA-backed project will investigate Tanbium, an alloy designed to meet the needs of extreme-environment applications (Courtesy Skyrora)](http://www.metal-am.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2025/11/skyora-close.jpg)

ESA-backed project will investigate Tanbium, a tantalum-niobium alloy designed to meet the needs of extreme-environment applications (Courtesy Skyrora)

Skyrora, headquartered in Cumbernauld, UK, has announced its participation as a prime contractor in the European Space Agency’s (ESA) General Support Technology Programme (GSTP). The project will focus on the Additive Manufacturing of Tanbium, a novel high-temperature tantalum-niobium alloy. Developed in collaboration with metal powder producer Metalysis, based in Rotherham, UK, and Thermo-Calc Solutions, located in Solna, Sweden, GSTP aims to validate the alloy’s production and performance for use in rocket engine components and other extreme-environment applications.

“This project reinforces Skyrora’s commitment to sovereign launch capability and materials innovation,” stated Derek Harris, Director of Business Development and Communications at Skyrora. “The UK and Europe are currently heavily dependent on the US for C103 alloy, which is used across aerospace propulsion. Tanbium will enable full domestic sourcing with the powder produced by Metalysis, and components printed and tested by Skyrora, which will be simulated by Thermo-Calc to optimise material behaviour before physical testing. As a European launch vehicle manufacturer, not only will Tanbium align with our long-term vision for sustainable, high-performance space hardware, but it will also contribute to the ESA’s Net Zero Space ambitions.”

Developed to overcome the challenges faced by existing aerospace alloys, Tanbium offers higher burn time and temperature capability, up to an estimated 30% in weight savings in engine components, up to 95% less material waste through Additive Manufacturing, and the potential for a 40% reduction in total component cost.

GSTP is said to represent a first Direct Energy Deposition (DED) Additive Manufacturing application, targeting rocket engine components, specifically nozzles and combustion chambers. The production of Tanbium is intended to reduce reliance on US imports of alloys, helping to localise a key material for the UK and European industrial sector.

![Skyrora will lead integration using its proprietary Skyprint 1 and 2 DED Additive Manufacturing machines (Courtesy Skyrora)](http://www.metal-am.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2025/11/skyora.jpg)

Skyrora will lead integration using its proprietary Skyprint 1 and 2 DED Additive Manufacturing machines (Courtesy Skyrora)

The nine-month ESA-funded project, which begins in Q4 2025, will include Additive Manufacturing trials, material validation, mechanical testing, and a business case analysis. It marks a strategic move in advancing propulsion manufacturing and will support vertical integration. Skyrora will lead integration using its proprietary Skyprint 1 and 2 DED Additive Manufacturing machines.

“Metalysis is very excited to be participating in this ESA funded project – utilising our alloy and high-entropy alloy experience to produce the new alloy Tanbium, which is predicted to significantly enhance space component lifetimes,” stated Nitesh Shah, CEO of Metalysis. “Skyrora came to us as the advanced materials partner because only our solid-state process can produce such a vast range of novel alloys. We look forward to successfully completing stage 1 of this project and moving to stages 2 and 3, and so making a real impact within the space propulsion market”.

Ida Berglund, Managing Director of Thermo-Calc Solutions, added, “Tanbium represents a major advancement in high-temperature alloy technology for space propulsion. Developed through an ICME-led design approach, Tanbium delivers performance and manufacturability gains that were previously out of reach – offering extended burn life, higher operating temperatures, and significant weight and cost reductions. Its validation in rocket engine components marks a key milestone, demonstrating both the maturity of ICME and the potential to secure a high-performance materials supply chain for Europe. We’re proud to see this breakthrough tested by such an experienced and forward-thinking partner alongside expert powder producers—an ideal team to showcase what Tanbium can achieve in rocket propulsion systems.”

Simon Hyde, Technical Officer at ESA, concluded, “Ultra-High Temperature capable materials for rocket motor applications are a key item in the ESA work plans. This project addresses the challenge in an outstanding way: It combines bespoke alloy design with a unique production approach. These technologies are perfectly wedded to direct energy deposition Additive Manufacturing. Using this Tanbium alloy, the consortium are addressing a critical challenge for ultra-high temperature applications in Europe. They are opening a potentially rich seam for space applications and providing Europe with a resilient supply chain.”
