args.research_topic: Research the specific metal thin films deposited by physical vapor deposition (PVD/sputtering), chemical vapor deposition (CVD), and atomic layer deposition (ALD) equipment in advanced semiconductor manufacturing nodes (7nm and below) by leading foundries like TSMC, Samsung, and Intel during 2023-2026. For each deposition technique, identify which specific metal or metal-compound thin films they deposit, such as tungsten (W), cobalt (Co), tantalum (Ta), titanium (Ti), titanium nitride (TiN), tantalum nitride (TaN), copper (Cu), ruthenium (Ru), molybdenum (Mo), aluminum (Al), etc. Also identify the application context for each film: barrier layer / adhesion layer, interconnect wiring layer, gate metal, contact layer, capping layer, or via fill. Cite equipment vendor technical materials from Applied Materials, Lam Research, ASM International, and Tokyo Electron, as well as SEMI / IRDS roadmap documents and industry public sources. Provide detailed technical information about which films are deposited by PVD sputtering (e.g., TaN/Ta barrier for copper interconnects, TiN, Ru liner, Cu seed), which by CVD (e.g., tungsten fill, cobalt fill, molybdenum, TiN from metal-organic precursors), and which by ALD (e.g., TiN, TaN, W nucleation, Ru, Co, molybdenum). Provide concrete examples from 7nm, 5nm, 3nm, 2nm nodes.

Research the technical reasons why specific metal deposition equipment (physical vapor deposition PVD, chemical vapor deposition CVD, atomic layer deposition ALD) is chosen for depositing particular metal thin films in advanced semiconductor manufacturing (7nm and below nodes, 2023-2026 era by TSMC, Samsung, Intel). Analyze the tradeoffs in terms of: thin film quality (purity, uniformity, step coverage / conformality in high-aspect-ratio vias and trenches, film stress), process temperature requirements (thermal budget compatibility with low-k dielectrics and FinFET/GAA transistors), deposition rate and throughput, compatibility with existing process steps (integration), and cost effectiveness. Explain specifically why PVD is used for TaN/Ta barrier and copper seed layers despite poor step coverage, why CVD is used for tungsten and cobalt gap fill due to good fill capability, why ALD is used for conformal barrier/liner layers on extreme high-aspect-ratio structures and for advanced gate metals, and why newer metals like ruthenium and molybdenum are being introduced for interconnect and via-fill at advanced nodes. Cite equipment vendor data (Applied Materials, Lam Research, ASM International, Tokyo Electron), SEMI/IRDS roadmaps, and technical papers.

Research how widely electron beam evaporation (e-beam evaporation) and molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) deposition equipment are actually used in high-volume manufacturing (HVM) of advanced-node semiconductor chips (7nm and below, TSMC, Samsung, Intel, 2023-2026). Determine whether these two techniques are primarily used in research and development (R&D) and laboratories rather than in mass production fabs. Analyze the reasons: e-beam evaporation gives poor step coverage and directionality making it unsuitable for filling high-aspect-ratio vias and trenches in advanced interconnect and contact structures, difficulty controlling uniformity and film stress at wafer scale, contamination and particle issues, and low throughput; MBE has extremely low growth rates, ultra-high-vacuum requirements, very high cost, and is mainly used for compound semiconductors, epitaxial layers for research, and specialized applications like magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJ) for MRAM and advanced gate stacks, not for mainstream metal interconnect films in CMOS logic mass production. Also mention where e-beam and MBE DO appear in advanced chip manufacturing or R&D: e.g., MBE for MRAM/STT-MRAM magnetic layers, MBE for quantum devices research, e-beam evaporation in some laboratories and for optical coatings, and possibly PVD alternatives. Cite SEMI/ITRS/IRDS roadmaps, equipment vendor information, and industry publications.

messages.content:
## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

**Search 1 (tavily_search):**
- "PVD sputtering metal films advanced nodes TSMC Samsung Intel barrier layer TaN Ta Cu seed interconnect"
- "Applied Materials CVD tungsten cobalt fill advanced node interconnect wiring barrier layer"
- "ALD atomic layer deposition metal films TiN TaN Ru Co W nucleation advanced semiconductor nodes"

**Search 2 (tavily_search):**
- "Lam Research ALTUS tungsten CVD cobalt fill molybdenum interconnect deposition advanced node"
- "ASM International ALD Pulsar Synergy TiN TaN tungsten nucleation atomic layer deposition semiconductor"
- "Tokyo Electron TEL CVD ALD metal films copper ruthenium molybdenum interconnects advanced nodes"

**Search 3 (tavily_search):**
- "ASM International ALD Pulsar Synergy TiN TaN W nucleation cobalt ruthenium molybdenum advanced node 3nm 2nm"
- "Applied Materials Endura PVD Cirrus HTX TaN Ta Cu seed TiN barrier advanced node interconnect"
- "IRDS roadmap interconnect metal molybdenum ruthenium cobalt tungsten 2nm node metallization"

**Think tool reflections:** Recorded twice to track gaps (missing ASM-specific tools, Applied Materials PVD specifics, node-specific applications, IRDS/SEMI roadmap details).

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### 1. PVD Sputtering — Targets, Films, and Applications

**PVD role and materials overview (SemiconductorX):** PVD deposits "every major metallization layer in semiconductor manufacturing, including copper seed layers for BEOL damascene interconnect, titanium/titanium nitride barrier layers, tantalum/tantalum nitride diffusion barriers, tungsten contact liners, aluminum bonding pads, cobalt advanced-node contacts, and emerging ruthenium/molybdenum alternatives at sub-5nm nodes." Targets require "5N to 7N purity (99.999% to 99.99999%) with specific grain structure, density, and dimensional tolerances." [4]

**Sputtering target market context (DataIntelo):** The global semiconductor sputtering targets market was valued at $4.8 billion in 2025, projected to reach $9.2 billion by 2034 (CAGR 7.5%). Pure metals dominate at 44.2% share ($2.12B); alloys hold 31.4% (fastest growth at 7.9% CAGR); compounds hold 24.4%. Integrated Circuits dominate applications at 42.1% ($2.02B). Growth drivers include fab capex exceeding $190B in 2025. Key opportunities explicitly tied to advanced nodes include "GAA transistor transitions at 2nm nodes (new ruthenium/molybdenum targets)" and "3D NAND stacking." Key threats include potential displacement by ALD/CVD. [1]

**JX Advanced Metals sputtering target specifics (the targets used in PVD tools):**
- **Ti Target:** Purity 4N5 (Ti 99.995%+), 5N, 5N5. Supports all sputtering equipment and wafer sizes. "Uses: interconnect barrier, hard masks, gate electrodes, UBM, TSV."
- **Cu Target:** 6N (99.9999%+) purity, reduced O, S, P impurities. "Uses: Cu interconnect seed layer, UBM, TSV."
- **Cu Alloy Target:** Uses 6N Cu; alloys include CuAl, CuMn, etc. "Used for Cu interconnect seed layers in leading-edge semiconductors."
- **Ta Target:** Purity 4N5 (effectively 5N+). "Uses: barrier in Cu interconnect process, TSV."
- **W Target:** 5N purity, density 99%+. Diffusion bonding for high-power sputtering. "Uses: gate electrodes." W-Si and W-Ti targets also available.
- **High-purity Co (5N) and Ni (5N), plus NiPt alloy (4N5):** "Uses: gate electrodes."
- JX supplies "Ti, Cu, and Ta coils, pins, caps, and parts sets" for Applied Materials (AMAT) sputtering equipment on 200mm and 300mm wafers — JX is an officially authorized supplier for Applied Materials. [2]

**Historical barrier material evolution for Cu interconnects (Allan Chemical):**
- "Late 1990s: Tantalum (Ta) and Tantalum Nitride (TaN) became the standard barrier materials, applied via physical vapor deposition (PVD), to prevent copper diffusion into dielectric layers."
- "By 2013 (16nm/14nm nodes): Cobalt (Co) liners replaced tantalum liners due to superior wetting properties, better copper adhesion, improved gap fill, and lower electrical resistance."
- "Current (2nm and beyond): Ruthenium-Cobalt (RuCo) alloys now dominate advanced nodes, combining ruthenium's diffusion-blocking strength with cobalt's conductivity and adhesion."
- "RuCo alloys reduce barrier thickness by 33% (down to just 20 angstroms) and cut resistance by up to 25% compared to tantalum-based processes."
- "Applied Materials demonstrated a 2.5% performance boost in 2 nm test chips using RuCo liners alongside advanced Black Diamond low-k dielectric materials."
- Dual-damascene deposition stages: "conformal barrier layer application (diffusion block), copper seed layer deposition via PVD, and copper electroplating to fill etched features." Deposition methods include PVD, CVD/PECVD, and ALD, "which achieves exceptional uniformity even in features with aspect ratios above 10:1." Barrier thicknesses typically range from 10 to 250 angstroms, with combined seed and barrier layers kept under 120 angstroms.
- Advanced barriers enable "void-free copper reflow, seedless copper electroplating (eliminating PVD seed layers)."
- "Advanced β-phase tantalum or ruthenium-based formulations achieve resistivities below 60 Ω/cm."
- Copper remains the preferred interconnect material even at 2nm dimensions, with focus on refining barrier/liner systems. [3]

**TSMC interconnect research history (relevant PVD/ALD/barrier context):**
- 2003: "High performance/reliability Cu interconnect with selective CoWP cap" — a selective CoWP metal cap replaced conventional dielectric cap after Cu CMP, achieving "5% reduction in RC delay and more than 10X improvement in electromigration for both via and trench, with 100% yield."
- 2002: "90 nm generation copper dual damascene with ALD TaN barrier" — ALD applied for TaN barrier in 90nm Cu dual damascene with low-k dielectrics (k=3.0), "providing conformal step coverage and thickness control (~10 Å), with superior reliability (electromigration, stress migration, bias temperature test) versus conventional PVD TaN."
- 2002: "CVD barriers for Cu with nanoporous ultra low-k" — feasibility study with "CVD TiN(Si) barrier for Cu dual damascene integration."
- 2000: "Evaluation of diffusion barrier performance of reactively sputtered TaNx layers" — grain boundary diffusivity of Cu in TaNx (x=0-0.62) extracted using Whipple analysis. [5]

**Applied Materials PVD platforms (BCC Research product catalog):**
- **Endura Platform** — metallization system with many systems:
  - Endura ALPS PVD (Cobalt): "High-efficiency silicide solution for gate and contact applications in high aspect ratio structures"
  - Endura Amber PVD: "Copper filling within interconnect trench and via structures"
  - Endura Avenir RF PVD: "For high k/metal gate applications and logic contact silicidation, extending to 22nm and beyond"
  - Endura Cirrus HT Co PVD: "Silicide coverage for reduced contact areas and increasing aspect ratios"
  - Endura Cirrus HTX PVD: "Hardmask solutions for next-gen devices beyond the 10nm node"
  - Endura Clover MRAM PVD: "For logic and memory applications at 3x/2x node and beyond"
  - Endura CuBS RF XT PVD: "Copper Barrier/Seed system for logic and memory from 3x/2x node onward"
  - Endura ILB PVD/ALD: "With Centinel chambers, addresses contact resistance as dimensions decrease"
  - Endura Impulse PCRAM PVD: For PCRAM/ReRAM
  - Endura Ioniq W PVD: "Pure tungsten (W) metallization across contact applications"
  - Endura PVD (core): "front-end metallization (cobalt, tungsten), aluminum/copper interconnects, and underbump metallization"
  - Endura Underbump: "UBM and bond pad solutions (NiV, Cu, Ti, TiW, CuCr, TaN, AI)"
  - Endura Ventura PVD: "For TSVs with aspect ratios ≥10:1 and 2.5D interposer applications"
  - Endura Versa XLR2 W PVD: "Deposits purer/smoother tungsten with resistivity 10-15% lower than current technology"
  - Endura Volta Cobalt CVD: "Ultra-thin seed-enhancing liners and selective cap layers (<20Å) for interconnect yield at 2Xnm node and beyond"
  - Endura Volta Selective W CVD: "Combines surface treatment with selective tungsten deposition"
  - Endura Volta W CVD: "Reduces contact resistance by up to 90%"
- **Charger Platform** — Charger UBM PVD for UBM, RDL, CMOS image sensors.
- **Axcela Platform** — Axcela PVD: "Maintains non-uniformities of <2% 1σ, handles thick films up to 8µm, each sputter chamber can deposit three distinct materials with co-sputtering flexibility." [33]

**Applied Materials Endura Cirrus HTX PVD:** "High-density, tensile Cirrus™ TiN produces tight line width control and via overlay alignment to preserve the pattern integrity of dense, complex interconnects." The Endura Cirrus HTX PVD system is described as a "breakthrough patterning hardmask" enabling copper interconnects at 10nm and beyond. [32][34]

---

### 2. CVD Films — Tungsten Fill, Cobalt Fill/Liner/Cap, Ruthenium Liner, Molybdenum

**Applied Materials — Cobalt CVD (Endura Volta) — the major conducting-material change:**
- SemiEngineering article by Kavita Shah (Applied Materials): "Advanced chips can feature up to 15 layers of copper metallization and more than 7 linear miles of wiring embedded in a square-inch 28nm chip layout." Applied Materials' "new Endura Volta CVD system" is "described as the biggest change in copper interconnects in the last 15 years," enabling two new cobalt process steps: (1) "A conformal cobalt liner deposited via CVD that enables thin, continuous deposition, optimizing the copper seed layer for good plating performance and reliable device performance"; (2) "A selective CVD cobalt capping layer deposited after chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) to reduce electro-migration by immobilizing copper atoms at the surface and promoting adhesion to the subsequent dielectric barrier layer." Together these "completely encapsulate the copper wiring," demonstrating "improved copper gap fill and an order-of-magnitude reduction in electro-migration... critical to extending Moore's Law beyond 20 nanometers." [6]
- Applied Materials blog (July 19, 2018, Jonathan Bakke): "This cobalt transition is described as the most significant conducting material change since copper dual damascene was introduced 20 years ago." Key technical points: "Tungsten contacts require liners, barriers, and adhesion layers that make extending to 7nm and beyond challenging; without scaling these layers, there would be no pure metal left in the contact by the 5nm node." "Cobalt contacts can use a thinner barrier layer, don't require a nucleation layer, and provide 6nm of fill volume at 5nm (versus tungsten), with lower resistance and the ability to remove seams via an anneal process." For copper interconnects, "adopting cobalt enables scaling liner/barrier thickness, though copper has better bulk resistivity; however, cobalt has significantly better electromigration properties, improving device reliability." The end-to-end solution: "deposition on the Endura platform (integrated PVD and CVD cobalt), anneal on the Producer system, planarization on the Reflexion LK Prime CMP system, and cobalt void detection via the PROVision platform's non-destructive electron beam method." "The cobalt can fill re-entrant features (narrower at top than bottom) without seams or voids." [7]
- Applied Materials blog (Dec 17, 2018, Mehul Naik, Ph.D.): "Tungsten requires a thick ALD titanium nitride barrier layer that doesn't scale proportionally with reduced critical dimensions, causing increased contact resistance and decreased on-state current." "Cobalt offers advantages over tungsten and copper at small geometries: it has bulk resistivity similar to tungsten but is ~1.5-2x less resistive due to impurities and grain boundary scattering in tungsten, and it works with thinner barriers." "Industry results show replacing tungsten contacts with cobalt provides approximately 60% improvement in contact line resistance, and cobalt local interconnects reduce via resistance and improve electromigration reliability." "Copper remains superior or adequate for CDs of 12-15nm and for longer metal levels above M1 where line resistance dominates. Copper extension requires co-optimization: replacing PVD tantalum nitride barriers with ALD tantalum nitride (enabling scaling below 36nm pitch) and using copper reflow on cobalt liners." "Beyond cobalt and copper, ruthenium and molybdenum are being explored but lag cobalt in maturity." References a 2018 IEDM paper (C. Auth et al.) on 10nm CMOS with "3rd generation FinFETs and cobalt local interconnects." [8]
- Applied Materials Endura Volta Cobalt CVD product page: "This high-quality layer in turn promotes void-free copper gap fill at the most advanced nodes. vital for avoiding EM failures." [9]

**Lam Research — Tungsten CVD/ALD (ALTUS family) and Molybdenum ALD (ALTUS Halo):**
- ALTUS Product Family page: "Lam's market-leading ALTUS® systems combine CVD and ALD technologies to deposit the highly conformal films needed for advanced metallization applications." Used "primarily for tungsten (W) and molybdenum (Mo) deposition to form conductive features like contacts, vias, and plugs on chips." Key challenges addressed: "Conventional CVD tungsten fill is limited by overhang from barrier films, leading to voids, higher resistance, and contact failure." Key capabilities: "Pulsed Nucleation Layer (PNL) ALD process with in-situ bulk CVD fill via Multi-Station Sequential Deposition (MSSD), lower resistivity thin W films, low-fluorine low-stress W fill for 3D NAND and DRAM, and high step coverage WN films using ALD." Product offerings: "ALTUS® Halo, Concept Two® ALTUS®, ALTUS® Max, ALTUS® Max ExtremeFill™, ALTUS® DirectFill™ Max, ALTUS® Max ICEFill®, and ALTUS® LFW." Key applications: "Plug, contact, and via fill; 3D NAND wordlines; low-stress composite interconnects; and WN barrier for via and contact metallization." [19]
- Lam Research press release (Feb 19, 2025): "Lam Research unveiled ALTUS Halo — the world's first atomic layer deposition (ALD) tool that enables the use of the metal molybdenum in leading-edge semiconductor production... the industry's first molybdenum deposition solution for high-volume manufacturing." Key advantages over tungsten: "molybdenum has lower resistivity in nano-scale wires, doesn't require adhesion or barrier layers (reducing process steps and boosting efficiency), and provides better than 50% improvement in resistance over conventional tungsten metallization in most instances." The tool is "currently in qualification and ramping with all leading chipmakers, with early adoption at high-volume 3D NAND manufacturers in Korea and Singapore and at advanced logic fabs, while development continues with DRAM customers." Addresses "1,000-layer 3D NAND, 4F2 DRAM, and advanced gate-all-around logic." Quote from Sesha Varadarajan (SVP, GM Global Products Group, Lam Research): "ALTUS Halo is the most significant breakthrough in atomic layer deposition in over 20 years." Quote from Mark Kiehlbauch (corporate VP of NAND development, Micron): "Lam's ALTUS Halo tool has made it possible for Micron to bring molybdenum into mass production." [15][16][17][18]
- Lam promotional video: "Lam pioneered tungsten ALD over 20 years ago and built the ALTUS system into the industry benchmark for tungsten fill productivity... As AI demand surges and scaling moves toward 1,000 NAND layers, tungsten-based metallization is hitting its limits, so chipmakers across NAND, DRAM, and foundry logic are transitioning to molybdenum for its low resistance and barrierless integration." ALTUS Halo "can deposit conformally or selectively with bottom-up feature fill using chemistry and thermal flexibility, plus plasma for temperature-sensitive applications." [18]

**Tokyo Electron — CVD Ruthenium liner (Trias Tandem):**
- TEL/Novellus press release (Dec 1, 2008): Jointly developed "an ionized PVD TaN or Ti barrier capped with an ultra-thin CVD Ruthenium (Ru) liner, coupled with a proprietary copper wet seed process (DirectSeed™) and copper electrochemical deposition," eliminating "the traditional PVD Cu seed process" for the 2Xnm generation. "The CVD Ru liner deposited using TEL's Trias Tandem™ system at thicknesses ≤2nm (20 Angstroms), offering exceptional conformality and the most attractive consumable costs compared to PVD or ALD Ru." Novellus's "DirectSeed™ wet copper seed process deposited in the SABRE® Extreme™ electrochemical deposition tool at thicknesses ≤3nm (30 Angstroms)." [23]

---

### 3. ALD Films — TaN Barrier, TiN, W Nucleation, Ru, Co, Mo

**ALD fundamentals (relevant to metal ALD):**
- Wikipedia ALD: "ALD is a thin-film deposition technique based on the sequential use of a gas-phase chemical process; it is a subclass of chemical vapour deposition." Metal ALD notes: "Copper ALD is of interest for interconnects (best performed ≤100°C to avoid agglomeration). Metals like tungsten and molybdenum can be deposited via fluorosilane elimination (e.g., WF6 + Si2H6 → W + SiF3H + 2H2, ∆H = –181 kcal). Novel strong reducing agents enabled low-temperature ALD of electropositive metals (Cr, Ti, Sn, Al)." [12]
- Patsnap Eureka ALD explainer: Each ALD cycle deposits "approximately 0.1–0.2 nanometers." Common materials deposited: "metal oxides (Al₂O₃, HfO₂, TiO₂, ZnO), metal nitrides (TiN, TaN), metals (Pt, Ru, Co), dielectrics (SiO₂, Si₃N₄), and conductors (W, Mo, Cu — emerging)." Applications include "barrier and encapsulation layers (preventing metal diffusion/moisture)" and "FinFET and GAAFET transistors (coating non-planar surfaces)." Future trends: "ALD for sub-5nm/3nm logic nodes." [10]
- IOPscience ALD chemistry review: Surface chemistry mechanisms classified into: ligand-exchange (including "halogen transfer (e.g., W and Mo ALD from WF6/MoF6 with Si2H6)" and "Cu deposition from Cu(dmap)2 and diethylzinc"), dissociative chemisorption (often "on catalytic surfaces like Ru, Ni, and Cu"), non-dissociative chemisorption, and oxidation/reduction. ALD is "essential for fabricating advanced microelectronic devices including FinFETs and gate-all-around (GAA) FETs, high-k gate dielectrics, DRAM capacitor dielectrics." [14]
- Springer review (Lee et al., Int. J. Precision Eng. Manuf., 2025): ALD typical growth-per-cycle of "0.05–0.1 nm/cycle"; limitations include "slow process times, narrow temperature windows below ~350°C, and high costs." Discusses Area-Selective Deposition (ASD) using "self-assembled monolayers/SAMs or small molecular inhibitors/SMIs" — relevant to selective metal deposition. Notes industry progress: "TSMC's 2-nm nanosheet GAA process and Intel's ribbon-style GAA FET at 3 nm silicon thickness, both unveiled at 2024 IEDM." [13]

**ALD TaN barrier for Cu interconnects (Applied Materials Endura iCuB/S):**
- Applied Materials' Endura iCuB/S integrated copper barrier/seed system (2002, for 65nm generation): "Uses new Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) technology to create an ultrathin, conformal tantalum nitride (TaN) barrier layer compatible with advanced low-k dielectric films... The ALD technology deposits a single atomic layer at a time, enabling ultrathin layers with uniform coverage on small 65nm features. The system's TaN chamber achieves virtually 100% side and bottom coverage." [30]

**Applied Materials Endura Copper Barrier Seed (2021, for 3nm):**
- Electronic Design: New Endura Copper Barrier Seed system "reduces interconnect resistance by 50%, allowing copper wires in 3-nm chips to achieve roughly the same overall resistance as current 5-nm chips, and enables scaling interconnect wires down to 15 nanometers." It "uses selective atomic layer deposition (ALD) to coat only the walls of interconnect trenches with tantalum (rather than blanketing the base), increasing the volume of copper in the via, and it eliminates the high-resistance tantalum barrier at the via-to-copper interface." The system "integrates multiple process technologies—surface treatment, interface engineering, ALD, PVD, CVD, copper reflow, and metrology—all within a vacuum-sealed chamber." Quote from Prabu Raja (SVP, Applied Materials): "A smartphone chip has tens of billions of copper interconnects, and the wiring already consumes up to a third of the chip's power." Resistance would "increase by a factor of 10 from 7-nm to the 3-nm nodes" if left unchecked. Tool already used by major foundry logic customers globally. [26]

**Lam Research — Ru ALD liner/fill (US Patent US10731250B2):**
- "Depositing ruthenium layers in interconnect metallization," assigned to Lam Research, for "sub-10nm technology nodes." Two-step process: (1) "Ru liner layer deposition via multiple atomic layer deposition (ALD) cycles performed under reducing conditions (using a reducing agent such as H2 or NH3, either thermal or plasma-enhanced)"; (2) "Ru fill operation where the feature is at least partially filled with ruthenium by reacting a ruthenium precursor with an oxidant." Protective Ru liner is "typically 1-2 nm thick." Context: "copper has an electron mean free path of ~39 nm, and no barrier material maintains integrity below 2.5nm thickness (barriers consume >50% of line cross-section at small dimensions). Ruthenium has a short inelastic mean free path, allowing better resistivity scaling than copper at sub-10nm dimensions, and can be used without a diffusion barrier." Applications: "sub-10nm MOL and BEOL logic interconnects, source/drain contact fill, vias, and trenches." Features may be "fully filled with Ru or other metals (Cu, W, Co, Mo, Ni, Al)." Liner layers can be deposited on WCN, TiN, WN, WC, or TaN. [24][37]

**Co and Ru nucleation in PE-ALD (Tyndall/Fudan research, J. Phys. Chem. C 2023):**
- "Ru and Co are being investigated as replacements for Cu in next-generation interconnects due to scaling challenges with Cu at the nanoscale." Reported Ru nucleation delays range "from 10 ALD cycles to 500 ALD cycles." Findings: on H:Si(100), both precursors show thermoneutral energy for first Cp ligand elimination but highly endothermic second elimination (2.83 eV for CoCp₂, 2.09 eV for RuCp₂); "RuCp₂ is not a useful precursor for Ru deposition" (explaining why more complex Cp-based Ru precursors like Ru(EtCp)₂, (MeCpPy)Ru are used experimentally); N₂/H₂ plasma pretreatment generating NHₓ terminations "can reduce the nucleation delay and promote faster deposition of metal films" for Co. [11]

**ASM International and TEL ALD positioning:**
- Patsnap ALD Landscape 2026: Key assignees in ALD reactor IP include "ASM Genitech Korea/ASM IP Holding B.V. (most prolific, broadest reactor IP), Samsung Electronics, Carl Zeiss SMT GmbH, Applied Materials, Beneq Oy." South Korea dominates filings (~35-40 patents), followed by China (12-15), Japan (4-5). The "5 nm node threshold driving ALD demand." [25]
- Tokyo Electron was "Platinum Sponsor of ALD/ALE2024" (Aug 4-7, 2024, Helsinki). TEL-affiliated presentations included: invited tutorial "Thin Film Process Technologies for the Atomic Scale Era" (Robert Clark, TEL Technology Center America), ALE Plenary Lecture "Atomic Layer Precision Process to Enable Advanced Patterning toward High-NA EUV Era" (Eric Liu), and technical presentations including "wet atomic layer etching of molybdenum and ruthenium." [27]

---

### 4. Industry Roadmap Context — imec, Node Transitions, 2nm/1nm Outlook

**imec logic technology roadmap (Horiguchi & Tokei, Semiconductor Digest 2020):**
- Current state: "7nm chips use FinFETs with 6T standard cells, 2 fins per device, and contact pitches as small as 57nm." "Most critical local interconnects (M1, M2) now have metal pitches as tight as 40nm." "Co is being adopted as an alternative metal at local level; airgaps used as alternative low-k dielectric at intermediate layers."
- Near-term: "Metal pitches of M1/M2 will reach 21nm; via critical dimensions as small as 12-14nm." **Hybrid metallization:** "Alternative via metal (Ru, W, or Mo) connects barrierless to the bottom of Cu lines, allowing thinner (2nm) Cu line barriers while maintaining electromigration reliability and lowering via resistance." **Semi-damascene:** "Proposed for metal pitches below 21nm; omits the CMP step; enables higher aspect ratio lines with lower resistance; uses patternable alternative metals (Ru, Mo)."
- MOL: "Buried power rails (BPRs)" demonstrated with tungsten BPR in FinFET CMOS test vehicle; "W-based BPR interfaced with Ru via for excellent resistance and electromigration results." "Wrap-around contacts (enabled by atomic layer deposition of metal)" proposed.
- Further out (toward 1nm): CFET devices; "New conductor materials: Ordered binary intermetallic compounds with low resistivity at scaled dimensions (e.g., AlNi, RuV3-based compounds)"; "Hybrid graphene/metal conductors (Metal (Cu, Ru, Mo) encapsulated by graphene)"; "ruthenium-based advanced MOL contacts proposed to reduce parasitic resistance of deep vias." [36]

**SemiEngineering "Interconnects Approach Tipping Point" (Feb 20, 2025, Laura Peters):**
- "The 1nm (10Å) node will have 20nm pitch metal lines, but the interconnect stack already consumes a third of device power and accounts for 75% of chip RC delay."
- "Potential transition from copper to ruthenium (Ru) interconnects at the lowest, tightest levels, possibly as soon as the 14 Å node, and from tungsten to molybdenum (Mo) in DRAM and 3D NAND applications."
- Ruthenium "can be deposited by PVD, CVD, ALD, or electroless plating. It requires no barrier layer, doesn't oxidize easily, has a shorter electron mean free path, and is compatible with air gaps (k=1.0)."
- "Molybdenum is emerging as the successor to tungsten for word lines in DRAM, contacts and plugs in 3D NAND, and contacts in logic. It offers low resistance at nanometer dimensions, requires no barrier layer (little intrinsic diffusivity into dielectrics), is low cost, and can be deposited via ion beam deposition at 400°C to achieve lower resistivity than tungsten. Nearly all major chipmakers are in various stages of molybdenum qualification."
- Copper extension efforts: "lower-resistance via processes, thinner TaN diffusion barriers via ALD, Ru-Co alternative liners, elimination of barrier layers at via bottoms, and self-aligned or fully aligned vias. Samsung reported a Ru-Co bilayer liner producing 87% fewer voids and 14% better line resistance at tight dimensions."
- "Backside power delivery (BPD) moves power delivery to the wafer backside so frontside interconnect levels only carry signals, potentially delaying ruthenium introduction by a device node."
- imec's Zsolt Tokei: "at 36nm pitches ruthenium performance is already slightly better than copper."
- Lam Research's Kaihan Ashtiani: "At the atomic dimensions required for advanced chipmaking, moly is emerging as the most suitable material to replace tungsten, creating a major inflection point in the industry." [21]

**imec ruthenium semi-damascene demonstration (eenewseurope):**
- imec demonstrated "electrically functional 2-metal-level interconnects... built using a ruthenium semi-damascene and airgap technology" at 30nm pitch (2020 IITC), "showing over 80% reproducibility with no evidence of shorting and a lifetime of more than 10 years." "A metal pitch of 24nm is seen as necessary for a 2nm process technology." Airgap technology promises "to improve performance by 10% while reducing power consumption by more than 5%"; high-aspect-ratio wires can reduce IR drop in the power network by 10%. Ruthenium "outperformed cobalt-filled vias (Ru on 0.3nm TiN liner without barrier vs. Co with 1.5nm TaN barrier)" and has been used "as a source/drain contact material with low contact resistivity on the order of 10^-9 Ωcm² on both p-SiGe and n-Si." Quote from Naoto Horiguchi: "Ru is a promising candidate for replacing Co in narrow MOL trenches." [32]

**Intel subtractive ruthenium (Vik's Newsletter, IEDM 2024):**
- "At IEDM 2024 in San Francisco, Intel unveiled a 'subtractive' ruthenium process that reduces line-to-line capacitance between metals smaller than 25nm in pitch." Intel claimed "to be the first to demonstrate a practical, cost-efficient, high-volume manufacturing compatible subtractive Ru integrated process with airgaps that does not require expensive lithographic airgap exclusion zones around vias or self-aligned via flows requiring selective etches. The airgaps provided up to 25% line-to-line capacitance reduction at pitches ≤25nm, and this solution could appear on Intel Foundry's future nodes."
- Technical rationale: dual-damascene requires "a tantalum nitride barrier layer and cobalt liner, reducing copper's effective cross-section by ~4nm total (2nm per side). Barrier and liner layers can make up ~30% of interconnect line width (~10nm at sub-25nm pitch)." Copper MFP ~40nm vs ruthenium MFP ~6-8nm. Ruthenium cohesive energy ~6.7 eV/atom vs copper ~3.5 eV/atom, providing "lower diffusion (ruthenium can be used without barrier layers)" and "better electromigration resistance." [33]

---

### 5. Node-by-Node Concrete Applications (7nm, 5nm, 3nm, 2nm)

**7nm foundry node (TSMC N7, etc.):**
- Applied Materials: "as the industry moves to foundry 7nm and below technology nodes, tungsten fill for contacts has reached the physical limits of scaling, and copper in the lowest level interconnects is facing multiple challenges." Cobalt contacts adopted: "Cobalt contacts can use a thinner barrier layer, don't require a nucleation layer, and provide 6nm of fill volume at 5nm (versus tungsten)." [7][8]
- "Replacing tungsten contacts with cobalt provides approximately 60% improvement in contact line resistance." [8]
- Copper interconnect extension: PVD TaN/Ta barrier + Cu seed + ECD Cu fill, with cobalt CVD liner/cap (Endura Volta) for "2Xnm node and beyond." [6][9]

**5nm node:**
- "Without scaling these layers, there would be no pure metal left in the contact by the 5nm node" (referring to W contact liner/barrier/nucleation stack). Cobalt "provide[s] 6nm of fill volume at 5nm (versus tungsten)." [7]
- Copper remains superior or adequate "for CDs of 12-15nm and for longer metal levels above M1." [8]
- ALD TaN barrier replacing PVD TaN "enabling scaling below 36nm pitch," with "copper reflow on cobalt liners." [8]
- Applied Materials Endura Copper Barrier Seed (2021): enables 3nm copper wires at "roughly the same overall resistance as the most advanced 5-nm chips available today," with selective ALD Ta coating of trench walls only. [26]

**3nm node:**
- Endura Copper Barrier Seed tool targets 3nm: resistance reduction of 50%, wires down to 15nm width, selective ALD Ta on trench walls only, elimination of high-resistance Ta barrier at via-to-copper interface. [26]
- Ru emerging "at 3nm and below, potentially barrierless integration" (SemiconductorX metallization). [20]
- Lam Ru ALD patent: sub-10nm MOL and BEOL logic interconnects (3nm-class geometries), Ru liner 1-2nm, Ru fill, no diffusion barrier needed. [24]

**2nm node:**
- GAA transition: "GAA transistor transitions at 2nm nodes (new ruthenium/molybdenum targets)" — DataIntelo. [1]
- "RuCo alloys now dominate advanced nodes" with barrier thickness down to 20 angstroms; Applied Materials demonstrated 2.5% performance boost in 2nm test chips with RuCo liners. [3]
- 24nm metal pitch needed for 2nm (imec); Ru semi-damascene + airgap demonstrated at 30nm pitch. [32]
- Intel IEDM 2024 subtractive Ru with airgaps at ≤25nm pitch, "could appear on Intel Foundry's future nodes." [33]
- TSMC 2nm nanosheet GAA and Intel ribbon-style GAA FET at 3nm Si thickness unveiled at 2024 IEDM (context for ALD/AE requirements). [13]
- Lam ALTUS Halo Mo ALD ramping "at advanced logic fabs" for GAA logic, 1,000-layer 3D NAND, 4F2 DRAM. [15][16]

---

### 6. General Metallization Landscape (SemiconductorX)

- A leading-edge logic chip has "10-15+ metal layers." Metallization equipment market spread across "Applied Materials (leading in PVD, ALD barriers, electroplating, and CMP), EBARA (primary CMP alternative), Lam Research (metal etch and deposition integration), and Tokyo Electron (BEOL etch, deposition, cleaning)."
- Consumables: "copper electroplating chemistry concentrates at Dow/DuPont, BASF, and Atotech (now part of MKS Instruments); specialty metal precursors for cobalt and ruthenium ALD come from an even narrower supplier base (Entegris, Merck/EMD, UP Chemical, Adeka, DNF); sputtering targets concentrate at JX Advanced Metals, Materion, and Honeywell."
- Each metal layer cycle: "dielectric deposition, via/trench patterning, barrier/liner deposition (TaN, TiN, Ru, Co via ALD/PVD), copper seed layer, electroplating fill, CMP planarization, and cap layer deposition."
- Interconnect metal generations: "Aluminum (legacy, displaced below 250nm, still used in mature-node/power/analog ICs and bond pads), Tungsten (MOL contacts, still extensively used), Copper (industry standard for BEOL since ~180nm, now approaching scaling limits), Cobalt (adopted from 10nm onward for MOL and lower BEOL due to better electromigration at small dimensions), Ruthenium (emerging at 3nm and below, potentially barrierless integration), and Molybdenum (research stage for post-copper and 3D NAND word lines)."
- The resistance problem: "A 2nm barrier in a 10nm trench consumes 40% of the trench, driving adoption of thinner ALD barriers and alternative liner materials." [20]
- Sputtering target supply chain: "tantalum from Central Africa (conflict-mineral regulated), cobalt from DRC ore/Chinese refining, ruthenium constrained by PGM byproduct production, and tungsten ~80% Chinese-controlled refining." Top suppliers: Materion, Honeywell Electronic Materials (strong at TSMC/Intel/Samsung), JX Nippon, Plansee, Mitsui Mining & Smelting, Tosoh, ULVAC Materials, Solar Applied Materials/SAM (TSMC regional anchor), and AT&M/Grikin (China, serving SMIC/YMTC/CXMT). [4]

---

# Research Report: Metal Deposition Equipment Selection for Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing (7nm and Below, 2023–2026)

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

The following searches were conducted via the Tavily search tool across three rounds:

**Round 1:**
- "PVD vs CVD vs ALD metal deposition advanced semiconductor 7nm interconnect barrier copper seed"
- "TaN Ta barrier PVD copper seed layer step coverage advanced nodes why PVD"
- "CVD tungsten cobalt gap fill interconnect advanced nodes deposition"
- "ALD conformal barrier liner high aspect ratio via trench semiconductor"

**Round 2:**
- "ruthenium interconnect via fill CVD ALD 2nm node semiconductor advanced metallization"
- "molybdenum interconnect via fill CVD semiconductor manufacturing 2024 2025"
- "Lam Research ALTUS tungsten CVD Applied Materials Endura Volta copper barrier seed PVD"
- "IRDS interconnect roadmap alternative metals ruthenium molybdenum copper scaling"

**Round 3:**
- "ASM International ALD Pulsar metal gate work function advanced logic production"
- "Tokyo Electron Triase ALD TiN 3D NAND high aspect ratio"
- "TSMC N2 Samsung GAA Intel 18A metal interconnect cobalt ruthenium molybdenum choice"
- "thermal budget BEOL interconnect deposition 400C low-k dielectric limit 3D NAND"
- "ALD throughput slow growth rate cost productivity semiconductor deposition"

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### 1. Foundational Comparison of PVD, CVD, and ALD

**General framework (Wafer World):** Thin-film deposition is a critical step in semiconductor fabrication involving ultra-thin material layers deposited onto silicon wafers. The three primary techniques are PVD, CVD, and ALD. In advanced manufacturing, these techniques are often combined within the same process stack (e.g., PVD seed layers, CVD interlayer dielectrics, ALD barrier layers) to balance cost, speed, and precision. [1]

**PVD (Physical Vapor Deposition):** PVD is a physical process (sputtering or evaporation) where material is vaporized from a solid source and condensed onto the wafer. Benefits include high deposition rates, low cost, and versatility with many materials. Limitations include poor step coverage on high-aspect-ratio structures, difficulty controlling film thickness at atomic scales, and line-of-sight shadowing effects. Best for thicker films, larger feature sizes (≥100 nm), and budget-conscious/high-throughput applications. [1]

Per SemiFlows, PVD is a high-vacuum thin-film deposition technique that uses physical methods (as opposed to chemical reactions in CVD) to produce constituent atoms that travel through a low-pressure gas phase and condense on a substrate. It encompasses two primary techniques: evaporation (heating a source until it vaporizes) and sputter deposition (bombarding a solid source with energetic plasma ions). Sputtering is the chief method for depositing aluminum, copper seeds, and other metals in modern manufacturing. PVD requires extremely low-pressure environments to enable transport without excessive scattering, and it avoids complex by-product contamination common in CVD. [3]

Sputter deposition relies on momentum transfer. The chamber is evacuated, argon sputtering gas is admitted, and an interelectrode voltage ionizes the argon to create plasma. The negatively biased target causes positively charged argon ions to accelerate toward it, physically ejecting target atoms via billiard-ball-like collisions. Sputter yield (atoms ejected per incident ion) peaks at an angle less than 90 degrees—glancing angles reflect ions while perfectly normal angles push atoms deeper into the target. Ejected atoms follow an approximately cosine angular distribution. [3]

Modern PVD systems primarily use DC magnetron sputtering, where a magnetic field confines electrons on a closed path near the target, creating a dense argon plasma at lower pressures. This enables high sputtering rates with lower applied potential, lower operating pressures, and less gas trapping in films. DC sputtering cannot deposit dielectric materials (charge buildup neutralizes cathode potential), requiring RF power supplies for insulating films. Reactive sputtering (e.g., titanium in nitrogen plasma to form TiN) combines sputtering with chemical reactions. Key process parameters—power, chamber pressure, gas flow ratios—govern mean free path, kinetic energy of arriving atoms, and film stress/density. Advantages include low operational cost, good film adhesion, and ability to deposit very high melting point materials. [3]

PVD challenges and failure modes include: Poor conformality (line-of-sight deposition causes shadowing effects in high-aspect-ratio structures, with overhang pinch-off before trench bottoms are filled); Ion-induced surface damage (high-energy bombardment creates unwanted interfacial electronic states that degrade device mobility and reliability); Target impurity/grain issues (e.g., PVD TiN films show small grains with (111) plane dominance, inducing higher interfacial oxidation and defect densities compared to ALD alternatives, relevant in ferroelectric memory with HfZrOx films); Adhesion/wetting failures (copper on improperly formed barriers exhibits 3D island growth rather than smooth wetting, causing adhesion failure during mechanical polishing). [3]

**CVD (Chemical Vapor Deposition):** CVD deposits solid material via gas-phase chemical reactions. It produces high-purity, conformal coatings including SiO₂, Si₃N₄, polysilicon, and tungsten. Advantages include uniform thickness on complex 3D geometries and dense, low-defect coatings. Limitations include high temperature requirements (400–900°C) and hazardous gases (silane, ammonia, hydrogen chloride). Best for high-purity conformal films and complex compounds. [1]

**ALD (Atomic Layer Deposition):** ALD deposits films one atomic layer at a time using sequential, self-limiting reactions. Used for high-k dielectrics (HfO₂, Al₂O₃) in CMOS, barrier layers in 3D NAND and DRAM, and MEMS/nanodevice coatings. Offers atomic-level thickness control, excellent step coverage on 3D geometries, and pinhole-free films. Limitations include slower deposition rates, higher costs, and limited material systems. Best for sub-10nm technologies and high-aspect-ratio features. [1]

Per Wikipedia, ALD is a thin-film deposition technique based on the sequential use of a gas-phase chemical process; it is a subclass of chemical vapour deposition. Most ALD reactions use two chemicals called precursors (or "reactants") that react with a material's surface one at a time in a sequential, self-limiting manner. ALD is a key process in fabricating semiconductor devices and part of the toolset for synthesizing nanomaterials. ALD grows films on a substrate by exposing its surface to alternate gaseous precursors in sequential, non-overlapping pulses (unlike CVD where precursors are present simultaneously). Each precursor reacts with the surface in a self-limiting way, terminating once all available surface sites are consumed. Growth is described in terms of "growth per cycle" rather than growth rate. [62]

**ALD history:** In the 1960s, Stanislav Koltsov and Valentin Aleskovsky experimentally developed ALD principles at Leningrad Technological Institute (LTI), based on Aleskovsky's 1952 "framework hypothesis," naming the technique "Molecular Layering" (ML) in 1965. In 1974, Tuomo Suntola independently devised ALD (initially called "atomic layer epitaxy" or ALE) at Instrumentarium Oy for thin-film electroluminescent (TFEL) displays. First experiments grew ZnS using elemental Zn and S. A breakthrough came with switching from high-vacuum to inert gas reactors, enabling compound reactants like metal chlorides, H₂S, and water vapor. In 1983, first large-scale ALE-EL displays were installed at Helsinki-Vantaa airport flight information boards. In 1987, Suntola began developing ALE for photovoltaic and catalyst applications at Microchemistry Ltd. (owned by Neste Oy). In 1999, Microchemistry Ltd. was sold to ASM International (Dutch), becoming ASM Microchemistry Oy — the only commercial ALD-reactor manufacturer in the 1990s. In the 2000s, Beneq Oy and Picosun Oy emerged in Finland. In 2000, Gurtej Singh Sandhu and Trung T. Doan of Micron Technology developed ALD high-κ films for DRAM (starting at 90-nm node). Intel used ALD for high-κ gate dielectric in its 45 nm CMOS technology. In 2004 and 2018, Suntola received the European SEMI award and the Millennium Technology Prize. The name "atomic layer deposition" was first proposed by Markku Leskelä at the ALE-1 conference (Espoo, Finland, 1990). [62]

**ALD surface reaction mechanisms:** Thermal ALD operates at room temperature (~20°C) to 350°C. Best-known example: Al₂O₃ from trimethylaluminum (TMA) and water. TMA dissociatively chemisorbs, leaving AlCH₃ on the surface; H₂O reacts with –CH₃ forming CH₄ and a hydroxylated Al₂O₃ surface. Plasma ALD (PA-ALD) uses high-reactivity plasma species to reduce deposition temperature without compromising film quality; enables wider range of precursors and materials, with better thickness control and uniformity. Spatial ALD (s-ALD) separates precursors in space (not time) via gas curtains; suitable for high-volume and roll-to-roll production. Deposition rate for Al₂O₃ increases from 100–300 nm/hour to 60 nm/minute. Photo-assisted ALD uses UV light to accelerate surface reactions, reducing reaction temperature. Metal ALD: copper ALD is of interest for interconnects (best performed ≤100°C to avoid agglomeration). Metals like tungsten and molybdenum can be deposited via fluorosilane elimination (e.g., WF₆ + Si₂H₆ → W + SiF₃H + 2H₂, ∆H = –181 kcal). Novel strong reducing agents enabled low-temperature ALD of electropositive metals (Cr, Ti, Sn, Al). Catalytic SiO₂ ALD requires Lewis base catalysts (NH₃, pyridine); without catalysts, temperatures must exceed 325°C and pressures exceed 10³ torr. Optimal temperature is 32°C with a common deposition rate of 1.35 Å per binary reaction sequence. [62]

**ALD advantages (Wikipedia):** Atomic-level thickness and composition control; highly conformal films on arbitrarily complex and large substrates; wide range of materials (oxides, metals, nitrides, sulfides, chalcogenides, fluorides). Disadvantages: economic viability (slower process compared to other deposition methods); reaction time (sequential pulses and purge steps limit throughput); chemical limitations (some materials, especially electropositive metals, are difficult or impossible to deposit thermally). [62]

**ALD conformality in 3D NAND (PatSnap Eureka):** ALD's self-limiting surface chemistry is the ONLY deposition method capable of reliably coating interior of aspect-ratio features exceeding 60:1 in current 3D NAND designs — a conclusion supported by more than 50 patents from Lam Research, Samsung, SanDisk, ASM IP, Applied Materials, and YMTC. Key stats: 60:1 minimum channel hole aspect ratio in current 3D NAND; 300:1 maximum AR ALD conformality confirmed (Applied Materials, 2024); 3–20 nm ALD sidewall passivation film thickness in RIE-ALD cycles. The standard ALD cycle (per Lam Research 2019) consists of four steps: (i) precursor adsorption to self-limiting monolayer, (ii) purge, (iii) co-reactant/oxidant reaction, (iv) purge of by-products. ALD outperforms CVD because it relies on sequential self-limiting surface reactions rather than continuous gas-phase decomposition. Thickness per cycle is bounded and flux-independent, enabling conformal coverage on all exposed surfaces. Samsung established ALD's step-coverage advantage over CVD as early as 2006. Thermal ALD is preferred over PEALD for channel fill uniformity. Non-conformal ALD prevents top-pinch-off voids via inhibitor plasma. Area-selective ALD enables sub-10 nm CD adjustment without lithography. [49]

**ALD general capabilities (GP Plasma):** ALD provides digital control over thickness on high aspect ratio substrates. First referenced in 1965 as "Molecular Layering," with the first production plant using ALD built for Electroluminescent Displays. Over a thousand well-characterized ALD chemistries exist. ALD can coat aspect ratios up to 4000:1 (compared to HiPIMS at 30:1), is compatible with large 3D structures and small feature sizes below 10 nm, can tune metal-semiconductor and semiconductor-semiconductor interfaces (fermi-states), and produces amorphous films. ALD has been shown to coat aspect ratios of 5000:1 with high conformality (Elam, 2003), and uniformities below 4% are achievable for high aspect ratio substrates (Elers, 2006), with 1% uniformity common for low aspect ratio wafers. A standard ALD cycle consists of four stages: Precursor A Dose, Precursor A Purge, Precursor B Dose, Precursor B Purge. Purge stages use inert gas to remove excess precursor and reaction products, preventing CVD-style deposition. "Super cycles" enable deposition of nanolaminate materials, graded layers, and alloys. Growth rates typically range from 0.2 to 1.3 Å/cycle. The pinhole-free nature of ALD films allows thinner films meeting the same performance criteria as other methods — ALD water/oxygen diffusion barriers can show superior performance at just 15 nm thickness (Higgs et al., 2014). [18]

**ALD market data (DataIntelo):** The ALD equipment market was valued at $3.98 billion in 2025, projected to reach $9.55 billion by 2034 at a CAGR of 10.2% (2026–2034). Thermal ALD holds the largest product share at 38.5%. Semiconductors application dominates with 52.0% revenue share. Asia Pacific leads regional market at 42.3% of global revenue (~$1.68 billion). Over 85% of leading-edge logic fab capacity additions are expected to incorporate ALD by 2030. Thermal ALD operates at 200–400°C with cycle times 100–300 ms; PEALD operates below 100°C (50–100°C); Spatial ALD has cycle times under 10 seconds. Top vendors (Applied Materials, ASM International, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron) command 52–55% of the global market. Lam Research holds ~12–14% of the global ALD market. [63]

**ALD seed layer market (Patsnap Eureka):** The ALD seed layer market was estimated at $2.3 billion in 2023, projected to grow at 11.7% CAGR through 2028. The semiconductor industry accounts for 65% of applications, followed by advanced packaging (18%) and MEMS (9%). Asia-Pacific leads with 58% market share, followed by North America (24%) and Europe (15%). Customer priorities: seed layer uniformity (73%), adhesion strength (68%), and resistivity (61%). The market value exceeds $500 million annually. ALD seed layer technology evolved from an experimental technique in the 1970s (as a CVD variant) to a critical semiconductor process in the early 2000s as PVD methods failed at sub-100nm nodes. As features shrank below 22nm, ALD became essential for conformal deposition in high-aspect-ratio structures (>100:1). Emerging focus areas include materials beyond copper (ruthenium, platinum, palladium, cobalt) and compatibility with Gate-All-Around (GAA) transistors, 3D NAND, and advanced logic interconnects. [4]

**ALD environmental benefits (Patsnap Eureka):** ALD can reduce water consumption by 30–40%, achieve up to 95% material utilization efficiency, yield 15–25% net energy savings, and reduce overall environmental impact by 20–35% compared to conventional approaches. Low-temperature ALD variants (80–120°C) further enhance sustainability. [4]

**ALD growth-rate enhancement (Patsnap Eureka):** The primary limitation of conventional ALD is its inherently slow growth rate of 0.5–2 Å per cycle (0.1–1.0 Å/cycle, or 1–10 nm/min), creating throughput challenges in high-volume manufacturing. Mixed precursor ALD can achieve 2–5x faster deposition rates (200–500% increase). Key challenges include kinetic barriers, steric hindrance from bulky organometallic precursors, thermal limitations (requiring 300–500°C temperatures), mass transport limitations in high-aspect-ratio structures, competitive adsorption, and extended purge times. Economic analysis shows mixed precursor ALD systems require 25–40% higher capital investment, but yield 30–50% reduction in processing costs and break-even within 18–24 months for high-volume production (over 10,000 wafers monthly). Applied Materials achieves 2–3x growth rates with mixed precursor systems on their Endura platform. [60]

**ALD conformality in deep features (AtomicLimits / Karsten Arts):** Plasma-assisted ALD can achieve excellent film conformality and seamless gap-filling in high-aspect-ratio semiconductor structures. TEM cross-sections of a stack of alternating TiO₂ and SiO₂ layers grown by plasma ALD showed conformality across trenches with initial aspect ratios ranging from approximately 0.6 to 6. "The ability of atomic layer deposition (ALD) to grow highly conformal thin films is one of the main reasons why ALD is so popular in research and heavily employed in the semiconductor industry." Applications of conformal plasma ALD of SiO₂ include sidewall spacers in self-aligned multiple patterning, dielectric lining of high-aspect-ratio channels in 3D NAND, and gap-filling around electrical contacts. [17]

**ALD optimization for high aspect ratios (Patsnap Eureka):** High aspect ratio structures (exceeding 10:1) present challenges including non-uniform film thickness and precursor penetration issues. Optimization goals: achieving uniform film thickness (>95% conformality) throughout deep features, complete precursor penetration, and minimizing process time. Modern 3D NAND flash and DRAM devices require conformal deposition in structures with aspect ratios exceeding 100:1. Foundry sector demand is driven by FinFET and gate-all-around transistor architectures. Core challenges: mass transport limitations in narrow geometries, precursor depletion (especially for high sticking coefficient precursors), temperature gradients within deep features, purging inefficiency leading to parasitic CVD reactions, and complex surface chemistry variations along sidewalls. Applied Materials (Olympia ALD platform, PEALD) achieves >95% conformality in high aspect ratios exceeding 50:1; ASM IP Holding (spatial ALD EmerALD system) achieves >90% step coverage up to 100:1 aspect ratios. Acceptance criteria typically require less than 5% thickness variation across aspect ratios exceeding 20:1. [19]

**Superconformal ALD research (PMC11891899):** A 2025 paper in The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters proposes a novel strategy for achieving superconformal thin-film deposition using ALD by adding a heavy inert gas as a diffusion additive. Adding krypton (Kr) as a diffusion additive improved step coverage in an 18:1 aspect ratio feature from 1 to 1.6 in an ALD process for aluminum nitride (AlN) deposited from Al(CH₃)₃ and NH₃. The proposed mechanism is that the heavier Kr (84 amu) promotes diffusion of the lighter NH₃ (17 amu) down the trenches, pushing NH₃ molecules to the trench bottom and resulting in lower growth per cycle at the trench openings. [20]

### 2. Why PVD is Used for TaN/Ta Barrier and Copper Seed Layers Despite Poor Step Coverage

**Historical context and node evolution (SemiFlows):** PVD was heavily used for all BEOL barrier layers (Ta/TaN) and copper seed layers at the 28nm planar node due to acceptable step coverage, high throughput, and material purity. However, at 14nm FinFET and 7nm FinFET nodes, extreme aspect-ratio vias made PVD unsuitable for continuous diffusion barriers due to shadowing. The industry transitioned to hybrid integration—using ALD for ultra-thin conformal barrier layers (like ALD TaN) while retaining specialized ionized PVD for copper seed layers requiring high purity and good wetting. "PVD is fundamentally a line-of-sight deposition process, which results in non-conformal step coverage caused by the shadowing effect in small feature size, high-aspect-ratio via geometries." [3]

**The copper seed problem (Applied Materials patent US10847463B2):** Copper seed layers deposited by PVD suffer from coverage gaps caused by copper agglomeration and discontinuous deposition (shadowing effects), which lead to voids in bulk copper, electromigration failures, and reduced device reliability. "Copper agglomeration occurs when the deposited copper coalesces into thicker coverage in some areas by pulling copper away from surrounding areas. Discontinuous deposition on the walls of the openings is typically due to a shadowing effect inherent to the copper seed physical vapor deposition (PVD) process for some opening geometries." As circuit densities increase and transistor dimensions shrink, wire interconnect resistance and conductivity dominate device performance metrics including power consumption, RC delay, and reliability. [2]

**The patent solution (US10847463B2, Applied Materials):** A seed layer with a stacked structure comprising: (1) a first copper layer (deposited by ALD, CVD, or PVD; typically ~0.5-20 nm thick, ~4 nm preferred); (2) a ruthenium layer disposed on the first copper layer (typically 1-20 Å thick); (3) a second copper layer disposed on the ruthenium layer (typically 0.5-200 nm, ~2 nm preferred). Since copper and ruthenium are generally immiscible, the ruthenium pins the copper at grain boundaries, preventing copper agglomeration and electromigration. The method also involves a barrier layer (e.g., tantalum nitride) on the dielectric material layer to prevent copper diffusion, and subsequent bulk copper deposition via electroplating or reflow/gap fill, followed by CMP. Benefits: suppressed copper agglomeration, reduced minimum seed layer thickness for continuous coverage, improved reflow fill, reduced liner thickness requirements (increasing bulk copper volume and reducing line resistance), suppressed copper electromigration for increased circuit density and reliability, and ruthenium diffuses more slowly into copper than cobalt or manganese so line resistance is not negatively impacted. Equipment: methods can be performed in ENDURA® PVD, PRODUCER® CVD, and OLYMPIA® ALD chambers from Applied Materials, Inc. Chambers can be connected under vacuum via a transfer chamber to prevent surface oxidation. [2]

**ALD process details from the patent:** ALD deposition of copper uses copper-containing organometallic precursors (e.g., Cu(DEAB)2, Cu(DMAP)2) with hydrogen, at chamber pressures of 1-30 Torr, substrate temperatures of 50-400°C, and plasma power of 100-1000 W (e.g., 400 W at 13.56 MHz). Ruthenium layer deposited using ruthenium-containing organometallics (e.g., methyl-cyclohexadine ruthenium tricarbonyl) with hydrogen, at 1-50 Torr and 100-400°C. The ratio of copper to ruthenium in the seed layer is between 99.9:1 and 4:1. [2]

**TaN/Ta barrier standard (Allan Chemical):** Late 1990s: Tantalum (Ta) and Tantalum Nitride (TaN) became standard barrier materials using physical vapor deposition (PVD). These worked well until features shrank below 20 nm, where barrier thickness couldn't scale proportionally, creating a trade-off between resistance and reliability (TDDB). ~2013 (16 nm/14 nm nodes): Cobalt liners replaced tantalum liners (with TaN barriers still used) due to superior wetting properties, better copper adhesion, improved gap fill, and lower electrical resistance. Current (2 nm+ nodes): Ruthenium-Cobalt (RuCo) alloys now dominate the most advanced process nodes, combining ruthenium's diffusion-blocking strength with cobalt's conductivity and adhesion. [6]

**RuCo alloy advantages (Allan Chemical):** Reduces barrier thickness by 33% (down to 20 angstroms); lowers resistance by up to 25% vs. tantalum-based processes; Applied Materials demonstrated a 2.5% performance boost in 2 nm test chips using RuCo liners with advanced Black Diamond low-k dielectric materials; provides exceptional resistance to plasma-induced damage during trench patterning; simplifies manufacturing by eliminating extra processing steps; enables seedless copper electroplating. [6]

**Dual-damascene manufacturing (Allan Chemical):** Process involves three deposition stages: conformal barrier layer, copper seed layer via PVD, then copper electroplating. Deposition methods include PVD, CVD/PECVD, and ALD (preferred for sub-20 nm nodes, achieving uniformity in features with aspect ratios above 10:1). Combined copper seed and barrier thickness typically kept under 120 angstroms to avoid void formation. CMP compatibility is critical for maintaining surface planarity for multilayer integration. [6]

**Copper seed requirement (ScienceDirect, Roule et al.):** Conventional metallization uses a TaN/Ta bi-layer barrier (TaN offers better thermal stability due to amorphous/nanocrystalline structure, while Ta provides better adhesion and barrier properties), followed by an electrochemical deposition (ECD) process where the wafer acts as the cathode. Because the barrier layer (α-Ta has resistivity of ~30 μΩ cm) is not an efficient cathode, a thin copper seed layer is required to initiate electrochemical deposition. Since physical vapor deposition (PVD) is a non-conformal technique, it produces discontinuous seeding of sidewalls in narrow features. The transition from aluminium to copper interconnects was driven by copper's lower resistivity (1.7 μΩ cm) and better electromigration resistance. [9]

**Seed layer enhancement (SLE) study:** A "seed layer enhancement" (SLE) electrolytic repair process for 300 mm wafer processing was evaluated as a solution for copper seeding at 45 nm node and below. A 10 nm thick PVD liner (which leads to severe degradation of line and via resistance) was efficiently repaired with only 20 nm of SLE deposition. All electrical performances (line and via resistance, dispersion, and yield) were fully recovered with implementation of the SLE step. The deposit was "extremely conformal, thus continuous inside the features." The process was successfully integrated into the existing metallization sequence without modification of subsequent steps, including electroplating. [9]

**Barrier layer science (PMC7664900 / Materials journal review):** The barrier layer in Cu technology prevents Cu from diffusing into the dielectric layer at high temperatures; therefore, it must have a high stability and good adhesion to both Cu and the dielectric layer. Ta/TaN has been the industry standard for ~30 years, but continuous down-scaling of Cu technology nodes (sub-20 or sub-10 nm) challenges traditional materials. Cu cannot be directly electrochemically deposited on Ta/TaN due to high resistivity, requiring a Cu seed layer via PVD or CVD, whose non-uniformity causes defects in modern nano-scale trenches. IBM replaced Al with Cu as interconnect material in 1997. Cu has lower resistivity than Al but requires the damascene process for patterning (dielectric patterned first, then barrier layer deposition, then Cu filling, then CMP). The "terminal effect" (IR drop across wafers) makes uniform Cu ED difficult on resistive substrates. Desirable barrier properties include: (1) good adhesion to Cu and dielectric; (2) immiscibility with Cu and high-temperature diffusion prevention; (3) good conductivity for direct ED of Cu; (4) simple ultra-thin uniform deposition. [7]

**Barrier materials comparison (Encyclopedia MDPI):** Ta/TaN: resistivity >13 μΩ·cm, melting point ~2996°C, deposited via PVD or CVD, expected thickness of a few nm. Platinum Group Metals (PGMs): Ru (~7 μΩ·cm, MP ~2334°C) and Ir (~4.7 μΩ·cm, MP ~2454°C), deposited via PVD, CVD, ALD, ED, or electroless deposition, thickness of a few nm. 2D materials (e.g., graphene): resistivity ~1 μΩ·cm, MP ~3652°C, deposited via CVD, thickness ~1 nm. SAMs: deposited via solution immersion as a monolayer. HEAs: poor resistivity, melting point normally >1000°C, deposited via magnetron sputtering, laser cladding, ED, or electron beam evaporation, thickness of a few nm. [8]

**Alternative barrier research (PMC7664900):** Ru has resistivity of 7.1 μΩ·cm (vs. Ta at 13 μΩ·cm), melting point 2334°C, negligible solubility in Cu, and excellent wettability with Cu. However, thin Ru films fail due to columnar grain structures that promote Cu penetration. Key findings: 20 nm Ru film prevents Cu diffusion at 450°C for 10 min but fails at 550°C; 5 nm Ru film only works at 300°C (Cu ED efficiency ~90%). Doping Ru with N, B, P, C, or metals (Ta, W, Cr) creates amorphous structures that eliminate columnar grain boundaries and significantly improve barrier performance. Ru-N failure temperature reaches 900°C vs. 700°C for pure Ru. RuO₂ is effective for corrosion resistance but has high resistivity (35.2 μΩ·cm) preventing direct Cu electroplating. Graphene (discovered 2004) is impermeable to metal atoms, thermally/electrically conductive, and thermally/chemically stable. CVD-grown graphene outperforms graphene oxide (GO) and reduced graphene oxide (rGO). Barrier performance improves with more layers: 1 nm-thick graphene tri-layer is stable to 700°C for 30 min (degradation at 750°C, breakdown at 800°C). Single-layer graphene with 10±2 µm grain size is stable to 900°C vs. 2±1 µm grain size stable only to 700°C. A 1.7 nm-thick P-containing SAM barrier has comparable lifetime to 20 nm-thick Ta film. -NH₂ terminated SAMs are most promising; Cu/NH2-SAM/SiO2 system works up to 400°C (with improved preparation up to 600°C). Coupling with -SH terminal groups increases interfacial adhesion energy by ~33%. High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) are formed by mixing 5+ metallic elements in equal molar ratios; key properties arise from high-entropy, sluggish diffusion, lattice distortion, and "cocktail" effects; fabricated via magnetron sputtering, laser cladding, electrochemical deposition, and electron beam evaporation. [7]

**TSMC's early ALD TaN work (TSMC research page):** A 2002 paper described 90nm Cu dual damascene with ALD TaN barrier: ALD provides conformal step coverage and ~10 Å thickness control; superior electrical (sheet resistance, via resistance, line-to-line leakage) and reliability (electromigration, stress migration, bias temperature test) performance vs. conventional PVD TaN. A 2010 TSMC paper described an enhancement layer (Ru or Co) between PVD Ta(N) barrier and Cu seed: improved Cu-to-barrier adhesion and gap fill; no voids in dual damascene with very thin seed; >2x electromigration lifetime improvement; enables seedless electroplating. A 2004 study found (Ti,Zr)N has better Cu diffusion barrier properties than TaN and TiN. [5]

**Applied Materials Endura history (Applied Materials press release, 2004):** The Applied Endura Cu Barrier/Seed system, which deposits tantalum nitride (TaN) barrier films and copper seed layers for copper interconnect circuits, is used by virtually all chipmakers engaged in copper production, including those using low-k dielectric films. The Endura iCuB/S system's ALD technology ensures extendibility to 45nm device generations and beyond. The latest Endura2 platform uses two high-speed XP robots supporting up to seven process chambers. Endura systems have processed over 1 billion wafers globally. "The combination of process excellence and legendary Endura PVD reliability made the Applied Endura Cu Barrier/Seed system the market leader from the beginning of copper chipmaking in the late 1990s... We've expanded this successful system to include ALD (atomic layer deposition) barriers for sub-65nm devices and a modified Endura2 platform that pushes manufacturing productivity to new heights as our customers move into widespread 90nm production." (Dr. Fusen Chen, vice president and general manager of Applied Materials' Copper, PVD and Integrated Systems Product Group). Gartner Dataquest analyst Dean Freeman expected copper interconnect process technologies (barrier/seed deposition, electrochemical deposition, low-k deposition, CMP, and dielectric etch) to grow at a CAGR greater than 18.5% from 2003–2007. [10]

**PVD future evolution (SemiFlows):** PVD is evolving toward highly ionized PVD (iPVD), which uses secondary RF coils to heavily ionize sputtered metal flux, enabling directional control via substrate biasing to defeat shadowing in deep trenches. Research is also exploring novel barrier materials like ruthenium and cobalt with superior copper wettability and lower size-effect resistivity than tantalum-based systems. In FEOL, PVD deposits work-function tuning metals and barrier layers in high-k metal gate processes. PVD liners enable orthogonal metal line patterning at the same metal level. In advanced packaging, PVD sputtering universally deposits under bump metallurgy (UBM) layers with titanium/tantalum diffusion barriers and copper seeds for electroplated pillars. [3]
