# Research Report: Metal Deposition Equipment Selection for Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing (7nm and Below, 2023–2026)

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

The following searches were conducted via the Tavily search tool across three rounds:

**Round 1:**
- "PVD vs CVD vs ALD metal deposition advanced semiconductor 7nm interconnect barrier copper seed"
- "TaN Ta barrier PVD copper seed layer step coverage advanced nodes why PVD"
- "CVD tungsten cobalt gap fill interconnect advanced nodes deposition"
- "ALD conformal barrier liner high aspect ratio via trench semiconductor"

**Round 2:**
- "ruthenium interconnect via fill CVD ALD 2nm node semiconductor advanced metallization"
- "molybdenum interconnect via fill CVD semiconductor manufacturing 2024 2025"
- "Lam Research ALTUS tungsten CVD Applied Materials Endura Volta copper barrier seed PVD"
- "IRDS interconnect roadmap alternative metals ruthenium molybdenum copper scaling"

**Round 3:**
- "ASM International ALD Pulsar metal gate work function advanced logic production"
- "Tokyo Electron Triase ALD TiN 3D NAND high aspect ratio"
- "TSMC N2 Samsung GAA Intel 18A metal interconnect cobalt ruthenium molybdenum choice"
- "thermal budget BEOL interconnect deposition 400C low-k dielectric limit 3D NAND"
- "ALD throughput slow growth rate cost productivity semiconductor deposition"

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### 1. Foundational Comparison of PVD, CVD, and ALD

**General framework (Wafer World):** Thin-film deposition is a critical step in semiconductor fabrication involving ultra-thin material layers deposited onto silicon wafers. The three primary techniques are PVD, CVD, and ALD. In advanced manufacturing, these techniques are often combined within the same process stack (e.g., PVD seed layers, CVD interlayer dielectrics, ALD barrier layers) to balance cost, speed, and precision. [1]

**PVD (Physical Vapor Deposition):** PVD is a physical process (sputtering or evaporation) where material is vaporized from a solid source and condensed onto the wafer. Benefits include high deposition rates, low cost, and versatility with many materials. Limitations include poor step coverage on high-aspect-ratio structures, difficulty controlling film thickness at atomic scales, and line-of-sight shadowing effects. Best for thicker films, larger feature sizes (≥100 nm), and budget-conscious/high-throughput applications. [1]

Per SemiFlows, PVD is a high-vacuum thin-film deposition technique that uses physical methods (as opposed to chemical reactions in CVD) to produce constituent atoms that travel through a low-pressure gas phase and condense on a substrate. It encompasses two primary techniques: evaporation (heating a source until it vaporizes) and sputter deposition (bombarding a solid source with energetic plasma ions). Sputtering is the chief method for depositing aluminum, copper seeds, and other metals in modern manufacturing. PVD requires extremely low-pressure environments to enable transport without excessive scattering, and it avoids complex by-product contamination common in CVD. [3]

Sputter deposition relies on momentum transfer. The chamber is evacuated, argon sputtering gas is admitted, and an interelectrode voltage ionizes the argon to create plasma. The negatively biased target causes positively charged argon ions to accelerate toward it, physically ejecting target atoms via billiard-ball-like collisions. Sputter yield (atoms ejected per incident ion) peaks at an angle less than 90 degrees—glancing angles reflect ions while perfectly normal angles push atoms deeper into the target. Ejected atoms follow an approximately cosine angular distribution. [3]

Modern PVD systems primarily use DC magnetron sputtering, where a magnetic field confines electrons on a closed path near the target, creating a dense argon plasma at lower pressures. This enables high sputtering rates with lower applied potential, lower operating pressures, and less gas trapping in films. DC sputtering cannot deposit dielectric materials (charge buildup neutralizes cathode potential), requiring RF power supplies for insulating films. Reactive sputtering (e.g., titanium in nitrogen plasma to form TiN) combines sputtering with chemical reactions. Key process parameters—power, chamber pressure, gas flow ratios—govern mean free path, kinetic energy of arriving atoms, and film stress/density. Advantages include low operational cost, good film adhesion, and ability to deposit very high melting point materials. [3]

PVD challenges and failure modes include: Poor conformality (line-of-sight deposition causes shadowing effects in high-aspect-ratio structures, with overhang pinch-off before trench bottoms are filled); Ion-induced surface damage (high-energy bombardment creates unwanted interfacial electronic states that degrade device mobility and reliability); Target impurity/grain issues (e.g., PVD TiN films show small grains with (111) plane dominance, inducing higher interfacial oxidation and defect densities compared to ALD alternatives, relevant in ferroelectric memory with HfZrOx films); Adhesion/wetting failures (copper on improperly formed barriers exhibits 3D island growth rather than smooth wetting, causing adhesion failure during mechanical polishing). [3]

**CVD (Chemical Vapor Deposition):** CVD deposits solid material via gas-phase chemical reactions. It produces high-purity, conformal coatings including SiO₂, Si₃N₄, polysilicon, and tungsten. Advantages include uniform thickness on complex 3D geometries and dense, low-defect coatings. Limitations include high temperature requirements (400–900°C) and hazardous gases (silane, ammonia, hydrogen chloride). Best for high-purity conformal films and complex compounds. [1]

**ALD (Atomic Layer Deposition):** ALD deposits films one atomic layer at a time using sequential, self-limiting reactions. Used for high-k dielectrics (HfO₂, Al₂O₃) in CMOS, barrier layers in 3D NAND and DRAM, and MEMS/nanodevice coatings. Offers atomic-level thickness control, excellent step coverage on 3D geometries, and pinhole-free films. Limitations include slower deposition rates, higher costs, and limited material systems. Best for sub-10nm technologies and high-aspect-ratio features. [1]

Per Wikipedia, ALD is a thin-film deposition technique based on the sequential use of a gas-phase chemical process; it is a subclass of chemical vapour deposition. Most ALD reactions use two chemicals called precursors (or "reactants") that react with a material's surface one at a time in a sequential, self-limiting manner. ALD is a key process in fabricating semiconductor devices and part of the toolset for synthesizing nanomaterials. ALD grows films on a substrate by exposing its surface to alternate gaseous precursors in sequential, non-overlapping pulses (unlike CVD where precursors are present simultaneously). Each precursor reacts with the surface in a self-limiting way, terminating once all available surface sites are consumed. Growth is described in terms of "growth per cycle" rather than growth rate. [62]

**ALD history:** In the 1960s, Stanislav Koltsov and Valentin Aleskovsky experimentally developed ALD principles at Leningrad Technological Institute (LTI), based on Aleskovsky's 1952 "framework hypothesis," naming the technique "Molecular Layering" (ML) in 1965. In 1974, Tuomo Suntola independently devised ALD (initially called "atomic layer epitaxy" or ALE) at Instrumentarium Oy for thin-film electroluminescent (TFEL) displays. First experiments grew ZnS using elemental Zn and S. A breakthrough came with switching from high-vacuum to inert gas reactors, enabling compound reactants like metal chlorides, H₂S, and water vapor. In 1983, first large-scale ALE-EL displays were installed at Helsinki-Vantaa airport flight information boards. In 1987, Suntola began developing ALE for photovoltaic and catalyst applications at Microchemistry Ltd. (owned by Neste Oy). In 1999, Microchemistry Ltd. was sold to ASM International (Dutch), becoming ASM Microchemistry Oy — the only commercial ALD-reactor manufacturer in the 1990s. In the 2000s, Beneq Oy and Picosun Oy emerged in Finland. In 2000, Gurtej Singh Sandhu and Trung T. Doan of Micron Technology developed ALD high-κ films for DRAM (starting at 90-nm node). Intel used ALD for high-κ gate dielectric in its 45 nm CMOS technology. In 2004 and 2018, Suntola received the European SEMI award and the Millennium Technology Prize. The name "atomic layer deposition" was first proposed by Markku Leskelä at the ALE-1 conference (Espoo, Finland, 1990). [62]

**ALD surface reaction mechanisms:** Thermal ALD operates at room temperature (~20°C) to 350°C. Best-known example: Al₂O₃ from trimethylaluminum (TMA) and water. TMA dissociatively chemisorbs, leaving AlCH₃ on the surface; H₂O reacts with –CH₃ forming CH₄ and a hydroxylated Al₂O₃ surface. Plasma ALD (PA-ALD) uses high-reactivity plasma species to reduce deposition temperature without compromising film quality; enables wider range of precursors and materials, with better thickness control and uniformity. Spatial ALD (s-ALD) separates precursors in space (not time) via gas curtains; suitable for high-volume and roll-to-roll production. Deposition rate for Al₂O₃ increases from 100–300 nm/hour to 60 nm/minute. Photo-assisted ALD uses UV light to accelerate surface reactions, reducing reaction temperature. Metal ALD: copper ALD is of interest for interconnects (best performed ≤100°C to avoid agglomeration). Metals like tungsten and molybdenum can be deposited via fluorosilane elimination (e.g., WF₆ + Si₂H₆ → W + SiF₃H + 2H₂, ∆H = –181 kcal). Novel strong reducing agents enabled low-temperature ALD of electropositive metals (Cr, Ti, Sn, Al). Catalytic SiO₂ ALD requires Lewis base catalysts (NH₃, pyridine); without catalysts, temperatures must exceed 325°C and pressures exceed 10³ torr. Optimal temperature is 32°C with a common deposition rate of 1.35 Å per binary reaction sequence. [62]

**ALD advantages (Wikipedia):** Atomic-level thickness and composition control; highly conformal films on arbitrarily complex and large substrates; wide range of materials (oxides, metals, nitrides, sulfides, chalcogenides, fluorides). Disadvantages: economic viability (slower process compared to other deposition methods); reaction time (sequential pulses and purge steps limit throughput); chemical limitations (some materials, especially electropositive metals, are difficult or impossible to deposit thermally). [62]

**ALD conformality in 3D NAND (PatSnap Eureka):** ALD's self-limiting surface chemistry is the ONLY deposition method capable of reliably coating interior of aspect-ratio features exceeding 60:1 in current 3D NAND designs — a conclusion supported by more than 50 patents from Lam Research, Samsung, SanDisk, ASM IP, Applied Materials, and YMTC. Key stats: 60:1 minimum channel hole aspect ratio in current 3D NAND; 300:1 maximum AR ALD conformality confirmed (Applied Materials, 2024); 3–20 nm ALD sidewall passivation film thickness in RIE-ALD cycles. The standard ALD cycle (per Lam Research 2019) consists of four steps: (i) precursor adsorption to self-limiting monolayer, (ii) purge, (iii) co-reactant/oxidant reaction, (iv) purge of by-products. ALD outperforms CVD because it relies on sequential self-limiting surface reactions rather than continuous gas-phase decomposition. Thickness per cycle is bounded and flux-independent, enabling conformal coverage on all exposed surfaces. Samsung established ALD's step-coverage advantage over CVD as early as 2006. Thermal ALD is preferred over PEALD for channel fill uniformity. Non-conformal ALD prevents top-pinch-off voids via inhibitor plasma. Area-selective ALD enables sub-10 nm CD adjustment without lithography. [49]

**ALD general capabilities (GP Plasma):** ALD provides digital control over thickness on high aspect ratio substrates. First referenced in 1965 as "Molecular Layering," with the first production plant using ALD built for Electroluminescent Displays. Over a thousand well-characterized ALD chemistries exist. ALD can coat aspect ratios up to 4000:1 (compared to HiPIMS at 30:1), is compatible with large 3D structures and small feature sizes below 10 nm, can tune metal-semiconductor and semiconductor-semiconductor interfaces (fermi-states), and produces amorphous films. ALD has been shown to coat aspect ratios of 5000:1 with high conformality (Elam, 2003), and uniformities below 4% are achievable for high aspect ratio substrates (Elers, 2006), with 1% uniformity common for low aspect ratio wafers. A standard ALD cycle consists of four stages: Precursor A Dose, Precursor A Purge, Precursor B Dose, Precursor B Purge. Purge stages use inert gas to remove excess precursor and reaction products, preventing CVD-style deposition. "Super cycles" enable deposition of nanolaminate materials, graded layers, and alloys. Growth rates typically range from 0.2 to 1.3 Å/cycle. The pinhole-free nature of ALD films allows thinner films meeting the same performance criteria as other methods — ALD water/oxygen diffusion barriers can show superior performance at just 15 nm thickness (Higgs et al., 2014). [18]

**ALD market data (DataIntelo):** The ALD equipment market was valued at $3.98 billion in 2025, projected to reach $9.55 billion by 2034 at a CAGR of 10.2% (2026–2034). Thermal ALD holds the largest product share at 38.5%. Semiconductors application dominates with 52.0% revenue share. Asia Pacific leads regional market at 42.3% of global revenue (~$1.68 billion). Over 85% of leading-edge logic fab capacity additions are expected to incorporate ALD by 2030. Thermal ALD operates at 200–400°C with cycle times 100–300 ms; PEALD operates below 100°C (50–100°C); Spatial ALD has cycle times under 10 seconds. Top vendors (Applied Materials, ASM International, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron) command 52–55% of the global market. Lam Research holds ~12–14% of the global ALD market. [63]

**ALD seed layer market (Patsnap Eureka):** The ALD seed layer market was estimated at $2.3 billion in 2023, projected to grow at 11.7% CAGR through 2028. The semiconductor industry accounts for 65% of applications, followed by advanced packaging (18%) and MEMS (9%). Asia-Pacific leads with 58% market share, followed by North America (24%) and Europe (15%). Customer priorities: seed layer uniformity (73%), adhesion strength (68%), and resistivity (61%). The market value exceeds $500 million annually. ALD seed layer technology evolved from an experimental technique in the 1970s (as a CVD variant) to a critical semiconductor process in the early 2000s as PVD methods failed at sub-100nm nodes. As features shrank below 22nm, ALD became essential for conformal deposition in high-aspect-ratio structures (>100:1). Emerging focus areas include materials beyond copper (ruthenium, platinum, palladium, cobalt) and compatibility with Gate-All-Around (GAA) transistors, 3D NAND, and advanced logic interconnects. [4]

**ALD environmental benefits (Patsnap Eureka):** ALD can reduce water consumption by 30–40%, achieve up to 95% material utilization efficiency, yield 15–25% net energy savings, and reduce overall environmental impact by 20–35% compared to conventional approaches. Low-temperature ALD variants (80–120°C) further enhance sustainability. [4]

**ALD growth-rate enhancement (Patsnap Eureka):** The primary limitation of conventional ALD is its inherently slow growth rate of 0.5–2 Å per cycle (0.1–1.0 Å/cycle, or 1–10 nm/min), creating throughput challenges in high-volume manufacturing. Mixed precursor ALD can achieve 2–5x faster deposition rates (200–500% increase). Key challenges include kinetic barriers, steric hindrance from bulky organometallic precursors, thermal limitations (requiring 300–500°C temperatures), mass transport limitations in high-aspect-ratio structures, competitive adsorption, and extended purge times. Economic analysis shows mixed precursor ALD systems require 25–40% higher capital investment, but yield 30–50% reduction in processing costs and break-even within 18–24 months for high-volume production (over 10,000 wafers monthly). Applied Materials achieves 2–3x growth rates with mixed precursor systems on their Endura platform. [60]

**ALD conformality in deep features (AtomicLimits / Karsten Arts):** Plasma-assisted ALD can achieve excellent film conformality and seamless gap-filling in high-aspect-ratio semiconductor structures. TEM cross-sections of a stack of alternating TiO₂ and SiO₂ layers grown by plasma ALD showed conformality across trenches with initial aspect ratios ranging from approximately 0.6 to 6. "The ability of atomic layer deposition (ALD) to grow highly conformal thin films is one of the main reasons why ALD is so popular in research and heavily employed in the semiconductor industry." Applications of conformal plasma ALD of SiO₂ include sidewall spacers in self-aligned multiple patterning, dielectric lining of high-aspect-ratio channels in 3D NAND, and gap-filling around electrical contacts. [17]

**ALD optimization for high aspect ratios (Patsnap Eureka):** High aspect ratio structures (exceeding 10:1) present challenges including non-uniform film thickness and precursor penetration issues. Optimization goals: achieving uniform film thickness (>95% conformality) throughout deep features, complete precursor penetration, and minimizing process time. Modern 3D NAND flash and DRAM devices require conformal deposition in structures with aspect ratios exceeding 100:1. Foundry sector demand is driven by FinFET and gate-all-around transistor architectures. Core challenges: mass transport limitations in narrow geometries, precursor depletion (especially for high sticking coefficient precursors), temperature gradients within deep features, purging inefficiency leading to parasitic CVD reactions, and complex surface chemistry variations along sidewalls. Applied Materials (Olympia ALD platform, PEALD) achieves >95% conformality in high aspect ratios exceeding 50:1; ASM IP Holding (spatial ALD EmerALD system) achieves >90% step coverage up to 100:1 aspect ratios. **Superconformal ALD research (PMC11891899):** A 2025 paper in The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters proposes a novel strategy for achieving superconformal thin-film deposition using ALD by adding a heavy inert gas as a diffusion additive. Adding krypton (Kr) as a diffusion additive improved step coverage in an 18:1 aspect ratio feature from 1 to 1.6 in an ALD process for aluminum nitride (AlN) deposited from Al(CH₃)₃ and NH₃. The proposed mechanism is that the heavier Kr (84 amu) promotes diffusion of the lighter NH₃ (17 amu) down the trenches, pushing NH₃ molecules to the trench bottom and resulting in lower growth per cycle at the trench openings. [20]

### 2. Why PVD is Used for TaN/Ta Barrier and Copper Seed Layers Despite Poor Step Coverage

**Historical context and node evolution (SemiFlows):** PVD was heavily used for all BEOL barrier layers (Ta/TaN) and copper seed layers at the 28nm planar node due to acceptable step coverage, high throughput, and material purity. However, at 14nm FinFET and 7nm FinFET nodes, extreme aspect-ratio vias made PVD unsuitable for continuous diffusion barriers due to shadowing. The industry transitioned to hybrid integration—using ALD for ultra-thin conformal barrier layers (like ALD TaN) while retaining specialized ionized PVD for copper seed layers requiring high purity and good wetting. "PVD is fundamentally a line-of-sight deposition process, which results in non-conformal step coverage caused by the shadowing effect in small feature size, high-aspect-ratio via geometries." [3]

**The copper seed problem (Applied Materials patent US10847463B2):** Copper seed layers deposited by PVD suffer from coverage gaps caused by copper agglomeration and discontinuous deposition (shadowing effects), which lead to voids in bulk copper, electromigration failures, and reduced device reliability. "Copper agglomeration occurs when the deposited copper coalesces into thicker coverage in some areas by pulling copper away from surrounding areas. Discontinuous deposition on the walls of the openings is typically due to a shadowing effect inherent to the copper seed physical vapor deposition (PVD) process for some opening geometries." As circuit densities increase and transistor dimensions shrink, wire interconnect resistance and conductivity dominate device performance metrics including power consumption, RC delay, and reliability. [2]

**The patent solution (US10847463B2, Applied Materials):** A seed layer with a stacked structure comprising: (1) a first copper layer (deposited by ALD, CVD, or PVD; typically ~0.5-20 nm thick, ~4 nm preferred); (2) a ruthenium layer disposed on the first copper layer (typically 1-20 Å thick); (3) a second copper layer disposed on the ruthenium layer (typically 0.5-200 nm, ~2 nm preferred). Since copper and ruthenium are generally immiscible, the ruthenium pins the copper at grain boundaries, preventing copper agglomeration and electromigration. The method also involves a barrier layer (e.g., tantalum nitride) on the dielectric material layer to prevent copper diffusion, and subsequent bulk copper deposition via electroplating or reflow/gap fill, followed by CMP. Benefits: suppressed copper agglomeration, reduced minimum seed layer thickness for continuous coverage, improved reflow fill, reduced liner thickness requirements (increasing bulk copper volume and reducing line resistance), suppressed copper electromigration for increased circuit density and reliability, and ruthenium diffuses more slowly into copper than cobalt or manganese so line resistance is not negatively impacted. Equipment: methods can be performed in ENDURA® PVD, PRODUCER® CVD, and OLYMPIA® ALD chambers from Applied Materials, Inc. Chambers can be connected under vacuum via a transfer chamber to prevent surface oxidation. [2]

**ALD process details from the patent:** ALD deposition of copper uses copper-containing organometallic precursors (e.g., Cu(DEAB)2, Cu(DMAP)2) with hydrogen, at chamber pressures of 1-30 Torr, substrate temperatures of 50-400°C, and plasma power of 100-1000 W (e.g., 400 W at 13.56 MHz). Ruthenium layer deposited using ruthenium-containing organometallics (e.g., methyl-cyclohexadine ruthenium tricarbonyl) with hydrogen, at 1-50 Torr and 100-400°C. The ratio of copper to ruthenium in the seed layer is between 99.9:1 and 4:1. [2]

**TaN/Ta barrier standard (Allan Chemical):** Late 1990s: Tantalum (Ta) and Tantalum Nitride (TaN) became standard barrier materials using physical vapor deposition (PVD). These worked well until features shrank below 20 nm, where barrier thickness couldn't scale proportionally, creating a trade-off between resistance and reliability (TDDB). ~2013 (16 nm/14 nm nodes): Cobalt liners replaced tantalum liners (with TaN barriers still used) due to superior wetting properties, better copper adhesion, improved gap fill, and lower electrical resistance. Current (2 nm+ nodes): Ruthenium-Cobalt (RuCo) alloys now dominate the most advanced process nodes, combining ruthenium's diffusion-blocking strength with cobalt's conductivity and adhesion. [6]

**RuCo alloy advantages (Allan Chemical):** Reduces barrier thickness by 33% (down to 20 angstroms); lowers resistance by up to 25% vs. tantalum-based processes; Applied Materials demonstrated a 2.5% performance boost in 2 nm test chips using RuCo liners with advanced Black Diamond low-k dielectric materials; provides exceptional resistance to plasma-induced damage during trench patterning; simplifies manufacturing by eliminating extra processing steps; enables seedless copper electroplating. [6]

**Dual-damascene manufacturing (Allan Chemical):** Process involves three deposition stages: conformal barrier layer, copper seed layer via PVD, then copper electroplating. Deposition methods include PVD, CVD/PECVD, and ALD (preferred for sub-20 nm nodes, achieving uniformity in features with aspect ratios above 10:1). Combined copper seed and barrier thickness typically kept under 120 angstroms to avoid void formation. CMP compatibility is critical for maintaining surface planarity for multilayer integration. [6]

**Copper seed requirement (ScienceDirect, Roule et al.):** Conventional metallization uses a TaN/Ta bi-layer barrier (TaN offers better thermal stability due to amorphous/nanocrystalline structure, while Ta provides better adhesion and barrier properties), followed by an electrochemical deposition (ECD) process where the wafer acts as the cathode. Because the barrier layer (α-Ta has resistivity of ~30 μΩ cm) is not an efficient cathode, a thin copper seed layer is required to initiate electrochemical deposition. Since physical vapor deposition (PVD) is a non-conformal technique, it produces discontinuous seeding of sidewalls in narrow features. The transition from aluminium to copper interconnects was driven by copper's lower resistivity (1.7 μΩ cm) and better electromigration resistance. [9]

**Seed layer enhancement (SLE) study:** A "seed layer enhancement" (SLE) electrolytic repair process for 300 mm wafer processing was evaluated as a solution for copper seeding at 45 nm node and below. A 10 nm thick PVD liner (which leads to severe degradation of line and via resistance) was efficiently repaired with only 20 nm of SLE deposition. All electrical performances (line and via resistance, dispersion, and yield) were fully recovered with implementation of the SLE step. The deposit was "extremely conformal, thus continuous inside the features." The process was successfully integrated into the existing metallization sequence without modification of subsequent steps, including electroplating. [9]

**Barrier layer science (PMC7664900 / Materials journal review):** The barrier layer in Cu technology prevents Cu from diffusing into the dielectric layer at high temperatures; therefore, it must have a high stability and good adhesion to both Cu and the dielectric layer. Ta/TaN has been the industry standard for ~30 years, but continuous down-scaling of Cu technology nodes (sub-20 or sub-10 nm) challenges traditional materials. Cu cannot be directly electrochemically deposited on Ta/TaN due to high resistivity, requiring a Cu seed layer via PVD or CVD, whose non-uniformity causes defects in modern nano-scale trenches. IBM replaced Al with Cu as interconnect material in 1997. Cu has lower resistivity than Al but requires the damascene process for patterning (dielectric patterned first, then barrier layer deposition, then Cu filling, then CMP). The "terminal effect" (IR drop across wafers) makes uniform Cu ED difficult on resistive substrates. Desirable barrier properties include: (1) good adhesion to Cu and dielectric; (2) immiscibility with Cu and high-temperature diffusion prevention; (3) good conductivity for direct ED of Cu; (4) simple ultra-thin uniform deposition. [7]

**Barrier materials comparison (Encyclopedia MDPI):** Ta/TaN: resistivity >13 μΩ·cm, melting point ~2996°C, deposited via PVD or CVD, expected thickness of a few nm. Platinum Group Metals (PGMs): Ru (~7 μΩ·cm, MP ~2334°C) and Ir (~4.7 μΩ·cm, MP ~2454°C), deposited via PVD, CVD, ALD, ED, or electroless deposition, thickness of a few nm. 2D materials (e.g., graphene): resistivity ~1 μΩ·cm, MP ~3652°C, deposited via CVD, thickness ~1 nm. SAMs: deposited via solution immersion as a monolayer. HEAs: poor resistivity, melting point normally >1000°C, deposited via magnetron sputtering, laser cladding, ED, or electron beam evaporation, thickness of a few nm. [8]

**Alternative barrier research (PMC7664900):** Ru has resistivity of 7.1 μΩ·cm (vs. Ta at 13 μΩ·cm), melting point 2334°C, negligible solubility in Cu, and excellent wettability with Cu. However, thin Ru films fail due to columnar grain structures that promote Cu penetration. Key findings: 20 nm Ru film prevents Cu diffusion at 450°C for 10 min but fails at 550°C; 5 nm Ru film only works at 300°C (Cu ED efficiency ~90%). Doping Ru with N, B, P, C, or metals (Ta, W, Cr) creates amorphous structures that eliminate columnar grain boundaries and significantly improve barrier performance. Ru-N failure temperature reaches 900°C vs. 700°C for pure Ru. RuO₂ is effective for corrosion resistance but has high resistivity (35.2 μΩ·cm) preventing direct Cu electroplating. Graphene (discovered 2004) is impermeable to metal atoms, thermally/electrically conductive, and thermally/chemically stable. CVD-grown graphene outperforms graphene oxide (GO) and reduced graphene oxide (rGO). Barrier performance improves with more layers: 1 nm-thick graphene tri-layer is stable to 700°C for 30 min (degradation at 750°C, breakdown at 800°C). Single-layer graphene with 10±2 µm grain size is stable to 900°C vs. 2±1 µm grain size stable only to 700°C. A 1.7 nm-thick P-containing SAM barrier has comparable lifetime to 20 nm-thick Ta film. -NH₂ terminated SAMs are most promising; Cu/NH2-SAM/SiO2 system works up to 400°C (with improved preparation up to 600°C). Coupling with -SH terminal groups increases interfacial adhesion energy by ~33%. High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) are formed by mixing 5+ metallic elements in equal molar ratios; key properties arise from high-entropy, sluggish diffusion, lattice distortion, and "cocktail" effects; fabricated via magnetron sputtering, laser cladding, electrochemical deposition, and electron beam evaporation. [7]

**TSMC's early ALD TaN work (TSMC research page):** A 2002 paper described 90nm Cu dual damascene with ALD TaN barrier: ALD provides conformal step coverage and ~10 Å thickness control; superior electrical (sheet resistance, via resistance, line-to-line leakage) and reliability (electromigration, stress migration, bias temperature test) performance vs. conventional PVD TaN. A 2010 TSMC paper described an enhancement layer (Ru or Co) between PVD Ta(N) barrier and Cu seed: improved Cu-to-barrier adhesion and gap fill; no voids in dual damascene with very thin seed; >2x electromigration lifetime improvement; enables seedless electroplating. A 2004 study found (Ti,Zr)N has better Cu diffusion barrier properties than TaN and TiN. [5]

**Applied Materials Endura history (Applied Materials press release, 2004):** The Applied Endura Cu Barrier/Seed system, which deposits tantalum nitride (TaN) barrier films and copper seed layers for copper interconnect circuits, is used by virtually all chipmakers engaged in copper production, including those using low-k dielectric films. The Endura iCuB/S system's ALD technology ensures extendibility to 45nm device generations and beyond. The latest Endura2 platform uses two high-speed XP robots supporting up to seven process chambers. Endura systems have processed over 1 billion wafers globally. "The combination of process excellence and legendary Endura PVD reliability made the Applied Endura Cu Barrier/Seed system the market leader from the beginning of copper chipmaking in the late 1990s... We've expanded this successful system to include ALD (atomic layer deposition) barriers for sub-65nm devices and a modified Endura2 platform that pushes manufacturing productivity to new heights as our customers move into widespread 90nm production." (Dr. Fusen Chen, vice president and general manager of Applied Materials' Copper, PVD and Integrated Systems Product Group). Gartner Dataquest analyst Dean Freeman expected copper interconnect process technologies (barrier/seed deposition, electrochemical deposition, low-k deposition, CMP, and dielectric etch) to grow at a CAGR greater than 18.5% from 2003–2007. [10]

**PVD future evolution (SemiFlows):** PVD is evolving toward highly ionized PVD (iPVD), which uses secondary RF coils to heavily ionize sputtered metal flux, enabling directional control via substrate biasing to defeat shadowing in deep trenches. Research is also exploring novel barrier materials like ruthenium and cobalt with superior copper wettability and lower size-effect resistivity than tantalum-based systems. In FEOL, PVD deposits work-function tuning metals and barrier layers in high-k metal gate processes. PVD liners enable orthogonal metal line patterning at the same metal level. In advanced packaging, PVD sputtering universally deposits under bump metallurgy (UBM) layers with titanium/tantalum diffusion barriers and copper seeds for electroplated pillars. [3]

### 3. Why CVD is Used for Tungsten and Cobalt Gap Fill Due to Good Fill Capability

**Tungsten fundamentals (SemiFlows):** Tungsten is a refractory metal primarily used to form contact plugs, local interconnects, and vias, serving as the critical conductive bridge between front-end-of-line (FEOL) active transistor structures and back-end-of-line (BEOL) multi-level wiring. It is selected for its high melting point, electromigration resistance, and excellent step coverage, while its low diffusivity in silicon dioxide and silicon substrates (compared to copper) prevents deep-level contamination. Tungsten deposition typically uses tungsten hexafluoride (WF₆) as the gaseous precursor. Two main reduction pathways exist: silane (SiH₄) reduction for the nucleation phase (forming a thin continuous seed layer, reacting rapidly at lower temperatures), followed by hydrogen (H₂) reduction for bulk film growth. The hydrogen reduction reaction (WF₆ + 3H₂ → W + 6HF) is thermally driven and surface-catalyzed. Hot-wire assisted ALD (HWALD) uses atomic hydrogen for low-temperature, self-limiting deposition, though this competes with fluorine-based etching reactions. A diffusion barrier—typically TiN or a Ti/TiN bilayer—is required between tungsten and silicon to prevent silicide consumption and fluorine penetration. [15]

**Tungsten process principles (SemiFlows):** Deposition temperature and chamber pressure are key parameters. Higher temperatures increase deposition rate (Arrhenius kinetics) but can cause rougher, non-conformal films; lower temperatures improve step coverage but reduce throughput. Tungsten crystallizes in two phases: the desired low-resistivity α-W (body-centered cubic) and the high-resistivity metastable β-W (A15 cubic), the latter stabilized by fluorine/oxygen impurities. High precursor purity and optimized H₂/WF₆ ratios are critical for α-W nucleation. [15]

**Tungsten failure modes (SemiFlows):** (1) Fluorine attack causing "volcano" defects—when WF₆ penetrates thin/discontinuous barriers and reacts with silicon or TiSi₂ to form volatile SiF₄ or TiF₄, creating voids that erupt during heating; (2) Grain boundary scattering—as contact dimensions shrink below 20nm, resistivity rises sharply due to electron scattering at surfaces/grain boundaries and fluorine impurities; (3) Loading effects during SF₆/Ar etchback—redeposition of tungsten or Ti-N-F byproducts causing incomplete clearing and electrical shorts; (4) High tensile stress leading to cracking, wafer warpage, or delamination. [15]

**Tungsten node evolution (SemiFlows):** At 28nm, contacts used TiSi₂ or CoSi₂ with Ti/TiN barrier + CVD W plug. At 14nm, ultra-thin ALD TiN barriers and NiSi silicide were adopted. "At the 7nm FinFET node and beyond, the volume of the contact plug became so small that the conventional TiN barrier and tungsten nucleation layer occupied more than half of the contact volume," driving innovations including barrierless tungsten (selective CVD directly on silicide), alternative metals (cobalt, ruthenium with shorter electron mean free paths), and dual-metal stacked vias (e.g., Mo or W stacks on primary contact metal). [15]

**Selective tungsten CVD (Applied Materials product page):** Tungsten has traditionally been used as a gapfill material in MOL contacts (the electrical links between transistors and interconnects) due to its low resistivity and bulk fill characteristics. However, as contact dimensions continue to scale down, contact resistance is becoming a performance bottleneck. As the contact cross-sectional area shrinks, an increasing proportion of volume is consumed by metal liner/barrier and nucleation layers, leaving less room for conducting metal fill, and multiple resistive interfaces contribute to higher contact resistance. The Endura Volta Selective W CVD system offers an Integrated Materials Solution that combines surface treatment chambers with selective tungsten deposition chambers. Selective deposition is enabled by unique process capabilities of the deposition chambers combined with specialized surface treatments using chemistries to prepare underlying metal and dielectrics of the contact, enabling bottom-up, metal-on-metal deposition. Key benefits: eliminates liner/barrier and nucleation layers, alleviating the device performance bottleneck; produces void-free and seam-free gapfill; all process steps performed in an ultra-clean, continuous high-vacuum environment, ensuring a pristine interface and defect-free contact fill; maximizes conducting metal volume, substantially improving contact resistivity compared to conventional liner/barrier contact fabrication; lower resistance facilitates higher device density and extends 2D scaling. [34]

**IEEE Spectrum on selective W (August 2020):** Applied Materials released a new chip manufacturing tool called the Endura Volta Selective Tungsten CVD system that solves the growing resistance bottleneck in vertical tungsten contacts. In existing manufacturing processes, tungsten contacts must be clad in titanium nitride, which serves two purposes: helping tungsten adhere to the hole walls (preventing flaking) and blocking fluorine used in the growth process from fouling the chip. However, while contact diameters have shrunk to 20 nanometers in 7-nanometer chips, the cladding thickness has not scaled down—leaving only 25% of the contact volume as tungsten, with the rest being cladding. The new machine deposits tungsten from the bottom of the contact hole upward (a "selective gapfill process") using different chemistry that eliminates the need for cladding entirely, reducing resistance by 40%. The process must be performed entirely in a vacuum, so the system is built around a sealed environment that moves wafers through multiple process steps without air exposure. "For devices on today's most advanced chips 'resistance is your key issue,' says Zhebo Chen, global product manager. 'With the transistor you've taken an economy car and turned it into a race car, but if the roads are congested it doesn't matter.'" "There's more than 100 kilometers of tungsten contact on a [300-millimeter] wafer. Doing this right in high-volume manufacturing is exceedingly difficult." The tool was introduced in July 2020 and is already being used in high-volume manufacturing by leading chipmakers. [35]

**Lam Research ALTUS product family:** Lam's market-leading ALTUS systems combine CVD and ALD technologies to deposit the highly conformal films needed for advanced metallization applications, used primarily for tungsten (W) and molybdenum (Mo) deposition to form conductive features like contacts, vias, and plugs. Conventional CVD tungsten fill is limited by overhang from barrier films, leading to voids, higher resistance, and contact failure. Key customer benefits: Quad Station Module (QSM) architecture, advanced ALD fill technology, wafer bow management with high-temperature vacuum-clamped ceramic pedestal, sub-fab sublimation cabinet for precursor delivery, integrated clean using advanced chemical etch (ACE), multi-station multi-temperature sequential/batch processes, thermal and plasma Mo ALD, CCP and remote plasma pretreatment options, Pulsed Nucleation Layer (PNL) ALD process with in-situ bulk CVD fill via Multi-Station Sequential Deposition (MSSD), lower resistivity thin W films, low-fluorine low-stress W fill for 3D NAND and DRAM, and high step coverage WN films using ALD. Products: ALTUS Halo, Concept Two ALTUS, ALTUS Max, ALTUS Max ExtremeFill, ALTUS DirectFill Max, ALTUS Max ICEFill, and ALTUS LFW. Applications: plug, contact, and via fill; 3D NAND wordlines; low-stress composite interconnects; and WN barrier for via and contact metallization. [33]

**Novellus/Lam ALTUS DirectFill (2004 press release):** The ALTUS DirectFill tungsten nitride/tungsten deposition system was designed for contact and via-fill needs at 65 nm and below. It eliminates the need for conventional titanium/titanium nitride (Ti/TiN) toolsets. The advanced plug-fill technique can reduce contact resistance (Rc) and lower overall cost of ownership (CoO) by 50 percent or more compared to existing processes. It simplifies tungsten deposition by replacing the standard multi-tool Ti/TiN/W approach with a single system integrating three process modules: (1) an advanced preclean process, (2) Novellus' proprietary pulsed nucleation layer (PNL) deposition of tungsten nitride (WN), and (3) combined PNL and chemical vapor deposition (CVD) tungsten (W) deposition. Technical benefits include: tungsten nitride barrier with atomic layer deposition (ALD) conformality that is substantially thinner than Ti/TiN liner-barrier, allowing more of the contact to be filled with lower resistivity tungsten; reduction of contact plug resistance by up to 50 percent at the 45-nm node; excellent barrier characteristics for tungsten; adhesion to a variety of dielectric materials; and all process temperatures below 400°C for compatibility with future process integration requirements. "Unlike the conventional PVD/MOCVD process sequence, our integrated single-architecture technology approach enhances current tungsten deposition applications, such as contact and bit line, while enabling future applications, such as capacitor electrode and metal gate electrode, where tungsten nitride and tungsten are currently being evaluated." (Karl Levy, vice president and general manager of Novellus' Tungsten Business Unit). [32]

**Area-selective deposition of W (AtomicLimits):** Area-selective CVD of W using WF₆ and H₂ was studied since the 1980s for metal gapfill. Both precursors contribute to selectivity (WF₆ adsorbs on metals/Si but not SiO₂; H₂ dissociates selectively on metals). However, the process failed commercially due to selectivity loss from two main causes: (1) pre-existing impurities on non-growth areas, and (2) intermediate reaction products (WFx and HF) formed during precursor adsorption that re-volatilize and re-adsorb on the SiO₂ non-growth area, causing undesired nucleation. In the 1980s, the technology node was ~1 µm, requiring 100 nm–1 µm of selective deposition—far more challenging than current applications. Applied Materials is selling a dedicated tool for area-selective CVD of W for metal gapfill, suggesting renewed industry interest. [12]

**Cobalt for contacts (Patsnap Eureka Cobalt page):** Cobalt contact plugs for 10/7/5 nm nodes displace tungsten due to superior gap-fill in aspect ratios >10:1; void-free fill with grain growth from 10–20 nm to 50–100 nm via annealing; contact resistance <5×10⁻⁹ Ω·cm² for 7 nm nodes. Co-W hybrid metallization: cobalt for contacts (aspect ratio 8:1–15:1) + tungsten for vias (3:1–6:1), reducing via chain resistance by 15–25%. TSMC uses hybrid Co-W metallization reducing via chain resistance 15–25%. Samsung uses cobalt capping layers for via resistance reduction. IBM uses BEOL cobalt contact technology for 10/7/5 nm nodes. Micron uses ALD cobalt nucleation process for FinFET/GAA architectures. [11]

**Cobalt deposition techniques (Patsnap Eureka Cobalt page):** Sputtering (PVD): argon at 0.1–1 mTorr, substrate temperature 200–370°C, RF bias 200–600 W, deposition rates 1.92–3.37 nm/s, surface roughness <0.5 nm RMS. ALD: enables conformal coating with sub-nanometer control; novel nucleation via TaN/TiN precursor pretreatment at 250–350°C; cobalt nucleation layer 0.5–1.5 nm; interface resistance <1×10⁻⁸ Ω·cm²; final films with resistivity <10 μΩ·cm. CVD/PECVD: 300–450°C thermal, 200–350°C PECVD; deposition rates 5–20 nm/min; post-deposition annealing in forming gas at 400–500°C reduces impurities to <1 at.%. ALD cobalt achieves step coverage >98% on 5:1 aspect ratio fins; parasitic source/drain resistance reduced 30–40% vs. tungsten. [11]

**Cobalt silicide formation (Patsnap Eureka Cobalt page):** Phase sequence: Co₂Si (400–550°C) → CoSi (550–700°C) → CoSi₂ (>700°C). CoSi₂ has lowest resistivity (15–20 μΩ·cm) but consumes excessive silicon, unsuitable for ultra-shallow junctions (<50 nm). Modern processes target CoSi phase (resistivity 50–70 μΩ·cm, Si:Co ratio 1:1). Co-Ti alloy films (5–15 at.% Ti) improve thermal stability and form TiN diffusion barriers; contact resistances <2×10⁻⁸ Ω·cm² for 0.13 μm nodes. Salicide process: 10–30 nm cobalt film, TiN capping layer (10–14 nm), RTA at 450–550°C, wet etch in H₂SO₄:H₂O₂ (4:1) at 60–80°C, second RTA at 700–800°C; achieves gate sheet resistance <5 Ω/sq for 45 nm nodes. [11]

**Cobalt purity requirements (Patsnap Eureka Cobalt page):** Crude cobalt has purity of 98–99.8%, containing detrimental impurities including transition metals (Ni, Fe, Cr), gas elements (O, N, S), and trace radioactive elements (U, Th). Copper impurities are especially problematic due to high diffusion rates in silicon. Semiconductor-grade cobalt targets require <5 ppm total impurities with specific limits: Cu <0.5 ppm, Ni <1 ppm, Fe <1 ppm, O <10 ppm, radioactive elements <0.01 ppb. Targets with <111> preferred orientation yield lower resistivity films (5–6 μΩ·cm at 25°C). ALD precursors (e.g., cobalt tricarbonyl nitrosyl, cobaltocene derivatives) require >99.999% purity. [11]

**Cobalt agglomeration and Ru doping (Applied Materials patent US20180211872A1):** As feature sizes shrink, traditional copper electroplating with barrier/liner layers becomes problematic because the low-conductivity barrier/liner layer (e.g., TaN) occupies a proportionally larger volume of smaller features. For example, a 3nm barrier layer occupies ~11% of cross-sectional area in larger features but ~33% in smaller ones. Cobalt has higher resistivity than copper (6.2 μΩ-cm vs 1.7 μΩ-cm) but may not need thick barrier/liner layers to prevent diffusion, making it attractive for smaller critical dimensions. "It has been found by the inventors that doping the cobalt layer with ruthenium reduces agglomeration." Ruthenium doping can be achieved by: (a) depositing a thin Ru layer prior to cobalt deposition, (b) co-flowing Ru precursors with cobalt precursors during deposition, (c) post-deposition exposure to ruthenium (via implant, soak in Ru-containing atmosphere, or thin Ru layer deposition), or (d) cyclic deposition of Ru and Co to form a multilayer laminate structure. Doping reduces agglomeration, allowing annealing to remove impurities and reduce resistance. Process details: barrier/liner layer (Ti, TiN, typically 2-100 Å thick, deposited by ALD/PE-ALD/CVD/PVD); plasma treatment (H2, N2, or NH3 at 0.1-100 Torr, 100-900°C, 100-800W RF power); ruthenium layer (1-30 Å thick, deposited by ALD/PE-ALD/CVD/PVD or MOCVD using precursors like ruthenium tricarbonyl compounds); cobalt seed layer deposition (1-100 Å, using cobalt precursors such as dicobalt hexacarbonyl acetyl compounds like CCTBA, deposited by ALD/PE-ALD/CVD at 150-400°C, 0.1-80 Torr); optional thermal annealing (200-1400°C). [14]

**Cobalt for EM reliability (Applied Materials Endura Volta Cobalt CVD page):** The system deposits thin, conformal CVD cobalt liners and selective cobalt caps that encapsulate copper interconnects, improving reliability and scalability beyond the 2Xnm node. It represents the first material change in more than 15 years of copper barrier/seed (CuBS) development. The technology enables deposition of seed-enhancing liner and selective cap layers less than 20Å thick, improving interconnect yield and reliability at the 2Xnm node and beyond. It is described as the industry's only vacuum-based electro-migration (EM) mitigation solution and the only CVD cobalt liner product integrated on the same platform with pre-clean, barrier, and copper seed processes. The cobalt liner improves copper wetting, promoting a thin, continuous, conformal seed layer that facilitates repair of discontinuities and forms a robust seed layer, enabling void-free copper gap fill at advanced nodes. The best-in-class (>100:1) selective metal capping process strengthens adhesion at the copper-dielectric interface, improving electro-migration performance by an order of magnitude without increasing line resistance or degrading time-dependent dielectric breakdown. Aggressive pitch scaling increases circuit density and creates need for high-performance interconnects running miles through multi-level devices; even a single void can render portions of a chip useless. [31]

**Co ASD success (AtomicLimits):** Co ASD is currently in production in high-volume manufacturing for capping Cu interconnects to improve electromigration (EM) reliability. Key reasons for success: (1) Co capping only requires a few nanometers of deposition (as thin as 1.6 nm), while gapfill required 10s of nanometers—most ASD processes lose selectivity after several nanometers; (2) Cu lines are slightly recessed after CMP (due to corrosion and dishing), which confines lateral growth (mushrooming) as long as Co thickness doesn't exceed recess depth; (3) the thinner deposition requirement makes selectivity more achievable. CMP leaves 10¹¹–10¹² atoms/cm² metal defects on dielectric surfaces; post-CMP cleaning reduces but doesn't eliminate them, causing nucleation even with perfect intrinsic selectivity. Yield and leakage current degrade for Co capping layers thicker than 3 nm. Co precursors studied include Co₂(CO)₈, Co₂(CO)₆(C₆H₁₀), and CoCp(CO)₂. Co-based alloys like CoWxPy can further improve EM reliability. Co, Ru, Mn, and W have been reported as candidate capping materials, with Co currently the material of choice. With Intel and TSMC implementing Co interconnects for bottom metal layers, ASD of Co for metal gapfill is being considered. ASD is likely best suited for target thicknesses below 10 nm. [12]

**Co(W) interconnect research (ScienceDirect, Microelectronics Reliability 2024):** Cobalt is explored as an alternative to copper (Cu) for nanoscale interconnects due to its higher melting point (1495°C vs. Cu's 1085°C), implying greater electromigration reliability, and a comparable product value of electrical resistivity and electron mean free path. A study used an all-wet self-assembled nanoseeding and electroless deposition process to fabricate Co interconnect lines with 0.06 at.% added tungsten. The Co(W) interconnect doubles the lifetime compared to pure Co. Electromigration tests under a nominal constant current density of 5.0×10⁷ A cm⁻² showed a gradual resistance increase (<14%) followed by localized line thinning. The Co(W) film has an adhesion strength of 55.0 MPa vs. 35.6 MPa for pure Co, and exhibits much lower current density scaling factor (n) values. "The super-diluted W into Co interconnects could maintain a low residual electrical resistivity." "The incorporation of diluted W (only 0.06 at.%) into Co interconnects could potentially avoid causing a significant increase in residual electrical resistivity." [13]

### 5. Why Newer Metals Like Ruthenium and Molybdenum are Being Introduced for Interconnect and Via-Fill at Advanced Nodes

#### 5.1 The Copper Scaling Problem

**Copper limitations (arXiv tutorial, "Selecting Alternative Metals for Advanced Interconnects"):** Current Cu dual-damascene metallization (which replaced Al-based metallization after 1999) faces growing issues at scaled dimensions. Cu requires diffusion barriers (typically TaN-based) and adhesion liners (typically Co) that cannot scale below a combined 2-3 nm thickness without losing function, leaving less space for actual Cu conductance. Additionally, Cu resistivity increases strongly at small dimensions due to grain boundary and surface scattering. "Today, interconnect resistance and reliability are key limiters for the performance of advanced CMOS circuits. As transistor scaling is slowing, interconnect scaling has become the main driver for circuit miniaturization." Projected interconnect scaling targets through 2035 show minimum metal pitch decreasing from 23 nm (2024/25, 2nm node) to 12 nm (2035, 3A node), with relevant interconnect line and via dimensions expected in the 5-10 nm range. [37]

**Physics of resistivity at nanoscale (arXiv):** The mean free path (λ) of charge carriers is a critical parameter. Cu's mean free path can reach up to 40 nm, which is large compared to interconnect dimensions. Metals with shorter λ are much less sensitive to interconnect scaling and grain boundary scattering effects. The paper introduces a ρ₀λ figure of merit that can be calculated via ab initio methods. Key considerations: predictive calculations of thin-film resistivity are impossible without detailed knowledge of microstructure, which is process-dependent; grain size dependence on film thickness depends on deposition process parameters, not uniquely on material; the reflection coefficient R and specularity p cannot be reliably predicted and are not purely materials properties; alloy scattering must be avoided in compound metals; only ordered intermetallics (not random alloys) are of potential interest for interconnects; anisotropy in Fermi surface can suppress surface scattering in 2D metals, but requires single-crystal lines with no current integration route yet; Matthiessen's rule is typically not valid for surface and grain boundary scattering in thin metallic films. [37]

**Copper barrier problem (Lam Research patent US10731250B2):** Copper interconnects are challenging at sub-10nm nodes because copper has an electron mean free path of ~39 nm, and no barrier material maintains integrity below 2.5nm thickness (barriers consume >50% of line cross-section at small dimensions). Ruthenium has a short inelastic mean free path, allowing better resistivity scaling than copper at sub-10nm dimensions, and can be used without a diffusion barrier. [21]

**Copper resistivity increase (LinkedIn post, Abhishekkumar Thakur):** Copper's resistivity increases up to 10x due to electron scattering as its line width falls below its 40nm mean free path. Copper requires a 3-4nm thick diffusion barrier, reducing effective copper width in a 10nm line to only 2-4nm, complicating fabrication and increasing resistance. Copper lacks a manufacturable etching process; lines are formed by etching dielectrics, depositing barriers and seed layers, then filling with copper (damascene approach). [24]

**Semiconductor Engineering 2024 (Ruthenium Interconnects On Tap):** Shrinking line dimensions are approaching copper's electron mean free path, and barrier layers consume an increasing share of line width. The industry introduced copper interconnects in 1997 (dual damascene scheme with electroplating and CMP), and is now approaching a similar crossroads nearly three decades later. Samsung researchers presented work on optimizing barrier and etch stop layers: a sidewall plasma pre-treatment reduced sidewall barrier thickness by a third (improving contact resistance by 2%); a polymeric inhibitor improved via-bottom selectivity (20% resistance reduction); via bottom barrier can account for more than 60% of via resistance; surface silylation/thermal recovery chemistry (Si-OH to Si-CH₃ termination) restores etch damage; and a plasma pretreatment before etch stop deposition gave 30% stress reduction in copper lines and 10% via resistance reduction. Samsung's Kang Sub Yim examined carbon depletion from dielectric surfaces by plasma etching: for features smaller than ~30nm, surface carbon depletion impacts capacitance more than the bulk dielectric constant; higher-density materials (k>3.0) are more resistant to plasma damage and may have lower effective k in sub-30nm features. [23]

**Vik's Newsletter on copper vs ruthenium:** Advanced nodes have 12-15 metal levels. Two major limitations emerge as features shrink: Resistance (smaller cross-sectional area means increased resistance, voltage drop, and thermal dissipation) and Capacitance (lines too close together increase crosstalk; low-k dielectrics (εr ~2.5 vs 4.2 for SiO₂) provided partial help, but resistance problems were unsolvable). The dual-damascene process requires a tantalum nitride barrier layer and cobalt liner, reducing copper's effective cross-section by ~4nm total (2nm per side). Barrier and liner layers can make up ~30% of interconnect line width (~10nm at sub-25nm pitch), significantly increasing resistance. Future nodes project metal pitches approaching 10nm. [25]

#### 5.2 Ruthenium (Ru)

**Material advantages of Ru (Vik's Newsletter):** (1) Bulk resistivity: Copper is superior at 1.68 μΩ-cm vs ruthenium's 7.1 μΩ-cm. (2) Mean free path (MFP): Copper has high MFP (~40nm), causing resistance to severely increase at small dimensions due to scattering. Ruthenium has low MFP (~6-8nm), making it insensitive to resistance increase at small sizes—this is the key advantage for narrow interconnects. (3) Cohesive energy: Ruthenium has ~6.7 eV/atom vs copper's ~3.5 eV/atom. This provides lower diffusion (ruthenium can be used without barrier layers, recovering cross-sectional area for current flow) and better electromigration resistance (atoms less prone to movement under current flow, reducing reliability concerns like opens and shorts). Ruthenium can be patterned with subtractive etching (like aluminum interconnects from the late 1990s) rather than requiring the complex dual-damascene process used for copper. [25]

**Ru physics (SemiFlows):** Ruthenium is thermodynamically immiscible with copper (zero solid solubility), making it an effective plateable Cu diffusion barrier without needing a separate seed layer. Sputter-deposited Ru films grow in columnar grain structures that force copper atoms along tortuous grain-boundary paths, extending barrier lifetime under thermal stress. Ru has a much shorter bulk electron mean free path than copper, meaning its resistivity rises far more gradually with linewidth scaling—allowing Ru to outperform Cu in RC delay at extremely small dimensions. PVD Ru on organosilicate glass (OSG) grows via Stranski-Krastanov (island) mode, creating weak adhesion requiring interface chemical modification (silicate layers or self-limiting precursors). During CMP, Ru must be oxidized (using H₂O₂-containing slurries), then dissolved via organic complexing agents like ethylenediamine (EDA) that coordinate with Ru d-orbitals. Galvanic corrosion between Cu and Ru is suppressed using pyridine carboxylate inhibitors (e.g., nicotinic acid) that form protective monolayers on copper. [22]

**Ru process principles (SemiFlows):** Deposition: CVD/ALD provide conformal coverage in high-aspect-ratio features but introduce impurities (C, O, N) that raise resistivity; PVD used for liner applications. Thermal annealing: Hydrogen-assisted RTA drives grain coalescence and removes interstitial impurities, dramatically reducing resistivity. Subtractive dry etching: Uses Cl₂/O₂ chemistries forming volatile RuOxCly species; cryogenic chuck temperatures and passivation layer formation control anisotropy and line-edge roughness. [22]

**Ru node evolution (SemiFlows):** 28nm–14nm nodes: Cu with Ta/TaN barriers sufficient; barrier thickness not yet restrictive. 7nm node: Barrier scaling to a few nanometers forced Ta/TaN replacement; Ru introduced as ultrathin liner enabling seedless direct Cu electroplating. Sub-3nm nodes: Shift to subtractive Ru metallization using EUV lithography and anisotropic dry etching, eliminating damascene trench filling bottlenecks; supports sub-30nm pitches with high current density and EM resistance. Ru is expanding into FEOL applications (work-function metal in HKMG stacks for FinFET/nanosheet devices), buried power rails (BPR) for standard cell height optimization, and integration with air-gap schemes to reduce parasitic capacitance in the angstrom era. [22]

**Ru interconnects on tap (Semiconductor Engineering 2024):** imec simulations showed ruthenium vias for the first four interconnect layers reduce overall resistance by up to 60%. A transitional hybrid scheme would combine copper lines with tungsten, ruthenium, or molybdenum vias. Ruthenium requires no barrier layer and can be deposited or etched in multiple ways, enabling flexible integration. TEL's Albany Technology Center (Jack Rogers) investigated how adhesion layer process conditions affect ruthenium deposition. Ru films on PVD vs. ALD TiN showed different grain orientations and resistivities; larger, more uniform Ru grains reduce resistivity. Optimized ruthenium etch/deposition is critical — tapered Ru profiles, footings, and incomplete TiN adhesion layer removal can cause leakage between lines. [23]

**Lam Research Ru patent (US10731250B2):** Methods and apparatus for depositing ruthenium (Ru) layers in semiconductor interconnect metallization, particularly for sub-10nm technology nodes. Two-step process: (1) Ru liner layer deposition via multiple ALD cycles performed under reducing conditions (using a reducing agent such as H₂ or NH₃, either thermal or plasma-enhanced); (2) Ru fill operation where the feature is at least partially filled with ruthenium by reacting a ruthenium precursor with an oxidant. The protective Ru liner layer (typically 1-2 nm thick) prevents oxidation of underlying adhesion/barrier layers and metal substrates during the subsequent oxidative fill step. It also serves as a barrier preventing oxygen from penetrating into underlying metal layers. ALD dose sequences include: Ru precursor → reductant; Ru precursor → oxidant → reductant; Ru precursor → oxidant mixed with reductant. Ru precursors include Ru(0) and Ru(II) organometallic compounds (e.g., (arene)(diene)Ru(0), (cyclopentadienyl)(ethyl)Ru(II)dicarbonyl). Applications include sub-10nm MOL and BEOL logic interconnects, source/drain contact fill, vias, and trenches. Features may be fully filled with Ru or other metals (Cu, W, Co, Mo, Ni, Al). Liner layers can be deposited on WCN, TiN, WN, WC, or TaN. Process parameters: temperatures 150-450°C, pressures 0.1-10 Torr, carrier gas flows 25-1000 sccm, dose times 0.5-20 seconds. [21]

**Intel subtractive Ru (IEDM 2024, via Vik's Newsletter):** Intel unveiled a "subtractive" ruthenium process that reduces line-to-line capacitance between metals smaller than 25nm in pitch. Intel claimed to be the first to demonstrate a practical, cost-efficient, high-volume manufacturing compatible subtractive Ru integrated process with airgaps that does not require expensive lithographic airgap exclusion zones around vias or self-aligned via flows requiring selective etches. The airgaps provided up to 25% line-to-line capacitance reduction at pitches ≤25nm, and this solution could appear on Intel Foundry's future nodes. [25]

**Ru challenges (LinkedIn post and comments):** Deposition (PVD, CVD, ALD) faces adhesion issues on SiO₂, requiring liners like TiN. Sputtering Ru in a nitrogen atmosphere or alloying with tungsten/cobalt creates amorphous structures enhancing barrier properties. Low-temperature electroless plating with succinic acid and post-annealing reduces resistivity by removing impurities. Ru resistivity varies by crystal orientation (25% lower resistance along the [001] axis), but epitaxial integration into CMOS is complex, requiring layer transfer. Expert comments: Dr. My Nghe Tran questioned cost comparison of metals; Avron Ger noted IMEC has been working on this path and questioned when it will go into HVM, noting it would only apply to the first metal levels; Rubina Sultan noted the key challenge is polishing and etching (unlike Cu with decades of well-established CMP and etch processes, Ru needs further development); James Swonger raised molybdenum (Mo) and alloy alternatives (CuW, CuMo, AgW, AgMo); Bernd Wildpanner questioned reliability data and formation of ruthenium chloride compounds; Kwanghyun Kim asked about Mo as alternative, mentioning integration challenges (anisotropic conductivity, grain structure control, adhesion); Simon Kirk noted post-etch residue cleaning and selectivity challenges; Ed Korczynski noted volatile toxic oxides form in CMP of Ru, increasing tool and process costs; Bijan Nowroozi noted Ru is hexagonal, making it an anisotropic conductor. [24]

#### 5.3 Molybdenum (Mo)

**Mo advantages (Entegris blog):** Molybdenum (Mo) is a promising metal for contacts and local interconnects because it offers a combination of low resistivity, high melting point, excellent thermal and chemical stability, and good electromigration resistance. It also is barrierless. Key advantages include up to 30% lower resistivity than tungsten in thin films, barrierless integration that simplifies manufacturing and improves yield, and scalability supporting high aspect ratio features and 3D architectures. Comparison table: Copper has very low bulk resistivity (~1.68 µΩ-cm) but high thin film resistivity in small features and requires a barrier (e.g., TaN); tungsten has higher resistivity (~5.6 µΩ-cm), requires barrier (e.g., TiN), and is reaching limits; molybdenum has moderate bulk resistivity (~5.3 µΩ-cm), lower thin film resistivity than tungsten in small features, and requires no barrier. Molybdenum uses ALD, CVD, and selective ALD deposition methods. Industry trend: copper is being phased out at local interconnects, tungsten at contacts and vias, with molybdenum emerging as the successor. [39]

**Mo limitations (Entegris):** Copper is NOT expected to be replaced at tight-pitch interconnect (TPI) levels (Metal 1 through Metal 4) because these layers sit adjacent to SRAM structures (especially L1 cache) where low resistance is essential. The critical dimension of SRAM features is 4-5 times larger than the smallest CDs at TPI, and molybdenum, tungsten, and iridium cannot meet the very low sheet resistance (Rs) requirements at those levels today. L1 cache is expected to remain on chip for the foreseeable future, even as L2 and L3 caches are pulled off-chip via hybrid bonding. Precision manufacturing: innovations in Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD), Area Selective Deposition (ASD), and Chemical Mechanical Planarization (CMP) enable molybdenum to be deposited with atomic-level precision, ensuring defect-free contacts and interconnects viable for high-volume manufacturing. [39]

**Mo via fill (Lam Research patent WO2021076636A1):** Methods and apparatus for filling semiconductor features (vias, contacts, trenches, wordlines in 3D NAND structures) with molybdenum (Mo). The core innovation involves depositing a first conformal layer of molybdenum in features and then treating it NON-CONFORMALLY — applying treatment preferentially near feature openings rather than in feature interiors — to enable void-free, "inside-out" fill. The non-conformal treatment can be either inhibition (e.g., nitrogen-containing chemistries like NH₃ that delay subsequent nucleation) or etching (e.g., halogen-containing chemistries like NF₃, NH₃/F₂, or molybdenum oxyhalides that remove film near openings). Deposition uses ALD processes with H₂ as a reducing agent and molybdenum oxyhalide or molybdenum halide precursors (e.g., MoO₂Cl₂, MoOxCly). Mo precursors can act as both deposition and etchant gases; higher precursor flux at openings causes lower net growth there. Process parameters (chamber pressure 3–40 Torr, precursor flow rate, dose time, partial pressure) tune precursor flux. Features addressed include re-entrant profiles, constrictions (15–20 nm wide), high aspect ratios (≥2:1 up to 25:1+), and 3D NAND wordlines with polysilicon pillar constrictions (1–20 nm gaps) that cause pinch-off during conventional fills. Mo is used as a lower-resistivity alternative to tungsten (lower electron mean free path). Mo may be deposited with or without diffusion barrier layers (TiN, Ti/TiN, WN, WCN). [26]

**Mo hybrid metallization (Lam Research Facebook post):** A Lam Research study explores molybdenum (Mo) hybrid metallization as an alternative to copper in BEOL interconnects. Results show it lowers via/line resistance by ~55% and reduces stress-related reliability risks. The research combined simulation and virtual fabrication to identify practical ways to optimize interconnect performance at advanced nodes. [27]

**Lam Research on Mo (Counterpoint Research interview):** Dr. Kaihan Ashtiani, CVP and GM of ALD/CVD Metals at Lam Research, discussed the industry transition from tungsten to molybdenum (moly) metallization. Lam introduced ALD of metals over 20 years ago with ALD tungsten and is now transitioning to ALD molybdenum. The transition is driven by the need for lower resistivity metals to support AI, cloud, and high-speed IO applications, as resistivity determines device speed and performance. All device types and customers are shifting toward Moly. Memory (particularly NAND) is expected to be the first adopter, followed closely by logic and DRAM. NAND is the most challenging to adopt Moly due to its 3D architecture with large surface areas and complex aspect ratios in both vertical and lateral dimensions. Lam began developing Moly technology close to 10 years ago, positioning them with a significant lead over competitors. Moly is sourced through a chemical precursor delivered via a bulk delivery system that Lam developed (a first in the industry) — the system sits in the sub-fab (not the main fab), taking up less cleanroom space. "So, this transition to Molly is very important from that perspective because we offer lower resistivity metal compared to what is used today such that our customers can advance their devices to the to the future." Molybdenum has lower resistance than tungsten in nano-scale wires and does not require a barrier layer. These qualities help boost efficiency and chip speed and reduce the number of process steps required in manufacturing. [28][29]

**Mo in high-volume manufacturing (Semiconductor Digest):** Tungsten has been the primary interconnect element for the past 25 years, but as 3D NAND and DRAM structures become more complex with shrinking wordline connections, tungsten is hitting limits in terms of resistance and reliability. Molybdenum offers superior performance with three key breakthroughs (lower resistance, higher yields, more efficient production) benefiting NAND, DRAM, and logic chips. Molybdenum had not been used in metallization until now because atomic layer deposition (ALD) methods had not been developed to meet its requirements. The ALTUS® Halo by Lam Research is the world's first ALD tool that overcomes the technical hurdles of molybdenum deposition at scale. Molybdenum is now being adopted in high-volume 3D NAND and advanced logic fabs, with DRAM in development. Micron is an early adopter using ALTUS Halo in production of its advanced NAND products. "As Moore's Law slows and architectures become more advanced, materials innovation is the next competitive frontier, with molybdenum representing 'a rare and pivotal inflection point.'" (Neil Shah, VP of research at Counterpoint). In 2024 alone, one trillion semiconductor chips were produced – or 100 chips for every human being on earth. [30]

**Mo in DRAM/3D NAND (Semiconductor Engineering, "Interconnects Approach Tipping Point," Feb 2025):** Molybdenum is emerging as the successor to tungsten for word lines in DRAM, contacts and plugs in 3D NAND, and contacts in logic. It offers low resistance at nanometer dimensions, requires no barrier layer (little intrinsic diffusivity into dielectrics), is low cost, and can be deposited via ion beam deposition at 400°C to achieve lower resistivity than tungsten. Nearly all major chipmakers are in various stages of molybdenum qualification. "There are a number of factors to consider in the selection of a metal, and resistivity is among the most important. At the atomic dimensions required for advanced chipmaking, moly is emerging as the most suitable material to replace tungsten, creating a major inflection point in the industry." (Kaihan Ashtiani, Lam Research). [59]

#### 5.4 Overall Transition Outlook

**Semiconductor Engineering tipping point (Feb 2025):** The 1nm (10Å) node will have 20nm pitch metal lines, but the interconnect stack already consumes a third of device power and accounts for 75% of chip RC delay. This is forcing a potential transition from copper to ruthenium (Ru) interconnects at the lowest, tightest levels, possibly as soon as the 14 Å node, and from tungsten to molybdenum (Mo) in DRAM and 3D NAND applications. Ruthenium appears furthest along in demonstrating manufacturability and reliability, and can be deposited by PVD, CVD, ALD, or electroless plating. It requires no barrier layer, doesn't oxidize easily, has a shorter electron mean free path, and is compatible with air gaps (k=1.0) to reduce RC delay, though air gaps reduce mechanical stability and would be used sparingly on alternating layers. The switch from damascene processing to subtractive (deposition-etch) schemes is likely because it enables more flexible, scalable paths to connect taller CFET devices, provides better line height control than CMP, and allows higher aspect ratio lines (beyond 2:1). imec's "semi-damascene" process is a two-layer module that could extend to multi-layer stacks, with data showing stacked via resistance remains important up to M5. Copper extension efforts include lower-resistance via processes, thinner TaN diffusion barriers via ALD, Ru-Co alternative liners, elimination of barrier layers at via bottoms, and self-aligned or fully aligned vias. Samsung reported a Ru-Co bilayer liner producing 87% fewer voids and 14% better line resistance at tight dimensions. Backside power delivery (BPD) moves power delivery to the wafer backside so frontside interconnect levels only carry signals, potentially delaying ruthenium introduction by a device node. Thermal concerns (Joule heating, electromigration, stress migration, TDDB) are exacerbated by scaling and low-k dielectric/air gap transitions, with heating now affecting more than just the first metal level. imec's Zsolt Tokei notes that at 36nm pitches ruthenium performance is already slightly better than copper, but the change is disruptive and requires full self-alignment, via-to-line leakage in spec, correct DPPM, air-gap compatibility, and passing electromigration and reliability testing. Material and architectural changes only happen when existing flows absolutely cannot meet performance specifications, so any metal replacement will occur gradually and step-wise due to massive existing investments in copper dual-damascene and tungsten metallization tooling. [59]

**TSMC interconnect research (TSMC research page):** On-chip interconnect today is based on copper/low-k wiring – in today's chips, there can be more than 100 km of copper wires. TSMC's leading-edge technologies use a novel copper gap-fill solution for smaller conductor lines, and new materials/processes reduce line and via resistance. Innovations in integration schemes, low-k materials, and low-k processes with selective deposition enhance performance through capacitance reduction and improved reliability. Beyond copper, TSMC is exploring single metallic elements, binary/ternary alloys, and 2D materials for future interconnect materials with academic partners. [5]
