### 7. IRDS / SEMI / imec Roadmap Data

**IRDS 2022 More Moore:** Ground rule scaling is expected to slow down and saturate around 2028. EUV will be the enabler of ground rule scaling while keeping cost under control. FinFET architecture expected to sustain scaling until 2025, with transition to gate-all-around (GAA) devices thereafter (sustaining another decade+); transition from 3 to 4 GAA devices around 2031. Physical channel length projected to saturate around 12nm. SiGe and 2D material channels gaining importance. "Interconnect resistance has entered exponential increase regime due to non-ideal barrier scaling for Cu; need for new barrier materials, ALD-based barriers, or non-Cu metallization." TDDB limits minimum spacing between adjacent lines for low-κ dielectrics. After 2031, no room for 2D geometry scaling; 3D VLSI (sequential/stacked integration) becomes necessary. Power density and thermal issues are significant challenges, particularly with 3D integration after 2031. Long-term challenges (2028-2037): integration of non-Cu metallization (buried power rails). Near-term challenges (2022-2028): interconnect scalability (resistance, EM, TDDB). Memory: 96 layers of flash currently at volume production; 128 layers achievable, with 192 and 256 possible; density increase continues via vertical stacking of memory layers (3D Flash). [36]

**imec logic technology roadmap:** The industry moved from planar MOSFET to FinFET architecture; first commercial 22nm FinFETs introduced in 2012; current 7nm chips use FinFETs with 6T standard cells, 2 fins per device, and contact pitches as small as 57nm. Cu-based dual damascene is the workhorse process for BEOL interconnects; most critical local interconnects (M1, M2) now have metal pitches as tight as 40nm. EUV lithography has been adopted by all leading logic manufacturers. Bottlenecks: routing congestion and dramatic RC delay; Co is being adopted as an alternative metal at local level; airgaps used as alternative low-k dielectric at intermediate layers. MOL: source/drain contact resistance has become a major concern due to shrinking contact areas. [38]

**imec near-term options:** FEOL - Gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors (natural evolution of FinFET; gate fully wraps around horizontal Si sheets providing superior channel control; imec has worked on this since 2015; developed processes to reduce vertical nanosheet separation below 10nm to cut parasitic capacitance). Forksheet devices proposed for the 2nm node and beyond (a dielectric wall isolates p- and nMOS gates allowing much tighter n-to-p spacing; expected to shrink track heights from 5T to 4.3T with lower parasitic capacitance and reduced SRAM cell area). BEOL - Metal pitches of M1/M2 will reach 21nm; via critical dimensions as small as 12-14nm. Hybrid metallization: Alternative via metal (Ru, W, or Mo) connects barrierless to the bottom of Cu lines, allowing thinner (2nm) Cu line barriers while maintaining electromigration reliability and lowering via resistance. Semi-damascene: proposed for metal pitches below 21nm; omits the CMP step; enables higher aspect ratio lines with lower resistance; uses patternable alternative metals (Ru, Mo) and eventually airgaps; envisioned for M1 and M2 layers. MOL - Buried power rails (BPRs): power rails buried in the FEOL instead of BEOL to free routing resources; at VLSI 2020, imec demonstrated a tungsten BPR in a FinFET CMOS test vehicle without adversely impacting CMOS characteristics. VBPRs: Via to BPR stitching with the MOL layer (M0A line); imec showed W-based BPR interfaced with Ru via for excellent resistance and electromigration results. Wrap-around contacts (enabled by atomic layer deposition of metal) proposed to replace diamond epi contacts, re-enlarging contact area and decreasing contact resistance. [38]

**imec further-out options:** FEOL - Complementary FET (CFET): folds nFET on top of pFET (fin-on-fin or sheet-on-sheet), fully exploiting 3D device scaling; strongest advantage is area scaling, eventually enabling 3T logic standard cells and significantly smaller SRAM cells. At VLSI 2020, imec demonstrated first experimental proof-of-concept of CFET fabricated in a monolithic process flow. BEOL - Hybrid height with zero via: splits each metal layer into three sub-layers (center line, extension above/below), allowing resistance/capacitance exchange flexibility within the same footprint. New conductor materials: ordered binary intermetallic compounds with low resistivity at scaled dimensions (e.g., AlNi, RuV₃-based compounds); figure of merit defined as product of bulk resistivity times mean free path. Hybrid graphene/metal conductors: Metal (Cu, Ru, Mo) encapsulated by graphene; imec demonstrated low electrical resistivity and high thermal stability. MOL: ruthenium-based advanced MOL contacts proposed to reduce parasitic resistance of deep vias. [38]

**imec thermal modeling (Sept 2023):** The BEOL is a complex wiring scheme with up to 15 metal layers (local Mx, intermediate My, and semi-global Mz layers), interconnected vertically via metal-filled via structures. Temperature increase in the BEOL can dramatically affect IC reliability, accelerating degradation of both BEOL (electromigration, stress migration) and FEOL (negative bias temperature instability). Main heat sources: transistors in the FEOL (logic cells dissipate ~10W/mm²) and Joule heating from currents in the interconnects. Joule heating worsens with each node due to scaling-induced rise in electrical resistivity, higher current densities, and poor thermal conductivity of low-k dielectrics. Measured thermal conductivity: 1.15 W/mK for SiO₂ and 0.3 W/mK for OSG3.0 organosilicate glass. Metal thermal conductivity significantly drops when line widths scale into the 10nm region (relevant for local interconnects at advanced nodes). Low-k dielectrics dominate thermal behavior: a fast temperature increase is observed when intermetal dielectric thermal conductivity drops below 1 W/mK (range of most current dielectrics like OSG3.0). Air gaps worsen this by ~30% increase in metal line self-heating (e.g., in A14 technology node). The choice of metal has minimal impact on thermal dissipation. Via layers contribute 86% of total thermal resistance in a 14-layer BEOL stack; line layers only contribute 14%. [57]

### 8. Thermal Budget Compatibility with Low-k Dielectrics and FinFET/GAA Transistors

**Thermal budget constraint (Emergent Mind):** BEOL integration encompasses processes after FEOL transistor formation but before passivation/package attachment. All steps must stay below a critical thermal budget of 400–450°C to preserve Cu/low-κ interconnects and dopant profiles. Graphene FET wafer-scale integration keeps processes under ~250°C. Photonic BEOL uses BCB bonding of thin-film lithium niobate at peak 300°C. [55]

**CVD temperature requirements (Wafer World):** CVD has high temperature requirements (400–900°C), which is a key limitation. [1]

**Low-k dielectric properties (IntechOpen chapter on Black Diamond):** As IC technology scales down, the industry transitioned from Al/SiO₂ to Cu/low-k interconnect technology to reduce RC delay, cross-talk noise, and power dissipation. Black Diamond™ (BD, low-k, SiOC:H) is a CVD-processed dielectric (by Applied Materials Inc.) with a dielectric constant of 2.5-2.7 and glass transition temperature above 450°C. Four interdependent properties govern thin film mechanical reliability: elastic modulus, hardness, fracture toughness, and interfacial adhesion. BD films of varying thickness (100-1200 nm) showed hardness values of 1.66-2.02 GPa and elastic modulus of 9.27-16.48 GPa. All films exhibited "pop-in" events (cracking/delamination) during indentation, with cracking occurring at approximately 60-65% of film thickness for films 300-1200 nm thick. Diffusion barrier effects (Ta and TaN): BD/Ta/Si had the highest values (hardness 1.91 GPa, modulus 10.03 GPa). Single stacks have slower CMP removal rates due to higher hardness. [56]

**Low-k dielectric families (PatSnap):** Low-k dielectric materials are insulating compounds with a dielectric constant (k) lower than that of silicon dioxide (k ≈ 3.9). In 3D IC packaging they are the primary means of controlling the RC delay and capacitive crosstalk that accumulate as interconnect densities increase. Ultra-low-k materials are classified at k below ~2.5, while air-gap dielectrics approach the theoretical lower bound of k ≈ 1.0. Four principal material families: (1) SiCOH (carbon-doped silicon oxide) — most widely deployed, k 2.7–3.3 via PECVD; porous variants reach ultra-low-k below 2.5. (2) Spin-on dielectric polymers (polyimides, benzocyclobutene/BCB) — k 2.5–3.0, valued for planarisation and hybrid bonding compatibility. (3) Air-gap dielectrics — effective k approaching 1.0, achieved by forming voids between metal lines; engineering challenge is mechanical stability during CMP and thermal cycling. (4) Porous SiCOH — achieve ultra-low-k below 2.5 via nanoscale voids. Key assignees: Device manufacturers (Intel, TSMC, Samsung) hold integration/device structure patents; materials suppliers (Applied Materials, Lam Research, ASM International, Dow Chemical, Merck KGaA) hold precursor chemistry, deposition equipment, and formulation patents. [58]

**Low-k damage and integration (TSMC research):** 2011 TSMC paper: Low damage etch (LRPE) for Cu interconnect: dual damascene process without k degradation on ELK (k=2.4) achieved 12% RC improvement, 15% via resistance reduction, and 3x IMD TDDB improvement vs. traditional etching. 2009 TSMC paper: Low capacitance approaches for 22nm Cu interconnect: K=2.0 low-k material integrated with Cu achieving up to 15% line-to-line capacitance reduction; cost-effective selective air-gap formation process developed. 2002 TSMC paper: 90nm Cu/CVD low-k (k<2.5) interconnect: 8-level dual damascene + 1 top Cu/USG level with 0.12/0.12 μm line width/space and 0.13 μm via; keff=2.6 achieved with nitrogen-free dielectrics. [5]

**Thermal budget for W deposition (Novellus ALTUS DirectFill):** All process temperatures are below 400°C, providing compatibility with future process integration requirements. [32]

**Thermal budget for Mo deposition (Semiconductor Engineering):** Mo can be deposited via ion beam deposition at 400°C to achieve lower resistivity than tungsten. [59]

**PEALD for low thermal budget (ASM):** PEALD uses RF-plasma cycling to provide reaction energy, enabling lower temperatures for low-thermal-budget applications. [40]

**ALD temperature ranges (Wikipedia):** Thermal ALD operates at room temperature (~20°C) to 350°C. Most depositions occur at 100-200°C (per atomiclayerdeposition.com). Substrate temperatures range from room temperature to 800°C. [62][61]

**TSMC 2010 enhancement layer (Ru or Co) between PVD Ta(N) barrier and Cu seed:** Improved Cu-to-barrier adhesion and gap fill; no voids in dual damascene with very thin seed; >2x electromigration lifetime improvement; enables seedless electroplating. [5]

**Samsung Ru-Co liner (Semiconductor Engineering):** Samsung reported a Ru-Co bilayer liner producing 87% fewer voids and 14% better line resistance at tight dimensions. [59]

### 9. Deposition Rate, Throughput, and Cost Effectiveness Tradeoffs

**ALD throughput challenge (Wikipedia):** Economic viability (slower process compared to other deposition methods) and reaction time (sequential pulses and purge steps limit throughput) are the main disadvantages. [62]

**ALD growth rates (Patsnap Eureka):** Conventional ALD has an inherently slow growth rate of 0.5–2 Å per cycle (0.1–1.0 Å/cycle, or 1–10 nm/min), creating throughput challenges in high-volume manufacturing. Mixed precursor ALD can achieve 200-500% increases in deposition rates. Mixed precursor ALD systems require 25–40% higher capital investment, but yield 30–50% reduction in processing costs and break-even within 18–24 months for high-volume production (over 10,000 wafers monthly). [60]

**ALD typical growth rates (GP Plasma):** Growth rates typically range from 0.2 to 1.3 Å/cycle. The pinhole-free nature of ALD films allows thinner films meeting the same performance criteria as other methods. [18]

**ALD growth rates (atomiclayerdeposition.com):** Typical growth rate is ~1 atomic layer/second, though fast flow reactors (1-5 nm/sec) and spatial ALD (1-10 nm/sec) are faster. [61]

**ASM throughput improvement:** ASM's high-speed ALD process doubled the throughput of HfO₂ films for 45 nm high-k gates, achieving throughput for 32 nm gate dielectrics comparable to MOCVD deposition methods while retaining ALD layer quality. [41]

**PVD cost/throughput advantages (Wafer World):** PVD offers high deposition rates, low cost, and versatility. [1] PVD advantages include low operational cost, good film adhesion, and ability to deposit very high melting point materials (SemiFlows). [3]

**CVD throughput (Wafer World):** CVD produces high-purity, conformal coatings with uniform thickness on complex 3D geometries. [1]

**SLE cost benefit (Roule et al.):** The SLE (seed layer enhancement) electrolytic repair process efficiently "repairs" discontinuous ultra-thin PVD copper liners, enabling efficient filling of narrow features for 45 nm node and beyond, integrated into the existing metallization sequence without modification of subsequent steps. [9]

**ALD market economics (DataIntelo):** ALD equipment market valued at $3.98 billion in 2025, projected to reach $9.55 billion by 2034 at a CAGR of 10.2%. Thermal ALD holds 38.5% product share; semiconductors application 52.0%; Asia Pacific 42.3% (~$1.68 billion). Over 85% of leading-edge logic fab capacity additions expected to incorporate ALD by 2030. [63]

**TEL cost of ownership:** Triase+ W features rapid wafer heat up/cool down and plasma-less chamber cleaning for higher productivity and lower CoO. [48] The ALTUS DirectFill reduced cost of ownership by 50 percent or more compared to existing processes. [32]

**ALD seed layer market (Patsnap Eureka):** $2.3 billion in 2023, projected to grow at 11.7% CAGR through 2028. Semiconductor industry accounts for 65% of applications. [4]

**Selective W cost/performance benefit (IEEE Spectrum):** In 7-nanometer chips, contacts are only 20 nanometers wide, and only 25 percent of their volume is tungsten; the rest is cladding. The Endura Volta Selective W CVD machine eliminates cladding entirely, reducing resistance by 40%. [35]

**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

Three rounds of Tavily web searches were performed:

**Round 1:**
- "e-beam evaporation PVD sputtering semiconductor manufacturing high volume production vs R&D"
- "molecular beam epitaxy MBE high volume manufacturing advanced node semiconductor"
- "electron beam evaporation step coverage high aspect ratio vias interconnect semiconductor"

**Round 2:**
- "MRAM STT-MRAM MBE magnetic tunnel junction production deposition PVD magnetron sputtering"
- "Applied Materials PVD Endura sputtering interconnect barrier liner advanced node 7nm"
- "IRDS ITRS interconnect metallization PVD sputtering roadmap BEOL"

**Round 3:**
- "MBE molecular beam epitaxy MTJ STT-MRAM deposition production magnetic layers PVD"
- "electron beam evaporation use optical coatings semiconductor research R&D labs applications"
- "physical vapor deposition interconnect advanced node sputtering vs evaporation industry"

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

**1. E-Beam Evaporation: Technical Characteristics**

*How it works:* Electron beam evaporation uses a focused beam of high-energy electrons to heat and evaporate materials. The electron beam is generated by a filament (5-10 kV, tungsten or tantalum) and steered by magnetic fields to strike the target material (the "evaporant"), which sits in a water-cooled copper crucible. Magnetic steering coils bend and direct the electron beam across the evaporant surface to control evaporation rate and uniformity. The vapor travels through a vacuum chamber (typically 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁷ Torr) and condenses onto the substrate. Because the electron beam can be focused to a spot just a few millimeters across, the power density is extremely high—allowing melting of virtually any material regardless of melting point. [12][33]

*Key advantage - water cooling/self-crucible:* Unlike thermal evaporation where the entire crucible heats up (causing contamination), in e-beam evaporation only the spot where the beam hits gets hot. The evaporant forms its own "self-crucible"—a molten pool surrounded by solid material of the same composition—eliminating container contamination. This allows evaporation of reactive materials (e.g., aluminum, which reacts with tungsten crucibles) and ultra-high-purity materials. [12]

*Deposition rates:* E-beam evaporation can deposit hundreds of nanometers per minute—much faster than sputtering for many materials. ScienceDirect states deposition rates are 2-3 orders of magnitude higher than sputtering: compounds can be deposited at ~100 nm/s, metals at ~1 µm/s. EBE can heat target materials up to 6000°C, making it suitable for high-melting-point materials. Denton Vacuum states e-beam evaporation offers a better deposition rate than sputtering or resistive thermal evaporation. ELETTRORAVA states deposition rates range from 1 nm per minute to several μm per minute, depending on required film control. Korvus Tech states deposition rates range from 0.1 to 100 nanometers per minute at low substrate temperatures. [14][37][33][35][12]

*Line-of-sight deposition / poor step coverage:* The vapor travels in a straight line (line of sight) to the wafer. Evaporation provides poor step coverage (directional flux); sputtering provides good step coverage (omnidirectional flux). [2] E-beam evaporation produces films that are line-of-sight (limited coverage on complex geometries), and film density is often lower than sputtered films. [3] Korvus Tech lists "line-of-sight deposition (unsuitable for complex geometries)" among e-beam limitations. [35]

*Lift-off compatibility:* Evaporation is excellent for lift-off (sidewalls stay uncoated); sputtering is poor for lift-off (coats sidewalls). [2] Polyteknik states e-beam evaporation has "excellent directionality (minimal sidewall coverage, ideal for lift-off processes)" and recommends its Flextura Evaporator Module for lift-off processes, either standalone or combined with a Flextura Cluster for high-volume production. E-beam evaporation is "the standard method for lift-off patterning in MEMS and microelectronics." [34]

*Alloy fidelity:* Evaporation struggles with alloys due to differing vapor pressures; sputtering preserves target composition faithfully. [2] Preferential evaporation of multi-component precursors with different melting points can affect film composition. [14]

*Adhesion and density:* Sputtered films are denser and adhere better (high-energy arrival, plus in situ RF etch); evaporated films often need a thin adhesion layer. [2] Evaporation coatings are line-of-sight and film density often lower than sputtered films. [3]

*Film purity:* Evaporation yields very high purity; sputtered films are high purity. [2] E-beam provides high purity due to elimination of crucible contamination. [12]

*Substrate heating:* Evaporation causes low heating; sputtering causes higher heating. [2] E-beam evaporation offers no substrate damage (mostly) since there is no plasma involved. [12]

*Uniformity concerns:* Evaporation cons: poor uniformity without planetary/masks, moderate complexity (e-beam). [1] ScienceDirect lists "deposition non-uniformity" and "spatter" among e-beam disadvantages, plus short filament lifetime, and thickness control less precise than sputtering systems. [14]

*Contamination/particle issues:* ScienceDirect lists as disadvantages: secondary electrons may ionize residual gas molecules, causing contamination; compounds may decompose when bombarded by high-energy electrons, affecting final film composition; short filament lifetime, deposition non-uniformity, and spatter. [14] Korvus Tech lists secondary electron emission and X-ray production causing energy loss, and filament degradation causing inconsistent evaporation rates. [35]

*Film stress:* Stanford Advanced Materials notes "low film stress compared to sputtered films—important for precision optics and thin membranes" as an e-beam advantage. [12]

*Materials that can be e-beam evaporated (with melting points):* Platinum (1,768°C) - electrodes, Schottky contacts; Gold (1,064°C) - electrical contacts, corrosion protection; Aluminum (660°C) - semiconductor interconnects, mirrors; Copper (1,085°C) - chip wiring; Titanium (1,668°C) - adhesion layers, biomedical; Tantalum (3,017°C) - diffusion barriers, capacitors; Tungsten (3,422°C) - X-ray targets, high-temperature electrodes; Molybdenum (2,623°C) - electrodes, solar cells; Silicon (1,414°C) - thin-film transistors; SiO₂ (1,710°C) - optical coatings, insulators; TiO₂ (1,843°C) - optical coatings, photocatalysts; ITO (~1,800°C) - transparent conductive films. [12]

*Applications where e-beam evaporation IS used:* Polyteknik lists typical applications: (1) Semiconductor fabrication—depositing metal contacts, gate electrodes, and barrier layers on silicon wafers, with excellent directionality making it the standard method for lift-off patterning in MEMS and microelectronics; (2) Optical coatings—anti-reflection coatings, mirrors, and bandpass filters using alternating layers of TiO₂ and SiO₂; (3) Research and advanced materials—developing novel thin film materials, surface functionalisation, and prototype devices across wafers, glass, ceramics, and polymer films. [34]

Korvus Tech lists e-beam applications: optical thin films (architectural glass, laser optics, solar panels, semiconductors, eyeglasses, cold filters blocking infrared), metallic films (wiring, decorative, electromagnetic shielding, and reflective films used in power packs, EL diode displays, SAW filters, watches, and lithium-ion batteries), and high-wear-resistant components for automotive and aerospace industries (cutting tools, machinery components, marine fittings). Multi-crucible four-pocket hearths allow sequential deposition of up to four material layers without breaking vacuum. [35]

ELETTRORAVA lists e-beam applications across industries including semiconductors, thin-film solar, aerospace, and cutting/tool industries for wear-resistant and thermal barrier coatings, plus "dielectric and optical coatings, Josephson junctions, and micro/nano-fabrication lift-off processes." [33]

ScienceDirect lists applications: thin film deposition for solar cells (dye-sensitized, perovskite, CZTS-based photovoltaic devices); gate dielectric deposition (e.g., Sm2O3 thin films on Si substrates for MOS devices); protective coating on porous metal supports for solid oxide cells; synthesis of 2D and 3D nanoparticle assemblies, carbon nanotubes, and graphene layers; silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries (graphene/Si multilayer structures); high barrier plastics using nanoscale inorganic films (SiO, SiO_x, Al2O3). [14]

Rogue Valley Microdevices lists typical applications: E-beam for lift-off metallization, precious metal contacts, multilayer stacks, thick high-purity films, optical coatings, refractory metals. Sputtering for alloy films (aluminum alloys, TiW), adhesion/barrier layers, conformal coatings, reactively sputtered dielectrics, interconnect metallization, and large-diameter wafers. [2]

**2. Sputtering (PVD) as the HVM Alternative: Technical Comparison**

*How sputtering works:* A target material is bombarded with energetic argon ions generated in a plasma (at low pressure). Momentum transfer ejects atoms that arrive at the wafer from many directions due to collisions with process gas, producing dense, well-adhered, conformal films. DC power is used for conductive targets; RF power for insulating targets. [2] Sputtering is preferred for materials with very high melting points (as it doesn't rely on vaporisation temperature) and can produce compound films via reactive sputtering. [1] Magnetron sputtering is the most scalable PVD process. [1]

*Selection workflow:* (1) Lift-off patterning → e-beam evaporation; (2) Conformal step coverage → sputter; (3) Alloy/compound composition fidelity → sputter; (4) Precious/refractory metals, multilayer stacks, thick high-purity films → e-beam evaporation; (5) Many successful flows use both methods at different steps. [2]

*Selection guidance:* Choose sputtering when you need high-density, uniform coatings or are working with complex geometries. Choose evaporation when you need faster deposition rates, simpler equipment, or are working with metals that vaporize cleanly. [3] Denton Vacuum states magnetron sputtering is better for highly automated high-volume production, particularly for thin films with short deposition times. [37] Sputtering offers better film quality, uniformity, and scalability at higher cost/complexity. [1]

*PVD step coverage limits (and why ALD/CVD take over at advanced nodes):* A Patsnap Eureka report states: "PVD faces fundamental limitations in step coverage for high-aspect-ratio structures, typically achieving only 20-30% step coverage in deep trenches compared to CVD's 80-90% conformality." PVD achieves <2% uniformity across 300mm wafers. "CVD dominates in applications requiring conformal coverage and gap-filling properties, particularly for dielectric layers and barrier films in advanced integrated circuits. PVD maintains strong market presence in metallization processes, where directional deposition and material purity are paramount." [38]

SemiFlows states: "PVD is fundamentally a line-of-sight deposition process, which results in non-conformal step coverage caused by the shadowing effect in small feature size, high-aspect-ratio via geometries." PVD was heavily used for all BEOL barrier layers (Ta/TaN) and copper seed layers at the 28nm planar node due to acceptable step coverage, high throughput, and material purity. However, at 14nm FinFET and 7nm FinFET nodes, extreme aspect-ratio vias made PVD unsuitable for continuous diffusion barriers due to shadowing. The industry transitioned to hybrid integration—using ALD for ultra-thin conformal barrier layers (like ALD TaN) while retaining specialized ionized PVD for copper seed layers requiring high purity and good wetting. PVD challenges include poor conformality (line-of-sight deposition causes shadowing effects in high-aspect-ratio structures, with overhang pinch-off before trench bottoms are filled), ion-induced surface damage, and adhesion/wetting failures. Future PVD is evolving toward highly ionized PVD (iPVD), which uses secondary RF coils to heavily ionize sputtered metal flux, enabling directional control via substrate biasing to defeat shadowing in deep trenches. [39]

*TSV fill limits:* Oerlikon Balzers (Semiconductor Digest) notes: "Copper is the preferred interconnect metal for advanced CMOS devices due to low resistivity and desirable electro-migration characteristics... The highest AR for features that could reliably be filled has been in the range 5:1 up to may be 10:1; limited by the ability of enhanced physical vapor deposition (PVD) techniques to deliver sufficient material to the lower sidewalls of the vias." Advanced directional sputtering (ADS) using a large target-to-substrate distance (~1.5× substrate diameter) plus RF bias provides 15% bottom coverage for Ti and 10% for Cu in 8:1 AR trenches. Highly ionized sputtering (HIS) using short (<0.2ms) high-current pulses (several hundred to >1000A) achieves >90% ionization of Ti near the target surface, achieving up to 20% bottom coverage in 10:1 AR trenches at 26 Å/s, with Ta deposition demonstrated at 30:1 AR. [11]

**3. PVD Sputtering Is the HVM Workhorse for Advanced-Node Interconnect Metallization**

*Applied Materials Endura platform:* "The Applied Endura platform is the most successful metallization system in the history of the semiconductor industry." "A vast majority of microchips made in the last 20 years have been created using an Endura system." The platform supports deposition capabilities spanning front-end metallization (cobalt, tungsten), aluminum and copper interconnects, and packaging applications such as underbump metallization. It can accommodate up to nine process chambers, including two preclean chambers for native oxide removal. [23]

*Endura history and installed base:* Launched in 1990, Endura is "the most successful metal deposition system in semiconductor equipment industry history, used by virtually all advanced chip manufacturers worldwide." The 2,000th system shipped in October 2000. The Endura entered the market when chipmakers needed "radically new sputtering technology to reach through the one micron barrier and create, for the first time, multiple layers of aluminum interconnects." It pioneered the industry's first production ultra-high vacuum (10⁻⁹ Torr) capability through staged vacuum wafer transfer chambers. Applications expanded from sputtered aluminum to include titanium/titanium nitride, tantalum/tantalum nitride barrier films, and copper seed layers, as well as integrated CVD/PVD processes. [22]

*Endura Integrated Liner/Barrier (100th shipment):* The system, announced in December 1996, features the industry's first integrated PVD and CVD process technologies on a single system, used to deposit conformal Ti/TiN liner/barrier films in tungsten-based contact and via structures of advanced metal interconnects. It uses Vectra IMP technology for highly directional Ti deposition with over 40% bottom coverage on aspect ratios higher than 4:1, extendible to 0.13-micron designs. Dr. Mark Liu of TSMC said: "This system's integrated PVD titanium and CVD titanium nitride processes have enabled us to extend our aluminum-based designs to next-generation products and achieve excellent device performance... The system is a manufacturing workhorse that contributes to our profitability and cost-effectiveness." [20]

*Endura Copper Barrier Seed (2021):* Applied Materials announced the Endura Copper Barrier Seed system to reduce electrical resistance in copper interconnects within advanced logic chips, addressing a key obstacle to future 3-nanometer node manufacturing. As chip interconnects shrink, their electrical resistance increases dramatically—by a factor of 10 from 7-nm to 3-nm nodes—causing power waste, heat buildup, and signal delays. The tool reduces interconnect resistance by 50%, allowing copper wires in 3-nm chips to achieve roughly the same overall resistance as current 5-nm chips, and enables scaling interconnect wires down to 15 nanometers. It uses selective ALD to coat only the walls of interconnect trenches with tantalum, and eliminates the high-resistance tantalum barrier at the via-to-copper interface, integrating surface treatment, interface engineering, ALD, PVD, CVD, copper reflow, and metrology in a vacuum-sealed chamber. Prabu Raja, senior VP: "A smartphone chip has tens of billions of copper interconnects, and the wiring already consumes up to a third of the chip's power." The tool was already being used by major foundry logic customers globally. [21]

*Endura Amber PVD:* Designed to address interconnect scaling challenges beyond the 20nm node, it combines cold deposition and high-temperature thermal copper reflow. Copper overhang around ultra-small via openings at the 1xnm node precludes conventional PVD from achieving required sidewall and bottom seed layer coverage. The two-step technique (PVD deposition + copper reflow) enables bottom-up fill. The copper seed technology is integrated on the Endura platform with pre-clean and EnCoRe II Ta(N) barrier technologies under high-vacuum conditions to enable high device yields in volume production. [24]

*Samsung PVD usage:* Samsung Electronics uses "hybrid PVD+CVD approach; proprietary low-temperature CVD below 150°C for flexible displays; magnetron sputtering for metal interconnects." [38]

**4. Why E-Beam Evaporation Is NOT Used for Mainstream Advanced-Node Interconnect/Contact Films**

The accumulated evidence from the sources above directly supports the thesis:

- E-beam evaporation provides poor step coverage (directional, line-of-sight flux); sputtering provides good step coverage (omnidirectional flux). [2][3] Advanced interconnect and contact structures at 7nm and below have high-aspect-ratio vias and trenches (at 5nm node, interconnect resistance affects ~50% of total RC delay [25]; M1/M2 metal pitches reaching 21nm with via CDs of 12-14nm per imec [27]). The line-of-sight nature of evaporation causes shadowing effects in high-aspect-ratio structures, with overhang pinch-off before trench bottoms are filled. [39]
- Evaporation produces less dense films (possible columnar structure); sputtered films are denser, better adhered, conformal. [3][2]
- Sputtering preserves alloy composition faithfully; evaporation struggles with alloys due to differing vapor pressures. [2]
- E-beam evaporation has known uniformity problems (poor uniformity without planetary/masks; deposition non-uniformity, spatter, short filament lifetime; thickness control less precise than sputtering). [1][14]
- Contamination issues: secondary electrons may ionize residual gas molecules causing contamination; compounds may decompose when bombarded by high-energy electrons; secondary electron emission and X-ray production cause energy loss. [14][35]
- Industry practice confirms: For HVM interconnect/barrier/seed films, the industry uses magnetron sputtering PVD (Applied Materials Endura platform, with >2,000 systems shipped and "virtually all advanced chip manufacturers worldwide" as customers [22][23]), supplemented by ALD/CVD for conformal barrier layers at 14nm/7nm and below [39]. Sputtering is explicitly the method for "interconnect metallization" and "large-diameter wafers," while e-beam is for "lift-off metallization, precious metal contacts, multilayer stacks, thick high-purity films, optical coatings, refractory metals." [2]
- PVD sputtering (not evaporation) is used for copper seed layers and barrier films at advanced nodes; Patsnap notes "PVD leads metallization processes requiring directional deposition and purity," but even sputtering PVD only achieves 20-30% step coverage in deep trenches, which is why ALD barriers are used at 14nm/7nm nodes. E-beam evaporation has even poorer step coverage than sputtering, making it even less suitable. [38][39]

**5. MBE: Technical Characteristics**

*Definition and method:* Molecular-beam epitaxy (MBE) is an epitaxy method for thin-film deposition of single crystals, widely used in the manufacture of semiconductor devices including transistors, diodes, and MOSFETs at microwave frequencies, as well as lasers used to read optical discs (CDs and DVDs). [10] MBE grows ultra-high-purity crystalline semiconductor layers one atomic layer at a time inside an ultra-high vacuum (UHV) chamber, using effusion cells to generate molecular or atomic beams (gallium, aluminum, indium, arsenic, phosphorus, silicon) that condense onto a heated substrate. Reflection High-Energy Electron Diffraction (RHEED) is used for real-time monitoring of crystal growth down to a single monolayer. [8][9]

*Ultra-high vacuum:* MBE takes place in high or ultra-high vacuum (10⁻⁸–10⁻¹² Torr). [10] Dataintelo reports UHV of 10⁻¹⁰ to 10⁻¹¹ Torr for MBE. [6]

*Extremely slow growth rates:* Deposition rates typically less than 3,000 nm per hour, allowing films to grow epitaxially. [10] Computer-controlled shutters allow precise layer thickness control, down to a single layer of atoms. [10] "Using high-precision shutters and stabilized fluxes, crystal growth is controlled down to one atomic layer every few dozen seconds, requiring ultra-high vacuum and stable temperature control." [30]

*Advantages:* atomic-scale thickness control, ultra-high purity, excellent crystal quality, precise doping profiles, sharp interfaces, ideal for quantum structures, and real-time growth monitoring with RHEED. [8] The absence of carrier gases and ultra-high vacuum result in the highest achievable film purity. [10]

*Applications:* MBE-grown materials include laser diodes, LEDs, photodetectors, solar cells, quantum computing devices, HEMT transistors, spintronic devices, infrared detectors, and advanced sensors. [8] MBE enables atomically flat and abrupt hetero-interfaces, allowing construction of nanowires and quantum structures for information processing, quantum communication/computing, and monolithical integration on silicon. [10] MBE systems can be modified with oxygen sources for depositing oxide materials for advanced electronic, magnetic, and optical applications. [10]

*Compound semiconductor / research focus:* The Prineas Research Group at the University of Iowa uses MBE to grow compound semiconductor materials for infrared photonics, with a major focus on III-V antimonide semiconductor systems enabling light emission and detection in near-, short-, mid-, and long-wave infrared. [9] Stanford's Shen Laboratory operates three MBE systems (a custom-built chalcogenide MBE, a Veeco GEN930 Oxide MBE, and a "Baby MBE") for growing ultra-thin 2D materials, topological insulators (Bi2Te3, Bi2Se3), and cuprate compounds, achieving significant results on FeSe superconductivity. [30] UniversityWafer documents MBE substrate applications including GaAs for high-speed electronics, sapphire for GaN growth in LEDs and power electronics, SiC for wide-bandgap/high-temperature/high-voltage devices, and MgO for magnetic thin films and superconducting materials. [8]

*MBE system sizes:* SVTA offers MBE systems by substrate size: Smart/Compact MBE Systems, 3"/4" substrate systems, and 6"/8" substrate systems, including a 200 mm cluster system—indicating MBE does not scale to mainstream 300mm HVM. [32]

*Magnetic-field-assisted MBE research:* A 2023 research paper (PMC) describes magnetic-field-assisted MBE of Fe3O4 ultrathin films on MgO(111) in a multi-chamber UHV system (PREVAC) with base pressure 2·10⁻¹⁰ mbar. This is reportedly the first implementation of UHV MBE under an external magnetic field, and "paves the way for tailoring magnetic properties of more complex heterostructures such as exchange bias systems or spin valves." [31]

**6. MBE: Market Data Demonstrating R&D/Specialty (Not Mainstream HVM) Role**

*Dataintelo report:* The global MBE market was valued at $0.84 billion in 2025, projected to reach $1.72 billion by 2034, growing at a CAGR of 8.3% (2026-2034). [6]

*End-user breakdown (2025):* Research Institutes: 52.3%, CAGR 7.5%—largest segment; Industrial Manufacturing: 35.1%, CAGR 9.7% (fastest); Others: 12.6%, CAGR 8.3%. [6]

*Application breakdown (2025):* Semiconductors: 42.5% ($0.36 billion); Optoelectronics: 27.3%; Quantum Computing: 15.4% (CAGR 13.8%, fastest growing); Others: 14.8%. [6]

*Key MBE facts:* Over 1,200 MBE systems installed globally, growing ~6.8% annually. MBE is preferred over MOCVD for quantum devices, specialty HEMT wafers, and infrared detectors; MOCVD dominates high-volume LED/power GaN production. MBE processes 1-4 wafers per run vs. 50-100+ for MOCVD. ~78% of global quantum dot/quantum well laser research programs use MBE as primary growth platform. Over 85% of leading quantum hardware companies rely on MBE-grown material. [6]

*MBE costs:* High capital costs ($1.5M-$5M per chamber, $15M+ for cluster tools), maintenance complexity, US-China export controls (dual-use classification). Threats include MOCVD encroachment. [6]

*Report Prime data:* MBE market valued at USD 1.65 billion in 2025, projected to reach USD 1.92 billion in 2026 and USD 3.02 billion by 2032, CAGR 7.83%. Restraints include high capital expenditure, shortage of specialized technical expertise, and competition from alternative epitaxy techniques. Top vendors include Veeco (USD 430M, production-scale focus), Riber (USD 210M, research/pilot-line specialist), Scienta Omicron (USD 160M), DCA (USD 95M, customized university/national lab tools), Svt Associates (USD 90M, custom compound semiconductor systems), SemiTeq JSC (USD 85M), Pascal (USD 80M), CreaTec Fischer (USD 75M), Dr. Eberl MBE-Komponenten (USD 70M), Prevac (USD 65M), Epiquest (USD 60M), EIKO ENGINEERING (USD 55M), SKY (USD 50M), GC inno (USD 50M). [7]

*Veeco as market leader:* Veeco Instruments Inc. is the MBE market leader with ~$145 million MBE revenue in 2025 (~17.3% share); platforms GEN10, GEN20, Lumina. Riber S.A. is second-largest at ~EUR 34.2 million revenue in 2025; MBE32, MBE49, Compact21 systems. [6]

*Note on market report caveats:* These figures should be contextualized against the broader semiconductor equipment market (PVD systems cost $100K-$500K research-grade to $1-3M industrial [38]; the global thin film deposition market exceeds $20 billion [38]), showing MBE (~$0.84-1.65B) is a small specialty segment.

**7. Where MBE DOES Appear in Advanced Chip Manufacturing / R&D**

*MRAM/STT-MRAM context:* STT-MRAM is an emerging memory technology combining non-volatility, high endurance, and ease of CMOS integration; initial applications include 1 Gb standalone memory for SSD write buffers and embedded non-volatile memory for microcontrollers (replacing embedded Flash). [18] STT-MRAM stores information using a Magnetic Tunnel Junction (MTJ), which contains two ferromagnetic layers and one tunnel barrier layer. [19] Everspin's STT-MRAM uses a perpendicular MTJ with high perpendicular magnetic anisotropy. [17] IBM history: spin-transfer-torque switching was invented at IBM in 1996; high magnetoresistance MgO tunnel barriers first published by IBM and AIST in 2004; perpendicularly magnetized STT-MRAM first published with Tohoku University in 2010; scaling to 11 nm tunnel junctions switching in 7.5 µA; first product-level yields (8 Mb demonstrator) with TDK in 2013. [18]

*MBE and MRAM magnetic layers:* The market report lists "magnetic applications" among MBE uses (SVTA lists MBE for "semiconductor, opto-electronic, photovoltaic, and magnetic applications" including Nitride MBE, Oxide MBE, III-V and II-VI MBE, Silicon MBE, Metal Organic Systems, Laser MBE) [32]. MgO substrates are supplied for "magnetic thin films and superconducting materials." [8] MBE systems "can be modified with oxygen sources for depositing oxide materials for advanced electronic, magnetic, and optical applications." [10] Magnetic-field-assisted MBE research targets "exchange bias systems or spin valves," which are related to MTJ/MRAM device structures. [31] However, no source found in this research states that MBE is used in high-volume production of MRAM; rather, MRAM production deposition is associated with PVD sputtering tools (e.g., Singulus TIMARIS deposition tool used in STT's OST-MRAM development and pre-commercial prototyping [16]) and CMOS-compatible processes. The MTJ patent (GlobalFoundries Singapore) describes fabrication methods involving forming bottom electrodes, ferromagnetic layers (CoFeC), and MgO tunnel barriers—materials commonly deposited by sputtering in production, with the MTJ able to withstand processing at about 400°C for at least 30 minutes for CMOS compatibility. [15]

*Quantum devices research:* Quantum computing is the fastest-growing MBE application segment (15.4% share in 2025, CAGR 13.8%). Quantum investment reached ~$2.35 billion in 2025, expected to surpass $7 billion annually by 2030. Microsoft's topological qubit program (InAs/Al heterostructures), IBM, Google, and IonQ are major demand drivers. [6] MBE enables "nanowires and quantum structures for information processing, quantum communication/computing, and monolithical integration on silicon." [10]

*Compound semiconductors / optoelectronics:* MBE is used for III-V compound semiconductors, 2D materials, and heterostructures; key drivers include 5G rollout, compound semiconductor proliferation, and photonic chip fabrication. [6] MBE-grown materials include laser diodes, LEDs, photodetectors, solar cells, HEMT transistors, spintronic devices, infrared detectors. [8]

**8. Roadmap Context: ITRS/IRDS and imec on Interconnect Metallization**

*ITRS/IRDS history:* The International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS) was a set of documents coordinated by the Semiconductor Research Corporation and produced by industry experts representing the Semiconductor Industry Associations of Taiwan, South Korea, the United States, Europe, Japan, and China. The last ITRS revision was published in 2013, and ITRS issued its final roadmap in 2016. Its successor is the International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IRDS), started through the IEEE's Rebooting Computing initiative. [26] Paolo Gargini states: "The IRDS is the ONLY roadmap that represents the continuation, enhancement and evolution of ITRS" (http://irds.ieee.org/, 2016). [28]

*IRDS 2022 More Moore:* The IRDS 2022 More Moore chapter provides physical, electrical, and reliability requirements for logic and memory technologies to sustain PPAC scaling over a 15-year horizon for mainstream/high-volume manufacturing (HVM). Key findings: "Ground rule scaling is expected to slow down and saturate around 2028. Extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) technology will be the enabler of ground rule scaling... Transition to 3D integration and use of beyond CMOS devices for complementary System-on-Chip (SoC) functions are projected after 2028." "Interconnect resistance has entered exponential increase regime due to non-ideal barrier scaling for Cu; need for new barrier materials, ALD-based barriers, or non-Cu metallization." On memory: "STT-MRAM seen as embedded (not standalone) memory, potential NOR Flash replacement for low-power IoT." [29]

*imec roadmap:* Cu-based dual damascene is the workhorse process for BEOL interconnects; most critical local interconnects (M1, M2) now have metal pitches as tight as 40nm (2020). Metal pitches of M1/M2 will reach 21nm; via critical dimensions as small as 12-14nm. Co is being adopted as an alternative metal at local level; airgaps used as alternative low-k dielectric. Hybrid metallization uses alternative via metal (Ru, W, or Mo) connecting barrierless to the bottom of Cu lines. Semi-damascene proposed for metal pitches below 21nm. [27]

*Interconnect materials review (Korea University/Samsung):* At the 5nm node, interconnect resistance affects ~50% of total RC delay. As linewidth shrinks below the electron mean free path, Cu interconnect resistivity increases dramatically—a 10nm linewidth causes ~10-fold increase in resistivity compared to bulk values due to surface and grain boundary electron scattering. IBM introduced Cu in 1997, replacing Al; Cu reduced wiring resistance by up to 45% and showed 100-fold improvement in EM failure time at 295°C. The review covers next-generation barrier materials (2D materials, self-assembled molecular layers, high-entropy alloys) and conductor alternatives (Co, Ru, intermetallic compounds, MAX phases). The research methodology framework includes thin-film experiments (PVD, CVD, electrodeposition, ALD). [25]

**9. Summary of the Core Thesis Supported by Sources**

The collected sources support the following conclusions:

1. **E-beam evaporation is primarily an R&D/laboratory and specialty technique, not a mainstream HVM tool for advanced-node interconnect metallization.** It offers high deposition rates and high purity [12], but its line-of-sight, directional flux gives poor step coverage [2][3], making it unsuitable for filling high-aspect-ratio vias and trenches in advanced interconnect and contact structures [11][39]. It has uniformity issues without planetary/masks [1], non-uniformity, spatter, short filament lifetime, and contamination concerns (secondary electrons ionizing residual gas, compound decomposition) [14][35]. Its primary semiconductor applications are lift-off metallization, precious metal contacts, multilayer stacks, and optical coatings [2][34].

2. **MBE is overwhelmingly an R&D and specialty technique**—the largest MBE end-user segment is Research Institutes at 52.3% [6]; it has extremely low growth rates (<3,000 nm/hour) [10], UHV requirements (10⁻⁸–10⁻¹² Torr) [10], very high capital costs ($1.5M-$5M per chamber, $15M+ for cluster tools) [6], processes only 1-4 wafers per run [6], and is used for compound semiconductors, quantum research, and specialized epitaxial applications [8][9][30]. It is not used for mainstream metal interconnect films in CMOS logic mass production—the MBE market is only ~$0.84-1.65B [6][7], and its applications are III-V compound semiconductors, quantum devices, optoelectronics, and magnetic/oxide research [6][8][10].

3. **The HVM workhorse for interconnect metallization is PVD sputtering**—specifically Applied Materials' Endura platform with 2,000+ systems shipped, used by "virtually all advanced chip manufacturers worldwide" [22][23], with TSMC explicitly calling an integrated PVD/CVD liner-barrier system "a manufacturing workhorse that contributes to our profitability and cost-effectiveness" [20]. At 14nm/7nm and below, ALD is used for conformal ultra-thin barriers while specialized ionized PVD is retained for copper seed layers [39].

4. **Where MBE does appear in advanced manufacturing/R&D:** MRAM/STT-MRAM magnetic layer research and related magnetic structures [8][10][31][32], quantum devices research (fastest-growing segment) [6][10], and compound semiconductor/optoelectronic applications [6][8][9]. Note that in MRAM production, deposition is associated with PVD sputtering tools (e.g., Singulus TIMARIS) [16] and CMOS-compatible fabrication [15], rather than MBE.

5. **Where e-beam evaporation does appear:** optical coatings (anti-reflection coatings, mirrors, bandpass filters) [34][35], laboratories and research [34], lift-off processes in MEMS and microelectronics [2][34], and specialty applications like Josephson junctions [33].

args.research_topic: Research the actual usage extent of electron beam evaporation (e-beam evaporation / e-beam physical vapor deposition) equipment in high-volume manufacturing (HVM) of advanced-node semiconductor logic chips (7nm and below) by TSMC, Samsung, Intel during 2023-2026. Determine whether e-beam evaporation is primarily used in research and development (R&D) rather than mass production. Analyze the technical reasons: e-beam evaporation produces highly directional, line-of-sight films with very poor step coverage in high-aspect-ratio vias and trenches, making it unsuitable for filling contact holes and interconnect trenches in advanced metallization; difficulty controlling film uniformity, composition, and stress at 300mm wafer scale; contamination/particle issues from the evaporation source and crucibles; low throughput; and incompatibility with damascene and dual-damascene integration flows. Also identify where e-beam evaporation IS actually used: e.g., in laboratories and research fabs for quick metal liftoff patterning, optical coatings, some compound semiconductor and discrete device manufacturing, MEMS, and possibly for certain metal stacks in R&D of next-generation devices. Contrast with why PVD magnetron sputtering replaced e-beam evaporation as the mainstream metal deposition method in semiconductor fabs. Cite SEMI / IRDS / ITRS roadmaps, equipment vendor information, and industry publications.

Research the actual usage extent of molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) equipment in high-volume manufacturing (HVM) of advanced-node semiconductor logic chips (7nm and below) by TSMC, Samsung, Intel during 2023-2026. Determine whether MBE is primarily used in research and development (R&D) rather than mass production for mainstream CMOS logic. Analyze the technical reasons: extremely slow deposition rates, ultra-high-vacuum (UHV) requirements, high equipment cost and low throughput, difficulty scaling to large 300mm wafers, and precision that is only needed for certain specialized layers. Also identify where MBE IS actually used in semiconductor manufacturing: e.g., magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) layers for STT-MRAM / MRAM embedded memory production, compound semiconductors (III-V like GaAs, InP, GaN) for RF and photonics, and R&D for quantum devices, new materials research, and advanced gate stacks. Note whether leading-edge logic fabs use MBE or instead use PVD sputtering / CVD / ALD for mainstream metal layers. Cite SEMI / IRDS / ITRS roadmaps, equipment vendor information (like Riber, Veeco, AIXTRON), and industry publications.

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### 1. PVD Sputtering — Targets, Films, and Applications

**PVD role and materials overview (SemiconductorX):** PVD deposits "every major metallization layer in semiconductor manufacturing, including copper seed layers for BEOL damascene interconnect, titanium/titanium nitride barrier layers, tantalum/tantalum nitride diffusion barriers, tungsten contact liners, aluminum bonding pads, cobalt advanced-node contacts, and emerging ruthenium/molybdenum alternatives at sub-5nm nodes." Targets require "5N to 7N purity (99.999% to 99.99999%) with specific grain structure, density, and dimensional tolerances." [4]

**Sputtering target market context (DataIntelo):** The global semiconductor sputtering targets market was valued at $4.8 billion in 2025, projected to reach $9.2 billion by 2034 (CAGR 7.5%). Pure metals dominate at 44.2% share ($2.12B); alloys hold 31.4% (fastest growth at 7.9% CAGR); compounds hold 24.4%. Integrated Circuits dominate applications at 42.1% ($2.02B). Growth drivers include fab capex exceeding $190B in 2025. Key opportunities explicitly tied to advanced nodes include "GAA transistor transitions at 2nm nodes (new ruthenium/molybdenum targets)" and "3D NAND stacking." Key threats include potential displacement by ALD/CVD. [1]

**JX Advanced Metals sputtering target specifics (the targets used in PVD tools):**
- **Ti Target:** Purity 4N5 (Ti 99.995%+), 5N, 5N5. Supports all sputtering equipment and wafer sizes. "Uses: interconnect barrier, hard masks, gate electrodes, UBM, TSV."
- **Cu Target:** 6N (99.9999%+) purity, reduced O, S, P impurities. "Uses: Cu interconnect seed layer, UBM, TSV."
- **Cu Alloy Target:** Uses 6N Cu; alloys include CuAl, CuMn, etc. "Used for Cu interconnect seed layers in leading-edge semiconductors."
- **Ta Target:** Purity 4N5 (effectively 5N+). "Uses: barrier in Cu interconnect process, TSV."
- **W Target:** 5N purity, density 99%+. Diffusion bonding for high-power sputtering. "Uses: gate electrodes." W-Si and W-Ti targets also available.
- **High-purity Co (5N) and Ni (5N), plus NiPt alloy (4N5):** "Uses: gate electrodes."
- JX supplies "Ti, Cu, and Ta coils, pins, caps, and parts sets" for Applied Materials (AMAT) sputtering equipment on 200mm and 300mm wafers — JX is an officially authorized supplier for Applied Materials. [2]

**Historical barrier material evolution for Cu interconnects (Allan Chemical):**
- "Late 1990s: Tantalum (Ta) and Tantalum Nitride (TaN) became the standard barrier materials, applied via physical vapor deposition (PVD), to prevent copper diffusion into dielectric layers."
- "By 2013 (16nm/14nm nodes): Cobalt (Co) liners replaced tantalum liners due to superior wetting properties, better copper adhesion, improved gap fill, and lower electrical resistance."
- "Current (2nm and beyond): Ruthenium-Cobalt (RuCo) alloys now dominate advanced nodes, combining ruthenium's diffusion-blocking strength with cobalt's conductivity and adhesion."
- "RuCo alloys reduce barrier thickness by 33% (down to just 20 angstroms) and cut resistance by up to 25% compared to tantalum-based processes."
- "Applied Materials demonstrated a 2.5% performance boost in 2 nm test chips using RuCo liners alongside advanced Black Diamond low-k dielectric materials."
- Dual-damascene deposition stages: "conformal barrier layer application (diffusion block), copper seed layer deposition via PVD, and copper electroplating to fill etched features." Deposition methods include PVD, CVD/PECVD, and ALD, "which achieves exceptional uniformity even in features with aspect ratios above 10:1." Barrier thicknesses typically range from 10 to 250 angstroms, with combined seed and barrier layers kept under 120 angstroms.
- Advanced barriers enable "void-free copper reflow, seedless copper electroplating (eliminating PVD seed layers)."
- "Advanced β-phase tantalum or ruthenium-based formulations achieve resistivities below 60 Ω/cm."
- Copper remains the preferred interconnect material even at 2nm dimensions, with focus on refining barrier/liner systems. [3]

**TSMC interconnect research history (relevant PVD/ALD/barrier context):**
- 2003: "High performance/reliability Cu interconnect with selective CoWP cap" — a selective CoWP metal cap replaced conventional dielectric cap after Cu CMP, achieving "5% reduction in RC delay and more than 10X improvement in electromigration for both via and trench, with 100% yield."
- 2002: "90 nm generation copper dual damascene with ALD TaN barrier" — ALD applied for TaN barrier in 90nm Cu dual damascene with low-k dielectrics (k=3.0), "providing conformal step coverage and thickness control (~10 Å), with superior reliability (electromigration, stress migration, bias temperature test) versus conventional PVD TaN."
- 2002: "CVD barriers for Cu with nanoporous ultra low-k" — feasibility study with "CVD TiN(Si) barrier for Cu dual damascene integration."
- 2000: "Evaluation of diffusion barrier performance of reactively sputtered TaNx layers" — grain boundary diffusivity of Cu in TaNx (x=0-0.62) extracted using Whipple analysis. [5]

**Applied Materials PVD platforms (BCC Research product catalog):**
- **Endura Platform** — metallization system with many systems:
  - Endura ALPS PVD (Cobalt): "High-efficiency silicide solution for gate and contact applications in high aspect ratio structures"
  - Endura Amber PVD: "Copper filling within interconnect trench and via structures"
  - Endura Avenir RF PVD: "For high k/metal gate applications and logic contact silicidation, extending to 22nm and beyond"
  - Endura Cirrus HT Co PVD: "Silicide coverage for reduced contact areas and increasing aspect ratios"
  - Endura Cirrus HTX PVD: "Hardmask solutions for next-gen devices beyond the 10nm node"
  - Endura Clover MRAM PVD: "For logic and memory applications at 3x/2x node and beyond"
  - Endura CuBS RF XT PVD: "Copper Barrier/Seed system for logic and memory from 3x/2x node onward"
  - Endura ILB PVD/ALD: "With Centinel chambers, addresses contact resistance as dimensions decrease"
  - Endura Impulse PCRAM PVD: For PCRAM/ReRAM
  - Endura Ioniq W PVD: "Pure tungsten (W) metallization across contact applications"
  - Endura PVD (core): "front-end metallization (cobalt, tungsten), aluminum/copper interconnects, and underbump metallization"
  - Endura Underbump: "UBM and bond pad solutions (NiV, Cu, Ti, TiW, CuCr, TaN, AI)"
  - Endura Ventura PVD: "For TSVs with aspect ratios ≥10:1 and 2.5D interposer applications"
  - Endura Versa XLR2 W PVD: "Deposits purer/smoother tungsten with resistivity 10-15% lower than current technology"
  - Endura Volta Cobalt CVD: "Ultra-thin seed-enhancing liners and selective cap layers (<20Å) for interconnect yield at 2Xnm node and beyond"
  - Endura Volta Selective W CVD: "Combines surface treatment with selective tungsten deposition"
  - Endura Volta W CVD: "Reduces contact resistance by up to 90%"
- **Charger Platform** — Charger UBM PVD for UBM, RDL, CMOS image sensors.
- **Axcela Platform** — Axcela PVD: "Maintains non-uniformities of <2% 1σ, handles thick films up to 8µm, each sputter chamber can deposit three distinct materials with co-sputtering flexibility." [33]

**Applied Materials Endura Cirrus HTX PVD:** "High-density, tensile Cirrus™ TiN produces tight line width control and via overlay alignment to preserve the pattern integrity of dense, complex interconnects." The Endura Cirrus HTX PVD system is described as a "breakthrough patterning hardmask" enabling copper interconnects at 10nm and beyond. [32][34]

---

### 2. CVD Films — Tungsten Fill, Cobalt Fill/Liner/Cap, Ruthenium Liner, Molybdenum

**Applied Materials — Cobalt CVD (Endura Volta) — the major conducting-material change:**
- SemiEngineering article by Kavita Shah (Applied Materials): "Advanced chips can feature up to 15 layers of copper metallization and more than 7 linear miles of wiring embedded in a square-inch 28nm chip layout." Applied Materials' "new Endura Volta CVD system" is "described as the biggest change in copper interconnects in the last 15 years," enabling two new cobalt process steps: (1) "A conformal cobalt liner deposited via CVD that enables thin, continuous deposition, optimizing the copper seed layer for good plating performance and reliable device performance"; (2) "A selective CVD cobalt capping layer deposited after chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) to reduce electro-migration by immobilizing copper atoms at the surface and promoting adhesion to the subsequent dielectric barrier layer." Together these "completely encapsulate the copper wiring," demonstrating "improved copper gap fill and an order-of-magnitude reduction in electro-migration... critical to extending Moore's Law beyond 20 nanometers." [6]
- Applied Materials blog (July 19, 2018, Jonathan Bakke): "This cobalt transition is described as the most significant conducting material change since copper dual damascene was introduced 20 years ago." Key technical points: "Tungsten contacts require liners, barriers, and adhesion layers that make extending to 7nm and beyond challenging; without scaling these layers, there would be no pure metal left in the contact by the 5nm node." "Cobalt contacts can use a thinner barrier layer, don't require a nucleation layer, and provide 6nm of fill volume at 5nm (versus tungsten), with lower resistance and the ability to remove seams via an anneal process." For copper interconnects, "adopting cobalt enables scaling liner/barrier thickness, though copper has better bulk resistivity; however, cobalt has significantly better electromigration properties, improving device reliability." The end-to-end solution: "deposition on the Endura platform (integrated PVD and CVD cobalt), anneal on the Producer system, planarization on the Reflexion LK Prime CMP system, and cobalt void detection via the PROVision platform's non-destructive electron beam method." "The cobalt can fill re-entrant features (narrower at top than bottom) without seams or voids." [7]
- Applied Materials blog (Dec 17, 2018, Mehul Naik, Ph.D.): "Tungsten requires a thick ALD titanium nitride barrier layer that doesn't scale proportionally with reduced critical dimensions, causing increased contact resistance and decreased on-state current." "Cobalt offers advantages over tungsten and copper at small geometries: it has bulk resistivity similar to tungsten but is ~1.5-2x less resistive due to impurities and grain boundary scattering in tungsten, and it works with thinner barriers." "Industry results show replacing tungsten contacts with cobalt provides approximately 60% improvement in contact line resistance, and cobalt local interconnects reduce via resistance and improve electromigration reliability." "Copper remains superior or adequate for CDs of 12-15nm and for longer metal levels above M1 where line resistance dominates. Copper extension requires co-optimization: replacing PVD tantalum nitride barriers with ALD tantalum nitride (enabling scaling below 36nm pitch) and using copper reflow on cobalt liners." "Beyond cobalt and copper, ruthenium and molybdenum are being explored but lag cobalt in maturity." References a 2018 IEDM paper (C. Auth et al.) on 10nm CMOS with "3rd generation FinFETs and cobalt local interconnects." [8]
- Applied Materials Endura Volta Cobalt CVD product page: "This high-quality layer in turn promotes void-free copper gap fill at the most advanced nodes. vital for avoiding EM failures." [9]

**Lam Research — Tungsten CVD/ALD (ALTUS family) and Molybdenum ALD (ALTUS Halo):**
- ALTUS Product Family page: "Lam's market-leading ALTUS® systems combine CVD and ALD technologies to deposit the highly conformal films needed for advanced metallization applications." Used "primarily for tungsten (W) and molybdenum (Mo) deposition to form conductive features like contacts, vias, and plugs on chips." Key challenges addressed: "Conventional CVD tungsten fill is limited by overhang from barrier films, leading to voids, higher resistance, and contact failure." Key capabilities: "Pulsed Nucleation Layer (PNL) ALD process with in-situ bulk CVD fill via Multi-Station Sequential Deposition (MSSD), lower resistivity thin W films, low-fluorine low-stress W fill for 3D NAND and DRAM, and high step coverage WN films using ALD." Product offerings: "ALTUS® Halo, Concept Two® ALTUS®, ALTUS® Max, ALTUS® Max ExtremeFill™, ALTUS® DirectFill™ Max, ALTUS® Max ICEFill®, and ALTUS® LFW." Key applications: "Plug, contact, and via fill; 3D NAND wordlines; low-stress composite interconnects; and WN barrier for via and contact metallization." [19]
- Lam Research press release (Feb 19, 2025): "Lam Research unveiled ALTUS Halo — the world's first atomic layer deposition (ALD) tool that enables the use of the metal molybdenum in leading-edge semiconductor production... the industry's first molybdenum deposition solution for high-volume manufacturing." Key advantages over tungsten: "molybdenum has lower resistivity in nano-scale wires, doesn't require adhesion or barrier layers (reducing process steps and boosting efficiency), and provides better than 50% improvement in resistance over conventional tungsten metallization in most instances." The tool is "currently in qualification and ramping with all leading chipmakers, with early adoption at high-volume 3D NAND manufacturers in Korea and Singapore and at advanced logic fabs, while development continues with DRAM customers." Addresses "1,000-layer 3D NAND, 4F2 DRAM, and advanced gate-all-around logic." Quote from Sesha Varadarajan (SVP, GM Global Products Group, Lam Research): "ALTUS Halo is the most significant breakthrough in atomic layer deposition in over 20 years." Quote from Mark Kiehlbauch (corporate VP of NAND development, Micron): "Lam's ALTUS Halo tool has made it possible for Micron to bring molybdenum into mass production." [15][16][17][18]
- Lam promotional video: "Lam pioneered tungsten ALD over 20 years ago and built the ALTUS system into the industry benchmark for tungsten fill productivity... As AI demand surges and scaling moves toward 1,000 NAND layers, tungsten-based metallization is hitting its limits, so chipmakers across NAND, DRAM, and foundry logic are transitioning to molybdenum for its low resistance and barrierless integration." ALTUS Halo "can deposit conformally or selectively with bottom-up feature fill using chemistry and thermal flexibility, plus plasma for temperature-sensitive applications." [18]

**Tokyo Electron — CVD Ruthenium liner (Trias Tandem):**
- TEL/Novellus press release (Dec 1, 2008): Jointly developed "an ionized PVD TaN or Ti barrier capped with an ultra-thin CVD Ruthenium (Ru) liner, coupled with a proprietary copper wet seed process (DirectSeed™) and copper electrochemical deposition," eliminating "the traditional PVD Cu seed process" for the 2Xnm generation. "The CVD Ru liner deposited using TEL's Trias Tandem™ system at thicknesses ≤2nm (20 Angstroms), offering exceptional conformality and the most attractive consumable costs compared to PVD or ALD Ru." Novellus's "DirectSeed™ wet copper seed process deposited in the SABRE® Extreme™ electrochemical deposition tool at thicknesses ≤3nm (30 Angstroms)." [23]

---

### 3. ALD Films — TaN Barrier, TiN, W Nucleation, Ru, Co, Mo

**ALD fundamentals (relevant to metal ALD):**
- Wikipedia ALD: "ALD is a thin-film deposition technique based on the sequential use of a gas-phase chemical process; it is a subclass of chemical vapour deposition." Metal ALD notes: "Copper ALD is of interest for interconnects (best performed ≤100°C to avoid agglomeration). Metals like tungsten and molybdenum can be deposited via fluorosilane elimination (e.g., WF6 + Si2H6 → W + SiF3H + 2H2, ∆H = –181 kcal). Novel strong reducing agents enabled low-temperature ALD of electropositive metals (Cr, Ti, Sn, Al)." [12]
- Patsnap Eureka ALD explainer: Each ALD cycle deposits "approximately 0.1–0.2 nanometers." Common materials deposited: "metal oxides (Al₂O₃, HfO₂, TiO₂, ZnO), metal nitrides (TiN, TaN), metals (Pt, Ru, Co), dielectrics (SiO₂, Si₃N₄), and conductors (W, Mo, Cu — emerging)." Applications include "barrier and encapsulation layers (preventing metal diffusion/moisture)" and "FinFET and GAAFET transistors (coating non-planar surfaces)." Future trends: "ALD for sub-5nm/3nm logic nodes." [10]
- IOPscience ALD chemistry review: Surface chemistry mechanisms classified into: ligand-exchange (including "halogen transfer (e.g., W and Mo ALD from WF6/MoF6 with Si2H6)" and "Cu deposition from Cu(dmap)2 and diethylzinc"), dissociative chemisorption (often "on catalytic surfaces like Ru, Ni, and Cu"), non-dissociative chemisorption, and oxidation/reduction. ALD is "essential for fabricating advanced microelectronic devices including FinFETs and gate-all-around (GAA) FETs, high-k gate dielectrics, DRAM capacitor dielectrics." [14]
- Springer review (Lee et al., Int. J. Precision Eng. Manuf., 2025): ALD typical growth-per-cycle of "0.05–0.1 nm/cycle"; limitations include "slow process times, narrow temperature windows below ~350°C, and high costs." Discusses Area-Selective Deposition (ASD) using "self-assembled monolayers/SAMs or small molecular inhibitors/SMIs" — relevant to selective metal deposition. Notes industry progress: "TSMC's 2-nm nanosheet GAA process and Intel's ribbon-style GAA FET at 3 nm silicon thickness, both unveiled at 2024 IEDM." [13]

**ALD TaN barrier for Cu interconnects (Applied Materials Endura iCuB/S):**
- Applied Materials' Endura iCuB/S integrated copper barrier/seed system (2002, for 65nm generation): "Uses new Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) technology to create an ultrathin, conformal tantalum nitride (TaN) barrier layer compatible with advanced low-k dielectric films... The ALD technology deposits a single atomic layer at a time, enabling ultrathin layers with uniform coverage on small 65nm features. The system's TaN chamber achieves virtually 100% side and bottom coverage." [30]

**Applied Materials Endura Copper Barrier Seed (2021, for 3nm):**
- Electronic Design: New Endura Copper Barrier Seed system "reduces interconnect resistance by 50%, allowing copper wires in 3-nm chips to achieve roughly the same overall resistance as current 5-nm chips, and enables scaling interconnect wires down to 15 nanometers." It "uses selective atomic layer deposition (ALD) to coat only the walls of interconnect trenches with tantalum (rather than blanketing the base), increasing the volume of copper in the via, and it eliminates the high-resistance tantalum barrier at the via-to-copper interface." The system "integrates multiple process technologies—surface treatment, interface engineering, ALD, PVD, CVD, copper reflow, and metrology—all within a vacuum-sealed chamber." Quote from Prabu Raja (SVP, Applied Materials): "A smartphone chip has tens of billions of copper interconnects, and the wiring already consumes up to a third of the chip's power." Resistance would "increase by a factor of 10 from 7-nm to the 3-nm nodes" if left unchecked. Tool already used by major foundry logic customers globally. [26]

**Lam Research — Ru ALD liner/fill (US Patent US10731250B2):**
- "Depositing ruthenium layers in interconnect metallization," assigned to Lam Research, for "sub-10nm technology nodes." Two-step process: (1) "Ru liner layer deposition via multiple atomic layer deposition (ALD) cycles performed under reducing conditions (using a reducing agent such as H2 or NH3, either thermal or plasma-enhanced)"; (2) "Ru fill operation where the feature is at least partially filled with ruthenium by reacting a ruthenium precursor with an oxidant." Protective Ru liner is "typically 1-2 nm thick." Context: "copper has an electron mean free path of ~39 nm, and no barrier material maintains integrity below 2.5nm thickness (barriers consume >50% of line cross-section at small dimensions). Ruthenium has a short inelastic mean free path, allowing better resistivity scaling than copper at sub-10nm dimensions, and can be used without a diffusion barrier." Applications: "sub-10nm MOL and BEOL logic interconnects, source/drain contact fill, vias, and trenches." Features may be "fully filled with Ru or other metals (Cu, W, Co, Mo, Ni, Al)." Liner layers can be deposited on WCN, TiN, WN, WC, or TaN. [24][37]

**Co and Ru nucleation in PE-ALD (Tyndall/Fudan research, J. Phys. Chem. C 2023):**
- "Ru and Co are being investigated as replacements for Cu in next-generation interconnects due to scaling challenges with Cu at the nanoscale." Reported Ru nucleation delays range "from 10 ALD cycles to 500 ALD cycles." Findings: on H:Si(100), both precursors show thermoneutral energy for first Cp ligand elimination but highly endothermic second elimination (2.83 eV for CoCp₂, 2.09 eV for RuCp₂); "RuCp₂ is not a useful precursor for Ru deposition" (explaining why more complex Cp-based Ru precursors like Ru(EtCp)₂, (MeCpPy)Ru are used experimentally); N₂/H₂ plasma pretreatment generating NHₓ terminations "can reduce the nucleation delay and promote faster deposition of metal films" for Co. [11]

**ASM International and TEL ALD positioning:**
- Patsnap ALD Landscape 2026: Key assignees in ALD reactor IP include "ASM Genitech Korea/ASM IP Holding B.V. (most prolific, broadest reactor IP), Samsung Electronics, Carl Zeiss SMT GmbH, Applied Materials, Beneq Oy." South Korea dominates filings (~35-40 patents), followed by China (12-15), Japan (4-5). The "5 nm node threshold driving ALD demand." [25]
- Tokyo Electron was "Platinum Sponsor of ALD/ALE2024" (Aug 4-7, 2024, Helsinki). TEL-affiliated presentations included: invited tutorial "Thin Film Process Technologies for the Atomic Scale Era" (Robert Clark, TEL Technology Center America), ALE Plenary Lecture "Atomic Layer Precision Process to Enable Advanced Patterning toward High-NA EUV Era" (Eric Liu), and technical presentations including "wet atomic layer etching of molybdenum and ruthenium." [27]

---

### 4. Industry Roadmap Context — imec, Node Transitions, 2nm/1nm Outlook

**imec logic technology roadmap (Horiguchi & Tokei, Semiconductor Digest 2020):**
- Current state: "7nm chips use FinFETs with 6T standard cells, 2 fins per device, and contact pitches as small as 57nm."
